topics.t: What is geography? The earth as our home
topics.h: Snow on Gulmarg, salt flats in the Rann of Kutch and paddy fields in Kerala, all in one country. Geography is the subject that asks why places are so different, and how people make each of them home.
p: The earth's surface is not uniform: it varies in physical features (mountains, plains, rivers, climate, soils) and in cultural features (houses, crops, roads, languages, settlements).
The word 'geography' was coined by the Greek scholar Eratosthenes, from 'geo' (earth) and 'graphos' (description). So geography literally means a description of the earth.
Geography is best understood as the study of the earth as the home of humankind.
Areal differentiation: geography studies how and why places differ from each other and also how they resemble each other.
The physical environment (nature) and the cultural environment (made by humans) interact all the time; humans use and modify nature, and the result keeps changing over time.

ex.q: Classify these features of a Himalayan village: a glacier-fed stream, terraced fields, a slate-roofed house and steep slopes.
st: Ask: was it made by nature or by people?
Glacier-fed stream and steep slopes are made by nature, so they are physical features.
Terraced fields and slate-roofed houses are made by people, so they are cultural features.
Notice the link: terraces are a human response to steep slopes.
ex.a: Physical: stream, steep slopes. Cultural: terraced fields, slate-roofed house.

topics.rl: Houses on stilts in Assam's flood plains and thick-walled houses in Rajasthan's desert show the same idea: people shape their cultural landscape to fit the physical one.

topics.t: What, where and why: the spatial perspective
topics.h: A good geographer is like a detective at a crime scene: first 'what is here?', then 'where exactly?', and finally the big one, 'why here and not somewhere else?'
p: Geography deals with spatial attributes: the location, distribution and arrangement of things over the earth's surface. This way of looking is the spatial perspective.
'What' questions identify patterns of natural and cultural features found over the earth's surface.
'Where' questions deal with the distribution of these features: where they are located and how they are spread out.
'Why' questions seek explanation: the causal relationships between features and the processes behind them. This makes geography a scientific discipline, not just a list of facts.
Geography studies interrelationships and associations between phenomena in space, so it is a discipline of synthesis rather than a study of isolated facts.

ex.q: Frame what, where and why questions about tea gardens in India.
st: What: What crop dominates the hill slopes of Assam and the Nilgiris? Tea.
Where: Where is it grown? Mainly in Assam, northern West Bengal (Darjeeling, Dooars) and the Nilgiris.
Why: Why there? Warm, humid climate, well-distributed rainfall and well-drained hill slopes suit tea.
ex.a: What = the pattern (tea), where = the distribution (Assam, Darjeeling, Nilgiris), why = the explanation (climate, rainfall, slopes).

topics.rl: When a delivery app decides where to open a new dark store, it asks the same three questions: what demand exists, where customers are, and why that spot works best.

topics.t: Nature and humans: determinism and humanisation
topics.h: A thousand years ago a desert meant 'no farming'. Today the Indira Gandhi Canal turns parts of the Thar green. Who is in control: nature or people?
p: The relationship between nature and humans is dynamic: it changes as human technology changes.

In early stages, with low technology, humans adapted to and were greatly influenced by nature. This is called the naturalisation of humans; the idea that nature controls human life is environmental determinism.
As technology improved, humans modified nature more and more, creating a cultural landscape. This is the humanisation of nature. Technology loosened the shackles (chains) of nature on humans.
The level of technology is an index of the cultural development of a society.
Possibilism: nature offers a range of possibilities, and humans choose among them according to their technology, needs and perception. Human perception of the environment also changes over time.

ex.q: Label each: (a) a hunter-gatherer group that moves with the seasons to find food; (b) farmers in Punjab using tube wells and canals to grow wheat and rice.
st: (a) Behaviour is dictated by nature's seasons and low technology.
So (a) shows naturalisation of humans (environmental determinism).
(b) People use technology to change how land and water are used.
So (b) shows humanisation of nature (people shaping nature).
ex.a: (a) Naturalisation of humans / determinism; (b) humanisation of nature.

topics.rl: Air-conditioned metro coaches in Delhi summers, drip irrigation in arid Rajasthan and Himalayan tunnels like Atal Tunnel all show technology loosening nature's grip.

topics.t: Geography as an integrating discipline: links with natural sciences
topics.h: Geography borrows from geology, meteorology, botany and more, then ties it all together on a map. Think of it as the group project leader of the sciences.
p: Geography is a discipline of spatial synthesis (it integrates phenomena over space), while history is a discipline of temporal synthesis (it integrates events over time).
Every science studies some reality that exists over space, so geography has close links with both natural and social sciences.

Physical geography links with natural sciences: geomorphology with geology, climatology with meteorology, hydrology with the study of water, soil geography with pedology, biogeography with botany and zoology.
Oceanography is shared with marine sciences; plant and animal geography draw on botany and zoology.
NCERT shows these links in a diagram of geography at the centre, connected to natural sciences on one side and social sciences on the other.

ex.q: A student studies why the Deccan has black soils. Which sister science will help her most, and which branch of geography is she working in?
st: Black soil formation is about soil-forming processes.
The science of soils is pedology.
The geography branch that studies soils is soil geography.
ex.a: Pedology; soil geography.

topics.rl: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) is meteorology in action, and climatologists use its decades of data to map India's climatic regions.

topics.t: Links with social sciences, maps and metaphors
topics.h: The 'mouth' of the Hooghly, the 'eye' of Cyclone Fani, the 'snout' of the Gangotri glacier: geography talks about the earth as if it had a body!
p: Human geography links with social sciences: economic geography with economics, political geography with political science, social/cultural geography with sociology, historical geography with history, population geography with demography, and with anthropology.
Maps are the main and most effective tool of a geographer: they show the three-dimensional earth on a two-dimensional surface.
Techniques linked with mathematics and computers include cartography (map making), quantitative/statistical methods, remote sensing, GIS (Geographic Information System) and GPS.

Physical and human phenomena are often described with metaphors from human anatomy: 'face' of the earth, 'eye' of the storm, 'mouth' of a river, 'snout' of a glacier, 'neck' of an isthmus and 'profile' of the soil.

ex.q: Which social science would help a geographer most in studying (a) the sex ratio across Indian states, (b) the movement of goods from ports?
st: (a) Sex ratio is a population attribute; population is studied by demography.
So population geography + demography.
(b) Movement of goods is an economic activity; studied by economics.
So economic geography + economics.
ex.a: (a) Demography; (b) Economics.

topics.rl: ISRO's Bhuvan portal and the Survey of India's digital maps use remote sensing and GIS, the modern toolkit of a geographer.

topics.t: Approaches: systematic and regional, and dualism
topics.h: Two German friends, two ways to study the world: one studies a single thing everywhere, the other studies everything in one place. Both are right!
p: There are two main approaches to studying geography: the systematic approach and the regional approach.

The systematic approach (same as general geography) was introduced by Alexander von Humboldt (1769–1859). A phenomenon is studied all over the world as a whole, and then typologies or spatial patterns are identified. Example: studying natural vegetation worldwide, then classifying it into equatorial forests, grasslands and so on.

The regional approach was developed by Karl Ritter (1779–1859), a contemporary of Humboldt. The world is divided into regions at different hierarchical levels, and then all geographical phenomena in a particular region are studied.
Dualism has been a main characteristic of geography from the beginning: physical versus human geography, and systematic versus regional geography.

ex.q: Identify the approach: (a) a study of rice cultivation in all countries of Asia; (b) a study of landforms, climate, crops and towns of the Bundelkhand region.
st: (a) One phenomenon (rice) is studied over a large area, then patterns are found → systematic approach.
(b) One region is chosen and all its phenomena are studied together → regional approach.
ex.a: (a) Systematic; (b) Regional.

topics.rl: A national report on groundwater levels in every Indian state is systematic; a development plan for the North Eastern Region covering everything from rivers to roads is regional.

topics.t: Branches of geography
topics.h: Geography is a big banyan tree. Its branches range from cyclones and soils to elections, cities and satellite mapping.
p: Branches based on the systematic approach: (1) Physical geography: geomorphology, climatology, hydrology, soil geography.
(2) Human geography: social/cultural geography, population and settlement geography, economic geography, historical geography, political geography.
(3) Biogeography: plant geography, zoo geography, ecology/ecosystem, environmental geography.
Branches based on the regional approach: regional studies/area studies, regional planning (country/rural and town/urban planning), regional development, regional analysis.

Two aspects are common to every discipline: philosophy (geographical thought; land and human interaction/human ecology) and methods and techniques (cartography including computer cartography, quantitative/statistical techniques, field survey methods, geo-informatics such as remote sensing, GIS and GPS).

ex.q: Place these in the correct branch: (a) zoo geography, (b) town planning, (c) GPS.
st: (a) Zoo geography studies animals over space → biogeography (systematic).
(b) Town planning → regional planning (regional approach).
(c) GPS is a technique → methods and techniques (geo-informatics), common to both.
ex.a: (a) Biogeography; (b) Regional planning; (c) Methods and techniques.

topics.rl: Smart City plans for Indore or Surat use regional planning, census data (population geography) and GIS together.

topics.t: Physical geography and its components
topics.h: The Himalaya (rock), the monsoon (air), the Bay of Bengal (water) and the Sundarbans tigers (life): physical geography covers all four spheres.
p: Physical geography studies the lithosphere (landforms, drainage, relief, physiography), atmosphere (composition, structure, weather and climate elements), hydrosphere (oceans, seas, lakes, the water realm) and biosphere (life forms, food chains, ecological balance). Soils are also studied.
Geomorphology studies landforms, their evolution and the related processes.
Climatology studies the structure of the atmosphere, the elements of weather and climate, and climatic types and regions.
Hydrology studies the realm of water on the earth's surface (oceans, lakes, rivers, other water bodies) and its effect on life forms, including humans.
Soil geography studies the processes of soil formation, soil types, their fertility status, distribution and use.

ex.q: Name the branch: (a) why the Ganga plain has deep alluvium; (b) why Cherrapunji gets heavy rain; (c) changes in water level of Wular lake.
st: (a) Alluvial deposits are landforms shaped by rivers → geomorphology (soil type can also be studied in soil geography).
(b) Rainfall is an element of climate → climatology.
(c) Lakes are part of the water realm → hydrology.
ex.a: (a) Geomorphology; (b) Climatology; (c) Hydrology.

topics.rl: The Central Water Commission tracks river flows (hydrology), IMD issues monsoon forecasts (climatology) and Soil Health Cards report soil fertility (soil geography).

topics.t: Why physical geography matters
topics.h: Why does Punjab grow wheat, Jharkhand mine coal and Himachal welcome tourists? The answer starts with physical geography.
p: Landforms provide the base for human activities: plains are used for agriculture; plateaus provide forests and minerals; mountains provide pastures, forests and tourist spots, and are sources of rivers that supply water to lower areas.
Climate influences house types, clothing and food habits, and strongly affects vegetation, cropping patterns, livestock farming and some industries.
Soils are renewable resources that support agriculture; water is vital for all life.
Physical geography is the basis for understanding natural resources, how humans use them, and how to plan for sustainable development without degrading the environment.
In exams: expect MCQs on approaches and branches, short answers on spatial synthesis and 'what-where-why', and long answers on geography as an integrating discipline.

ex.q: Explain with Indian examples how landforms provide a base for human activities.
st: Plains: the Indo-Gangetic plains support intensive farming and dense population.
Plateaus: the Chota Nagpur plateau provides minerals like coal and iron ore and forests.
Mountains: the Himalaya provide pastures, forests, tourist spots like Shimla and are the source of rivers like the Ganga.
Conclude: each landform offers different resources and activities.
ex.a: Plains → agriculture; plateaus → minerals and forests; mountains → pastures, forests, tourism and river water.

topics.rl: Hydropower projects in the Himalaya, coal mining in Jharkhand and the paddy belt of the deltas all depend on physical geography, which is why planners study it before building.

topics.ch: Physical: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
topics.t: Early theories on the origin of the earth
topics.h: Before telescopes could see far into space, thinkers argued over one question: did the planets come from a spinning cloud, or were they ripped out of the sun by a passing star?
p: Nebular hypothesis: proposed by the German philosopher Immanuel Kant and revised by the mathematician Laplace in 1796. Planets formed out of a cloud of material associated with a youthful sun that was slowly rotating.

In 1900, Chamberlain and Moulton suggested that a wandering star approached the sun. Its pull drew out a cigar-shaped extension of material from the solar surface; as the star moved away, this material kept revolving around the sun and slowly condensed into planets.
Sir James Jeans and later Sir Harold Jeffrey supported this idea. Later arguments considered a companion star coexisting with the sun; these are called binary theories.

In 1950, Otto Schmidt in Russia and Carl Weizascar in Germany revised the nebular hypothesis: the sun was surrounded by a solar nebula containing mostly hydrogen and helium along with dust. Friction and collision of particles formed a disk-shaped cloud, and the planets formed through accretion.

ex.q: Arrange the early theories in chronological order and name the key idea of each.
st: 1796: Laplace revises Kant's nebular hypothesis → rotating cloud around a young sun.
1900: Chamberlain and Moulton → wandering star pulls out cigar-shaped material.
Supported by Jeans and Jeffrey; companion-star versions are binary theories.
1950: Otto Schmidt and Carl Weizascar → revised nebular hypothesis with solar nebula of H, He and dust; accretion.
ex.a: Kant–Laplace (1796) → Chamberlain–Moulton (1900) → Schmidt–Weizascar (1950).

topics.rl: Science changes with evidence, just like ISRO's Chandrayaan missions revised what we knew about water on the Moon.

topics.ch: Physical: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
topics.t: The Big Bang and the expanding universe
topics.h: Draw dots on a balloon and blow it up: every dot moves away from every other dot. That simple trick explains how our universe behaves.
p: The most popular modern theory of the origin of the universe is the Big Bang Theory, also called the expanding universe hypothesis.
In 1920, Edwin Hubble provided evidence that the universe is expanding: galaxies move farther apart as time passes.
Balloon analogy: points on a balloon move apart as it is inflated. In reality, it is the space between galaxies that increases; the galaxies themselves are not expanding.
An alternative idea was Hoyle's steady state concept, which considered the universe to be roughly the same at any point of time.
With growing evidence of expansion, the scientific community today favours the expanding universe (Big Bang) view.

ex.q: A balloon has three ink dots. As it is blown up, the dots move apart. What do the dots and the rubber stand for in the Big Bang model?
st: The dots represent galaxies.
The stretching rubber represents space.
As space expands, the distance between galaxies increases.
So galaxies appear to move away from each other, as Hubble observed.
ex.a: Dots = galaxies; stretching rubber = expanding space between galaxies.

topics.rl: Indian astronomers using the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune study distant galaxies whose light carries the signature of an expanding universe.

topics.ch: Physical: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
topics.t: Stages of the Big Bang
topics.h: Everything you see, from the Himalaya to your phone, was once squeezed into something smaller than a dot. Then: bang.
p: Stage 1: In the beginning, all matter forming the universe existed in one place as a 'tiny ball' (singular atom) with an unimaginably small volume, infinite temperature and infinite density.

Stage 2: At the Big Bang, the tiny ball exploded violently, leading to a huge expansion. It is generally accepted that this happened 13.7 billion years before the present. The expansion continues even today.
As it grew, some energy was converted into matter. Expansion was very rapid within fractions of a second, then slowed down. Within the first three minutes, the first atoms began to form.
Stage 3: Within 300,000 years from the Big Bang, the temperature dropped to 4,500 K and gave rise to atomic matter. The universe became transparent.

ex.q: How long after the Big Bang did the universe become transparent, and what was its temperature then?
st: Recall stage 3 of the Big Bang.
Within 300,000 years the temperature fell.
It fell to 4,500 K and atomic matter formed.
At that point the universe became transparent.
ex.a: Within 300,000 years; about 4,500 K.

topics.rl: The 13.7-billion-year figure is like the universe's birth certificate. Everything in the Indian Space Research Organisation's star catalogues is younger than that.

topics.ch: Physical: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
topics.t: Formation of stars and galaxies
topics.h: The Milky Way is so wide that light, the fastest thing there is, needs about a hundred thousand years to cross it.
p: Matter and energy were distributed unevenly in the early universe. These density differences allowed gravitational forces to pull matter together, forming galaxies.
A galaxy contains a large number of stars. Galaxies spread over vast distances measured in thousands of light years; individual galaxies have diameters from 80,000 to 150,000 light years.
A galaxy starts to form by accumulating hydrogen gas as a very large cloud called a nebula. The growing nebula develops localised clumps of gas, which grow into denser bodies and give rise to stars.
The formation of stars is believed to have taken place some 5–6 billion years ago.
A light year is a measure of distance, not time: the distance light travels in one year. Light moves at about 300,000 km per second, so one light year is about 9.461 × 10¹² km.

ex.q: Light travels at 300,000 km per second. How far does it travel in one minute?
st: Distance = speed × time.
Time = 1 minute = 60 seconds.

topics.rl: On a clear night in Hanle, Ladakh, home to the Indian Astronomical Observatory, you can see the band of our own galaxy stretched across the sky.

topics.ch: Physical: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
topics.t: Formation of planets and our solar system
topics.h: Planets did not appear fully formed. They grew like snowballs rolling downhill, from dust to pebbles to worlds.
p: Stage 1: Stars are localised lumps of gas within a nebula. Gravity inside the lumps forms a core, and a huge rotating disc of gas and dust develops around the core.
Stage 2: The gas cloud starts condensing, and matter around the core develops into small rounded objects. By cohesion these grow into planetesimals.
Stage 3: Larger bodies form by collision and gravitational attraction. The small planetesimals accrete to form a few large bodies: the planets.
Our solar system has the sun (star), 8 planets, their satellites (moons), and millions of smaller bodies such as asteroids, comets, dust and gases.
The nebula's collapse and core formation began about 5–5.6 billion years ago, and the planets formed about 4.6 billion years ago.

ex.q: Put the planet-forming steps in order: planetesimals collide, rotating disc around a core, small rounded objects form.
st: First gravity forms a core with a rotating disc of gas and dust.
Then the gas condenses into small rounded objects, which grow into planetesimals.
Finally planetesimals collide and accrete into planets.
ex.a: Rotating disc around a core → small rounded objects/planetesimals → collision and accretion into planets.

topics.rl: Asteroids and comets are leftover building blocks. ISRO and other agencies study them to learn what the early solar system was made of.

topics.ch: Physical: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
topics.t: Terrestrial and Jovian planets
topics.h: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are rocky little worlds. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are giant gas balls. Why such a sharp split?
p: The four inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars), between the sun and the asteroid belt, are terrestrial planets: earth-like, made of rock and metals, with relatively high densities and small size.

The four outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are Jovian or gas giant planets: Jupiter-like, much larger than the terrestrial planets, with thick atmospheres mostly of helium and hydrogen.
Reason 1: terrestrial planets formed close to the parent star, where it was too warm for gases to condense into solid particles; Jovian planets formed at quite a distant location.

Reason 2: the solar wind was most intense nearer the sun, so it blew off lots of gas and dust from the terrestrial planets. Reason 3: being smaller, terrestrial planets had lower gravity and could not hold the escaping gases.

Planet data (NCERT table): Earth's density is about 5.517 g/cm³, the highest of all planets; Saturn's density, about 0.70 g/cm³, is the lowest (less than water). Jupiter's radius is about 11 times Earth's. Mars has 2 satellites; Mercury and Venus have none.

ex.q: Using the densities Mars = 3.945 g/cm³ and Saturn = 0.70 g/cm³, which is a terrestrial planet and why?
st: Terrestrial planets are rocky and dense.
Mars has a density of nearly 4 g/cm³, so it is rocky.
Saturn's density is less than water (1 g/cm³), so it is mostly gas.
So Mars is terrestrial and Saturn is Jovian.
ex.a: Mars is terrestrial (high density, rocky); Saturn is Jovian (very low density, gaseous).

topics.rl: ISRO's Mangalyaan studied Mars, a terrestrial planet. Its rocky surface is why it can be photographed in such detail, unlike the cloud-covered gas giants.

topics.ch: Physical: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
topics.t: The Moon and the layering of the earth
topics.h: The Moon may be a chunk of the young earth, knocked off when a Mars-sized body crashed into us. Scientists call it the 'big splat'.
p: Sir George Darwin suggested earlier that the earth and the moon formed a single rapidly rotating body that took a dumb-bell shape and broke apart.

Today's accepted view is the giant impact or 'big splat': a body one to three times the size of Mars collided with the earth shortly after the earth formed, blasting out material that formed the moon. This happened about 4.44 billion years ago.
The early earth was a barren, rocky and hot object with a thin atmosphere of hydrogen and helium.
The earth has a layered structure; the density of material increases from the surface towards the centre.

Differentiation: as density increased, heavier materials (like iron) sank towards the centre and lighter ones moved to the surface. The earth cooled, solidified and formed a crust. The moon-forming impact heated the earth again, and differentiation produced the crust, mantle, outer core and inner core.

ex.q: Explain why iron is concentrated in the earth's core while lighter rocks form the crust.
st: The early earth was partly molten (volatile state).
Materials separated according to their density.
Heavier materials like iron sank towards the centre.
Lighter materials rose to the surface and formed the crust.
This process is called differentiation.
ex.a: By differentiation: heavy iron sank to the core and lighter material rose to form the crust.

topics.rl: Chandrayaan missions study lunar rocks and soil, which helps scientists test the giant impact idea of the Moon's origin.

topics.ch: Physical: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
topics.t: Evolution of the atmosphere and hydrosphere
topics.h: The air you breathe is not the earth's first atmosphere. It is the third version, edited by volcanoes and then by tiny ocean life.
p: The present atmosphere evolved in three stages: (1) loss of the primordial atmosphere, (2) the hot interior contributing gases and water vapour, (3) modification by the living world through photosynthesis.
Stage 1: the primordial atmosphere of hydrogen and helium was stripped off by the solar winds.

Stage 2: during cooling, gases and water vapour were released from the interior. This degassing happened through volcanic eruptions. The early atmosphere was largely water vapour, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, methane, ammonia and very little free oxygen.

Continuous volcanic eruptions added water vapour; as the earth cooled, it condensed, and rain filled the depressions, giving rise to oceans within 500 million years of the earth's formation. Oceans are about 4,000 million years old. Carbon dioxide dissolved in rainwater and further cooled the earth.

Stage 3: around 2,500–3,000 million years ago, photosynthesis evolved in the oceans. Oceans were eventually saturated with oxygen, and about 2,000 million years ago oxygen began to flood the atmosphere.

ex.q: Why did the early atmosphere have very little free oxygen, while today's has about 21%?
st: Early atmosphere came from degassing: water vapour, N₂, CO₂, CH₄, NH₃ with very little O₂.
Life evolved in the oceans and developed photosynthesis.
Photosynthesis released oxygen; the oceans became saturated with it.
About 2,000 million years ago oxygen began to flood the atmosphere.
ex.a: Oxygen was added later by photosynthesising life in the oceans.

topics.rl: Gases from Barren Island, India's only active volcano in the Andamans, are a small modern example of degassing.

topics.ch: Physical: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
topics.t: Origin of life and the geological time scale
topics.h: Squeeze the earth's 4.6-billion-year history into one day and humans show up only in the last few seconds before midnight.
p: Modern scientists see the origin of life as a kind of chemical reaction that first produced complex organic molecules, which assembled into molecules able to duplicate themselves, turning inanimate matter into living substance.
Life is believed to have begun evolving about 3,800 million years ago.
Fossil evidence: microscopic structures closely related to present-day blue-green algae have been found in rocks much older than 3,000 million years.

The geological time scale divides earth history into eons, eras, periods and epochs. Examples: the Cainozoic era (from about 65 million years ago to the present); the Jurassic period is the age of dinosaurs; dinosaurs became extinct at the end of the Cretaceous; the Holocene epoch (the last 10,000 years) is the time of modern humans.
Exam tip: practise MCQs on Big Bang, planets and the moon; differences between terrestrial and Jovian planets; the stages of the Big Bang; and the evolution of the atmosphere.

ex.q: Order these: origin of life, oxygen floods the atmosphere, age of dinosaurs, modern humans.
st: Origin of life: about 3,800 million years ago.
Oxygen floods the atmosphere: about 2,000 million years ago.
Age of dinosaurs: Jurassic period (Mesozoic era).
Modern humans: Holocene epoch (last 10,000 years).
ex.a: Origin of life → oxygen in atmosphere → dinosaurs (Jurassic) → modern humans (Holocene).

topics.rl: Dinosaur fossils and eggs found in the Narmada valley of Madhya Pradesh and at Balasinor in Gujarat are evidence from the Mesozoic era.

topics.t: Why study the interior? Direct sources
topics.h: The deepest hole humans have ever drilled, the Kola borehole, goes about 12 km down. The earth's radius is 6,370 km. We have barely scratched the skin!
p: Most landforms on the earth's surface are produced by processes operating in the interior (endogenic processes) together with surface processes, so understanding the interior helps explain the surface.
The earth's radius is about 6,370 km. Nobody can reach the centre, and even the deepest drill, at Kola in the Arctic, has reached only about 12 km.
Direct sources give actual materials. Surface rock and rocks from mining: for example, gold mines in South Africa go as deep as 3–4 km.
Deep drilling projects: the Deep Ocean Drilling Project and the Integrated Ocean Drilling Project, plus the Kola superdeep borehole, provide samples from deeper layers.
Volcanic eruptions bring magma from the interior to the surface, where it can be analysed in laboratories. However, it is hard to know the exact depth it came from.

ex.q: What fraction of the earth's radius has the deepest drill (12 km) reached? Take the radius as 6,370 km and give a rough percentage.
st: Fraction = 12 ÷ 6,370.
As a percentage ≈ 0.19%, i.e., less than 0.2% of the radius.
ex.a: Less than 0.2% of the radius, so direct sources tell us very little about the deep interior.

topics.rl: The Kolar Gold Fields in Karnataka were among the deepest mines in the world, giving geologists rare rock samples from kilometres below the surface.

topics.t: Indirect sources of information
topics.h: Doctors see inside you using X-rays without cutting you open. Geologists 'X-ray' the earth using earthquakes, gravity and magnetism.
p: Temperature, pressure and density all increase with depth. Knowing the thickness of the earth and these rates of change, scientists estimate values at different depths.
Meteors (meteorites) that reach the earth are solid bodies made of materials similar to the earth's, formed in the same nebula, so their structure gives clues to the interior.

Gravitation: the force of gravity is greater near the poles and less at the equator, because of the distance from the centre. Observed gravity also varies with the mass of material below. The difference between expected and observed gravity is called a gravity anomaly; it tells us how mass is distributed in the crust.
Magnetic surveys give information about the distribution of magnetic materials in the crust.
Seismic activity (earthquake waves) is the most important indirect source of information about the interior.

ex.q: A survey finds gravity at a place is higher than expected. What does this anomaly suggest?
st: Gravity depends on the mass of material below.
Higher-than-expected gravity means more mass (denser rock) lies beneath.
So the anomaly reveals a concentration of dense material in the crust.
ex.a: Denser or heavier material lies beneath that place.

topics.rl: The National Geophysical Research Institute in Hyderabad uses gravity and magnetic surveys to locate mineral deposits and study India's crust.

topics.t: Earthquakes: focus, epicentre and the seismograph
topics.h: On 26 January 2001, as India celebrated Republic Day, the ground in Kachchh, Gujarat, began to shake violently. What had happened kilometres below?
p: An earthquake is the shaking of the earth caused by a release of energy, which generates waves that travel in all directions.

The energy is released along a fault, a sharp break in crustal rocks. Rocks along a fault tend to move in opposite directions; friction locks them until the stress overcomes it, and the blocks suddenly shift, releasing energy.
The point inside the earth where the energy is released is the focus, also called the hypocentre.
The epicentre is the point on the surface nearest to the focus (directly above it). It is the first place to experience the waves.
Earthquake waves reaching the surface are recorded by an instrument called a seismograph.

ex.q: An earthquake's focus is 20 km below a village. Which place is the epicentre and which feels the waves first?
st: The focus is the point of energy release, 20 km underground.
The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus.
Here, the village directly above is the epicentre.
The epicentre is the first point on the surface to experience the waves.
ex.a: The village directly above the focus is the epicentre and feels the waves first.

topics.rl: The National Center for Seismology, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, runs a network of seismographs across India and reports the epicentre of every significant earthquake.

topics.t: Earthquake waves: P, S and surface waves
topics.h: Within seconds of a quake, three messengers race out. The first is fast but gentle, the second shakes harder, and the last is the one that knocks down buildings.
p: Earthquake waves are of two types: body waves and surface waves. Body waves are generated by the release of energy at the focus and move through the body of the earth. Body waves interact with surface rocks to generate surface waves.

P-waves (primary waves) are the fastest and first to arrive. They are similar to sound waves, travel through gaseous, liquid and solid materials, and vibrate parallel to the direction of the wave, causing compression and rarefaction (squeezing and stretching).

S-waves (secondary waves) arrive after a time lag and travel only through solid materials. Their vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation in the vertical plane, creating troughs and crests.
Surface waves are the last to be recorded on the seismograph and are the most destructive: they cause displacement of rocks and the collapse of structures.

The velocity of waves changes as they pass through materials of different density (denser material, higher velocity). Their direction also changes as they reflect or refract at boundaries between layers.

ex.q: A seismograph records three wave arrivals: first a fast, weak one; then a stronger one; finally a slow, very damaging one. Name each.
st: The first to arrive are always the fastest: P-waves.
Next, after a time lag: S-waves.
Last and most destructive: surface waves.
ex.a: P-waves → S-waves → surface waves.

topics.rl: Earthquake early-warning apps use the head start of fast P-waves to send alerts a few seconds before the damaging waves arrive, enough time to stop metro trains or move away from glass.

topics.t: Shadow zones and what they reveal
topics.h: After a big quake, some seismographs around the world record nothing at all. That 'silence' told scientists the earth has a liquid outer core.
p: P-waves make material squeeze and stretch along their path; S-waves make it vibrate up and down at right angles to their path (as drawn in NCERT's diagram).
A shadow zone is an area on the surface where earthquake waves are not recorded.
Seismographs within 105° of the epicentre record both P- and S-waves.
Seismographs beyond 145° record P-waves but not S-waves. The zone between 105° and 145° is the shadow zone for both types of waves.

The entire area beyond 105° receives no S-waves, so the S-wave shadow zone is much larger: a little over 40% of the earth's surface. Since S-waves cannot pass through liquids, this shows that the outer core is liquid.

ex.q: Three stations are 80°, 120° and 160° from an epicentre. Which waves does each record?
st: 80° is within 105° → both P and S waves.
120° lies between 105° and 145° → shadow zone for both; no direct P or S waves.
160° is beyond 145° → P-waves only (no S-waves).
ex.a: 80°: P and S; 120°: neither; 160°: P only.

topics.rl: A strong quake in Japan is recorded with both P and S waves at Indian stations, but stations on the far side of the globe receive no S-waves, a daily reminder of the liquid outer core.

topics.t: Types of earthquakes
topics.h: Not every tremor comes from moving plates. Some come from volcanoes, some from collapsing mines, some from bombs and some even from giant dams.
p: Tectonic earthquakes are the most common. They are caused by the sliding of rocks along a fault plane.
Volcanic earthquakes are a special class of tectonic earthquake, confined to areas of active volcanoes.
Collapse earthquakes are minor tremors that occur in areas of intense mining when the roofs of underground mines collapse.
Explosion earthquakes are tremors caused by the explosion of chemical or nuclear devices.
Reservoir induced earthquakes occur in areas of large reservoirs (behind big dams).

ex.q: Classify: (a) tremors near the Koyna dam reservoir in Maharashtra; (b) ground shaking during an underground nuclear test; (c) the 2001 Bhuj earthquake caused by fault movement.
st: (a) Linked to a large reservoir → reservoir induced earthquake.
(b) Caused by an explosion → explosion earthquake.
(c) Caused by sliding of rocks along a fault → tectonic earthquake.
ex.a: (a) Reservoir induced; (b) Explosion; (c) Tectonic.

topics.rl: The 1967 Koyna earthquake in Maharashtra is a famous case studied worldwide as a reservoir-linked earthquake.

topics.t: Measuring earthquakes: magnitude and intensity
topics.h: Two people describe the same earthquake: one says 'magnitude 7', the other says 'intensity X'. Both are right, because they measure different things.
p: The magnitude scale, known as the Richter scale, measures the energy released during an earthquake. It is expressed in absolute numbers, 0–10.
The intensity scale, named after Mercalli, an Italian seismologist, measures the visible damage caused by the event. It ranges from 1 to 12.
Magnitude is one value for an earthquake (energy at the source); intensity varies from place to place depending on distance, ground and buildings.
Higher-magnitude earthquakes are rare: quakes of magnitude 8+ occur about once in 1–2 years, while tiny ones occur almost every minute.
Indian case: the Bhuj (Kachchh, Gujarat) earthquake of 26 January 2001 caused heavy loss of life and property.

ex.q: An earthquake damages old buildings badly in town X near the epicentre and only rattles windows in town Y far away. Which value is the same for both towns and which differs?
st: Magnitude measures energy released at the source, so it is a single value for the earthquake.
Intensity measures damage seen at a place, so it is higher in X and lower in Y.
ex.a: Magnitude is the same; intensity differs (higher in X).

topics.rl: After a quake, the National Center for Seismology reports the magnitude; damage surveys by the state disaster authority describe the intensity in each district.

topics.t: Effects of earthquakes
topics.h: In an earthquake, it is mostly falling buildings, fires and floods, not the shaking itself, that hurt people.
p: Earthquakes are a natural hazard. Immediate hazard-causing effects include: ground shaking, differential ground settlement, land and mud slides, soil liquefaction, ground lurching and avalanches.
Other effects: ground displacement, floods from dam and levee failures, and fires.
Further effects: structural collapse, falling objects and tsunami.
The first six effects (ground shaking to avalanches) have some bearing on landforms, while the others are effects of immediate concern to life and property.
A tsunami occurs only if the epicentre is below oceanic waters and the magnitude is sufficiently high.

ex.q: Sort these effects into 'bearing on landforms' or 'immediate concern to life and property': soil liquefaction, fires, avalanches, falling objects.
st: NCERT lists 12 effects; the first six (ground shaking, differential settlement, land/mud slides, soil liquefaction, ground lurching, avalanches) affect landforms.
Soil liquefaction and avalanches → landforms.
Fires and falling objects are among the remaining six → life and property.
ex.a: Landforms: soil liquefaction, avalanches. Life and property: fires, falling objects.

topics.rl: The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) campaigns on 'Drop, Cover and Hold' because falling objects and collapsing structures are the main killers in quakes.

topics.t: Structure of the earth: crust and mantle
topics.h: If the earth were an apple, the crust would be thinner than its skin, yet it holds every mountain, ocean and city.
p: The crust is the outermost solid part of the earth. It is brittle in nature. Its thickness varies: about 5 km under the oceans, about 30 km on continents, and as much as 70 km under major mountain systems such as the Himalaya.
The crust is made up of rocks with a density of about 3 g/cm³; the rock of the oceanic crust is basalt.
The mantle extends from the Moho discontinuity (the crust–mantle boundary) to a depth of 2,900 km.
The upper portion of the mantle is the asthenosphere ('astheno' = weak), extending up to about 400 km. It is the main source of magma and has a higher density than the crust (about 3.4 g/cm³).
The crust and the uppermost part of the mantle together form the lithosphere, 10–200 km thick. The lower mantle, beyond the asthenosphere, is in a solid state.

ex.q: How much thicker is the continental crust under the Himalaya (70 km) than the oceanic crust (5 km)?
st: Difference = 70 − 5 = 65 km.
ex.a: 65 km thicker, or 14 times as thick.

topics.rl: The Himalaya's thick crustal root (up to about 70 km) is part of why the region is so geologically active and earthquake-prone.

topics.t: The core and the full picture of the interior
topics.h: At the centre of the earth, about 6,300 km down, material is about 13 times as dense as water. It is a giant ball of metal.
p: The core–mantle boundary lies at a depth of 2,900 km (the Gutenberg discontinuity).
The outer core is in a liquid state; the inner core is in a solid state.
Density is around 5 g/cm³ at the mantle–core boundary and around 13 g/cm³ at the centre of the earth (at about 6,300 km).
The core is made of very heavy material, mostly nickel and iron. It is sometimes called the 'nife' layer (Ni + Fe).
Diagram practice: label crust, Moho discontinuity, upper mantle (asthenosphere), lower mantle, Gutenberg discontinuity at 2,900 km, liquid outer core and solid inner core.

ex.q: Why is the core called the 'nife' layer?
st: The core is made mostly of very heavy materials.
These are nickel (chemical symbol Ni) and iron (Fe).
Ni + Fe → 'nife'.
ex.a: Because it is made mostly of nickel (Ni) and iron (Fe).

topics.rl: The earth's magnetic field, which compasses and migrating birds use, is linked to the movement of molten iron in the liquid outer core.

topics.t: Volcanoes, volcanic materials and shield volcanoes
topics.h: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is India's only active volcano. Its smoke and lava are messages sent up from the asthenosphere.
p: A volcano is a place where gases, ashes and/or molten rock material (lava) escape to the ground.
A volcano is called active if these materials are being released or have been released in the recent past.
Molten rock in the upper mantle (asthenosphere) is called magma. Once it starts moving towards the crust or reaches the surface, it is called lava.

Materials that reach the ground include lava flows, pyroclastic debris, volcanic bombs, ash and dust, and gases such as nitrogen compounds, sulphur compounds and minor amounts of chlorine, hydrogen and argon.

Shield volcanoes are the largest of all volcanoes (barring basalt flows), e.g. the Hawaiian volcanoes. They are mostly basalt, a lava that is very fluid when erupted, so they are not steep. They have low explosivity, but become explosive if water gets into the vent. Lava fountains can build a cinder cone at the top.

ex.q: A volcano has gentle slopes, is built of fluid basaltic lava and erupts quietly. Identify its type and explain the gentle slope.
st: Gentle slopes + basalt + quiet eruption → shield volcano.
Basaltic lava is very fluid (low viscosity).
Fluid lava flows far before cooling, so it builds a broad, gently sloping shape.
ex.a: Shield volcano; its fluid basaltic lava spreads widely, giving gentle slopes.

topics.rl: Barren Island, about 135 km north-east of Port Blair, has erupted several times in recent decades and is monitored by Indian scientists.

topics.t: Composite volcanoes, calderas, flood basalts and mid-ocean ridges
topics.h: Some volcanoes build tall cones, some blow themselves apart, and some flood whole regions. The Deccan Traps of Maharashtra are lava floods frozen in stone.
p: Composite volcanoes erupt cooler and more viscous lavas than basalt and often cause explosive eruptions. Large quantities of pyroclastic material and ash accumulate near the vent, forming layers; that layering gives them the name composite.

Calderas are the most explosive volcanoes. They are so explosive that they collapse on themselves instead of building tall structures; the collapsed depressions are calderas. Their explosiveness shows that the magma chamber is huge and close to the surface.
Flood basalt provinces: highly fluid lava flows for long distances, covering thousands of sq km. Some flows are more than 50 m thick, and individual flows extend for hundreds of km.
The Deccan Traps of India, which now cover most of the Maharashtra plateau, are a much larger flood basalt province; they once covered an even larger area.
Mid-ocean ridge volcanoes occur in the oceans. A system of mid-ocean ridges more than 70,000 km long runs through all the ocean basins, and its central portion has frequent eruptions.

ex.q: Identify the volcano type: (a) a huge depression formed when a volcano collapses after a violent eruption; (b) cones with alternate layers of lava and ash; (c) thick lava sheets covering the Maharashtra plateau.
st: (a) Collapse into a depression → caldera.
(b) Layers of lava and pyroclastic material → composite volcano.
(c) Extensive thick flows of fluid lava → flood basalt province (Deccan Traps).
ex.a: (a) Caldera; (b) Composite volcano; (c) Flood basalt province.

topics.rl: The flat-topped hills of the Western Ghats near Mahabaleshwar and Lonavala are stacked layers of Deccan basalt, like a giant stone layer cake.

topics.t: Intrusive volcanic landforms
topics.h: Not all lava reaches the surface. Some cools underground into domes, saucers and walls, which erosion later uncovers, like the granite domes of Karnataka.
p: Lava that cools on the surface forms volcanic rocks; lava that cools within the crust forms plutonic rocks. Forms cooled inside the crust are called intrusive forms.

Batholiths: large bodies of magma that cool deep in the crust as large domes. They are granitic, cover large areas, can be several km deep, and appear on the surface only after denudation removes the overlying material. They are the cooled portions of magma chambers.

Lacoliths: large dome-shaped intrusive bodies with a level base, connected by a pipe-like conduit from below. The Karnataka plateau is dotted with granite domal hills, mostly now exfoliated, that are examples of lacoliths or batholiths.

Lapolith: a saucer-shaped body, concave to the sky. Phacolith: a wavy mass of intrusive rock found at the base of synclines or the top of anticlines in folded igneous country, with a conduit to a magma chamber below.

Sills and sheets are near-horizontal intrusive bodies: thick ones are sills, thin ones are sheets. Dykes are wall-like structures formed when lava solidifies almost perpendicular to the ground in cracks; they are the most common intrusive forms in western Maharashtra and are considered the feeders of the Deccan Traps.

ex.q: A geologist finds a vertical, wall-like band of basalt cutting across horizontal rock layers in western Maharashtra. Name it and state its significance.
st: A vertical wall-like intrusion that cuts across layers is a dyke.
Dykes are the most common intrusive forms in western Maharashtra.
They are considered the feeders (channels) for the lava eruptions that built the Deccan Traps.
ex.a: A dyke, a feeder for the Deccan Trap eruptions.

topics.rl: The rounded granite hills around Bengaluru and Hampi in Karnataka are exfoliated domes linked with batholiths and lacoliths, now popular rock-climbing spots.

topics.ch: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents
topics.t: Continental drift: Wegener, Pangaea and Panthalassa
topics.h: Look at a world map: the bulge of Brazil seems to fit into the curve of West Africa like jigsaw pieces. A weather scientist took that hint seriously.
p: Continents cover about 29% of the earth's surface; the rest is under oceans. The positions of continents and oceans have not always been the same.

Early ideas: Abraham Ortelius, a Dutch map maker, suggested as early as 1596 that the Americas, Europe and Africa were once joined. Antonio Pellegrini drew a map showing the three continents together.
Alfred Wegener, a German meteorologist, gave a comprehensive argument in 1912: the continental drift theory.
Wegener said all continents formed one supercontinent, Pangaea ('all earth'), surrounded by one mega-ocean, Panthalassa ('all water').
Around 200 million years ago, Pangaea began to split, first into two large landmasses: Laurasia (northern) and Gondwanaland (southern). These later broke into today's continents.

ex.q: Name the two landmasses Pangaea first split into and say which one India was part of.
st: About 200 million years ago Pangaea split into two.
The northern part was Laurasia.
The southern part was Gondwanaland.
India lies with the southern landmasses (Africa, South America, Australia, Antarctica), so it was part of Gondwanaland.
ex.a: Laurasia (north) and Gondwanaland (south); India was in Gondwanaland.

topics.rl: The Gondwana coalfields of the Damodar, Mahanadi and Godavari valleys get their name from Gondwanaland, the ancient southern supercontinent.

topics.ch: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents
topics.t: Evidence for drift: jigsaw fit, rock ages and tillite
topics.h: Ancient glacier deposits are found in hot India and Africa today. Ice never formed there in the present climate, so the land itself must have moved.
p: Jigsaw fit: the facing shorelines of Africa and South America match remarkably. In 1964 Bullard used a computer programme to find the best fit of the Atlantic margins; the fit was almost perfect at the 1,000-fathom line rather than the present shoreline.
Rocks of the same age across oceans: radiometric dating shows that a belt of ancient rocks, 2,000 million years old, on the Brazil coast matches rocks in western Africa.
The earliest marine deposits along the coasts of South America and Africa are of Jurassic age, suggesting that the ocean did not exist before that time.

Tillite is a sedimentary rock formed from glacial deposits. The Gondwana system of sediments of India has counterparts in six landmasses of the Southern Hemisphere (Africa, Falkland Islands, Madagascar, Antarctica and Australia, besides India).
Thick tillite at the base of the Gondwana system shows extensive, prolonged glaciation. It is clear evidence of past climates and of the drifting of continents.

ex.q: Why was Bullard's 1964 fit done at the 1,000-fathom line and not at today's coastline?
st: Present coastlines change with sea level, erosion and deposition.
The true edge of a continent is the continental margin, below sea level.
Matching at the 1,000-fathom depth line compares the real continental edges.
This gave an almost perfect fit.
ex.a: Because the 1,000-fathom line is closer to the true edge of the continents than the shifting shoreline.

topics.rl: Talchir tillite in Odisha, part of India's Gondwana rocks, records an ice age when India lay much closer to the South Pole.

topics.ch: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents
topics.t: Evidence for drift: placers and fossils; Wegener's forces
topics.h: Ghana's coast has rich gold deposits but no gold-bearing rock nearby. The 'source' lies across the Atlantic, in Brazil!
p: Placer deposits: rich placer gold deposits occur on the Ghana coast, but there are no source rocks there. The gold-bearing veins are in Brazil, so Ghana's gold must have come from the Brazil plateau when the two continents lay side by side.
Distribution of fossils: identical land or freshwater species on either side of marine barriers need an explanation.
Lemurs occur in India, Madagascar and Africa, which led some to imagine a connecting landmass called 'Lemuria'.
Mesosaurus, a small reptile of shallow brackish water, is found only in the southern Cape province of South Africa and the Iraver formations of Brazil, now 4,800 km apart with an ocean between them.

Force for drifting: Wegener suggested the pole-fleeing force (linked to the earth's rotation and its equatorial bulge) and the tidal force (due to the attraction of the moon and the sun). Most scholars considered these forces totally inadequate.

ex.q: Why is Mesosaurus strong evidence for drift?
st: Mesosaurus lived in shallow brackish water.
It could not have swum across a 4,800 km wide ocean.
Yet its fossils occur in both South Africa and Brazil.
So the two areas must once have been joined.
ex.a: A shallow-water reptile could not cross an ocean, so South Africa and Brazil must have been connected.

topics.rl: Grey slender lorises of Sri Lanka and India belong to the same primate group as Madagascar's lemurs, part of the puzzle that once inspired the 'Lemuria' idea.

topics.ch: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents
topics.t: Post-drift studies: convection currents and ocean floor mapping
topics.h: Wegener's big gap was 'What pushes the continents?' Two decades later, Arthur Holmes suggested the answer: the mantle is slowly boiling.
p: Convectional current theory: in the 1930s Arthur Holmes discussed convection currents in the mantle, generated by radioactive elements causing thermal differences. He argued that a system of such currents exists throughout the mantle.
Mapping of the ocean floor in the post-Second World War period showed that the ocean floor is not a vast plain but full of relief.
It revealed submerged mountain ranges and deep trenches, mostly located closer to the continental margins. Mid-oceanic ridges were found to be the most active in volcanic eruptions.
Dating showed that the oceanic crust is much younger than the continental areas.
Rocks equidistant from the crest of a mid-oceanic ridge, on either side, are remarkably similar in their constituents and age.

ex.q: How did ocean floor mapping help revive the idea of moving continents?
st: It found mid-oceanic ridges with active volcanism, i.e. a place where new crust may form.
It found deep trenches near continents, i.e. a place where crust may sink.
Ocean crust turned out to be young, and rocks matched symmetrically about the ridge.
These suggested the ocean floor itself is moving, leading to sea floor spreading.
ex.a: By revealing active ridges, trenches, young ocean crust and symmetric rocks: signs of a moving ocean floor.

topics.rl: India's National Institute of Oceanography in Goa and the research vessel Sagar Kanya have mapped parts of the Indian Ocean ridges using similar techniques.

topics.ch: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents
topics.t: Ocean floor configuration
topics.h: The longest mountain chain on earth is not the Himalaya or the Andes. It is hidden under the oceans.
p: Based on depth and relief, the ocean floor is divided into three major divisions: continental margins, deep sea basins and mid-ocean ridges.
Continental margins form the transition between continental shores and deep-sea basins. They include the continental shelf, continental slope, continental rise and deep oceanic trenches.
Abyssal plains are extensive plains between the continental margins and mid-oceanic ridges. Continental sediments that move beyond the margins are deposited here.
Mid-oceanic ridges form an interconnected chain of mountains within the ocean: the longest mountain chain on the earth's surface, though submerged.
A mid-oceanic ridge has a central rift system at the crest, a fractionated plateau, and a flank zone along its length. The rift at the crest is a zone of intense volcanic activity.

ex.q: A ship sails from the coast of Mumbai straight to the Carlsberg Ridge in the Arabian Sea. List the ocean-floor features it crosses in order.
st: Near the coast: continental shelf.
Then the steep continental slope and the continental rise.
Then the deep, flat abyssal plain (deep sea basin).
Finally the mid-oceanic ridge (Carlsberg Ridge) with its central rift.
ex.a: Shelf → slope → rise → abyssal plain → mid-oceanic ridge.

topics.rl: Mumbai High, India's biggest offshore oilfield, lies on the continental shelf, the shallow part of the continental margin.

topics.ch: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents
topics.t: Distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes
topics.h: Plot every earthquake and volcano on a world map and they are not scattered randomly. They draw lines, and those lines outline the plates.
p: A line of earthquake dots runs through the central Atlantic Ocean, almost parallel to the coastlines, and extends into the Indian Ocean. It coincides with the mid-oceanic ridges.
In the Indian Ocean the line branches a little south of the Indian subcontinent: one branch goes into East Africa and the other meets a line running from Myanmar to New Guinea.
A second belt of concentration coincides with the Alpine-Himalayan system and the rim of the Pacific Ocean.
Earthquake foci along mid-oceanic ridges are at shallow depths, while along the Alpine-Himalayan belt and the Pacific rim they are deep-seated.
Volcanoes show a similar pattern. The rim of the Pacific is called the 'rim of fire' (Ring of Fire) because of its many active volcanoes. Map work: locate the Ring of Fire and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

ex.q: An earthquake has a shallow focus and lies in the middle of the Atlantic. Another has a deep focus near Japan. Explain the difference.
st: The mid-Atlantic quake lies on the mid-oceanic ridge, where plates pull apart; foci there are shallow.
The Japan quake lies on the Pacific rim, where one plate sinks under another; foci there are deep-seated.
So the type of zone decides the focal depth.
ex.a: Ridges have shallow-focus quakes; the Pacific rim (and Alpine-Himalayan belt) has deep-seated quakes.

topics.rl: India sits next to the Alpine-Himalayan belt, which is why the Himalayan states and the North-East fall in India's highest seismic zone.

topics.ch: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents
topics.t: Sea floor spreading: the evidence
topics.h: The ocean floor is like a giant tape recorder: as new rock forms at the ridges, it 'records' the earth's magnetic field, which keeps flipping.
p: Palaeomagnetic studies show that rocks on either side of a mid-oceanic ridge form parallel stripes of normal and reverse magnetic polarity, matching on both sides.

Rocks equidistant from the crest are similar in age, chemical composition and magnetic properties. Rocks closest to the ridge have normal polarity and are the youngest; age increases with distance from the crest.
Ocean crust rocks are much younger than continental rocks: no oceanic crust is more than 200 million years old, while some continental rocks are as old as 3,200 million years.
Sediments on the ocean floor are unexpectedly thin. If the ocean floor were as old as the continents, much thicker sediments would have collected.
Deep trenches have deep-seated earthquakes, while mid-oceanic ridges have shallow-focus earthquakes.

ex.q: Rock A lies 10 km from a ridge crest and rock B lies 200 km away on the same side. Which is older and why?
st: New crust forms at the ridge crest and moves outwards.
Rocks nearer the crest formed more recently.
Rock A is nearer the crest, so it is younger.
Rock B, farther away, formed earlier and is older.
ex.a: Rock B is older, because age increases away from the ridge crest.

topics.rl: Indian scientists aboard ocean research cruises collect basalt from the Central Indian Ridge to date the youngest crust on earth.

topics.ch: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents
topics.t: Hess's sea floor spreading and the idea of plates
topics.h: If new ocean floor forms at the ridges every year, the earth should be growing. It isn't. So where does old ocean floor go?
p: Harry Hess (1961) proposed sea floor spreading: constant eruptions at the crest of ridges rupture the oceanic crust; new lava wedges in and pushes the crust on either side, so the ocean floor spreads.

Because the spreading of one ocean does not shrink another and the ocean crust is young, Hess argued that the ocean floor pushed away from the ridge sinks at oceanic trenches and is consumed (subduction).
In the NCERT diagram, magma rises at the ridge, the floor moves away on both sides, and old floor sinks at a trench near a continent.
Plate tectonics was proposed in 1967 by McKenzie and Parker, and independently by Morgan.

A tectonic (lithospheric) plate is a massive, irregularly shaped slab of solid rock, generally made of both continental and oceanic lithosphere, moving horizontally over the asthenosphere as a rigid unit. The lithosphere is 5–100 km thick under oceans and about 200 km in continental areas.

ex.q: Put Hess's model in order: crust sinks at trenches, magma erupts at the ridge, crust is pushed sideways.
st: Magma erupts at the ridge crest and ruptures the crust.
New lava wedges in and pushes the crust to either side.
The floor moves away and finally sinks at an oceanic trench, where it is consumed.
ex.a: Eruption at ridge → crust pushed apart (spreading) → sinking and consumption at trench.

topics.rl: The Andaman–Sumatra trench, where the Indian plate sinks below the Burma microplate, is the zone that produced the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.

topics.ch: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents
topics.t: Major and minor lithospheric plates
topics.h: The earth's surface is cracked into about seven giant pieces and many smaller ones, slowly jostling like rafts on a pond.
p: Seven major plates: Antarctica and the surrounding oceanic plate; North American plate; South American plate; Pacific plate; India-Australia-New Zealand plate; Africa with the eastern Atlantic floor plate; Eurasia and the adjacent oceanic plate.

Important minor plates: Cocos (between Central America and the Pacific plate), Nazca (between South America and the Pacific plate), Arabian (mostly the Saudi Arabian landmass), Philippine (between the Asiatic and Pacific plates), Caroline (between the Philippine and Indian plates, north of New Guinea) and Fuji (north-east of Australia).
A plate is called continental or oceanic depending on which occupies a larger part: the Pacific plate is largely oceanic; the Eurasian plate may be called continental.
It is the plate that moves, not the continent alone as Wegener believed. Continents are part of plates.
Palaeomagnetic data help reconstruct past positions of continents; the position of the Indian subcontinent (mostly Peninsular India) has been traced using rocks from the Nagpur area.

ex.q: Locate the Nazca plate in words.
st: Recall: Nazca is a minor plate.
It lies between South America and the Pacific plate.
So it is off the west coast of South America, under the Pacific Ocean.
ex.a: Between the South American plate and the Pacific plate, west of South America.

topics.rl: India sits on the India-Australia-New Zealand plate, which is still pushing north into the Eurasian plate. This is why Delhi and the Himalayan region feel tremors.

topics.ch: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents
topics.t: Types of plate boundaries
topics.h: Plates can pull apart, crash together or grind sideways. Each kind of meeting builds a different landscape.
p: Divergent boundaries: new crust is generated as plates pull away from each other. These sites are called spreading sites. The best-known example is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the American plate(s) separate from the Eurasian and African plates.
Convergent boundaries: crust is destroyed as one plate dives under another. The place where a plate sinks is called a subduction zone.
Convergence can occur in three ways: between an oceanic and a continental plate; between two oceanic plates; and between two continental plates.
Transform boundaries: crust is neither produced nor destroyed; plates slide horizontally past each other.

Transform faults are planes of separation generally perpendicular to mid-oceanic ridges. They form because eruptions do not occur all along the crest at the same time, causing differential movement, and the earth's rotation also affects the separated blocks.

ex.q: Classify each boundary: (a) Mid-Atlantic Ridge; (b) India pushing into Eurasia along the Himalaya; (c) plates sliding past each other along a fault crossing a ridge.
st: (a) Plates pull apart, new crust forms → divergent.
(b) Two continental plates collide → convergent (continent–continent).
(c) Horizontal sliding, no crust made or destroyed → transform.
ex.a: (a) Divergent; (b) Convergent; (c) Transform.

topics.rl: The Himalaya are a continent–continent convergent boundary, while the Andaman trench is an ocean–continent type of convergence affecting India's islands.

topics.ch: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents
topics.t: Rates and forces of plate movement; drift vs plate tectonics
topics.h: Plates move at roughly the speed your fingernails grow, yet over millions of years that adds up to whole oceans.
p: The strips of normal and reverse magnetic field parallel to mid-oceanic ridges help scientists determine the rates of plate movement.
Rates vary a lot: the Arctic Ridge is slowest (less than 2.5 cm/yr); the East Pacific Rise near Easter Island, in the South Pacific about 3,400 km west of Chile, is fastest (more than 15 cm/yr).

Force: the mantle is slowly convecting. Heated material rises, spreads, cools and sinks back, forming convection cells. The heat comes from radioactive decay and residual heat. Holmes first considered this in the 1930s, and it influenced Hess's ideas.

Continental drift (Wegener): continents move, driven by pole-fleeing and tidal forces. Plate tectonics: lithospheric plates, carrying both continents and ocean floor, move over the asthenosphere, driven by mantle convection.

ex.q: A plate moves at 5 cm per year. How far does it move in 1 million years, in km?
ex.a: 50 km.

topics.rl: GPS stations of the Survey of India show the Indian plate moving north-east by a few centimetres every year.

topics.ch: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents
topics.t: Movement of the Indian plate
topics.h: India was once an island near Australia. It then raced north across an ocean and crashed into Asia, and the Himalaya are the wreckage.
p: The Indian plate includes Peninsular India and the Australian continental portions.

Boundaries: the northern boundary is a continent–continent convergence along the Himalaya. In the east it extends through the Rakinyoma Mountains of Myanmar towards the island arc along the Java Trench. The western margin follows the Kirthar Mountains of Pakistan and extends along the Makrana coast.

India was a large island off the Australian coast, separated from Asia by the Tethys Sea till about 225 million years ago. It began its northward journey about 200 million years ago, when Pangaea broke.

About 140 million years ago, the subcontinent lay as far south as 50°S. The outpouring of lava that formed the Deccan Traps began about 60 million years ago, while India was still close to the equator.
India collided with Asia about 40–50 million years ago, causing rapid uplift of the Himalaya. The process continues and the Himalaya are still rising.

ex.q: Arrange in time order: Deccan Traps begin, India near 50°S, collision with Asia, start of the northward journey.
st: Start of the northward journey: about 200 million years ago.
India near 50°S: about 140 million years ago.
Deccan Traps begin: about 60 million years ago.
Collision with Asia: about 40–50 million years ago.
ex.a: Northward journey (200 Ma) → near 50°S (140 Ma) → Deccan Traps (60 Ma) → collision (40–50 Ma).

topics.rl: Marine fossils found high in the Himalaya, near Spiti and in Ladakh, are leftovers of the Tethys Sea floor lifted up by India's collision.

topics.t: Geomorphic processes and agents
topics.h: The Himalaya are still rising, yet the Ganga carries away millions of tonnes of their rock every year. The earth's surface is a tug-of-war between building up and wearing down.
p: Endogenic forces (internal) build up or elevate parts of the earth's surface; exogenic forces (external) wear down relief (degradation) and fill up basins (aggradation). Wearing down of relief through erosion is called gradation.

Geomorphic processes are the endogenic and exogenic forces that cause physical stresses and chemical actions on earth materials and change the configuration of the earth's surface. Diastrophism and volcanism are endogenic; weathering, mass wasting, erosion and deposition are exogenic.
A geomorphic agent is a mobile medium that removes, transports and deposits earth materials: running water, groundwater, glaciers, wind, waves and currents.
Gravity is a directional force that activates all downslope movements of matter and also causes stresses on earth materials. All movements occur due to gradients, from higher to lower levels.

ex.q: Classify as endogenic or exogenic: (a) uplift of a plateau; (b) a river carrying sand to the sea; (c) a volcanic eruption; (d) breaking of rock by frost.
st: Endogenic processes come from inside the earth: uplift (a) and volcanism (c).
Exogenic processes act on the surface using external energy: river transport (b) and frost weathering (d).
ex.a: Endogenic: (a), (c). Exogenic: (b), (d).

topics.rl: The Brahmaputra deposits huge amounts of sediment in Assam's valley (aggradation), while the Himalaya it drains are lifted by endogenic forces.

topics.t: Endogenic processes: energy and diastrophism
topics.h: The heat that lifts the Himalaya comes from deep inside the earth: radioactive elements and heat left over from the planet's birth.
p: The energy from within the earth drives endogenic processes. It is mostly generated by radioactivity, rotational and tidal friction, and primordial heat from the origin of the earth. Through geothermal gradients and heat flow, it induces diastrophism and volcanism.
Diastrophism: all processes that move, elevate or build up portions of the earth's crust.
Orogeny (orogenic processes): mountain building through severe folding, affecting long and narrow belts of the crust.
Epeirogeny (epeirogenic processes): uplift or warping of large parts of the crust. It causes simple deformation; it is a continent-building process, while orogeny is mountain building.

Diastrophism also includes earthquakes (local, relatively minor movements) and plate tectonics (horizontal movements of crustal plates). Diastrophism produces faulting and fracturing, and changes in pressure, volume and temperature that can cause metamorphism.

ex.q: Distinguish orogeny and epeirogeny with one feature each.
st: Orogeny: severe folding in long, narrow belts → mountains (e.g. Himalaya).
Epeirogeny: uplift or warping of large parts of the crust with simple deformation → continent building.
So the key difference is severe folding of narrow belts vs broad uplift of large areas.
ex.a: Orogeny = mountain building by severe folding of narrow belts; epeirogeny = broad uplift/warping of large areas (continent building).

topics.rl: Hot springs at Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh and Bakreshwar in West Bengal are surface signs of the earth's internal heat.

topics.t: Volcanism and the exogenic processes
topics.h: Push on a stack of books from the side and the top ones slide. Rocks feel the same 'shear', and that is how they start to break.
p: Volcanism (an endogenic process) includes the movement of molten rock (magma) onto or towards the earth's surface, and the formation of intrusive and extrusive volcanic forms.
Exogenic processes get their energy from the atmosphere, determined ultimately by the sun, and from the gradients created by tectonic factors.

Stress is force applied per unit area. It is produced in a solid by pushing or pulling and causes deformation. Forces acting along the faces of earth materials are shear stresses (separating forces); they break rocks and cause angular displacement or slippage.

Earth materials also face molecular stresses from temperature changes, crystallisation and melting. Chemical processes loosen bonds between grains. When stress exceeds a material's resistance, it breaks.
Weathering, mass wasting/movements, erosion and transportation are together called denudation, which means to strip off or uncover.

ex.q: A force of 600 newtons acts on a rock face of area 3 m². What is the stress (force per unit area)?
st: Stress = force ÷ area.
= 200 newtons per m².

topics.rl: When engineers cut roads through hills on the Mumbai–Pune expressway, they study shear stress on rock faces to prevent slope failures.

topics.t: Climate, rocks and exogenic processes
topics.h: The same granite crumbles in a different way in Rajasthan's heat, Kerala's rain and Ladakh's frost. Climate decides which exogenic processes rule.
p: Exogenic processes depend on the type of climate. Temperature and precipitation are the two most important climatic elements controlling them.
Vegetation density and type, which depend on precipitation and temperature, also influence exogenic processes indirectly.

Within a climatic region, there are local variations due to altitude, aspect (north- vs south-facing slopes receiving different insolation), wind speed and direction, rainfall intensity, and freeze-thaw cycles.
Rock type and structure matter too: differences in rocks lead to differential erosion, so soft rocks wear away faster than hard ones.
NCERT's diagram shows denudational processes (weathering, mass wasting, erosion and transportation) together with the driving forces behind them, such as solar energy, gravity and gradients.

ex.q: Two slopes of the same hill in the mid-latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere face north and south. Why might exogenic processes differ on them?
st: The south-facing slope receives more sunlight (insolation).
It is warmer and drier; the north-facing slope is cooler and moister.
Different temperature and moisture lead to different weathering and vegetation.
So aspect causes local differences in exogenic processes.
ex.a: Because of aspect: the sunnier south-facing slope is warmer and drier than the cooler, moister north-facing slope.

topics.rl: In the Kumaon Himalaya, villages and orchards prefer the sunny south-facing slopes, while north-facing slopes keep denser, moister forests.

topics.t: Weathering: meaning, factors and significance
topics.h: Without weathering there would be no soil, no forests and no bauxite for aluminium. Slow-motion rock breaking is the foundation of life and industry.
p: Weathering is the mechanical disintegration and chemical decomposition of rocks through the actions of the elements of weather and climate.
Very little or no motion of material takes place in weathering, so it is an in-situ or on-site process.
Weathering is controlled by many geological, climatic, topographic and vegetative factors. Weathering processes are grouped as chemical, physical (mechanical) and biological.

Significance: weathering breaks rocks into smaller fragments, preparing the way for regolith and soils, and for erosion and mass movements. Forests and biodiversity depend on the depth of the weathering mantle.

Weathering helps in the enrichment and concentration of valuable ores of iron, manganese, aluminium and copper. When some materials are leached away, the concentration of the remaining valuable material rises, making it economic to mine. This is called enrichment.

ex.q: A rock contains 20 kg of aluminium ore mixed in 100 kg of material. Weathering leaches away 50 kg of other material. What is the new percentage of ore?
st: Original ore share = 20 ÷ 100 = 20%.
After leaching, total = 100 − 50 = 50 kg; ore is still 20 kg.
Ore concentration has doubled: enrichment.
ex.a: 40%, the ore has been enriched by weathering.

topics.rl: India's bauxite deposits in Odisha and Jharkhand, the source of aluminium, formed by intense weathering that removed other minerals and concentrated aluminium.

topics.t: Chemical weathering processes
topics.h: Rainwater is slightly acidic. Given enough time, it can dissolve whole caves out of limestone.
p: Chemical weathering processes include solution, carbonation, hydration, oxidation and reduction. They act on rocks to decompose, dissolve or reduce them to fine particles, with water and air and heat speeding them up.

Solution: minerals dissolve in water or acids. Nitrates, sulphates and potassium are very soluble; common salt (sodium chloride) also dissolves. Calcium carbonate and calcium magnesium bicarbonate in limestones dissolve in water containing carbonic acid.

Carbonation: the reaction of carbonate and bicarbonate with minerals. Carbon dioxide from the air and soil air dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, a weak acid, which dissolves calcium and magnesium carbonates. This helps form caves.

Hydration: chemical addition of water. Minerals take up water and expand, increasing volume. Calcium sulphate takes in water and turns into gypsum, which is more unstable. Repeated hydration causes fatigue in rocks and may lead to disintegration.

Oxidation: combination of a mineral with oxygen to form oxides or hydroxides, where air and oxygenated water are available; iron, manganese and sulphur are commonly involved (rusting of iron is an example). Reduction occurs when oxidised minerals are placed where oxygen is absent, e.g. below the water table or in waterlogged ground.

ex.q: Identify the process: (a) limestone dissolving in rainwater containing CO₂; (b) calcium sulphate becoming gypsum; (c) iron minerals in a rock rusting.
st: (a) CO₂ + water → carbonic acid, which dissolves carbonates → carbonation.
(b) Addition of water to a mineral → hydration.
(c) Combination with oxygen → oxidation.
ex.a: (a) Carbonation; (b) Hydration; (c) Oxidation.

topics.rl: The limestone caves of Borra (Andhra Pradesh) and Mawsmai (Meghalaya) were dissolved out by carbonation over thousands of years.

topics.t: Physical weathering: unloading, temperature and exfoliation
