topics.h: The smooth, rounded granite domes and boulders of the Deccan look polished, but no one polished them. The rock peeled itself like an onion.
p: Physical (mechanical) weathering depends on applied forces: gravitational forces (overburden pressure, load, shearing stress); expansion forces due to temperature changes, crystal growth or animal activity; and water pressure controlled by wetting and drying cycles.

Unloading and expansion: continued erosion removes the overlying rock load, releasing vertical pressure. The upper layers expand, and fractures develop roughly parallel to the surface. On curved surfaces this produces exfoliation sheets and large, smooth rounded exfoliation domes.

Temperature changes and expansion: surface layers expand more than deeper rock, creating stress that causes heaving and fracturing parallel to the surface. Differential heating and cooling leads to exfoliation and smooth rounded surfaces; in granites, rounded boulders called tors form.
Exfoliation is a result, not a process: it is the flaking off of curved sheets of rock. Exfoliation domes result from unloading, and tors from thermal expansion.

ex.q: A granite hill has become a huge smooth dome after the overlying rocks were eroded away. Explain the weathering involved.
st: Erosion removed the overlying load from the granite.
Pressure release allowed the upper granite layers to expand.
Fractures developed parallel to the curved surface.
Curved sheets peeled off (exfoliation), producing a smooth exfoliation dome.
ex.a: Unloading and expansion produced exfoliation, forming an exfoliation dome.

topics.rl: Hampi's piled-up rounded granite boulders and the domes around Bengaluru are classic results of exfoliation.

topics.t: Frost, salt and biological weathering
topics.h: Water expands when it freezes, salt crystals grow in desert rocks, and tree roots push like hydraulic jacks. Small forces, repeated endlessly, crack mountains.
p: Frost weathering occurs due to the growth of ice in pores and cracks during repeated cycles of freezing and melting. It is most effective at high elevations in mid-latitudes, where freezing and thawing are repeated often; glacial areas face frost wedging daily. Rapid freezing causes sudden expansion and high pressure.

Salt weathering: salts in rocks expand due to thermal action, hydration and crystallisation. Salts of calcium, sodium, magnesium, potassium and barium tend to expand. High surface temperatures of 30–50°C in deserts favour salt expansion.

Salt crystals in near-surface pores split grains, which fall off: granular disintegration or granular foliation. Salt crystallisation is the most effective salt-weathering process, favoured by alternate wetting and drying.

Biological weathering: burrowing and wedging by earthworms, termites and rodents expose new surfaces to chemical attack; humans disturb vegetation and plough soils. Decaying plant and animal matter produces humic, carbonic and other acids. Plant roots exert tremendous pressure and break rocks apart.

ex.q: Match each place to its most effective weathering: (a) high-altitude slopes of Himachal with daily freeze-thaw; (b) the hot, dry Thar desert with salty soils; (c) a forest where tree roots grow into rock cracks.
st: (a) Repeated freezing and thawing → frost wedging.
(b) High temperatures and salts → salt weathering (salt crystallisation).
(c) Roots growing in cracks → biological weathering.
ex.a: (a) Frost wedging; (b) Salt weathering; (c) Biological weathering.

topics.rl: Termite mounds in central India and earthworms in farm soils constantly rework the soil, exposing fresh material to weathering.

topics.t: Mass movements: causes, forms and slow movements
topics.h: Ever seen electric poles on a hillside all leaning downhill? The soil beneath them is creeping, too slowly to see.
p: Mass movements transfer rock debris down slopes under the direct influence of gravity. Air, water or ice do not carry the debris; rather, the debris may carry air, water or ice with it. Mass movements do not come under erosion.

Factors favouring them: weak unconsolidated materials, thinly bedded rocks, faults, steep slopes, heavy rainfall and scarce vegetation. Activating causes include removal of support from below, increase in gradient and height of slopes, overloading (by materials or heavy rain and saturation), earthquakes, explosions or machinery, excessive seepage, drawdown of water from reservoirs, and removal of natural vegetation.
Three forms of movement: heave (heaving up of soils due to frost growth and other causes), flow and slide.

Slow movements: creep occurs on moderately steep, soil-covered slopes and is extremely slow and imperceptible; leaning fence posts and poles show soil creep. Types include soil creep, talus creep, rock creep and rock-glacier creep.

Solifluction is the slow downslope flow of soil or fine debris saturated or lubricated with water. It is common in moist temperate areas, where surface melting of deeply frozen ground and long continued rain occur.

ex.q: After road widening on a Himalayan hill, the toe of a slope is cut away and heavy monsoon rain follows. Which activating causes of mass movement are present?
st: Cutting the toe removes support from below.
It also steepens the slope (increase in gradient).
Heavy rain saturates and overloads slope materials.
Together these make mass movement likely.
ex.a: Removal of support, increased gradient, and overloading/saturation by heavy rain.

topics.rl: Leaning trees and cracked retaining walls along hill roads in Uttarakhand and Sikkim are tell-tale signs of soil creep.

topics.t: Rapid movements and landslides
topics.h: In the Himalaya, a single night of cloudburst can send a hillside crashing onto a highway. Why do the Himalaya suffer more than the Western Ghats?
p: Rapid movements are common in humid regions on gentle to steep slopes. Earthflow: water-saturated clayey or silty material moves down low-angle terraces or hillsides, often slumping into step-like terraces.

Mudflow: with heavy rain and no vegetation, thick weathered layers saturated with water flow down definite channels like streams of mud. They can engulf roads, bridges and houses, and occur often on slopes of erupting or recently erupted volcanoes. Debris avalanche: on steep slopes in narrow tracks, even faster than mudflow, similar to a snow avalanche.

Landslides are relatively rapid and perceptible movements of relatively dry material. Types: slump (slipping with a backward rotation), debris slide (rolling or sliding without backward rotation), debris fall (nearly free fall from a vertical face), rock slide (sliding of rock masses down bedding, joint or fault surfaces) and rock fall (free fall of rock blocks from a steep slope).
Debris avalanches and landslides are very frequent in the Himalaya because they are tectonically active, made mostly of sedimentary rocks and unconsolidated deposits, and have very steep slopes.

The Nilgiris and Western Ghats are tectonically stable and made of hard rocks, yet landslides occur there because of very steep slopes and cliffs, strong mechanical weathering due to temperature changes, and heavy rainfall over short periods.

ex.q: A block of earth slips downhill and tilts backwards as it moves. Name the movement and contrast it with a debris slide.
st: Slipping with backward rotation is a slump.
A debris slide is rapid rolling or sliding of debris without backward rotation.
So the key difference is the backward rotation.
ex.a: Slump (with backward rotation); a debris slide has no backward rotation.

topics.rl: Landslides on the Konkan Railway during heavy monsoon spells show that even the hard-rock Western Ghats are vulnerable on steep cuttings.

topics.t: Erosion and deposition
topics.h: Weathering is a rock breaking at home. Erosion is the rock leaving home, on a river, a glacier or a gust of wind.
p: Erosion involves the acquisition and transportation of rock debris. It is largely responsible for the continuous changes in the earth's surface.
Weathering is in-situ and involves no motion; erosion involves movement of material. Weathering aids erosion, but it is not a pre-condition for erosion.

Erosion and transportation are controlled by kinetic energy. The agents are running water, wind, glaciers, waves and groundwater; the first three are controlled by climate. Abrasion by debris carried by agents greatly aids erosion.

Running water is the most important agent in humid regions with heavy rainfall; wind operates mainly in hot dry deserts; glaciers work in high latitudes and high altitudes; waves act along coasts; groundwater is effective in limestone areas.

Deposition is a consequence of erosion: when agents lose velocity and energy on gentler slopes, they drop their load. Coarser materials are deposited first and finer ones later. Deposition is not the work of a separate agent.

ex.q: A river slows down as it enters the plains from the hills. What happens to its load and in what order?
st: Velocity drops on the gentler slope, so energy falls.
The river can no longer carry all its load and starts depositing.
Coarse material (boulders, gravel) settles first.
Finer material (sand, silt, clay) is carried farther and settles later.
ex.a: It deposits its load: coarse material first, finer material later.

topics.rl: The Kosi drops gravel near the foothills and carries fine silt far into the plains of Bihar, a textbook example of sorted deposition.

topics.t: Soil formation: process, profile, parent material and topography
topics.h: A handful of good soil can take centuries to form, and it starts with bacteria, lichens and mosses settling on broken rock.
p: Soil is a collection of natural bodies on the earth's surface containing living matter and supporting or capable of supporting plants. It is a dynamic medium with constant chemical, physical and biological activity.

Soil formation (pedogenesis) depends first on weathering; the weathering mantle is the basic input. Weathered material or transported deposits are colonised by bacteria and simple plants like mosses and lichens; dead remains build humus; grasses, ferns, bushes and trees follow. Roots and burrowing animals make it porous; a mature soil, a mix of mineral and organic products, forms and develops layers (horizons) seen in a soil profile.
Five soil-forming factors: parent material, topography, climate, biological activity and time. They act together.

Parent material is a passive control factor. It can be in-situ weathered rock debris (residual soils) or transported deposits (transported soils). Texture, structure and mineral composition of the debris matter.

Topography is another passive factor: soils are thin on steep slopes and thick on flat uplands; gentle slopes with slow erosion and good percolation favour soil formation. In middle latitudes, sunny south-facing slopes and cool, moist north-facing slopes develop different soils and vegetation.

ex.q: Why is soil usually thin on a steep hillside but thick on a flat upland?
st: On steep slopes, erosion removes weathered material quickly.
Water runs off instead of percolating, so less weathering at depth.
On flat uplands, material stays in place and water percolates well.
So soil accumulates and becomes thick.
ex.a: Steep slopes lose material to erosion; flat uplands retain it, so soil is thicker there.

topics.rl: Alluvial soils of the Ganga plain are transported soils, while the black soils of the Deccan formed in place from basalt: residual soils.

topics.t: Soil formation: climate, biological activity and time
topics.h: The same parent rock can give a deep red soil in Kerala and a thin, stony soil in Ladakh. Climate, life and time make the difference.
p: Climate is an important active factor: moisture (intensity, frequency and duration of precipitation; evaporation; humidity) and temperature (seasonal and daily variation).

Excess water moves soil components downward (eluviation) and deposits them below (illuviation). In wet equatorial areas, calcium, sodium, magnesium, potassium and much of the silica are removed; removal of silica is desilication. In dry climates, evaporation exceeds precipitation, groundwater rises by capillary action and leaves salts that form a crust called hardpan. In tropical areas with intermediate rainfall, calcium carbonate nodules (kanker) form.
Higher temperature increases chemical activity (except carbonation), so tropical soils have deeper profiles; in frozen tundra, soils are mainly mechanically broken material.

Biological activity: vegetation and organisms add organic matter, moisture retention and nitrogen. Dead plants give humus. In cold climates, slow bacterial activity lets humus and peat accumulate; in humid tropics, intense bacterial action leaves low humus. Nitrogen fixation: Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules of leguminous plants fix nitrogen. Earthworms, ants, termites and rodents rework the soil.

Time: the length of time soil-forming processes operate determines maturity and profile development. Soils on recent alluvium or glacial till are young, with no or poorly developed horizons. No fixed absolute time can be set for soils to mature.

ex.q: Why do humid tropical soils have low humus even though plant growth is heavy?
st: Humid tropics are hot and wet.
Bacterial growth and action are intense there.
Dead vegetation is rapidly oxidised (decomposed).
So little humus accumulates in the soil.
ex.a: Intense bacterial activity rapidly decomposes dead matter, leaving little humus.

topics.rl: Farmers in India grow pulses like moong and arhar partly because Rhizobium in their root nodules fixes nitrogen and enriches the soil.

topics.t: Landforms, landscapes and their evolution
topics.h: A river valley in Uttarakhand, a sand dune in Jaisalmer and a sea cliff in Goa each have a life story: youth, maturity and old age.
p: After weathering, geomorphic agents such as running water, groundwater, wind, glaciers and waves erode, transport and deposit material, and in the process create landforms.
Landforms are small to medium tracts or parcels of the earth's surface. Several related landforms together make up a landscape, a large tract of the earth's surface.
Each landform has its own physical shape, size and materials, and is the result of certain geomorphic processes and agents. Landforms change slowly or quickly as processes and agents change.
Landform evolution means the stages of transformation of a landform or landscape. Like living beings, landforms pass through youth, maturity and old age.
Two aspects matter when studying landforms: the stages of development, and the processes and agents shaping them. Each agent produces its own assemblage of landforms.

ex.q: Is the entire Indo-Gangetic plain a landform or a landscape? Is a single oxbow lake a landform or a landscape?
st: A landscape is a large tract made up of several related landforms.
The Indo-Gangetic plain contains floodplains, levees, oxbow lakes and more → a landscape.
A single oxbow lake is a small tract with its own shape and origin → a landform.
ex.a: Indo-Gangetic plain = landscape; oxbow lake = landform.

topics.rl: Tourism brochures for Himachal describe 'landscapes', but a geography field trip zooms in on each landform: a moraine, a terrace, a gorge.

topics.t: Running water: stages of a river landscape
topics.h: Follow a river landscape through time and you see a young, energetic stream turning into a slow, meandering elder that has flattened almost everything around it.
p: In humid regions with heavy rainfall, running water is the most important geomorphic agent. It has two components: overland flow as a sheet over the land, and linear flow as streams and rivers in valleys.

Youth: streams are few with poor integration; they flow over original slopes in shallow V-shaped valleys with no or very narrow floodplains. Stream divides are broad and flat with marshes, swamps and lakes. Waterfalls and rapids may exist where local hard rocks are exposed.
Maturity: streams are plenty with good integration. Valleys are still V-shaped but deep; trunk streams have wider floodplains with meanders. Divides become sharp, and waterfalls and rapids disappear.

Old age: smaller tributaries are few, with gentle gradients. Streams meander freely over vast floodplains with natural levees and oxbow lakes. Divides are broad and flat with lakes, swamps and marshes; most of the land is at or slightly above sea level.
Over a long time, relief can be reduced to an almost plain, a peneplain, with low resistant remnants called monadnocks standing out.

ex.q: A region has many well-integrated streams in deep V-shaped valleys with wide floodplains and sharp divides, but no waterfalls. Which stage is it?
st: Many well-integrated streams → not youth.
Deep V-shaped valleys and wide floodplains with sharp divides → maturity.
Waterfalls and rapids have disappeared → maturity.
Old age would have very gentle gradients and vast floodplains with oxbow lakes.
ex.a: Mature stage.

topics.rl: The upper Ganga near Rishikesh shows youthful features, while the lower Ganga in West Bengal and Bangladesh meanders across vast floodplains, showing old-age features.

topics.t: Erosional landforms of running water
topics.h: At Hogenakkal, the Kaveri squeezes through a deep rocky gorge. Upstream, pebbles spinning in eddies have drilled perfect round holes in the riverbed rock.
p: Valleys begin as small, narrow rills, which grow into long, wide gullies, which deepen, widen and lengthen into valleys. Types include V-shaped valley, gorge and canyon.

A gorge is a deep valley with very steep to straight sides, almost equal in width at the top and bottom; it forms in hard rocks. A canyon has steep, step-like side slopes, is wider at the top than at the bottom, and commonly forms in horizontally bedded sedimentary rocks; a canyon is a variant of a gorge (e.g. the Grand Canyon of the Colorado River; the Kaveri gorge near Hogenakkal).

Potholes are more or less circular depressions on rocky beds of hill streams, formed by stream erosion aided by abrasion of rock fragments that rotate in them. Large, deep holes at the base of waterfalls are plunge pools; they help deepen valleys.

Incised or entrenched meanders are very deep, wide meanders cut in hard rocks. The loops formed on original gentle surfaces get entrenched due to erosion or slow, continued uplift; they indicate the status of the original land surface.

River terraces mark old valley-floor or floodplain levels. They are products of erosion: the stream cuts vertically into its own floodplain. Paired terraces are at the same height on both sides; unpaired terraces are on one side only or at different heights. Causes: receding water after peak flow, change in hydrological regime due to climate change, tectonic uplift and sea-level change.

ex.q: Distinguish between a gorge and a canyon.
st: Shape of sides: gorge has very steep to straight sides; canyon has steep step-like sides.
Width: gorge is almost equal at top and bottom; canyon is wider at the top.
Rock: gorges form in hard rocks; canyons commonly in horizontally bedded sedimentary rocks.
ex.a: Gorge: straight sides, equal width, hard rock. Canyon: step-like sides, wider at top, horizontal sedimentary rock.

topics.rl: The Gandikota gorge on the Penner river in Andhra Pradesh is often called the 'Grand Canyon of India'.

topics.t: Depositional landforms: fans, deltas, floodplains and levees
topics.h: Fly over Andhra Pradesh and the Krishna spreads into many fingers before meeting the Bay of Bengal, building land into the sea year after year.
p: Alluvial fans form when streams from higher levels break into foot-slope plains of low gradient. The heavy, coarse load is dumped as a broad cone-shaped deposit. Streams on fans shift and form many channels called distributaries. Fans are low cones with gentle slopes in humid areas and high cones with steep slopes in arid and semi-arid areas.

Deltas are like alluvial fans but form where rivers meet the sea. Unlike fans, delta deposits are very well sorted with clear stratification: coarse material settles first, finer silt and clay are carried farther. Distributaries lengthen as the delta grows into the sea (e.g. the Krishna delta).

Floodplains are major landforms of river deposition. The riverbed made of river deposits is the active floodplain; the floodplain above the bank is the inactive floodplain, with flood deposits (finer silt and clay) and channel deposits (coarser, from abandoned channels). Floodplains in a delta are called delta plains.

Natural levees are low, linear, parallel ridges of coarse deposits along the banks of large rivers. When floodwater spills over the bank, its velocity falls and coarse, heavy material is dumped next to the bank. Levees are high near the bank and slope gently away from it.

ex.q: Why are deposits in a delta well sorted while those in an alluvial fan are not?
st: A fan forms suddenly at the foot of a slope, where coarse load is dumped quickly → poor sorting.
A delta forms where the river slows gradually into the sea.
Coarse material settles first, finer silt and clay are carried farther → well sorted and stratified.
ex.a: The gradual loss of velocity into the sea sorts delta deposits by size; fans are dumped abruptly.

topics.rl: The Kosi's huge alluvial fan in Bihar explains why the river keeps shifting its course, earning it the name 'Sorrow of Bihar'.

topics.t: Meanders, point bars and oxbow lakes
topics.h: On the plains of Bihar, the Ganga and its tributaries loop like a garden hose left on the floor. Sometimes a loop gets cut off and turns into a lake.
p: Meanders are loop-like channel patterns that develop over flood and delta plains. A meander is not a landform but a type of channel pattern.

Meanders form because of (i) the tendency of water on very gentle gradients to work laterally on the banks, (ii) unconsolidated alluvial banks with many irregularities, and (iii) the Coriolis force deflecting the flowing water.
The concave bank of a meander (cut-off bank) is a steep, eroding scarp; the convex bank has a long, gentle profile.

Point bars (meander bars) are sediments deposited in a linear fashion on the convex side of meanders of large rivers. They are almost uniform in profile and width and contain mixed sizes of sediment. As point bars build on the convex side, the concave bank erodes actively.

When meanders grow into deep loops, they may be cut off by erosion at the inflection points, leaving oxbow lakes. Natural levees (coarse ridges along the banks from floodwater spill) differ from point bars (mixed sediments on the convex side of meanders).

ex.q: Differentiate natural levees and point bars.
st: Location: levees are along the banks of large rivers; point bars are on the convex side of meanders.
Formation: levees form when floodwater spills over and slows; point bars form from deposition by flowing water along the inner bank.
Material: levees are coarse deposits; point bars have mixed sizes of sediment.
ex.a: Levees: bank ridges of coarse flood deposits. Point bars: convex-side meander deposits of mixed sediments.

topics.rl: Kanwar Lake (Kabar Tal) in Begusarai, Bihar, is often described as a residual oxbow lake left by a meandering river.

topics.t: Groundwater and karst: erosional landforms
topics.h: In parts of Meghalaya, a stream suddenly vanishes into a hole in the ground and reappears kilometres away. Welcome to karst country.
p: Groundwater does effective geomorphic work in rocks like limestone and dolomite, rich in calcium carbonate. The processes are mainly solution and precipitation (deposition).

Any limestone or dolomite region showing typical landforms produced by groundwater through solution and deposition is called karst topography, named after the Karst region in the Balkans, next to the Adriatic Sea.

Swallow holes are small to medium, round to sub-rounded shallow depressions formed on limestone surfaces through solution. A sinkhole is an opening more or less circular at the top and funnel-shaped towards the bottom; sizes range from a few sq m to a hectare, depths from under half a metre to 30 m or more.

Solution sinks form solely by solution. Collapse sinks form when the bottom of a sinkhole is the roof of a cave that collapses; the term doline is sometimes used for collapse sinks. Solution sinks are more common than collapse sinks.

When sinkholes and dolines join, long, narrow to wide trenches called valley sinks or uvalas form. The limestone surface is eaten into a maze of grooves and ridges called lapies, formed by differential solution along joints; lapies may turn into smooth limestone pavements.

ex.q: A sinkhole has a circular opening at the top that funnels down, but its floor suddenly gives way into an underground void. What type of sink does it become?
st: A sinkhole formed by solution alone is a solution sink.
If its bottom is the roof of an underground cave and collapses, it opens into the void.
That makes it a collapse sink, also called a doline.
ex.a: A collapse sink (doline).

topics.rl: The Cherrapunji–Mawsmai area of Meghalaya has limestone with sinkholes and caves, a classic karst landscape in India.

topics.t: Caves, stalactites, stalagmites and underground drainage
topics.h: Inside the Borra Caves of Andhra Pradesh, stone icicles hang from the roof while stone columns grow up from the floor, one drip at a time.
p: Caves form prominently where limestone or dolomite alternates with other rocks (shales, sandstones, quartzites), or where limestone is dense, massive and thickly bedded. Water percolates through cracks and joints, then moves horizontally along bedding planes, dissolving limestone into long, narrow to wide gaps called caves.
Caves usually have an opening through which cave streams are discharged. Caves with openings at both ends are called tunnels.
Calcium carbonate dissolved in carbonated water is deposited when the water evaporates or loses its carbon dioxide as it trickles over rough rock surfaces.

Stalactites hang from cave roofs like icicles; they are broad at their bases and taper towards the free ends. Stalagmites rise up from the cave floor, formed by water dripping from the surface or through the thin pipe of a stalactite above. Stalactites and stalagmites eventually fuse to form columns and pillars.
In karst areas, surface run-off often goes down swallow holes and sinkholes, flows as underground streams, and re-emerges downstream through cave openings, so surface drainage is scarce.

ex.q: How can you remember which grows from the roof and which from the floor?
st: StalaCtites hold tight to the Ceiling (C for ceiling).
StalaGmites rise from the Ground (G for ground).
When they meet, they fuse into a pillar or column.
ex.a: Stalactites hang from the ceiling; stalagmites rise from the ground; together they form pillars.

topics.rl: The Borra Caves near Visakhapatnam and the Belum Caves in Nandyal district (formerly part of Kurnool district) are among India's best-known limestone caves, drawing thousands of tourists.

topics.t: Glaciers: erosion, cirques and horns
topics.h: The holy Ganga begins as meltwater from the Gangotri glacier's snout at Gaumukh, a 'cow's mouth' of ice.
p: Glaciers are masses of ice moving as sheets over land (continental glacier, or piedmont glacier when a vast ice sheet spreads over plains at the foot of mountains) or as linear flows down mountain slopes in broad trough-like valleys (mountain or valley glaciers). They move slowly, from a few centimetres to a few metres a day, basically due to gravity.

Glacial erosion is tremendous because of friction caused by the sheer weight of ice. Material plucked from the land is dragged along valley floors and sides, causing great damage through abrasion and plucking.
Example: the Gangotri glacier's snout is at Gaumukh, where the Bhagirathi emerges. The Bhagirathi and Alaknanda join at Devprayag (Deoprayag) to form the Ganga.

Cirques are deep, long and wide troughs or basins with very steep concave to vertical walls at the head and sides, often at the heads of glacial valleys. After the glacier disappears, a lake called a cirque or tarn lake may form inside.

Horns form by headward erosion of cirque walls: when three or more radiating glaciers cut back until their cirques meet, sharp, steep peaks result. Narrowed divides become serrated or saw-toothed ridges called arêtes. The Matterhorn (Alps) and Everest (Himalaya) are horns.

ex.q: Explain how a horn like the Matterhorn forms.
st: Several glaciers radiate from a mountain top, each carving a cirque.
Each cirque erodes headward (backwards into the mountain).
When three or more cirques meet, only a sharp, steep-sided peak remains.
This pyramid-like peak is a horn.
ex.a: By headward erosion of three or more radiating cirques meeting at the top.

topics.rl: Hemkund in Uttarakhand and many lakes in the Himalaya sit in glacial basins, while the retreat of Gangotri's snout is closely monitored as a sign of climate change.

topics.t: Glacial valleys, till and moraines
topics.h: A river carves a V. A glacier bulldozes a U. Look at a valley's cross-section and you can tell who made it.
p: Glaciated valleys are trough-like and U-shaped, with broad floors and relatively smooth, steep sides. They may contain debris, moraines and lakes gouged from the rocky floor.

Hanging valleys may lie at a height on one or both sides of the main glacial valley; their truncated spurs look like triangular facets. Very deep glacial troughs filled with sea water and forming shorelines in high latitudes are fjords (fiords).

Glacial till is the unassorted coarse and fine debris dropped by melting glaciers; its fragments are angular to sub-angular. Outwash deposits are washed down by meltwater streams; unlike till, they are roughly stratified and assorted, with somewhat rounded fragments.

Moraines are long ridges of glacial till. Terminal moraines form at the end (toe) of glaciers; lateral moraines form along the sides parallel to the valley and may join a terminal moraine in a horse-shoe shape.

Ground moraines are irregular sheets of till left over valley floors by rapidly retreating glaciers. A medial moraine lies in the centre of a glacial valley flanked by lateral moraines; it is imperfectly formed and may be indistinguishable from ground moraines.

ex.q: Differentiate glacial till from outwash deposits.
st: Till: dropped directly by melting ice → unassorted coarse and fine debris, angular to sub-angular.
Outwash: carried and deposited by meltwater streams → roughly stratified and assorted, somewhat rounded.
So the key difference is sorting and roundness, due to water transport.
ex.a: Till is unsorted and angular; outwash is sorted, stratified and rounded.

topics.rl: Trekkers to Gaumukh walk over hummocks of moraine debris dumped by the retreating Gangotri glacier.

topics.t: Eskers, outwash plains and drumlins
topics.h: Some glacial landforms are made by rivers that once flowed beneath the ice, and they still point in the direction the ice was moving.
p: Eskers: in summer, meltwater flows on, along or through the ice and collects beneath the glacier, flowing like a stream with ice as its banks. Coarse material like boulders and blocks settles in this ice channel; when the ice melts, a sinuous ridge called an esker remains.

Outwash plains: plains at the foot of glacial mountains or beyond continental ice sheets are covered with glacio-fluvial deposits as broad, flat alluvial fans, which may join to form outwash plains of gravel, silt, sand and clay.

Drumlins are smooth, oval, ridge-like features made mainly of glacial till with some gravel and sand. Their long axes are parallel to the direction of ice movement. They may be up to 1 km long and about 30 m high.

The end of a drumlin facing the glacier, the stoss end, is blunter and steeper than the other end, called the tail. Drumlins form by dumping of debris beneath heavily loaded ice and indicate the direction of glacier movement.

Key differences: glacial valleys are U-shaped while river valleys are V-shaped; till is unsorted while alluvium is sorted; outwash plains are built by meltwater from glaciers while alluvial plains are built by rivers.

ex.q: A drumlin's steep, blunt end faces north and its gentle tail points south. Which way did the ice move?
st: The stoss end (blunt, steep) faces the oncoming glacier.
The stoss end faces north, so the ice came from the north.
The tail points in the direction the ice moved, i.e., south.
ex.a: From north to south.

topics.rl: Geologists mapping old glacial deposits in Ladakh and Himachal use features like moraines and outwash to reconstruct how far glaciers once extended.

topics.t: Coasts: high rocky and low sedimentary
topics.h: Goa's cliffs and headlands look nothing like the long flat beaches and lagoons of Odisha. India's two coasts behave in opposite ways.
p: Coastal processes are the most dynamic and hence the most destructive. Most erosion and deposition is by waves; storm waves and tsunami waves can cause far-reaching changes in a short time.
Two types of coasts: (i) high, rocky coasts (submerged coasts) and (ii) low, smooth and gently sloping sedimentary coasts (emerged coasts).

High rocky coasts: rivers appear drowned; the coastline is highly irregular and indented; hill sides drop sharply into water. Erosion features dominate: waves pound hill sides into cliffs that retreat, leaving wave-cut platforms. The west coast of India is a high rocky retreating coast.

Low sedimentary coasts: rivers extend their length by building coastal plains and deltas; the coastline is smooth with lagoons and tidal creeks; land slopes gently into the water; marshes and swamps may abound. Depositional features dominate. The east coast of India is a low sedimentary coast.
Differences in short: high rocky = submerged, irregular, erosion dominant, cliffs; low sedimentary = emerged, smooth, deposition dominant, lagoons, bars and deltas.

ex.q: Why does the east coast of India have large deltas while the west coast has very few?
st: The east coast is a low sedimentary coast where deposition dominates.
Large rivers like the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri bring huge sediment loads to it.
The west coast is a high rocky coast where erosion dominates and rivers are short and swift.
So deltas form on the east coast, not on the west.
ex.a: The east coast is a low sedimentary, deposition-dominated coast fed by large rivers; the west coast is high, rocky and erosion-dominated.

topics.rl: Chilika and Pulicat lagoons on the east coast and the cliffs of Ratnagiri and Goa on the west coast are textbook contrasts.

topics.t: Coastal landforms: cliffs, stacks, beaches, bars and spits
topics.h: During the 2004 tsunami, villages behind healthy mangroves and sand dunes on the Tamil Nadu coast suffered less. Coastal landforms are natural shock absorbers.
p: Erosional landforms: sea cliffs are steep (a few metres to 30 m or more). At their foot lies a wave-cut platform; when it is above the average height of waves it is a wave-cut terrace. Waves and debris lashing the cliff base create hollows that grow into sea caves; cave roofs collapse and cliffs retreat. Isolated remnants of the cliff standing off the shore are sea stacks.

Depositional landforms: beaches dominate depositional shores. Most are made of sand; shingle beaches have small pebbles and even cobbles. Beaches are temporary features. Behind the beach, sand dunes often form long ridges parallel to the coast.

An offshore bar is a ridge of sand and shingle in the offshore zone, roughly parallel to the coast. When it is exposed above water, it is a barrier bar. A barrier bar keyed up to one end of a bay, or attached to a headland, is a spit (e.g. spits in the Godavari delta).
When bars and spits nearly close the mouth of a bay, it becomes a lagoon, which gradually fills with sediment to become a coastal plain.

Offshore bars are the first buffer against storm and tsunami waves; then come barriers, beaches, beach dunes and mangroves. Disturbing the sediment budget or mangroves exposes settlements to storms and tsunamis.

ex.q: Arrange the stages by which a sea stack forms.
st: Waves attack the base of a cliff, forming hollows.
Hollows grow into sea caves.
Cave roofs collapse and the cliff retreats inland.
A resistant mass of rock is left standing off the shore: a sea stack.
ex.a: Wave attack → sea cave → roof collapse and cliff retreat → isolated sea stack.

topics.rl: Kerala's backwaters (kayals) are lagoons behind sand bars, while the Sundarbans mangroves shield Kolkata's hinterland from cyclones.

topics.t: Desert landforms: wind erosion, pediments and playas
topics.h: Deserts are not just sand. Rocky floors, lonely hills and dazzling salt flats like the Rann of Kutch are all carved by wind and sudden floods.
p: Wind is one of the two dominant agents in hot deserts; the other is running water as sheet floods after rare, torrential rain. Desert floors heat up quickly, creating vertical air currents and turbulent winds.

Wind causes deflation (lifting and removal of dust and small particles), abrasion (sand and silt carried by wind wearing down surfaces) and impact (sheer force of momentum when sand is blown against rock).

Pediments are gently inclined rocky floors close to mountains at their foot, with or without a thin cover of debris. They form by erosion of the mountain front through lateral erosion by streams and sheet flooding. The steep wash slope and free face retreat backwards (parallel retreat of slopes through backwasting), so pediments extend at the expense of the mountain.
An inselberg is the remnant of a mountain left after pediments extend backwards. High desert relief is reduced to low featureless plains called pediplains.

In basins surrounded by hills, a nearly level plain forms at the centre. When covered by shallow water for a short time, it is a playa; playas often contain salt deposits. A playa plain covered with salts is an alkali flat.

ex.q: Arrange the stages by which a mountain in a desert becomes a pediplain.
st: Streams and sheet floods erode the mountain front laterally.
A gently sloping rocky floor, the pediment, forms at the foot.
The slopes retreat backwards (parallel retreat), extending the pediment.
Only a remnant hill, the inselberg, is left.
Finally the area becomes a low, featureless pediplain.
ex.a: Mountain front erosion → pediment → parallel retreat → inselberg → pediplain.

topics.rl: The Great Rann of Kutch turns into a shallow water body in the monsoon and a shimmering salt flat in winter, much like a playa and alkali flat.

topics.t: Desert landforms: hollows, mushroom rocks and sand dunes
topics.h: Barchans march across the Thar like crescent moons, their horns always pointing the way the wind blows.
p: Deflation hollows: persistent wind in one direction blows away weathered mantle or bare soil, creating shallow depressions. Deflation also creates small pits on rock surfaces. Wind-borne sand first makes shallow depressions called blow outs, some of which deepen into caves.

Mushroom, table and pedestal rocks: rock outcrops worn by wind deflation and abrasion leave resistant remnants polished into a mushroom shape (slender stalk, broad rounded cap), a table top, or pedestals.

Sand dunes form well in dry hot deserts. Barchans are crescent-shaped with points (wings) directed away from the wind, i.e. downwind; they form where wind direction is constant and moderate over a uniform surface. Parabolic dunes form where sandy surfaces are partly covered by vegetation; they are reversed barchans with the same wind direction.

A seif is like a barchan but with only one wing, formed when wind conditions shift; the lone wing can grow very long and high. Longitudinal dunes form when sand supply is poor and wind direction is constant: long but low ridges. Transverse dunes are aligned perpendicular to the wind; they form when wind direction is constant and the sand source is an elongated feature at right angles to the wind.
Exam practice: identify a landform from its description; explain river valley stages; contrast how limestone behaves in humid (karst) and arid climates; explain glacial and desert landforms.

ex.q: A dune is crescent-shaped with its horns pointing east. From which direction is the wind blowing?
st: In a barchan, the horns point downwind (away from the wind direction).
The horns point east, so the wind is blowing towards the east.
So the wind comes from the west.
ex.a: From the west (westerly wind).

topics.rl: Shifting barchans near Jaisalmer can bury roads and fields, which is why shelterbelts and grasses are planted in western Rajasthan to stabilise moving sand.

topics.ch: Physical: Composition and Structure of Atmosphere
topics.t: The atmosphere and its permanent gases
topics.h: Climbers on Everest carry oxygen cylinders even though the air there has the same gases. The problem is how thin the air gets with height.
p: The atmosphere is the envelope of air around the earth: a mixture of gases, water vapour and dust particles. It is essential for life and protects us from the sun's harmful radiation.
Air is densely compressed near the surface; its density falls rapidly with height. About 99% of the total mass of the atmosphere lies within 32 km of the earth's surface.
Permanent gases by volume in dry air (NCERT table): nitrogen 78.08%, oxygen 20.95%, argon 0.93%, carbon dioxide 0.036%, neon 0.002%, helium 0.0005%, krypton 0.001%, xenon 0.00009%, hydrogen 0.00005%.
The proportion of gases changes in the higher layers: oxygen is almost negligible at a height of 120 km, and carbon dioxide and water vapour are found only up to 90 km from the surface.

ex.q: Using NCERT's table, what is the combined percentage of nitrogen and oxygen in dry air?
st: Nitrogen = 78.08%.
Oxygen = 20.95%.
ex.a: 99.03%, so nitrogen and oxygen together make up about 99% of dry air.

topics.rl: Indian Air Force pilots flying at high altitudes use pressurised cabins and oxygen masks because the air gets too thin to breathe normally.

topics.ch: Physical: Composition and Structure of Atmosphere
topics.t: Carbon dioxide and ozone
topics.h: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.036% of the air, yet it helps decide whether the earth is cosy or overheated. Ozone, even rarer, guards us from sunburn and worse.
p: Carbon dioxide is meteorologically very important: it is transparent to incoming solar radiation but opaque to outgoing terrestrial radiation.
It absorbs part of the terrestrial radiation and reflects some back to the earth's surface. It is largely responsible for the greenhouse effect.
The volume of other gases is constant, but carbon dioxide has been rising in recent decades, mainly due to the burning of fossil fuels, which has increased air temperature.
Ozone is found between 10 and 50 km above the earth's surface. It acts as a filter, absorbing ultraviolet rays from the sun and preventing them from reaching the surface.

ex.q: Explain why carbon dioxide is called a greenhouse gas.
st: Sunlight (short waves) passes easily through CO₂ to heat the surface.
The heated earth radiates long-wave terrestrial radiation.
CO₂ absorbs part of this radiation and sends some back to the surface.
This traps heat like the glass of a greenhouse.
ex.a: Because it lets incoming solar radiation through but traps outgoing terrestrial radiation.

topics.rl: India's push for solar energy, electric buses and the National Action Plan on Climate Change aims partly to slow the rise of carbon dioxide from fossil fuels.

topics.ch: Physical: Composition and Structure of Atmosphere
topics.t: Water vapour and dust particles
topics.h: Without tiny specks of dust and sea salt floating in the air, there would be no clouds and no monsoon rain.
p: Water vapour is a variable gas that decreases with altitude. In warm, wet tropics it may be 4% of air by volume; in dry, cold deserts and polar regions it may be less than 1%. It also decreases from the equator towards the poles.

Water vapour absorbs part of the insolation and preserves the earth's radiated heat, acting like a blanket so the earth is neither too cold nor too hot. It also contributes to stability and instability in the air.
Dust particles come from sea salt, fine soil, smoke-soot, ash, pollen, dust and disintegrated meteors. They are concentrated in the lower layers, though convection can carry them high.
Higher concentrations of dust are found in subtropical and temperate regions, due to dry winds, compared with equatorial and polar regions.
Dust and salt particles act as hygroscopic nuclei around which water vapour condenses to form clouds.

ex.q: Why do deserts get very hot by day and very cold at night, while humid coastal places do not?
st: Water vapour acts like a blanket, absorbing and holding heat.
Deserts have very little water vapour (less than 1%).
By day sunlight heats the ground strongly; at night heat escapes quickly.
Humid places have more water vapour that holds heat, so the range is smaller.
ex.a: Low water vapour in deserts means little blanket effect, so they heat and cool rapidly.

topics.rl: Dust storms from the Thar in May–June raise dust levels over north India, and sea salt from the Arabian Sea helps seed monsoon clouds over the Western Ghats.

topics.ch: Physical: Composition and Structure of Atmosphere
topics.t: Layers of the atmosphere: troposphere and tropopause
topics.h: Every cloud, every monsoon shower and every thunderstorm you have ever seen happened in the bottom layer of the atmosphere.
p: Based on temperature, the atmosphere has five layers: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere.

The troposphere is the lowest layer. Its average height is 13 km: about 8 km near the poles and about 18 km at the equator. It is thickest at the equator because strong convectional currents carry heat to great heights.
The troposphere contains dust particles and water vapour, and all changes in weather and climate take place here. It is the most important layer for all biological activity.
In the troposphere, temperature decreases at the rate of 1°C for every 165 m of height (normal lapse rate).

The tropopause separates the troposphere from the stratosphere. Air temperature there is about −80°C over the equator and about −45°C over the poles; since temperature is nearly constant there, it is called the tropopause.

ex.q: The temperature at sea level is 30°C. Using a fall of 1°C per 165 m, what is the temperature at a height of 1,650 m?
st: Temperature = 30 − 10 = 20°C.

topics.rl: Hill stations like Shimla and Ooty are cooler than the plains around them because temperature falls with height in the troposphere.

topics.ch: Physical: Composition and Structure of Atmosphere
topics.t: Stratosphere, mesosphere, ionosphere and exosphere
topics.h: Your AM radio can hear stations from far away at night because a layer 80 km up bounces radio waves back to earth.
p: The stratosphere lies above the tropopause and extends up to 50 km. It contains the ozone layer, which absorbs ultraviolet radiation and shields life from this intense, harmful energy.
The mesosphere lies above the stratosphere up to 80 km. Here temperature again decreases with altitude, reaching −100°C at 80 km. Its upper limit is the mesopause.

The ionosphere lies between 80 and 400 km, above the mesopause. It contains electrically charged particles called ions. Radio waves transmitted from the earth are reflected back by this layer. Temperature here increases with height. (NCERT lists this layer as the thermosphere in the five-layer division.)
The exosphere is the uppermost layer, above the thermosphere. Very little is known about it; its contents are extremely rarefied and it gradually merges with outer space.

Diagram practice: draw the layers with heights (troposphere up to about 13 km average, stratosphere to 50 km, mesosphere to 80 km, ionosphere 80–400 km, exosphere above) and the temperature trend in each.

ex.q: In which layers does temperature fall with height, and in which does it rise?
st: Troposphere: falls with height.
Stratosphere: contains ozone, which absorbs UV (temperature does not fall like the troposphere).
Mesosphere: falls again, to −100°C at 80 km.
Ionosphere/thermosphere: rises with height.
ex.a: Falls in the troposphere and mesosphere; rises in the ionosphere (thermosphere).

topics.rl: Long-distance radio broadcasts, such as All India Radio's short-wave services, depend on the ionosphere reflecting signals back to earth.

topics.ch: Physical: Composition and Structure of Atmosphere
topics.t: Elements of weather and climate
topics.h: When IMD forecasts '38°C, humid, light winds, chance of thundershowers', it is describing the elements of weather.
p: The main elements of weather and climate are temperature, pressure, winds, humidity, clouds and precipitation. Each is studied in detail in the following chapters.
Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a place over a short time; climate is the average weather over a long period. Both are described using the same elements.
These elements interact: temperature affects pressure, pressure differences cause winds, winds carry moisture, and humidity leads to clouds and precipitation.

Exam focus for this chapter: percentages of gases, the layers of the atmosphere and their heights, the importance of water vapour and dust, why the troposphere is the most important layer, and the role of ozone.

ex.q: Identify the elements of weather in this forecast: 'Delhi: 41°C, 996 hPa, hot westerly loo winds at 25 km/h, humidity 15%, clear skies, no rain.'
st: 41°C → temperature.
996 hPa → pressure.
Loo winds at 25 km/h → winds.
Humidity 15% → humidity.
Clear skies → clouds; no rain → precipitation.
ex.a: Temperature, pressure, winds, humidity, clouds and precipitation.

topics.rl: Farmers check IMD's agromet advisories, which use these elements to decide when to sow, spray or harvest.

topics.ch: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
topics.t: Insolation, aphelion and perihelion
topics.h: Here's a surprise: the earth is closest to the sun in January, yet that is when Delhi shivers in winter.
p: The energy received by the earth from the sun is called incoming solar radiation, or insolation. The earth's surface receives most of it in short wavelengths.
Because the earth is a geoid resembling a sphere, the sun's rays fall obliquely at the top of the atmosphere, and the earth intercepts only a very small portion of the sun's energy.
On average, the earth receives 1.94 calories per sq cm per minute at the top of its atmosphere.

On 4 July the earth is farthest from the sun (152 million km): aphelion. On 3 January it is nearest (147 million km): perihelion. So annual insolation received on 3 January is slightly more than on 4 July.
This variation is masked by other factors such as the distribution of land and sea and atmospheric circulation, so it has no great effect on daily weather.

ex.q: How much closer to the sun is the earth at perihelion than at aphelion?
st: Aphelion distance = 152 million km.
Perihelion distance = 147 million km.
Difference = 152 − 147 = 5 million km.
ex.a: 5 million km closer at perihelion (3 January).

topics.rl: ISRO's Aditya-L1 solar observatory measures the sun's output from space, above the atmosphere, where insolation is not reduced by clouds or dust.

topics.ch: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
topics.t: Why insolation varies: axis, angle and day length
topics.h: Shine a torch straight down and you get a small bright circle; tilt it and the light spreads into a dim oval. That is why the poles are cold.
p: The amount and intensity of insolation vary during a day, a season and a year. The factors are: (i) rotation of the earth on its axis, (ii) angle of inclination of the sun's rays, (iii) length of the day, (iv) transparency of the atmosphere, (v) configuration of land in terms of its aspect. The last two have less influence.
The earth's axis makes an angle of 66½° with the plane of its orbit around the sun. This greatly influences the insolation received at different latitudes.
The angle of the sun's rays depends on latitude. The higher the latitude, the smaller the angle the rays make with the surface, giving slant rays.
Slant rays spread over a larger area than vertical rays, so energy per unit area falls. They also pass through a greater depth of atmosphere, causing more absorption, scattering and diffusion.

ex.q: The earth's axis makes 66½° with the plane of its orbit. What angle does it make with the perpendicular to that plane?
st: The perpendicular makes 90° with the plane.
Tilt from the perpendicular = 90° − 66½°.

topics.rl: Solar panels in Ladakh are tilted at a steeper angle than those in Tamil Nadu so that the sun's rays strike them more directly.

topics.ch: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
topics.t: Insolation through the atmosphere and its distribution
topics.h: Why is the sky blue at noon and the sun red at sunset? Blame scattering by tiny particles in the air.
p: The atmosphere is largely transparent to short-wave solar radiation. In the troposphere, water vapour, ozone and other gases absorb much of the near-infrared radiation.

Very small suspended particles in the troposphere scatter the visible spectrum both to space and towards the surface. The blue colour of the sky and the red colour of the rising and setting sun are results of scattering.
Insolation at the surface varies from about 320 W/m² in the tropics to about 70 W/m² at the poles.
Maximum insolation is received over the subtropical deserts, where cloudiness is least. The equator receives comparatively less insolation than the tropics.
At the same latitude, insolation is generally more over continents than over oceans. In winter, middle and higher latitudes receive less radiation than in summer.

ex.q: Why do subtropical deserts receive more insolation than the equator, even though the sun is higher over the equator?
st: Insolation reaching the surface depends on cloudiness as well as sun angle.
The equator has thick clouds and heavy rain, which reflect and absorb insolation.
Subtropical deserts have the least cloudiness.
So more insolation reaches the surface in subtropical deserts.
ex.a: Because subtropical deserts have the least cloud cover, while the equator is very cloudy.

topics.rl: Rajasthan's Bhadla Solar Park sits in the dry subtropics, where clear skies give some of the highest solar energy in India.

topics.ch: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
topics.t: Heating the atmosphere: conduction, convection and advection
topics.h: In May, a scorching wind called the loo sweeps across north India and can push temperatures past 45°C. It is heat delivered sideways by advection.
p: The earth, heated by insolation, transmits heat to the layers of the atmosphere near it in long-wave form.

Conduction: when two bodies of unequal temperature are in contact, energy flows from the warmer to the cooler body until both reach the same temperature or contact is broken. Air in contact with land gets heated, and the layers above get heated by contact. Conduction is important in heating the lower layers of the atmosphere.
Convection: heated air near the surface rises vertically in currents and transmits heat upward. This vertical heating is convection; it is confined to the troposphere.

Advection: transfer of heat through horizontal movement of air. Horizontal movement is relatively more important than vertical movement. In middle latitudes, most diurnal variation in daily weather is caused by advection alone.
In tropical regions, especially northern India in summer, the local wind called 'loo' is the outcome of advection.

ex.q: Name the heat-transfer process: (a) a warm road heating the air just above it; (b) a column of hot air rising over farmland on a summer afternoon; (c) hot loo winds blowing across Uttar Pradesh.
st: (a) Heat passing to air in contact with the surface → conduction.
(b) Heated air rising vertically → convection.
(c) Heat carried horizontally by wind → advection.
ex.a: (a) Conduction; (b) Convection; (c) Advection.

topics.rl: IMD issues heatwave alerts when loo winds carry desert heat across Rajasthan, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh in May and June.

topics.ch: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
topics.t: Terrestrial radiation, Planck's law and specific heat
topics.h: The sun heats the ground, and the ground heats the air. That's why it's cooler on a mountain top even though it's closer to the sun.
p: Insolation in short waves heats the earth's surface. The heated earth becomes a radiating body and radiates energy to the atmosphere in long-wave form. This is terrestrial radiation; it heats the atmosphere from below.
Long-wave radiation is absorbed by atmospheric gases, particularly carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases. So the atmosphere is indirectly heated by the earth's radiation.

The atmosphere in turn radiates and transmits heat to space. The heat received from the sun is finally returned to space, maintaining a constant temperature at the surface and in the atmosphere over time.
Planck's law: the hotter a body, the more energy it radiates and the shorter the wavelength of that radiation. That is why the very hot sun emits short waves and the cooler earth emits long waves.
Specific heat is the energy needed to raise the temperature of one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius.

ex.q: Use Planck's law to explain why the sun emits short waves and the earth emits long waves.
st: Planck's law: hotter bodies radiate more energy at shorter wavelengths.
The sun is extremely hot, so its radiation is short-wave.
The earth is much cooler, so it radiates long-wave (terrestrial) radiation.
ex.a: The sun is much hotter, so it radiates at shorter wavelengths; the cooler earth radiates long waves.

topics.rl: Thermal cameras used by firefighters and in airport fever screening detect the long-wave radiation that warm bodies give off.

topics.ch: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
topics.t: Heat budget I: reflection, albedo and absorption
topics.h: Imagine the sun pays the earth 100 rupees of energy every day. Where does every rupee go? The heat budget is that account book.
p: The earth as a whole does not accumulate or lose heat; it maintains its temperature. This happens because the insolation received is balanced by the radiation sent back to space.

Take insolation at the top of the atmosphere as 100 units. About 35 units are sent back to space before reaching the surface: 27 units reflected from the tops of clouds, 2 units reflected from snow and ice-covered areas, and 6 units scattered to space.
The reflected amount of radiation is called the albedo of the earth.
The remaining 65 units are absorbed: 14 units within the atmosphere and 51 units by the earth's surface.

ex.q: Check that the units add up: 35 units lost before reaching the surface and 65 absorbed.
st: Lost: 27 (clouds) + 2 (snow and ice) + 6 (scattered) = 35.
Absorbed: 14 (atmosphere) + 51 (surface) = 65.
Total: 35 + 65 = 100 units.
ex.a: 35 + 65 = 100 units, so all incoming insolation is accounted for.

topics.rl: Melting Himalayan snow lowers the region's albedo, so the ground absorbs more heat and warms faster, a worrying feedback watched by Indian climate scientists.

topics.ch: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
topics.t: Heat budget II: terrestrial radiation and the balance
topics.h: The ground absorbs 51 units. It gives them all back, but not all in the same way. Some go straight to space, some warm the air, and some ride up with evaporated water.
p: The earth radiates back the 51 units it absorbed, as terrestrial radiation.

Of these, 17 units are radiated directly to space. The remaining 34 units are absorbed by the atmosphere: 6 units absorbed directly, 9 units through convection and turbulence, and 19 units through latent heat of condensation.
The atmosphere absorbs 48 units in total (14 from insolation + 34 from terrestrial radiation) and radiates them back into space.
Total radiation returning to space from the earth and the atmosphere = 17 + 48 = 65 units, which balances the 65 units absorbed from the sun. This is the heat budget or heat balance of the earth.
NCERT's flow diagram shows these units moving between space, the atmosphere and the earth's surface.

ex.q: Show that the heat budget balances.
st: Absorbed from the sun: 14 (atmosphere) + 51 (surface) = 65 units.
Surface gives back 51: 17 directly to space + 34 to the atmosphere (6 + 9 + 19).
Atmosphere radiates 14 + 34 = 48 units to space.
Returned to space: 17 + 48 = 65 units = absorbed.
ex.a: 65 units in = 65 units out, so the earth's heat budget balances.

topics.rl: Monsoon clouds over India release enormous latent heat when vapour condenses into rain, part of the 19 units in the heat budget.

topics.ch: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
topics.t: Variation in the net heat budget
topics.h: The tropics get more energy than they lose, and the poles lose more than they get. Without a heat delivery service, the tropics would bake and the poles would freeze solid.
p: The heat budget balances for the whole earth, but not for every latitude.
There is a surplus of net radiation between 40°N and 40°S, and the regions near the poles have a deficit.
The surplus heat from the tropics is redistributed polewards by winds and ocean currents.
As a result, the tropics do not get progressively hotter from accumulating excess heat, and the high latitudes do not get permanently frozen.
NCERT shows this as a graph of net radiation against latitude: positive (surplus) in low latitudes, negative (deficit) towards the poles.

ex.q: Kolkata (about 22°N) and a station in Norway (about 70°N): which has a net radiation surplus and which a deficit?
st: Surplus zone: between 40°N and 40°S.
22°N lies within it → surplus.
70°N lies poleward of 40°N → deficit.
ex.a: Kolkata: surplus; the Norwegian station: deficit.

topics.rl: Warm ocean currents like the North Atlantic Drift carry tropical heat to north-west Europe, keeping its ports ice-free, an example of heat redistribution.

topics.ch: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
topics.t: Temperature and the factors controlling it
topics.h: Mumbai and Nagpur are at almost the same latitude, but Nagpur roasts in May while Mumbai stays milder. Distance from the sea explains a lot.
p: Heat represents the molecular movement of particles in a substance; temperature is the measurement in degrees of how hot or cold a thing or place is.
Factors controlling temperature distribution: (i) latitude, (ii) altitude, (iii) distance from the sea, (iv) air-mass circulation, (v) warm and cold ocean currents, and local aspects.

Latitude: temperature depends on insolation, which varies with latitude. Altitude: the atmosphere is heated from below, so places near sea level are warmer; temperature generally falls with height at the normal lapse rate of 6.5°C per 1,000 m.

Distance from the sea: the sea heats and cools slowly; land heats and cools quickly. Places near the sea come under the moderating influence of sea and land breezes, so their temperature range is smaller.
Air masses and ocean currents: places under warm air masses are warmer, those under cold air masses colder. Coasts with warm ocean currents are warmer than coasts with cold currents.

ex.q: The temperature at sea level is 30°C. Using the normal lapse rate of 6.5°C per 1,000 m, what is the temperature at 2,000 m?
st: Temperature = 30 − 13 = 17°C.

topics.rl: Chennai's summer range is smaller than Delhi's partly because sea breezes moderate the coast, while inland Delhi feels the full effect of continentality.

topics.ch: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
topics.t: Distribution of temperature: January and July isotherms
topics.h: Draw lines joining places with equal temperature on a world map and they bend in curious ways, revealing hidden warm currents and frozen continents.
p: Isotherms are lines joining places having equal temperature. They are generally parallel to latitudes, showing the effect of latitude; deviations are more pronounced in January than in July, especially in the Northern Hemisphere.

In January (Northern Hemisphere winter), isotherms deviate to the north over the ocean and to the south over the continent. Warm currents, the Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift, make the North Atlantic warmer so isotherms bend north; over Europe and especially the Siberian plain, temperatures fall sharply and isotherms bend south.
January means: over 27°C in equatorial oceans, over 24°C in the tropics, 2°C to 0°C in middle latitudes, and −18°C to −48°C in the Eurasian continental interior.
In the Southern Hemisphere, larger oceans make isotherms more regular and roughly parallel to latitudes; the 20°C, 10°C and 0°C isotherms run along about 35°S, 45°S and 60°S in January.

In July, isotherms generally run parallel to latitudes. Equatorial oceans exceed 27°C; over 30°C is found over subtropical continental Asia along 30°N. The highest annual range of temperature, more than 60°C, is over north-eastern Eurasia, due to continentality; the least range, 3°C, is between 20°S and 15°N.

ex.q: On a January map, isotherms over the North Atlantic bend sharply northwards. What does this tell you?
st: A northward bend means warm temperatures extend to higher latitudes over that area.
In the North Atlantic, the warm Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift flow north-east.
So the ocean there is warmer than other areas at the same latitude in January.
ex.a: Warm ocean currents (Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift) are warming the North Atlantic.

topics.rl: In January, Srinagar can be below freezing while Thiruvananthapuram stays warm, a gradient you could draw with isotherms across India.

topics.ch: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
topics.t: Inversion of temperature and air drainage
topics.h: On winter mornings in Delhi, smog and fog hug the ground and flights get delayed. Above that grey blanket, the air is actually warmer.
p: Normally temperature decreases with height (normal lapse rate). When this is reversed and temperature increases with height, it is called inversion of temperature. Inversions are usually short but quite common; over polar areas, inversion is normal throughout the year.
Ideal conditions: a long winter night with clear skies and still air. The day's heat is radiated off at night, so by early morning the earth is cooler than the air above.

Surface inversion promotes stability in the lower atmosphere. Smoke and dust collect beneath the inversion layer and spread horizontally; dense morning fogs are common, especially in winter. The inversion usually lasts a few hours until the sun warms the earth.

Air drainage: in hills and mountains, cold, dense air formed at night flows downslope under gravity, like water, and piles up in pockets and valley bottoms with warm air above. This is why valley floors get frost while slopes are warmer; it protects plants on the slopes from frost damage.
Exam tip: be ready to explain the heat budget, factors controlling temperature, why subtropics get more insolation than the equator, isotherm patterns and conditions for inversion.

ex.q: A farmer in a hill valley plants his orchard on the mid-slope instead of the valley floor. Why is this wise?
st: On clear, calm nights, cold dense air drains down the slopes.
It collects in the valley bottom, causing frost there.
The mid-slopes stay relatively warmer (inversion).
So orchards on slopes are protected from frost damage.
ex.a: Because air drainage collects frost-forming cold air in the valley floor, while slopes stay warmer.

topics.rl: Apple orchards in Himachal and tea gardens in Darjeeling are often on slopes rather than valley floors, partly to avoid frost pockets created by air drainage.

topics.ch: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
topics.t: Atmospheric pressure and its vertical variation
topics.h: A sealed packet of chips puffs up when you drive up to Mussoorie. The air outside is pressing on it less.
p: Atmospheric pressure is the weight of a column of air contained in a unit area from mean sea level to the top of the atmosphere. It is expressed in millibars (mb).
The average atmospheric pressure at sea level is 1,013.2 mb. Due to gravity, the air at the surface is denser and so has higher pressure.
Pressure is measured with a mercury barometer or an aneroid barometer.
In the lower atmosphere, pressure decreases rapidly with height, by about 1 mb for each 10 m increase in elevation (not always at the same rate).

The vertical pressure gradient force is much larger than the horizontal one, but it is generally balanced by a nearly equal and opposite gravitational force. Hence we do not experience strong upward winds.

ex.q: Pressure at sea level is 1,013 mb. Using a fall of about 1 mb per 10 m, estimate the pressure at a hill town 500 m above sea level.
st: Pressure = 1,013 − 50 = 963 mb.
ex.a: About 963 mb.

topics.rl: Aircraft altimeters work like aneroid barometers, converting the drop in air pressure into a height reading.

topics.ch: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
topics.t: Isobars and horizontal distribution of pressure
topics.h: A weather map full of tightly packed lines over the Bay of Bengal is a warning: a strong wind system is brewing.
p: Small differences in horizontal pressure are highly significant for wind direction and velocity.
Isobars are lines connecting places having equal pressure. To remove the effect of altitude, pressure at every station is reduced to sea level before comparison.
A low-pressure system is enclosed by one or more isobars with the lowest pressure at the centre; a high-pressure system has the highest pressure at the centre.
The pressure gradient is the rate of change of pressure with distance. It is strong (steep) where isobars are close together and weak (gentle) where isobars are far apart.
Map reading: on world maps of sea-level pressure in January and July, the pressure belts can be traced, and their shift between the two months is visible.

ex.q: On a map, isobars over region A are 50 km apart and over region B 200 km apart, with the same pressure interval. Where will winds be stronger?
st: Closer isobars mean a steeper pressure gradient.
A steeper pressure gradient produces stronger winds.
Region A has isobars closer together.
ex.a: Region A, because its closely spaced isobars show a steep pressure gradient.

topics.rl: IMD's daily weather charts show isobars; closely spaced isobars around a depression in the Bay of Bengal mean strong winds and a warning for fishermen.

topics.ch: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
topics.t: World pressure belts and their seasonal shift
topics.h: The earth wears belts of pressure, alternating low and high from the equator to the poles, and the whole set shifts north and south with the seasons.
p: Near the equator, sea-level pressure is low: the equatorial low (equatorial trough).
Along 30°N and 30°S lie high-pressure areas called the subtropical highs.
Further polewards, along 60°N and 60°S, are low-pressure belts called the subpolar lows. Near the poles the pressure is high: the polar highs.
These pressure belts are not permanent in position. They oscillate with the apparent movement of the sun: in the Northern Hemisphere they move southwards in winter and northwards in summer.

ex.q: List the pressure belts you cross flying from the North Pole to the equator.
st: Start at the pole: polar high.
Around 60°N: subpolar low.
Around 30°N: subtropical high.
At the equator: equatorial low.
ex.a: Polar high → subpolar low (60°N) → subtropical high (30°N) → equatorial low.

topics.rl: The northward shift of the equatorial low in summer over north India helps pull the south-west monsoon winds into the subcontinent.

topics.ch: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
topics.t: Forces affecting winds: pressure gradient, friction and Coriolis
topics.h: Why do cyclones never form right at the equator? Because one invisible force, the Coriolis force, is zero there.
p: Wind is air moving from high pressure to low pressure. Its velocity and direction depend on three forces: the pressure gradient force, the frictional force and the Coriolis force (gravity acts downwards).
Pressure gradient force: the rate of change of pressure with distance. It is strong where isobars are close and weak where they are apart; it acts perpendicular to the isobars.
Frictional force affects wind speed. It is greatest at the surface and its influence generally extends up to 1–3 km. Friction is minimal over the sea surface.

Coriolis force, named after the French physicist who described it in 1844, results from the earth's rotation. It deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. Deflection is more when wind velocity is high.

The Coriolis force is directly proportional to the angle of latitude: maximum at the poles and absent at the equator. At the equator, wind blows perpendicular to the isobars and a low pressure fills up instead of intensifying, which is why tropical cyclones do not form near the equator.

ex.q: A wind blows from south to north in the Northern Hemisphere. Which way will the Coriolis force deflect it?
st: In the Northern Hemisphere, deflection is to the right of the direction of motion.
Facing north, your right is east.
So the wind is deflected towards the east (becoming south-westerly).
ex.a: To the right, i.e., towards the east.

topics.rl: The south-east trade winds crossing the equator into the Indian Ocean are deflected to the right and arrive in India as the south-west monsoon.

topics.ch: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
topics.t: Geostrophic wind, cyclonic and anticyclonic circulation
topics.h: In the Northern Hemisphere, a cyclone spins anticlockwise. Cross the equator, and the same storm would spin clockwise.
p: Winds in the upper atmosphere, 2–3 km above the surface, are free from surface friction and are controlled by the pressure gradient and the Coriolis force.
When isobars are straight and there is no friction, the pressure gradient force is balanced by the Coriolis force and the wind blows parallel to the isobars. This is the geostrophic wind.
Wind circulation around a low is cyclonic circulation; around a high it is anticyclonic circulation.

Directions (NCERT table): around a low (cyclone), anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere; around a high (anticyclone), clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

Over low-pressure areas, air converges and rises; over high-pressure areas, air subsides from above and diverges at the surface. Rising air (also from eddies, convection, orographic uplift and fronts) is essential for clouds and precipitation.

ex.q: A low-pressure system lies over Australia. In which direction do its winds circulate?
st: Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere.
Circulation around a low is cyclonic.
In the Southern Hemisphere, cyclonic circulation is clockwise.
ex.a: Clockwise.

topics.rl: Satellite images of cyclones hitting Odisha always show an anticlockwise swirl, because the Bay of Bengal is in the Northern Hemisphere.

topics.ch: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
topics.t: General circulation: ITCZ and the three cells
topics.h: The atmosphere runs like three giant conveyor belts in each hemisphere, carrying heat from the tropics towards the poles.
p: The pattern of planetary winds depends on: latitudinal variation of heating, emergence of pressure belts, migration of the belts with the sun's apparent path, distribution of continents and oceans, and the earth's rotation.

At the Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), high insolation causes convection and low pressure. Winds from the tropics converge here; the air rises to the top of the troposphere (up to about 14 km) and moves polewards.

Hadley cell (tropics): the air accumulates and sinks at about 30°N and S, forming the subtropical high. Near the surface, air flows back towards the equator as the easterlies (trade winds), which converge at the ITCZ.
Ferrel cell (middle latitudes): sinking cold air from the poles and rising warm air from the subtropical high; at the surface the winds are the westerlies.

Polar cell: cold, dense air subsides near the poles and blows towards the middle latitudes as the polar easterlies. These three cells set the pattern of general circulation, and the transfer of heat from lower to higher latitudes maintains it.

ex.q: Name the surface winds in each cell of the Northern Hemisphere, from the equator to the pole.
st: Hadley cell (0°–30°N): easterlies, i.e., the north-east trade winds.
Ferrel cell (30°–60°N): westerlies.
Polar cell (60°–90°N): polar easterlies.
ex.a: Trade winds (easterlies) → westerlies → polar easterlies.

topics.rl: In July, the ITCZ shifts north over the Ganga plain, part of the system that draws the monsoon into India.

topics.ch: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
topics.t: El Nino, ENSO and seasonal winds
topics.h: Warm water appearing off the coast of Peru can mean a weak monsoon in India. The atmosphere and the oceans are deeply linked.
p: The general circulation affects the oceans: large-scale winds start large, slow ocean currents, and oceans in turn supply energy and water vapour to the air.

Warming and cooling of the Pacific Ocean is most important. Warm water of the central Pacific slowly drifts towards the South American coast and replaces the cool Peruvian current. This appearance of warm water off Peru is called El Nino.
El Nino is closely linked with pressure changes in the Central Pacific and Australia; this change in pressure over the Pacific is the Southern Oscillation. The combined phenomenon is ENSO.
In strong ENSO years, the arid west coast of South America gets heavy rain, Australia faces drought (sometimes India too), and China faces floods. ENSO is monitored for long-range forecasting.

Seasonal winds: wind circulation is modified in different seasons by the shift of regions of maximum heating, pressure and wind belts. The most pronounced effect is the monsoon, especially over South-east Asia.

ex.q: Why does IMD watch Pacific Ocean temperatures before forecasting India's monsoon?
st: Warm water off Peru (El Nino) is linked with pressure changes over the Pacific (Southern Oscillation).
Strong ENSO causes large-scale weather variations around the world.
These can include drought in Australia and sometimes in India.
So ENSO helps in long-range monsoon forecasting.
ex.a: Because El Nino/ENSO can weaken India's monsoon, so it is used for long-range forecasting.

topics.rl: IMD's long-range monsoon forecast each April mentions whether El Nino or La Nina conditions are expected in the Pacific.

topics.ch: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
topics.t: Local winds: land and sea breezes, mountain and valley winds
topics.h: On Marina Beach in Chennai, the afternoon sea breeze brings relief. At night, the wind quietly reverses and blows out to sea.
p: Land and sea absorb and transfer heat differently. By day, land heats faster than the sea, so air over land rises and pressure falls, while the cooler sea has relatively high pressure. Wind blows from sea to land: the sea breeze.
At night the reverse happens: land loses heat faster and becomes cooler than the sea, so the pressure gradient is from land to sea, giving a land breeze.
