Mountain and valley winds: by day, slopes heat up and air moves upslope, and air from the valley blows up the valley: the valley breeze. At night, slopes cool and dense air descends into the valley as the mountain wind.
Cool air from high plateaus and ice fields draining into valleys is called katabatic wind.

Warm winds occur on the leeward side of mountain ranges: moisture condenses and precipitates on the windward side; the dry air descending the leeward slope is warmed adiabatically and can melt snow quickly. Examples include the Foehn in the Alps and the Chinook in the Rockies.

ex.q: At 3 p.m. on a sunny day in Mumbai, which way does the local wind blow? At 3 a.m.?
st: 3 p.m.: land is warmer than the sea, so low pressure over land.
Wind blows from sea to land → sea breeze.
3 a.m.: land is cooler than the sea, so higher pressure over land.
Wind blows from land to sea → land breeze.
ex.a: 3 p.m.: sea breeze (sea to land); 3 a.m.: land breeze (land to sea).

topics.rl: Fishermen along the Kerala coast traditionally sail out with the early-morning land breeze and return with the afternoon sea breeze.

topics.ch: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
topics.t: Air masses and their source regions
topics.h: A cold wave that sweeps into north India in January carries the 'personality' of the frozen lands where its air was born.
p: When air stays over a homogeneous area (a vast ocean or plain) long enough, it acquires the characteristics of that area. Air with distinctive temperature and humidity is an air mass: a large body of air with little horizontal variation in temperature and moisture.
The homogeneous surfaces over which air masses form are their source regions. Air masses are classified by source region.

Five major source regions: (i) warm tropical and subtropical oceans; (ii) subtropical hot deserts; (iii) relatively cold high-latitude oceans; (iv) very cold snow-covered continents in high latitudes; (v) permanently ice-covered continents in the Arctic and Antarctica.
Types: maritime tropical (mT), continental tropical (cT), maritime polar (mP), continental polar (cP) and continental arctic (cA).
Tropical air masses are warm; polar air masses are cold. Maritime ones are moist; continental ones are dry.

ex.q: Classify an air mass formed over the hot Sahara desert.
st: Over land → continental (c).
Hot subtropical desert → tropical (T).
So it is continental tropical (cT): warm and dry.
ex.a: Continental tropical (cT), warm and dry.

topics.rl: Moist maritime tropical air from the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal feeds India's monsoon, while dry continental air dominates its winter.

topics.ch: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
topics.t: Fronts
topics.h: When a cold air mass charges into warm air, it acts like a snowplough, shoving the warm air up into towering clouds.
p: When two different air masses meet, the boundary zone between them is called a front. The process of formation of fronts is frontogenesis.
There are four types of fronts: cold, warm, stationary and occluded.
When cold air moves towards a warm air mass, the contact zone is a cold front. When warm air moves towards a cold air mass, the contact zone is a warm front.

When the front remains stationary, it is a stationary front. When an air mass is fully lifted above the land surface, it is an occluded front (this happens when a faster cold front overtakes a warm front).
Fronts occur in middle latitudes and are marked by steep gradients of temperature and pressure. They bring abrupt changes in temperature and cause air to rise, forming clouds and precipitation.

ex.q: Name the front: (a) a cold air mass pushing into warm air; (b) a boundary that does not move for days; (c) warm air completely lifted off the ground by a cold front catching up.
st: (a) Cold air advancing → cold front.
(b) Not moving → stationary front.
(c) Warm air fully lifted off the surface → occluded front.
ex.a: (a) Cold front; (b) Stationary front; (c) Occluded front.

topics.rl: Western disturbances that bring winter rain and snow to north-west India are mid-latitude systems with frontal characteristics, originating over the Mediterranean region.

topics.ch: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
topics.t: Extra-tropical cyclones
topics.h: Most of Europe's rainy, windy weather comes from cyclones born where cold polar air meets warmer air: no warm ocean required.
p: Systems developing in mid and high latitudes, beyond the tropics, are called middle-latitude or extra-tropical cyclones. They form along the polar front.

Initially the front is stationary. In the Northern Hemisphere, warm air blows from the south and cold air from the north of the front. When pressure drops along the front, warm air moves north and cold air south, setting up an anticlockwise cyclonic circulation with a warm front and a cold front.

A warm sector is wedged between the forward and rear cold air. Warm air glides over the cold air ahead of the warm front, bringing a sequence of clouds and precipitation; behind, the cold front pushes the warm air up, forming cumulus clouds.
The cold front moves faster and overtakes the warm front. The warm air is completely lifted, the front is occluded, and the cyclone dissipates.

Differences from tropical cyclones: extra-tropical cyclones have a clear frontal system, cover a larger area, can originate over land and sea, and move from west to east; tropical cyclones have no fronts, originate only over seas and dissipate on land, have much higher wind velocity and are more destructive, and move from east to west.

ex.q: Arrange the life cycle of an extra-tropical cyclone.
st: A stationary polar front separates cold and warm air.
Pressure drops; warm air moves poleward and cold air equatorward; cyclonic circulation starts.
A warm front and a cold front develop with a warm sector between.
The faster cold front overtakes the warm front.
The warm air is lifted completely (occlusion) and the cyclone dies.
ex.a: Stationary front → wave and circulation → warm and cold fronts with warm sector → cold front overtakes → occlusion and dissipation.

topics.rl: Western disturbances that bring snow to Kashmir and Himachal and winter rain to Punjab are linked with mid-latitude systems moving from west to east.

topics.ch: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
topics.t: Tropical cyclones
topics.h: Cyclone Fani in 2019 struck Odisha with ferocious winds, yet timely evacuation of over a million people saved countless lives. Knowing how cyclones work saves lives.
p: Tropical cyclones are violent storms that originate over tropical oceans and move to coastal areas, causing destruction through violent winds, very heavy rain and storm surges. They are called cyclones in the Indian Ocean, hurricanes in the Atlantic, typhoons in the western Pacific and South China Sea, and willy-willies in western Australia.

Favourable conditions: (i) large sea surface with temperature higher than 27°C; (ii) presence of the Coriolis force; (iii) small variations in vertical wind speed; (iv) a pre-existing weak low-pressure area or low-level cyclonic circulation; (v) upper divergence above the sea-level system.

Energy comes from condensation in towering cumulonimbus clouds around the centre; a continuous supply of moisture from the sea strengthens the storm. On reaching land, the moisture supply is cut off and the storm dissipates. The place where it crosses the coast is the landfall.

Structure: the eye is a calm centre with subsiding air. Around it, the eye wall has strong spiralling ascent of air up to the tropopause, maximum winds (up to about 250 km/h) and torrential rain. Rain bands radiate outwards. The strongly circulating core around the eye can be 150–250 km across.

The whole storm system over the Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean is larger, about 600–1,200 km across, and it moves slowly, about 300–500 km per day. Cyclones crossing 20°N generally recurve and are more destructive. Storm surges inundate coastal lowlands.

ex.q: A cyclone moves at 400 km per day. How long will it take to reach a coast 1,000 km away?
st: Time = distance ÷ speed.
= 2.5 days.
ex.a: 2.5 days (about 60 hours).

topics.rl: IMD's cyclone warnings and Odisha's network of cyclone shelters have made India a global example in reducing deaths from tropical cyclones.

topics.ch: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems
topics.t: Thunderstorms and tornadoes
topics.h: In April and May, Kolkata often gets sudden evening storms called Kalbaisakhi: towering clouds, lightning and hail, all from one giant cumulonimbus.
p: Thunderstorms and tornadoes are severe local storms: of short duration and over a small area, but violent.

Thunderstorms are caused by intense convection on moist, hot days. A thunderstorm is a well-grown cumulonimbus cloud producing thunder and lightning. When clouds extend to heights with sub-zero temperature, hail forms and falls as a hailstorm. With insufficient moisture, a thunderstorm can generate dust storms.
A thunderstorm has an intense updraft of rising warm air that makes clouds grow taller, causing precipitation; later a downdraft brings cool air and rain to the ground.

From severe thunderstorms, a spiralling wind sometimes descends like an elephant's trunk with great force and very low pressure at the centre, causing massive destruction. This is a tornado. Tornadoes generally occur in middle latitudes; over the sea they are called water spouts.
These violent storms are the atmosphere's way of adjusting to uneven energy distribution: potential and heat energy are converted into kinetic energy, and the atmosphere returns to a stable state.

ex.q: Why are thunderstorms more common on hot, humid afternoons?
st: Strong heating makes air rise rapidly (intense convection).
Moist air cools as it rises and water vapour condenses.
Condensation releases heat, fuelling a towering cumulonimbus.
The cloud produces thunder, lightning and heavy rain.
ex.a: Because intense convection of moist, hot air builds cumulonimbus clouds by afternoon.

topics.rl: IMD issues 'nowcasts' warning of thunderstorms and lightning a few hours ahead, and the Damini app alerts people about nearby lightning strikes.

topics.t: Humidity: absolute and relative
topics.h: Mumbai at 32°C feels far stickier than Jaipur at 38°C. The difference is the water vapour in the air.
p: Water vapour in the air varies from zero to four per cent by volume of the atmosphere. Water moves continuously between the atmosphere, oceans and continents through evaporation, transpiration, condensation and precipitation.
Water vapour present in the air is called humidity.
Absolute humidity is the actual amount of water vapour present: the weight of water vapour per unit volume of air, expressed in grams per cubic metre. It differs from place to place.
The ability of air to hold water vapour depends entirely on its temperature.

Relative humidity is the percentage of moisture present in the atmosphere compared with its full capacity at a given temperature. RH = (actual vapour ÷ capacity at that temperature) × 100. When temperature changes, the capacity changes, so relative humidity changes.

ex.q: Air at 30°C can hold 30 g/m³ of water vapour but actually holds 18 g/m³. Find its absolute and relative humidity.
st: Absolute humidity = actual vapour = 18 g/m³.
Relative humidity = 18 ÷ 30 × 100.
ex.a: Absolute humidity 18 g/m³; relative humidity 60%.

topics.rl: Weather apps show relative humidity because it tells you how close the air is to saturation, which is why 80% RH in Chennai feels so muggy.

topics.t: Saturation, dew point and evaporation
topics.h: On a hot day a glass of cold water 'sweats'. The air touching it has cooled to its dew point.
p: Air holding moisture to its full capacity at a given temperature is saturated: it cannot hold any more water vapour at that temperature.
The temperature at which saturation occurs in a given sample of air is its dew point.
Relative humidity is greater over the oceans and least over the continents.
Evaporation is the process by which water changes from liquid to gas. Heat is the main cause; the heat absorbed in this change is the latent heat of vaporisation.

Evaporation increases with (i) higher temperature, which raises the air's capacity to hold moisture, (ii) low moisture content (unsaturated air can absorb more), and (iii) air movement, which replaces the saturated layer with unsaturated air.

ex.q: Why do clothes dry faster on a hot, dry, windy day than on a humid, still day?
st: High temperature increases the air's capacity to hold vapour.
Dry (unsaturated) air can absorb more moisture.
Wind replaces the moist layer next to the clothes with drier air.
All three increase evaporation.
ex.a: Because high temperature, dry air and wind all speed up evaporation.

topics.rl: Salt pans in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu rely on hot sun and dry winds to evaporate sea water and leave salt behind.

topics.t: Condensation and sublimation
topics.h: Every raindrop starts as invisible vapour clinging to a speck of dust, salt or smoke.
p: Condensation is the transformation of water vapour into water. It is caused by loss of heat. When moist air cools to the point where it can no longer hold its vapour, the excess condenses.
If vapour changes directly into the solid form (ice), it is called sublimation.

In free air, condensation occurs around very small particles called hygroscopic condensation nuclei: dust, smoke and salt from the ocean are good nuclei because they absorb water. Condensation also occurs when moist air touches a colder object, or when the temperature is close to the dew point.

Condensation takes place: (i) when air temperature is reduced to the dew point with volume constant; (ii) when both volume and temperature are reduced; (iii) when moisture is added through evaporation. The most favourable condition is a decrease in air temperature.
Condensation depends on the amount of cooling and the relative humidity. After condensation, moisture takes the form of dew, frost, fog or clouds, depending on temperature and location.

ex.q: Identify the process: (a) water vapour forming droplets around salt particles over the Arabian Sea; (b) water vapour turning straight into ice crystals on a freezing night.
st: (a) Vapour → liquid droplets around nuclei → condensation.
(b) Vapour → solid ice directly, skipping the liquid → sublimation.
ex.a: (a) Condensation; (b) Sublimation.

topics.rl: Delhi's winter smog becomes thicker fog partly because pollution particles act as plentiful condensation nuclei.

topics.t: Forms of condensation: dew, frost, fog, mist and clouds
topics.h: Winter mornings in Punjab bring fog so thick that trains run hours late. Up in Shimla, the same chill leaves sparkling frost on rooftops.
p: Dew: moisture deposited as water droplets on cooler surfaces of solid objects (stones, grass blades, leaves) rather than on nuclei in the air. Ideal conditions: clear sky, calm air, high relative humidity, and cold, long nights. The dew point must be above the freezing point.

Frost: forms on cold surfaces when condensation takes place below freezing point (0°C), i.e., when the dew point is at or below freezing. Excess moisture is deposited as minute ice crystals. Conditions for white frost are the same as for dew, except the air temperature must be at or below freezing.

Fog: when the temperature of an air mass with much water vapour falls suddenly, condensation takes place within it on fine dust particles. Fog is a cloud with its base at or very near the ground; visibility becomes poor to zero. Fog mixed with smoke in urban and industrial areas is smog.

Mist contains more moisture than fog (each nucleus has a thicker layer of moisture). Mists are frequent over mountains where rising warm air meets cold surfaces; fogs are drier and occur where warm air currents meet cold currents.
Clouds are masses of minute water droplets or tiny ice crystals formed by condensation of water vapour in free air at considerable elevations.

ex.q: On a clear, calm, cold night, the dew point is 3°C. Will dew or frost form, and why?
st: Dew forms when the dew point is above freezing (0°C).
Frost forms when the dew point is at or below freezing.
Here the dew point is 3°C, above 0°C.
So dew will form.
ex.a: Dew, because the dew point (3°C) is above freezing.

topics.rl: Indian Railways runs anti-fog devices on locomotives in the Indo-Gangetic plain every winter because dense fog cuts visibility to near zero.

topics.t: Types of clouds
topics.h: Wispy white streaks high in a blue sky, cotton-wool puffs on a summer afternoon, a dark grey blanket before the monsoon burst: each tells you something about the weather.
p: Clouds are grouped by their height, expanse, density and transparency or opaqueness into four basic types: cirrus, cumulus, stratus and nimbus.
Cirrus: formed at high altitudes (8,000–12,000 m); thin, detached and feathery; always white.
Cumulus: look like cotton wool; generally formed at 4,000–7,000 m; exist in scattered patches with a flat base.

Stratus: layered clouds covering large portions of the sky, formed by loss of heat or mixing of air masses with different temperatures. Nimbus: black or dark grey, formed at middle levels or very near the surface; extremely dense and opaque to the sun's rays; shapeless masses of thick vapour, sometimes so low they seem to touch the ground.

Combinations: high clouds (cirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus); middle clouds (altostratus, altocumulus); low clouds (stratocumulus, nimbostratus); clouds with extensive vertical development (cumulus, cumulonimbus).

ex.q: Identify the cloud: thin, white and feathery at about 10,000 m.
st: High altitude (8,000–12,000 m) → high cloud.
Thin, detached, feathery and white.
These match cirrus.
ex.a: Cirrus.

topics.rl: Pilots and IMD observers note cumulonimbus clouds carefully, as they bring thunderstorms and turbulence to flights over India.

topics.t: Precipitation: rain, snow, sleet and hail
topics.h: Cut a hailstone in half and you will see rings like an onion, a record of its trips up and down inside a storm cloud.
p: Continuous condensation in free air makes condensed particles grow. When air resistance can no longer hold them against gravity, they fall to the earth. This release of moisture after condensation is precipitation; it can be liquid or solid.

Precipitation in the form of water is rainfall. When the temperature is lower than 0°C, precipitation takes place as fine flakes of snow (snowfall); moisture is released as hexagonal crystals that form snowflakes.

Sleet is frozen raindrops and refrozen melted snow-water. It occurs when a layer of air above freezing overlies a sub-freezing layer near the ground: raindrops leaving the warmer air solidify in the colder air and reach the ground as small ice pellets, not bigger than the raindrops.

Hailstones are rain drops that, after being released by the clouds, solidify into small rounded pieces of ice while passing through colder layers. They have several concentric layers of ice, one over the other.
Sleet and hail are limited in occurrence and sporadic in both time and space.

ex.q: Rain falls from a warm layer of air into a freezing layer near the ground and reaches the surface as small ice pellets the size of raindrops. What is this?
st: A warm layer over a sub-freezing layer near the ground.
Raindrops freeze in the cold layer.
Ice pellets no bigger than the raindrops reach the ground.
This is sleet.
ex.a: Sleet.

topics.rl: Hailstorms in March and April damage wheat and mustard crops in Punjab, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh, and farmers can claim insurance under crop insurance schemes.

topics.t: Types of rainfall
topics.h: Mangaluru gets over 300 cm of rain a year, but Bengaluru, not far east, gets only about 100 cm. The Western Ghats stand in between.
p: On the basis of origin, rainfall is of three main types: convectional, orographic (relief) and cyclonic (frontal).

Convectional rain: heated air becomes light and rises in convection currents; it expands, loses heat and condenses into cumulus clouds. Heavy rain with thunder and lightning falls but does not last long. It is common in summer or the hotter part of the day, in equatorial regions and interior parts of continents, especially in the Northern Hemisphere.
Orographic (relief) rain: a saturated air mass meeting a mountain is forced to rise; it expands, cools and its moisture condenses. The windward slopes receive greater rainfall.

After crossing the mountain, the air descends the leeward slope and warms up, increasing its capacity to hold moisture, so leeward slopes remain dry. The area on the leeward side that gets less rain is the rain-shadow area. A diagram of a mountain with rainy windward and dry leeward slopes shows this.
Cyclonic (frontal) rain is associated with cyclones and fronts, as studied in the chapter on atmospheric circulation and weather systems.

ex.q: Explain why Mumbai gets heavy monsoon rain while Pune, east of the Western Ghats, gets much less.
st: South-west monsoon winds blow from the Arabian Sea towards the Western Ghats.
They rise up the windward (western) slopes, cool and give heavy orographic rain to Mumbai and the Konkan.
After crossing the Ghats, the air descends and warms on the leeward side.
Pune lies in this rain-shadow area, so it gets less rain.
ex.a: Mumbai is on the windward side (orographic rain); Pune lies in the rain shadow.

topics.rl: Agumbe in Karnataka, on the windward Ghats, gets very heavy rain, while districts like Chitradurga in the rain shadow are drought-prone.

topics.t: World distribution of rainfall
topics.h: Why does western Europe get rain all year, while eastern coasts in the 35°–40° belt get heavier rain than western ones? Latitude, winds and mountains decide.
p: In general, rainfall decreases steadily from the equator towards the poles.
Coastal areas receive more rain than the interiors of continents. Rainfall is more over the oceans than over landmasses, because oceans are great sources of water.
Between 35° and 40° N and S, rain is heavier on the eastern coasts and decreases towards the west.
Between 45° and 65° N and S, due to the westerlies, rainfall is first received on the western margins of continents and decreases towards the east.
Wherever mountains run parallel to the coast, rain is greater on the coastal plain on the windward side and decreases towards the leeward side.

ex.q: A continent at 55°N gets rain-bearing westerlies. Which coast will be wetter, and why?
st: Between 45° and 65° N, the westerlies blow from the west.
They bring moisture from the ocean first to the western margin.
Rainfall decreases eastwards into the interior.
So the western coast is wetter.
ex.a: The western coast, because the westerlies bring rain to the western margins first.

topics.rl: India's own pattern mirrors these rules: the windward Western Ghats and the north-east (with mountains facing moist winds) are wet, while interior Rajasthan is dry.

topics.t: Rainfall regimes and seasonal distribution
topics.h: Two places can both get 100 cm of rain a year, yet one is lush and one is parched. When the rain falls matters as much as how much.
p: Over 200 cm per year: the equatorial belt, the windward slopes of mountains along the western coasts in the cool temperate zone, and the coastal areas of the monsoon lands.
100–200 cm per year: interior continental areas (moderate rainfall); coastal areas of continents also receive moderate amounts.
50–100 cm per year: the central parts of tropical lands and the eastern and interior parts of temperate lands.
Less than 50 cm per year: areas in the rain-shadow zone of the interiors of continents and high latitudes.

Seasonal distribution matters for effectiveness. In the equatorial belt and western parts of cool temperate regions, rain is distributed evenly through the year; monsoon lands get most rain in summer; Mediterranean lands get rain mainly in winter. Exam tip: practise absolute vs relative humidity, forms of condensation, types of rainfall with diagrams, and reading world rainfall maps.

ex.q: Classify the rainfall regime: (a) Konkan coast of India, about 250 cm; (b) a rain-shadow interior plateau, about 40 cm.
st: (a) Over 200 cm and a coastal monsoon land → heavy rainfall regime (over 200 cm).
(b) Less than 50 cm in a rain-shadow interior → very low rainfall regime.
ex.a: (a) Over 200 cm (heavy); (b) Less than 50 cm (very low).

topics.rl: Indian agriculture depends on the summer monsoon season, which brings most of the country's annual rainfall in June to September.

topics.ch: Physical: World Climate and Climate Change
topics.t: Classifying climate: approaches and Koeppen's scheme
topics.h: Kerala, Rajasthan and Ladakh have wildly different climates. To compare climates worldwide, scientists needed a common alphabet, and Koeppen gave them one.
p: Three broad approaches to classifying climate: empirical (based on observed data, especially temperature and precipitation), genetic (organising climates by their causes) and applied (for a specific purpose).
The most widely used scheme is the empirical classification developed by V. Koeppen. He found a close relationship between the distribution of vegetation and climate.

Koeppen selected values of temperature and precipitation, related them to vegetation, and used mean annual and mean monthly temperature and precipitation data. Developed in 1918 and modified over time, it is still popular.

Koeppen recognised five major climatic groups, four based on temperature and one on precipitation. Capital letters A, C, D and E delineate humid climates, and B dry climates (H is used for highlands).

ex.q: Which approach is used when climates are grouped by their causes, such as air masses and pressure belts?
st: Empirical = based on observed data (temperature, rainfall).
Genetic = based on causes.
Applied = for a specific purpose.
Grouping by causes → genetic.
ex.a: The genetic approach.

topics.rl: Climate maps in Indian atlases use Koeppen codes such as Am for the Konkan coast and BWhw for western Rajasthan.

topics.ch: Physical: World Climate and Climate Change
topics.t: Koeppen's letters and climatic groups
topics.h: 'Cs', 'Aw', 'BWh': these codes look like passwords, but each letter tells you something precise about a place's climate.
p: Small letters show seasons of dryness: f = no dry season, m = monsoon climate, w = winter dry season, s = summer dry season.
Small letters a, b, c and d refer to the degree of severity of temperature. In dry climates, h and k indicate hot (low-latitude) and cold (mid-latitude) dry climates.
The B (dry) group is subdivided using capital letters S for steppe (semi-arid) and W for desert.

Koeppen's groups (NCERT table): A Tropical: coldest month 18°C or higher; B Dry: potential evaporation exceeds precipitation; C Warm temperate: coldest month above −3°C but below 18°C; D Cold snow forest: coldest month −3°C or below; E Cold: all months below 10°C; H Highland: cold due to elevation.

Example types: Af tropical wet, Am tropical monsoon, Aw tropical wet and dry, BSh/BWh subtropical steppe/desert, BSk/BWk mid-latitude steppe/desert, Cfa humid subtropical, Cs Mediterranean, Cfb marine west coast, Df humid continental, Dw subarctic, ET tundra, EF polar ice cap.

ex.q: Decode 'Cs'.
st: C = warm temperate: coldest month above −3°C but below 18°C.
s = summer dry season.
So Cs is a warm temperate climate with a dry summer: the Mediterranean type.
ex.a: Warm temperate climate with dry summers (Mediterranean).

topics.rl: Much of the Indian subcontinent is coded Am or Aw, showing tropical climates with a pronounced dry season and monsoon rain.

topics.ch: Physical: World Climate and Climate Change
topics.t: Group A: tropical humid climates
topics.h: In the Amazon it rains almost every afternoon, like clockwork. In India, rain comes in one big monsoon season. Both are 'tropical', yet very different.
p: Tropical humid climates lie between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn. The sun overhead throughout the year and the ITCZ make them hot and humid; the annual range of temperature is very low and annual rainfall is high.

Tropical wet climate (Af): near the equator; Amazon Basin, western equatorial Africa and the islands of the East Indies. Significant rain in every month as afternoon thundershowers. Temperature is uniformly high (maximum about 30°C, minimum about 20°C); annual range negligible. Tropical evergreen forests with dense canopy and large biodiversity.
Tropical monsoon climate (Am): Indian subcontinent, north-eastern South America and northern Australia. Heavy rainfall mostly in summer; winter is dry.

Tropical wet and dry climate (Aw): north and south of Af regions, e.g. north and south of the Amazon in Brazil and adjoining Bolivia and Paraguay, Sudan and south of Central Africa. Rainfall is considerably less and variable; the wet season is shorter and the dry season longer and more severe. Diurnal ranges are greatest in the dry season. Deciduous forests and tree-shredded grasslands (savanna) occur.

ex.q: A place has rain every month as afternoon thundershowers and temperatures between about 20°C and 30°C all year. Classify it.
st: Coldest month above 18°C → group A.
Rain every month, no dry season → f.
So it is Af, tropical wet climate.
ex.a: Af (tropical wet climate).

topics.rl: Most of India falls under Am and Aw: heavy monsoon rain from June to September followed by a long dry season.

topics.ch: Physical: World Climate and Climate Change
topics.t: Group B: dry climates
topics.h: NCERT records a shade temperature of 58°C at Al Aziziyah in Libya on 13 September 1922. Deserts take temperature to the extreme.
p: Dry climates have very low rainfall, not adequate for plant growth. They cover a very large area, from 15° to 60° north and south of the equator.

At low latitudes (15°–30°), they occur in the subtropical high, where subsidence and inversion of temperature do not produce rain. Next to cold currents, especially on the west coast of South America, they extend further towards the equator on the coast. In middle latitudes (35°–60°), they are confined to continental interiors that maritime winds do not reach, often surrounded by mountains.
They are divided into steppe or semi-arid (BS) and desert (BW): subtropical steppe (BSh) and subtropical desert (BWh) at 15°–35°; mid-latitude steppe (BSk) and mid-latitude desert (BWk) at 35°–60°.

Steppe gets slightly more rain than desert, enough for sparse grasslands. Rainfall is highly variable; variability affects steppe life more, often causing famine. Desert rain comes in short, intense thundershowers that do not build soil moisture. Fog is common in coastal deserts bordering cold currents.

Maximum summer temperature is very high: NCERT cites a shade temperature of 58°C at Al Aziziyah, Libya, on 13 September 1922 (the World Meteorological Organization later rejected this reading, but it is the figure used in the textbook). Annual and diurnal ranges are also high.

ex.q: Classify a semi-arid grassland at 45°N in the interior of Asia.
st: Low rainfall → group B.
Semi-arid with sparse grassland → steppe (S).
At 35°–60° → mid-latitude, cold dry (k).
So it is BSk.
ex.a: BSk (mid-latitude steppe).

topics.rl: Western Rajasthan's Thar desert is a BWh climate, while the surrounding semi-arid belt of Kutch and Haryana shows steppe-like conditions.

topics.ch: Physical: World Climate and Climate Change
topics.t: Group C: warm temperate (mid-latitude) climates
topics.h: Grapes and olives grow on hot, dry summers in the Mediterranean, while north-west Europe stays green with drizzle all year. Both are C climates.
p: Warm temperate (mid-latitude) climates extend from 30° to 50° latitude, mainly on the eastern and western margins of continents. They generally have warm summers and mild winters. Four types: Cwa, Cs, Cfa and Cfb.

Humid subtropical with dry winter (Cwa): poleward of the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, mainly in the North Indian plains and the South China interior plains. Similar to Aw except that winter is warm.

Mediterranean (Cs): around the Mediterranean Sea and on west coasts of continents at 30°–40° (central California, central Chile, south-eastern and south-western Australia). Under the subtropical high in summer and westerlies in winter: hot, dry summer and mild, rainy winter. Summer around 25°C, winter below 10°C; annual precipitation 35–90 cm.

Humid subtropical with no dry season (Cfa): eastern parts of continents in subtropical latitudes (eastern USA, southern and eastern China, southern Japan, north-eastern Argentina, coastal South Africa, eastern Australia). Unstable air masses give rain throughout the year (75–150 cm); summer thunderstorms and winter frontal rain.

Marine west coast (Cfb): poleward of the Mediterranean on west coasts (north-western Europe, west coast of North America north of California, southern Chile, south-eastern Australia, New Zealand). Marine influence gives moderate temperatures (summer 15°–20°C, winter 4°–10°C); small ranges; precipitation throughout the year (50–250 cm).

ex.q: Why does the Mediterranean climate have dry summers and rainy winters?
st: In summer, the pressure belts shift north and the region comes under the subtropical high: sinking air, no rain.
In winter, the belts shift south and the westerlies arrive, bringing rain-bearing systems.
So summers are hot and dry, winters mild and rainy.
ex.a: Subtropical high in summer (dry) and westerlies in winter (rain).

topics.rl: Delhi and the Ganga plain fall in the Cwa type: hot, rainy summers and cool, dry winters, very different from Mediterranean lands at a similar latitude.

topics.ch: Physical: World Climate and Climate Change
topics.t: Group D: cold snow forest climates and highland climates
topics.h: In north-eastern Siberia, some places stay below freezing for up to seven months a year, yet they still have a summer monsoon-like wind reversal.
p: Cold snow forest climates occur in large continental areas of the Northern Hemisphere between 40° and 70°N in Europe, Asia and North America. Winter severity increases towards higher latitudes. Two types: Df and Dw.

Cold climate with humid winters (Df): poleward of the marine west coast climate and mid-latitude steppe. Winters are cold and snowy; the frost-free season is short; annual ranges are large; weather changes are abrupt; poleward, winters are more severe.

Cold climate with dry winters (Dw): mainly over north-eastern Asia. A pronounced winter anticyclone that weakens in summer sets up a monsoon-like reversal of wind. Winter temperatures are extremely low, with many places below freezing for up to seven months; precipitation occurs in summer and is low (12–15 cm a year).

Highland climates (H) are governed by topography. In high mountains, large changes in mean temperature occur over short distances, and precipitation type and intensity vary. There is vertical zonation of climatic types with elevation.

ex.q: Why does the Dw climate of north-eastern Asia have dry winters?
st: In winter a strong anticyclone (high pressure) forms over the cold continent.
Air sinks and flows outward, so moist air cannot come in.
Little precipitation falls; winters are dry and extremely cold.
In summer the high weakens, winds reverse and bring some rain.
ex.a: A pronounced winter anticyclone keeps winters dry; summer wind reversal brings the little rain it gets.

topics.rl: Climbing from the plains of Uttarakhand to Kedarnath, you pass through subtropical, temperate and alpine zones in a single day: highland (H) vertical zonation.

topics.ch: Physical: World Climate and Climate Change
topics.t: Group E: polar climates
topics.h: In the tundra, summer daylight can last almost around the clock, yet the ground a little below stays frozen forever.
p: Polar climates exist poleward beyond 70° latitude. There are two types: tundra (ET) and ice cap (EF).
Tundra (ET) is named after its vegetation: low-growing mosses, lichens and flowering plants. It is a region of permafrost, where the subsoil is permanently frozen.
The short growing season and waterlogging support only low-growing plants. In summer, tundra regions have very long daylight.
Ice cap (EF) occurs over interior Greenland and Antarctica. Even in summer the temperature is below freezing. The area receives very little precipitation.

Snow and ice accumulate; the mounting pressure deforms the ice sheets and they break, moving as icebergs that float in Arctic and Antarctic waters. Plateau Station in Antarctica (79°S) portrays this climate.

ex.q: Why do only low-growing plants survive in the tundra?
st: The subsoil is permanently frozen (permafrost), so roots cannot go deep.
The growing season is very short.
Meltwater cannot drain through the frozen ground, causing waterlogging.
So only low plants like mosses and lichens survive.
ex.a: Because of permafrost, a short growing season and waterlogging.

topics.rl: India's research stations in Antarctica, Maitri and Bharati, operate in polar conditions where summer temperatures can still stay low.

topics.ch: Physical: World Climate and Climate Change
topics.t: Climate change: past evidence and causes
topics.h: The Thar desert was once wet and cool, and the Harappans flourished nearby. Climate has always changed. The question now is how fast, and why.
p: The earth has witnessed many variations in climate. Geological records show alternating glacial and inter-glacial periods; landforms in high altitudes and latitudes show advances and retreats of glaciers; sediments in glacial lakes reveal warm and cold periods; tree rings give clues about wet and dry periods; historical records describe climate's vagaries.
During the Pleistocene epoch, glacial and inter-glacial periods occurred; the last major peak glacial period was about 18,000 years ago, and the present inter-glacial began about 10,000 years ago.

India: archaeological findings show the Rajasthan desert had a wet and cool climate around 8,000 BC; 3,000–1,700 BC had higher rainfall; from about 2,000–1,700 BC it was the centre of the Harappan civilisation; dry conditions increased afterwards. Europe witnessed the 'Little Ice Age' from 1550 to about 1850.

Natural (astronomical and terrestrial) causes: changes in solar output linked with sunspots (dark, cooler patches whose numbers rise and fall cyclically); Milankovitch oscillations (cycles in the earth's orbit, its wobble and changes in axial tilt) that alter insolation; and volcanism, which throws aerosols into the air that reduce sunlight reaching the surface.
The most important anthropogenic (human) cause is the increasing concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, which is likely to cause global warming.

ex.q: How long did Europe's Little Ice Age last if it ran from 1550 to about 1850?
st: End year = 1850.
Start year = 1550.
Duration = 1850 − 1550 = 300 years.
ex.a: About 300 years.

topics.rl: Scientists at Indian institutes study tree rings from the Himalaya and lake sediments in Ladakh to reconstruct India's past monsoons.

topics.ch: Physical: World Climate and Climate Change
topics.t: Global warming and greenhouse gases
topics.h: A car parked in the sun with windows closed gets very hot inside: light gets in, heat cannot get out. The atmosphere does something similar.
p: Due to greenhouse gases, the atmosphere behaves like a greenhouse: it transmits incoming solar radiation but absorbs most of the long-wave radiation emitted by the earth. The gases that absorb long-wave radiation are greenhouse gases (GHGs); the warming processes together are the greenhouse effect.

The primary GHGs of concern are carbon dioxide (CO₂), chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O) and ozone (O₃). Nitric oxide and carbon monoxide react with GHGs and affect their concentration.

A GHG's effectiveness depends on the increase in its concentration, its lifetime in the atmosphere and the wavelength of radiation it absorbs. CFCs are highly effective. Ozone in the lower troposphere absorbs terrestrial radiation effectively. The longer a GHG stays, the longer the system takes to recover.

CO₂ has the largest concentration among GHGs. It comes mainly from fossil fuel combustion (oil, gas, coal). Forests and oceans are sinks for CO₂, so deforestation increases its concentration. Atmospheric CO₂ takes 20–50 years to adjust to changes in sources and sinks and is rising at about 0.5% annually.
CFCs are products of human activity (used in refrigeration and aerosol sprays). Methane comes from sources such as wetlands, paddy fields and livestock.

ex.q: Why does cutting forests add to global warming even if no fuel is burnt?
st: Forests use CO₂ for growth, acting as carbon sinks.
Deforestation removes this sink.
Less CO₂ is absorbed, so its concentration in the air rises.
More CO₂ traps more long-wave radiation, increasing warming.
ex.a: Because forests are CO₂ sinks; removing them increases CO₂ in the atmosphere.

topics.rl: India's National Mission for a Green India aims to increase forest cover, partly to strengthen carbon sinks.

topics.ch: Physical: World Climate and Climate Change
topics.t: Ozone depletion, the Kyoto Protocol and effects of warming
topics.h: In the 1980s, scientists discovered a 'hole' in the ozone layer over Antarctica, a warning sign that human-made chemicals can change the sky itself.
p: Ozone forms in the stratosphere where ultraviolet rays convert oxygen into ozone, so UV rays do not reach the surface. CFCs drifting into the stratosphere destroy ozone. Large depletion occurs over Antarctica; this depletion is called the ozone hole, and it allows UV rays to pass into the troposphere.

International efforts aim to reduce GHG emissions. The most important was the Kyoto Protocol, proclaimed in 1997 and in effect from 2005, ratified by 141 nations. It bound 35 industrialised countries to reduce emissions by 2012 to 5% below 1990 levels. Later international agreements continue these efforts.
Once global warming sets in, it is difficult to reverse. Its effects may not be uniform everywhere, but they will harm life-supporting systems.

Effects include rise in sea level due to melting of glaciers and ice caps and thermal expansion of seawater, which may inundate large coastal areas and islands, causing social problems; changes in agriculture and in extreme weather.
Exam tip: expect MCQs on Koeppen letters and climate types, comparisons like tundra vs Mediterranean, causes of climate change, and greenhouse gases and their effects.

ex.q: Under the Kyoto Protocol, a country emitted 200 million tonnes in 1990. What was its 2012 target if it had to be 5% below the 1990 level?
st: 5% of 200 = 10 million tonnes.
Target = 200 − 10 = 190 million tonnes.
ex.a: 190 million tonnes.

topics.rl: Low-lying island nations and coastal areas, including the Sundarbans and Lakshadweep, are especially threatened by sea-level rise from global warming.

topics.t: The blue planet and where the earth's water is
topics.h: Seen from space, the earth looks blue. Yet almost all that water is salty: only a tiny fraction is fresh water we can drink.
p: The earth is called the blue planet because water covers about 71% of its surface.
Most of the planet's water is in the oceans. The remaining water is held as fresh water in glaciers and ice caps, groundwater, lakes, soil moisture, the atmosphere, streams and within living things.

NCERT's table of water on the earth's surface shows oceans holding about 97.3% of all water, and ice caps and glaciers about 2%. Groundwater, lakes, the atmosphere and rivers together hold only tiny fractions.
So fresh water that is easily usable (lakes, rivers, shallow groundwater) is a very small part of the earth's total water.

ex.q: If oceans hold about 97.3% of the earth's water, what percentage is held everywhere else?
st: Total = 100%.
Everything else = 100 − 97.3.
ex.a: About 2.7%, most of it locked in ice caps and glaciers.

topics.rl: Even though India has a long coastline, most cities depend on rivers, reservoirs and groundwater, the small fresh-water fraction, for drinking water.

topics.t: The hydrological cycle
topics.h: The water in your morning tea may once have been part of a Himalayan glacier, a Bay of Bengal cyclone or a dinosaur's drink.
p: The hydrological cycle is the circulation of water within the earth's hydrosphere in different forms: liquid, solid and gas. It is the continuous exchange of water between the oceans, atmosphere, land surface, subsurface and organisms.
Water stored in oceans enters the atmosphere through evaporation, evapotranspiration (from plants and land) and sublimation (from ice).
In the atmosphere, water vapour undergoes condensation and returns as precipitation.

Water stored as ice and snow reaches streams as snowmelt runoff. Surface runoff moves as stream flow into fresh-water storage and also infiltrates the ground. Groundwater storage is released as groundwater discharge and springs.
Water is a cyclic resource, but rising demand is causing water stress in many parts of the world. It must be used and managed sustainably.

ex.q: Trace a drop of water from the Arabian Sea to a well in Maharashtra.
st: Evaporation from the Arabian Sea → water vapour.
Monsoon winds carry vapour inland; it condenses into clouds.
Precipitation falls on the Western Ghats.
Some water infiltrates into the ground → groundwater storage.
It is drawn up from a well.
ex.a: Evaporation → condensation → precipitation → infiltration → groundwater → well.

topics.rl: The Jal Shakti Abhiyan's 'Catch the Rain' campaign encourages rainwater harvesting so more water infiltrates and recharges groundwater.

topics.t: Ocean floor: continental shelf and slope
topics.h: Mumbai High oil field sits beneath shallow water on the continental shelf. Shelves are the oceans' richest real estate.
p: Oceans are confined to the great depressions of the earth's outer layer. Geographers divide them into five: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic oceans.
The ocean floor has four major divisions: continental shelf, continental slope, deep sea plain and oceanic deeps. Besides these, there are ridges, hills, seamounts, guyots, trenches and canyons.

Continental shelf: the extended margin of each continent under relatively shallow seas and gulfs. It is the shallowest part of the ocean, with an average gradient of 1° or less, ending at a steep drop called the shelf break. Average width about 80 km; almost absent along Chile and the west coast of Sumatra; the Siberian shelf in the Arctic Ocean, the largest, is about 1,500 km wide. Depth varies from about 30 m to 600 m.
Shelves are covered with sediments brought by rivers, glaciers and wind; massive deposits over long periods become the source of fossil fuels.

Continental slope: connects the shelf with the ocean basins. Gradient 2°–5°; depth 200–3,000 m. At its seaward edge it gives rise to the continental rise. The slope boundary marks the end of the continents. Canyons and trenches are observed here.

ex.q: How many times wider is the Siberian shelf (1,500 km) than the average continental shelf (80 km)? (Nearest whole number.)
st: Nearest whole number = 19.
ex.a: About 19 times wider.

topics.rl: India's Exclusive Economic Zone includes large shelf areas off Gujarat and Maharashtra, where oil and gas are produced.

topics.t: Deep sea plains and oceanic deeps
topics.h: The flattest places on earth are not deserts or plains on land. They lie 3–6 km under the sea.
p: Deep sea plains (abyssal plains) are gently sloping areas of the ocean basins. They are the flattest and smoothest regions of the world.
Their depths vary between 3,000 and 6,000 m, and they are covered with fine-grained sediments such as clay and silt.
Oceanic deeps or trenches are the deepest parts of the oceans: relatively steep-sided, narrow basins some 3–5 km deeper than the surrounding ocean floor.
Trenches occur at the bases of continental slopes and along island arcs, and are associated with active volcanoes and strong earthquakes, so they are important for studying plate movements.
As many as 57 deeps have been explored: 32 in the Pacific Ocean, 19 in the Atlantic and 6 in the Indian Ocean.

ex.q: Of the 57 deeps explored, 32 are in the Pacific and 19 in the Atlantic. How many are in the Indian Ocean?
st: Pacific + Atlantic = 32 + 19 = 51.
Indian Ocean = 57 − 51 = 6.

topics.rl: The Sunda (Java) Trench near the Andaman–Nicobar region is linked with the earthquake that triggered the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.

topics.t: Minor relief features of the ocean floor
topics.h: Lakshadweep's islands are atolls: rings of coral around turquoise lagoons, built by tiny animals over thousands of years.
p: Mid-oceanic ridge: two chains of mountains separated by a large depression. Peaks can rise to 2,500 m, and some reach above the surface; Iceland, part of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, is an example.

Seamount: a mountain with a pointed summit rising from the seafloor that does not reach the surface. Seamounts are volcanic in origin and can be 3,000–4,500 m tall; the Emperor seamount, an extension of the Hawaiian Islands in the Pacific, is an example.

Submarine canyons: deep valleys, some comparable to the Grand Canyon, cutting across continental shelves and slopes, often extending from the mouths of large rivers. The Hudson Canyon is the best known.
Guyot: a flat-topped seamount that shows evidence of gradual subsidence. More than 10,000 seamounts and guyots are estimated in the Pacific alone.

Atoll: low islands in tropical oceans consisting of coral reefs surrounding a central depression, which may be a lagoon or a body of fresh, brackish or highly saline water. A labelled diagram of ocean floor relief shows all these features.

ex.q: Distinguish between a seamount and a guyot.
st: Both are underwater mountains, mostly volcanic.
A seamount has a pointed summit that does not reach the surface.
A guyot has a flat top, showing gradual subsidence.
ex.a: Seamount = pointed summit; guyot = flat-topped seamount.

topics.rl: Lakshadweep, India's coral island territory in the Arabian Sea, is made of atolls and coral reefs, home to rich marine life.

topics.t: Temperature of ocean waters: factors and horizontal distribution
topics.h: Swimmers at Goa's beaches enjoy warm water almost all year, while the sea off Norway is chilly even in summer. Why?
p: Ocean water is heated by solar energy. It heats up and cools down more slowly than land.

Factors affecting temperature distribution: (i) latitude: surface water temperature decreases from the equator to the poles as insolation decreases; (ii) unequal distribution of land and water: Northern Hemisphere oceans receive more heat due to contact with more land; (iii) prevailing winds: offshore winds drive warm surface water away, causing upwelling of cold water, while onshore winds pile up warm water near the coast; (iv) ocean currents: warm currents raise temperature in cold areas, cold currents lower it in warm areas (e.g. the Gulf Stream warms the east coast of North America and the west coast of Europe; the Labrador current cools the north-east coast of North America).
Enclosed seas in low latitudes are warmer than open seas; enclosed seas in high latitudes are colder than open seas.
The average surface temperature of oceans is about 27°C and decreases from the equator to the poles at about 0.5°C per degree of latitude: about 22°C at 20°, 14°C at 40° and 0°C near the poles.
Northern Hemisphere oceans are warmer than Southern Hemisphere oceans (average about 19°C vs 16°C). The highest temperature is recorded not at the equator but slightly north of it.

ex.q: NCERT gives average annual ocean temperatures of about 19°C for the Northern Hemisphere and 16°C for the Southern Hemisphere. How much warmer are northern oceans, and why?
st: Difference = 19 − 16 = 3°C.
The Northern Hemisphere has a much larger extent of land.
Oceans there are in contact with more land and receive more heat.
ex.a: About 3°C warmer, because of the unequal distribution of land and water.

topics.rl: Upwelling of cold water off the Somali coast during the south-west monsoon makes the western Arabian Sea cooler, affecting fisheries and weather.

topics.t: Vertical distribution of ocean temperature
topics.h: Dive in the Bay of Bengal: the top layer feels warm, then within a few hundred metres the water suddenly turns cold. You've hit the thermocline.
p: Ocean temperature decreases with increasing depth. A boundary region between surface waters and deeper layers, with a rapid decrease in temperature, is the thermocline. It usually begins around 100–400 m below the surface and extends several hundred metres down.
About 90% of the total volume of ocean water lies below the thermocline, where temperatures approach 0°C.

In middle and low latitudes, temperature structure is a three-layer system: (1) top layer of warm water about 500 m thick, 20°–25°C (present all year in the tropics; only in summer in mid-latitudes); (2) the thermocline layer, 500–1,000 m thick, with rapid fall in temperature; (3) a very cold layer extending to the deep ocean floor.
In the Arctic and Antarctic circles, surface water temperatures are close to 0°C, so temperature changes very little with depth: only one layer of cold water exists from surface to floor.

ex.q: Why is there no thermocline in polar seas?
st: A thermocline needs warm surface water over cold deep water.
In polar seas, surface water is already close to 0°C.
Deep water is also near 0°C.
So temperature barely changes with depth; only one cold layer exists.
ex.a: Because surface and deep waters are both near 0°C, so there is no sharp temperature drop.

topics.rl: Indian Navy submarines and fishing fleets study the thermocline, since it affects how sound travels underwater and where fish gather.

topics.t: Salinity of sea water: meaning and factors
topics.h: Sea water tastes salty because every kilogram of it carries about 35 grams of dissolved salts, mostly the same stuff as table salt.
p: Salinity is the total content of dissolved salts in sea water. It is calculated as the amount of salt (in grams) dissolved in 1,000 g (1 kg) of sea water and expressed as parts per thousand (‰ or ppt).
A salinity of 24.7‰ is considered the upper limit to demarcate brackish water.

NCERT's table of dissolved salts shows chlorine and sodium (the components of common salt) as the most abundant dissolved constituents, followed by others such as sulphate, magnesium, calcium and potassium.

Factors: (i) surface salinity depends mainly on evaporation and precipitation; (ii) in coastal regions it is influenced by fresh water from rivers, and in polar regions by freezing and thawing of ice; (iii) wind transfers water to other areas; (iv) ocean currents contribute to variations.
Salinity, temperature and density are interrelated. Other factors being constant, higher salinity increases density, so high-salinity water generally sinks below lower-salinity water.

ex.q: A 2 kg sample of sea water contains 70 g of dissolved salts. What is its salinity in parts per thousand?
st: Salinity = grams of salt per 1,000 g of water.
Salinity = 35‰.
ex.a: 35‰ (parts per thousand).

topics.rl: Salt pans along the Gujarat coast evaporate sea water to concentrate salts, the same process that raises salinity in hot, dry seas.

topics.t: Distribution of salinity
topics.h: The Arabian Sea is saltier than the Bay of Bengal, though both wash India's shores. The Ganga makes the difference.
p: The salinity of the normal open ocean ranges between 33‰ and 37‰. In the land-locked Red Sea it is as high as 41‰; in estuaries and the Arctic it fluctuates seasonally from 0 to 35‰; in hot, dry areas with high evaporation it can reach 70‰. Inland water bodies such as the Dead Sea, the Great Salt Lake and Lake Van are extremely saline.

Atlantic: average about 36‰; the highest salinity is between 15° and 20° latitude, with maximum (37‰) between 20°N–30°N and 20°W–60°W. The North Sea has higher salinity due to saline water from the North Atlantic Drift; the Baltic Sea is low due to large river inflow; the Mediterranean is high due to high evaporation; the Black Sea is very low due to enormous fresh water inflow.
Indian Ocean: average about 35‰. The Bay of Bengal has low salinity due to the inflow of the Ganga; the Arabian Sea has higher salinity due to high evaporation and low fresh-water inflow.

Vertical distribution: surface salinity increases with loss of water to ice or evaporation and decreases with fresh-water input; salinity at depth is very much fixed. Lower-salinity water rests above denser higher-salinity water. Salinity generally increases with depth, and the zone where it increases sharply is the halocline.
Map reading: on a world map of surface salinity, note high values in the subtropics and enclosed seas with high evaporation, and low values near large rivers and polar melt.

ex.q: Explain why the Bay of Bengal is less saline than the Arabian Sea.
st: Salinity falls with fresh-water inflow and rises with evaporation.
The Bay of Bengal receives huge fresh water from the Ganga (and Brahmaputra).
The Arabian Sea has high evaporation and low fresh-water inflow.
So the Bay of Bengal has lower salinity.
ex.a: Large inflow of river water into the Bay of Bengal versus high evaporation and little inflow in the Arabian Sea.

topics.rl: Low-salinity surface water in the Bay of Bengal affects monsoon depressions and cyclone strength, which IMD and INCOIS scientists study closely.

topics.t: Movements of ocean water: an overview
topics.h: The sea is never still. Waves ripple its surface, tides lift it twice a day, and giant currents carry it across whole oceans.
p: Ocean water is dynamic. Its physical characteristics (temperature, salinity, density) and external forces (the sun, the moon and the winds) influence its movement.
Horizontal motion refers to ocean currents and waves. Vertical motion refers to tides, and also to upwelling of cold sub-surface water and sinking of surface water.
Ocean currents are the continuous flow of huge amounts of water in a definite direction; the water itself moves from one place to another.
Waves are the horizontal motion of the water surface. In waves the water does not move ahead; the wave trains do.
Due to the attraction of the sun and the moon, ocean water rises and falls twice a day: the tides.

ex.q: Classify each as horizontal or vertical motion: (a) Gulf Stream; (b) high tide at Mumbai; (c) cold water rising off the coast of Peru; (d) waves at Puri beach.
st: (a) Current → horizontal.
(b) Tide → vertical.
(c) Upwelling → vertical.
(d) Waves → horizontal.
ex.a: Horizontal: (a), (d). Vertical: (b), (c).

topics.rl: Fishermen, port authorities and the Indian Navy all depend on forecasts of waves, tides and currents issued by INCOIS, Hyderabad.

topics.t: Waves: how they form and break
topics.h: Surfers at Kovalam ride waves that may have been born thousands of kilometres away, in storms across the Indian Ocean.
p: Waves are energy, not water, moving across the ocean surface. Water particles only travel in small circles as a wave passes: up and forward as the wave approaches, down and back as it passes.

Wind provides energy to waves. Most waves are caused by wind driving against water. Wind makes waves travel across the ocean, and the energy is released on shorelines. The largest waves are found in the open oceans.

Waves grow larger as they move and absorb energy from the wind. Maximum wave height depends on the strength of the wind, how long it blows, and the area (distance) over which it blows in one direction (often called the fetch).

Steep waves are young ones, probably formed by local wind; slow and steady waves come from far away, possibly another hemisphere. Waves travel because wind pushes the water while gravity pulls the crests down.
As a wave approaches the beach, it slows due to friction with the sea floor. When the depth of water is less than half the wavelength, the wave breaks and dissolves as surf.

ex.q: A wave has a wavelength of 40 m. Below what depth of water will it break as it approaches the shore?
st: A wave breaks when water depth is less than half its wavelength.
Half of 40 m = 20 m.
So it breaks when the depth is less than 20 m.
ex.a: Less than 20 m.

topics.rl: INCOIS issues high-wave and swell-surge alerts for the Kerala and Tamil Nadu coasts, when long-travelled swells from distant storms arrive.

topics.t: Characteristics of waves
topics.h: Engineers designing ports at Vizhinjam or Paradip need exact wave numbers: height, period, wavelength. Here is the vocabulary they use.
p: Wave crest and trough: the highest and lowest points of a wave.
Wave height: the vertical distance from the bottom of a trough to the top of a crest. Wave amplitude: one-half of the wave height.
Wave period: the time interval between two successive wave crests or troughs passing a fixed point. Wavelength: the horizontal distance between two successive crests.
Wave speed: the rate at which the wave moves through the water, measured in knots. Wave frequency: the number of waves passing a given point in a one-second interval.
NCERT's diagram shows the circular motion of water molecules beneath a passing wave, with the circles shrinking with depth.

ex.q: A wave's crest is 3 m above its trough. What are its height and amplitude?
st: Wave height = vertical distance from trough to crest = 3 m.
Amplitude = half of wave height = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 m.
ex.a: Height 3 m; amplitude 1.5 m.

topics.rl: Wave-rider buoys moored off Indian ports record wave height and period to help ships enter safely.

topics.t: Tides: causes and tidal bulges
topics.h: In the Bay of Fundy, Canada, the tide can rise by 15–16 m, and boats sitting on mud at low tide float again within hours.
p: A tide is the periodical rise and fall of the sea level, once or twice a day, mainly due to the attraction of the sun and the moon.
Movements of water caused by meteorological effects (winds and atmospheric pressure changes) are called surges. Surges are not regular like tides.

The moon's gravitational pull, to a great extent, and the sun's, to a lesser extent, are the major causes of tides. Centrifugal force counterbalances gravity. Together they create two major tidal bulges: one on the side facing the moon (gravitational pull) and one on the opposite side (centrifugal force). The tide-generating force is the difference between the moon's gravitational attraction and the centrifugal force.

Tidal bulges on wide continental shelves are higher; when they hit mid-oceanic islands they become low. Funnel-shaped bays and estuaries greatly magnify tidal heights. Tides channelled between islands or into bays and estuaries are called tidal currents.

The highest tides in the world occur in the Bay of Fundy in Nova Scotia, Canada, with a tidal bulge of 15–16 m. With two high and two low tides a day, the tide comes in within about six hours, rising roughly 240 cm an hour.

ex.q: In the Bay of Fundy the tide rises about 14.4 m (1,440 cm) in about 6 hours. What is the average rise per hour?
st: Rise per hour = 1,440 ÷ 6.
= 240 cm per hour.
ex.a: About 240 cm (2.4 m) per hour.

topics.rl: In the Gulf of Khambhat in Gujarat, funnel-shaped coastlines produce large tidal ranges, which is why it is studied for tidal power.

topics.t: Types of tides
topics.h: Fishermen of the Sundarbans know that full-moon and new-moon days bring the highest tides. That is no superstition: the sun, moon and earth line up.
p: Based on frequency: semi-diurnal tide (most common): two high tides and two low tides each day, successive ones of about the same height; diurnal tide: only one high and one low tide each day; mixed tide: tides with variations in height, generally along the west coast of North America and many Pacific islands.
Spring tides: when the sun, moon and earth are in a straight line, tides are higher. They occur twice a month, at full moon and at new moon.

Neap tides: normally about seven days after spring tides, when the sun and moon are at right angles to each other and their forces counteract. The moon's attraction, though more than twice as strong as the sun's, is reduced by the sun's counteracting pull, so tidal ranges are smaller.

Once a month, when the moon is closest to the earth (perigee), unusually high and low tides occur and the tidal range is greater. Two weeks later, at apogee (moon farthest), tidal ranges are less than average. At perihelion (earth closest to the sun, around 3 January) tidal ranges are greater; at aphelion (around 4 July) they are less.

Ebb: the time between high tide and low tide when water level is falling. Flow or flood: the time between low tide and high tide when the tide is rising. Successive high tides occur about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.

ex.q: A high tide occurs at 6:00 a.m. at a port with semi-diurnal tides. Roughly when will the next high tide occur?
st: Successive high tides are about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.
ex.a: About 6:25 p.m.

topics.rl: Kolkata Port and Haldia schedule large ships to enter the Hooghly on high tides, especially spring tides, for safe passage.

topics.t: Importance of tides; ocean currents and their forces
topics.h: India's first tidal power project was planned at Durgaduani in the Sundarbans. Tides are a predictable, renewable rhythm we can use.
p: Because tides depend on the earth–moon–sun positions, which are known accurately, they can be predicted well in advance, helping navigators and fishermen plan. Tidal heights are very important for harbours near rivers and estuaries with shallow 'bars' at the entrance (e.g. tidal ports such as Kolkata). Tides also help desilt sediments and remove polluted water from estuaries.

Tides are used to generate electricity in Canada, France, Russia and China. In India, a 3 MW tidal power project at Durgaduani in the Sundarbans (West Bengal) was taken up; the Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat also have tidal energy potential.
Ocean currents are like rivers in the ocean: a regular volume of water in a definite path and direction.

Primary forces that start currents: (i) heating by solar energy, which expands water so that near the equator the ocean is about 8 cm higher than in middle latitudes, creating a slight gradient; (ii) wind, which pushes surface water; (iii) gravity, which pulls water down the pile; (iv) the Coriolis force, which deflects water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.

Secondary forces: differences in water density due to temperature and salinity. Saltier water and colder water are denser and sink; lighter water rises. Cold currents form when cold polar water sinks and slowly moves towards the equator, while warm currents flow out from the equator along the surface towards the poles.

ex.q: Why is the ocean surface near the equator about 8 cm higher than in middle latitudes, and what does this cause?
st: Solar heating near the equator makes water expand.
Expanded water stands slightly higher.
This creates a gentle slope (gradient).
Water tends to flow down this slope, helping start currents.
ex.a: Solar heating expands equatorial water, creating a slope that helps drive currents.

topics.rl: Kolkata Port lies about 200 km up the Hooghly, and ships depend on tides to cross shallow stretches safely.

topics.t: Types of ocean currents and gyres
topics.h: Ninety per cent of ocean water moves in a slow, hidden conveyor belt deep below the surface, driven by cold and salt.
p: By depth: surface currents make up about 10% of all ocean water, in the upper 400 m. Deep water currents make up the other 90%; they move around ocean basins due to differences in density and gravity, sinking in high latitudes where cold temperatures increase density.

By temperature: cold currents bring cold water into warm areas; they are usually on the west coasts of continents in low and middle latitudes (both hemispheres) and on east coasts in higher latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere. Warm currents bring warm water into cold areas; they are usually on the east coasts of continents in low and middle latitudes, and on west coasts in high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere.

The speed of a current is called its drift, measured in knots. Currents are strongest near the surface (may exceed 5 knots) and slow at depth (usually less than 0.5 knots); most currents have speeds of 5 knots or less.

Major currents are greatly influenced by the prevailing winds and the Coriolis force. Large accumulations of water and the flow around them are called gyres: large circular currents in all ocean basins.

In the middle latitudes the circulation is mainly anticyclonic: clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere, following the atmospheric circulation. In monsoon regions, monsoon winds influence current movements.

ex.q: Off the west coast of South America at 20°S flows a current. Is it likely to be warm or cold?
st: Cold currents are usually on west coasts in low and middle latitudes.
20°S lies in low latitudes.
So the current is likely cold (it is the Humboldt or Peru current).
ex.a: Cold (the Humboldt/Peru current).

topics.rl: In the north Indian Ocean, currents reverse direction with the monsoon, which affects fishing seasons along India's coasts.

topics.t: Major warm and cold ocean currents
topics.h: The Gulf Stream carries tropical warmth across the Atlantic, while the Humboldt current brings Antarctic chill up South America's coast.
p: Warm currents (from low to high latitudes) include: Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift (North Atlantic), Kuroshio (North Pacific, off Japan), Brazil current (South Atlantic), Agulhas current (south-west Indian Ocean, off south-east Africa), Alaska current (North Pacific) and East Australian current.

Cold currents (from high to low latitudes) include: Labrador current (north-west Atlantic, off Canada), Canaries current (off north-west Africa), California current (off western USA), Humboldt or Peru current (off western South America), Benguela current (off south-west Africa), Falkland current (off south-east South America), West Australian current and Oyashio (north-west Pacific, off northern Japan).
Pattern to remember: warm currents generally flow along east coasts of continents in low and middle latitudes; cold currents along west coasts in low and middle latitudes.
Map work: on a world map, trace warm currents in red and cold currents in blue, and note the clockwise gyres of the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise gyres of the Southern Hemisphere.

ex.q: Two currents flow off southern Africa: one on the west coast, one on the east coast. Name them and say which is warm.
st: West coast of southern Africa (low-middle latitude) → cold current: Benguela.
East coast of southern Africa → warm current: Agulhas.
So the Agulhas is warm and the Benguela is cold.
ex.a: Benguela (west, cold) and Agulhas (east, warm).

topics.rl: The cold Benguela current helps keep the Namib desert dry, while the warm Agulhas makes Durban's coast humid: two currents, two climates.

topics.t: Effects of ocean currents
topics.h: Some of the world's richest fishing grounds lie where warm and cold currents meet, like the Grand Banks off Newfoundland.
p: West coasts of continents in tropical and subtropical latitudes (except near the equator) are bordered by cool waters. Their average temperatures are relatively low with narrow diurnal and annual ranges; there is fog, but generally the areas are arid (e.g. the Atacama, Namib and Sahara coasts).

West coasts of continents in middle and higher latitudes are bordered by warm waters, giving a distinct marine climate: cool summers, relatively mild winters and a narrow annual range (e.g. north-western Europe).

Warm currents flowing parallel to the east coasts of continents in tropical and subtropical latitudes give warm and rainy climates; these areas lie on the western margins of the subtropical anticyclones.

Mixing of warm and cold currents replenishes oxygen and favours the growth of plankton, the primary food of fish. The best fishing grounds exist mainly in these mixing zones, e.g. the Grand Banks near Newfoundland (Gulf Stream meets Labrador current) and the waters near Hokkaido, Japan (Kuroshio meets Oyashio).
Exam tip: revise types and importance of tides, forces behind currents, effects of warm and cold currents, and wave characteristics.

ex.q: Why are the waters around Newfoundland among the best fishing grounds in the world?
st: The warm Gulf Stream meets the cold Labrador current here.
Mixing replenishes oxygen in the water.
This favours rich growth of plankton.
Plankton is the primary food of fish, so fish are abundant.
ex.a: Mixing of the warm Gulf Stream and cold Labrador current boosts plankton and fish.

topics.rl: Upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water off India's south-west coast during the monsoon supports big sardine and mackerel catches in Kerala.

topics.t: What is biodiversity?
topics.h: A single hectare of rainforest in the Western Ghats can hold more tree species than many entire countries in cold regions.
p: Biodiversity is the number and variety of organisms found within a specified geographic region. It refers to the varieties of plants, animals and micro-organisms, the genes they contain and the ecosystems they form.

Today's biodiversity is the result of 2.5–3.5 billion years of evolution. Before the advent of humans, the earth supported more biodiversity than in any other period; since then it has declined rapidly.

Biodiversity is a system in constant evolution: the average half-life of a species is estimated at one to four million years, and 99% of species that ever lived are now extinct. Estimates of the number of species range from 2 million to 100 million, with 10 million as the best estimate.
Biodiversity is not found evenly on the earth. It is consistently richer in the tropics. Towards the poles, one finds larger and larger populations of fewer and fewer species.

ex.q: Compare biodiversity in the Andaman rainforests and the Ladakh cold desert.
st: The Andamans lie in the tropics with high heat and rainfall.
Tropical regions are consistently richer in biodiversity.
Ladakh is cold and dry at high altitude.
It has fewer species, often with larger populations of each.
ex.a: The Andamans have far higher biodiversity; Ladakh has fewer species.

topics.rl: India is one of the world's megadiverse countries, with ecosystems from coral reefs to alpine meadows.

topics.t: Levels of biodiversity
topics.h: India has thousands of traditional rice varieties. Each carries different genes for taste, drought or flood tolerance. That is biodiversity at the level of genes.
p: Genetic diversity: genes are the basic building blocks of life forms. Genetic diversity is the variation of genes within a species. For example, human beings all belong to Homo sapiens but differ in height, colour and physical appearance because of genetic diversity. It is essential for healthy breeding of populations.
Species diversity: the variety of species in a defined area. It is measured through richness, abundance and types. Areas rich in species diversity are called hotspots of diversity.
Ecosystem diversity: the broad differences between ecosystem types, and the diversity of habitats and ecological processes within each type.
The boundaries of communities and ecosystems are not rigidly defined, so demarcating ecosystem boundaries is difficult and complex.

ex.q: Identify the level: (a) many varieties of mango such as Alphonso, Dasheri and Langra; (b) tigers, deer, mangroves and crabs in the Sundarbans; (c) India having deserts, rainforests, wetlands and coral reefs.
st: (a) Variation within one species (mango) → genetic diversity.
(b) Many different species in one area → species diversity.
(c) Many different ecosystem types → ecosystem diversity.
ex.a: (a) Genetic; (b) Species; (c) Ecosystem.

topics.rl: The National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources in New Delhi stores seeds of thousands of crop varieties to protect genetic diversity.

topics.t: Why biodiversity matters
topics.h: The neem tree gives us medicine, honeybees pollinate our crops and earthworms build our soils. Every species has a job.
p: Ecological role: species of many kinds perform functions in an ecosystem. They capture and store energy, produce and decompose organic material, help cycle water and nutrients, fix atmospheric gases and help regulate the climate. These functions are vital for ecosystems and human survival.
Every organism, besides extracting its needs, contributes something useful to other organisms. The more diverse an ecosystem, the better its chances of surviving adversities.
Economic role: biodiversity provides food crops, livestock, forestry, fish and medicinal resources, and raw materials for industries such as dyes, fibres, fragrances, oils, rubber and timber.
Scientific role: each species can give clues about how life evolved and will evolve, and helps us understand how life functions and the role of each species in sustaining ecosystems.
Ethical value: we share the earth with other species; all species have a right to exist, and humans have a responsibility to 'live and let live'.

ex.q: Classify each role of biodiversity: (a) bees pollinating mustard crops; (b) rubber from trees used to make tyres; (c) studying fossils and living relatives to understand evolution.
st: (a) Supporting an ecological process (pollination) → ecological role.
(b) Raw material for industry → economic role.
(c) Understanding evolution and how life functions → scientific role.
ex.a: (a) Ecological; (b) Economic; (c) Scientific.

topics.rl: Ayurveda and modern pharmacy in India draw on medicinal plants like ashwagandha, tulsi and neem, an economic value of biodiversity.

topics.t: Loss of biodiversity
topics.h: The cheetah vanished from India in the 1950s and had to be brought back from Africa in 2022. Losing a species is easy; getting it back is very hard.
p: Growth in human population has increased consumption of natural resources, accelerating loss of species and habitats.

Tropical regions occupy only about one-fourth of the world's area but contain about three-fourths of its population. Over-exploitation and deforestation are rampant there. Since tropical rainforests contain 50% of the species on earth, destroying them is disastrous.
Natural calamities such as earthquakes, floods, volcanic eruptions, forest fires and droughts damage flora and fauna.
Pesticides and pollutants such as hydrocarbons and toxic heavy metals destroy weak and sensitive species.

Exotic species, which are not natural inhabitants of a habitat but are introduced, can damage natural biotic communities. Poaching of tigers, elephants, rhinoceros, crocodiles, minks and birds for horns, tusks and hides has pushed many into the endangered category.

ex.q: Identify the cause of biodiversity loss: (a) Lantana spreading in Indian forests and crowding out native plants; (b) rhinos killed for their horns in Assam; (c) a river's fish dying after pesticide runoff.
st: (a) An introduced plant harming natives → exotic species.
(b) Killing for horns → poaching.
(c) Chemical runoff killing sensitive species → pesticides and pollutants.
ex.a: (a) Exotic species; (b) Poaching; (c) Pesticides and pollution.

topics.rl: Kaziranga's rangers protect the one-horned rhinoceros from poachers, and their success has helped its numbers grow.

topics.t: IUCN categories of threatened species
topics.h: The great Indian bustard, once common in Rajasthan's grasslands, now numbers only in the low hundreds. Global lists help decide which species need urgent protection.
