p: The International Union for the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (IUCN) has classified threatened species of plants and animals into categories for the purpose of their conservation.

Endangered species: species in danger of extinction. The IUCN publishes information about endangered species worldwide as the Red List of threatened species (earlier popularly known as the Red Data Book).
Vulnerable species: species likely to be in danger of extinction in the near future if the factors threatening them continue. Their survival is not assured, as their population has reduced greatly.
Rare species: species whose world population is very small; they are confined to limited areas or thinly scattered over a wider area.
Other categories used in conservation lists include extinct species (no longer found alive) and insufficiently known species (not enough information to classify them).

ex.q: A plant species is found only in a few valleys of the Western Ghats in small numbers, though not currently declining. Which IUCN category best fits it?
st: Its world population is very small.
It is confined to a limited area.
It is not described as in immediate danger of extinction.
This fits the rare category.
ex.a: Rare species.

topics.rl: Project Great Indian Bustard in Rajasthan and Gujarat breeds and protects the bird because it is among the most threatened species in India.

topics.t: Conservation of biodiversity
topics.h: Project Tiger began in 1973 with nine reserves. Today India has over 50 tiger reserves, showing what determined conservation can do.
p: Biodiversity is important for human existence. All life forms are closely interlinked, so disturbance in one causes imbalance in others. People must adopt environment-friendly practices so that development is harmonious with other life forms and sustainable.

The World Conservation Strategy suggests steps such as: preserving endangered species; proper planning and management to prevent extinction; preserving varieties of food crops, forage plants, timber trees, livestock and their wild relatives; each country identifying and protecting habitats of wild relatives; safeguarding habitats where species feed, breed, rest and nurse their young; and regulating international trade in wild plants and animals.

In India, the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 was passed to protect, preserve and propagate the variety of species within natural boundaries; under it, national parks and sanctuaries were established and biosphere reserves declared. The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 further strengthened environmental protection.
India, along with 155 other nations, signed the Convention on Biological Diversity at the Earth Summit held at Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in June 1992.

ex.q: Which conservation step applies to protecting the nesting beaches of Olive Ridley turtles at Gahirmatha, Odisha?
st: Olive Ridleys come ashore to breed and lay eggs.
The World Conservation Strategy says habitats where species feed, breed, rest and nurse their young should be safeguarded.
So protecting nesting beaches applies this step.
ex.a: Safeguarding habitats where species breed and nurse their young.

topics.rl: Gahirmatha Marine Sanctuary in Odisha, one of the world's largest Olive Ridley nesting sites, shows habitat protection in action.

topics.t: Megadiversity countries and biodiversity hotspots
topics.h: In Madagascar, about 85% of plants and animals are found nowhere else on earth. Places like this are the world's biodiversity treasure chests.
p: Some countries in the tropical region possess a large share of the world's species diversity; they are called megadiversity centres. NCERT lists 12: Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Brazil, Democratic Republic of Congo, Madagascar, China, India, Malaysia, Indonesia and Australia.

To concentrate resources on the most vulnerable areas, the IUCN has identified certain areas as biodiversity hotspots. Hotspots are areas very rich in species, with many endemic species (found nowhere else), that are under threat. The hotspot concept was first proposed by ecologist Norman Myers.

Hotspots are defined according to their vegetation, because plants determine the primary productivity of an ecosystem. Many hotspots rely on species-rich ecosystems for food, firewood, cropland and timber income. In Madagascar, about 85% of plants and animals are found nowhere else.
Hotspots in wealthy places face other pressures: the islands of Hawaii have unique species threatened by introduced species and land development.

Map work: locate hotspots such as the Eastern Himalaya, the Western Ghats, Indonesia, eastern Madagascar, the Upper Guinean forests of West Africa, the Atlantic forest of Brazil and the Tropical Andes.

ex.q: Which two biodiversity hotspots lie wholly or partly in India?
st: India's north-east lies in the eastern part of the Himalaya, a species-rich, threatened area.
The Western Ghats along India's west coast are also species-rich with many endemics.
Both are recognised hotspots.
ex.a: The Eastern Himalaya and the Western Ghats.

topics.rl: The Silent Valley National Park in Kerala, part of the Western Ghats hotspot, was protected after a famous public campaign against a dam in the 1970s–80s.

topics.t: India's location and extent
topics.h: From the snows of Kashmir to the waves at Kanniyakumari is over 3,200 km. India's extent explains much of its variety.
p: The mainland of India extends from Kashmir in the north to Kanniyakumari in the south, and from Arunachal Pradesh in the east to Gujarat in the west.
India's territorial limit extends into the sea up to 12 nautical miles (about 21.9 km) from the coast.

Latitudinal extent of the mainland: 8°4'N to 37°6'N. Longitudinal extent: 68°7'E to 97°25'E. Both are roughly about 30 degrees. (The southern boundary of the country reaches 6°45'N in the Bay of Bengal, at Indira Point.)

The north–south extent is about 3,214 km, but the east–west extent is only about 2,933 km. This is because the distance between two lines of longitude decreases towards the poles, whereas the distance between two lines of latitude remains the same everywhere.

ex.q: Calculate India's latitudinal extent of the mainland from 8°4'N to 37°6'N.
st: Degrees: 37 − 8 = 29°; minutes: 6' − 4' = 2'.
Extent = 29°2', i.e., roughly 29 degrees (about 30 degrees).
ex.a: 29°2', roughly 30 degrees.

topics.rl: The Indian Coast Guard patrols up to 12 nautical miles as India's territorial waters, and further in the Exclusive Economic Zone.

topics.t: The Tropic of Cancer and effects of India's extent
topics.h: The Tropic of Cancer passes through eight Indian states. North of it the climate is subtropical; south of it, tropical.
p: The Tropic of Cancer (23°30'N) divides India almost into two equal parts. The southern part lies within the tropics, and the northern part lies in the subtropical or warm temperate zone.
Because of this latitudinal extent, day length varies: the difference between day and night is small near Kanniyakumari but much larger in Kashmir, especially in summer and winter.
India's longitudinal extent of nearly 30 degrees causes a time difference of nearly two hours between the easternmost and westernmost parts of the country (4 minutes per degree of longitude).
So the sun rises in Arunachal Pradesh about two hours earlier than in western Gujarat.

ex.q: How much earlier does the sun rise at 97°E than at 68°E? (Earth rotates 1° in 4 minutes.)
st: Difference in longitude = 97 − 68 = 29°.
Time difference = 29 × 4 = 116 minutes.
116 minutes = 1 hour 56 minutes, nearly two hours.
ex.a: About 1 hour 56 minutes, nearly two hours earlier.

topics.rl: Many in the North-East have long argued for an earlier time zone because sunrise there can be before 5 a.m. in summer, well ahead of office hours based on IST.

topics.t: Indian Standard Time
topics.h: Trains in India run on one clock from Dwarka to Dibrugarh. That clock is set by a line passing near Mirzapur.
p: To avoid confusion from different local times, India uses one standard time. The Standard Meridian of India is 82°30'E, passing through Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. Time along it is Indian Standard Time (IST).
IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT): 82.5° × 4 minutes = 330 minutes = 5 h 30 min.
Countries usually choose a standard meridian that is a multiple of 7°30' (half-hour time steps), so their time differs from GMT in clean half-hour units. 82°30' = 11 × 7°30'.
Some countries with vast east–west extent use more than one standard meridian; for example, the USA has seven time zones.
To find local time: each degree of longitude = 4 minutes; places east of a meridian are ahead, places west are behind.

ex.q: When it is 12:00 noon IST, what is the local time at 90°E (near Dhubri, Assam)?
st: Longitude difference = 90° − 82.5° = 7.5°.
Time difference = 7.5 × 4 = 30 minutes.
90°E is east of the Standard Meridian, so local time is ahead.
Local time = 12:00 + 30 min = 12:30 p.m.

topics.rl: Every Indian Railways timetable, ISRO launch countdown and RBI clearing schedule follows IST, keeping the whole country in sync.

topics.t: Size, coastline and boundaries of India
topics.h: India is the seventh largest country, yet it packs in the world's highest mountains, a great desert, vast plains, two seas and hundreds of islands.
p: India's area is 3.28 million sq km, about 2.4% of the world's total land area. It is the seventh largest country in the world.

Its size gives it great physical diversity: the Himalaya in the north, the Indian Ocean in the south, a desert in the west and forested hills in the east. Its location in the tropics and subtropics, between the Himalaya and the Indian Ocean, also gives it a monsoon climate, which is classified in detail (including Koeppen's scheme for India) in the chapter on climate.
The mainland coastline is about 6,100 km; including the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep, the total coastline is about 7,517 km.

India is bounded by young fold mountains in the north-west, north and north-east. South of about 22°N, the peninsula begins to taper and extends into the Indian Ocean, dividing it into the Arabian Sea on the west and the Bay of Bengal on the east.

ex.q: How much of India's total coastline (7,517 km) belongs to its islands, if the mainland coastline is 6,100 km?
st: Island coastline = 7,517 − 6,100.
ex.a: About 1,417 km.

topics.rl: India's long coastline supports major ports such as JNPT (Mumbai), Chennai and Visakhapatnam, and millions of fishing families.

topics.t: India and its neighbours
topics.h: India sits at the head of the Indian Ocean, the only ocean named after a country. Its location connects it to West Asia, Africa, South-east Asia and beyond.
p: India is located in the south-central part of Asia, bordering the Indian Ocean and its two arms, the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal. This maritime location provides links with neighbouring regions by sea and air.
India's central location at the head of the Indian Ocean is strategically important for trade routes between east and west.
Land neighbours: Pakistan and Afghanistan in the north-west; China (Tibet), Nepal and Bhutan in the north; Myanmar and Bangladesh in the east.
Island neighbours: Sri Lanka, separated from India by the Gulf of Mannar and the Palk Strait; and the Maldives, located south of the Lakshadweep Islands.
Map work: mark the latitudinal and longitudinal extent, the Standard Meridian (82°30'E), the Tropic of Cancer, Kanniyakumari, and India's neighbours on an outline map.

ex.q: Which water bodies separate India from Sri Lanka?
st: Sri Lanka lies south-east of India's southern tip.
The narrow strait between them is the Palk Strait.
South of it lies the Gulf of Mannar.
ex.a: The Palk Strait and the Gulf of Mannar.

topics.rl: Ferry services between Nagapattinam in Tamil Nadu and Kankesanthurai in Sri Lanka cross the Palk Strait region, linking two close neighbours.

topics.t: Structure of India: three geological divisions
topics.h: The rocks under Bengaluru are among the oldest on earth, while the Himalaya are among the youngest mountains. India holds both extremes.
p: The earth is about 4,600 million years old. Over this time, endogenic and exogenic forces have shaped its surface features.
The Indian plate was once south of the equator. Its northward movement and collision with the Eurasian plate led to the formation of the Himalaya.

Based on variations in geological structure and formation, India is divided into three geological divisions: (i) the Peninsular Block; (ii) the Himalayas and other Peninsular mountains; (iii) the Indo-Ganga-Brahmaputra Plain.

ex.q: Place each in its geological division: Deccan Plateau, Shiwalik hills, Ganga plain near Patna.
st: Deccan Plateau: ancient rigid landmass → Peninsular Block.
Shiwalik hills: young folded mountains → Himalayas and other Peninsular mountains.
Ganga plain near Patna: alluvial plain → Indo-Ganga-Brahmaputra Plain.
ex.a: Deccan Plateau → Peninsular Block; Shiwalik → Himalayas; Ganga plain → Indo-Ganga-Brahmaputra Plain.

topics.rl: The Geological Survey of India, founded in 1851, maps these divisions, which guide everything from mining to earthquake zoning.

topics.t: The Peninsular Block
topics.h: The Peninsular Block has stood like a rigid rock shield since the Cambrian period, over 500 million years.
p: The northern boundary of the Peninsular Block is an irregular line from Kachchh, along the western flank of the Aravali Range near Delhi, then roughly parallel to the Yamuna and Ganga up to the Rajmahal Hills and the Ganga delta. The Karbi Anglong and Meghalaya Plateau in the north-east, and Rajasthan in the west, are its extensions; the north-eastern parts are separated from the Chotanagpur plateau by the Malda fault in West Bengal.
The Peninsula is made essentially of a great complex of very ancient gneisses and granites.

Since the Cambrian period it has stood like a rigid block, except for parts of its western coast that are submerged beneath the sea and some areas changed by tectonic activity without affecting the basement.
As part of the Indo-Australian plate, it has faced vertical movements and block faulting: the rift valleys of the Narmada, Tapi and Mahanadi and the Satpura block mountains are examples.

It mostly consists of relict and residual mountains like the Aravali, Nallamala, Javadi and Veliconda hills, the Palkonda range and the Mahendragiri hills. Its river valleys are shallow with low gradients.

ex.q: Why do the Narmada and Tapi flow through rift valleys?
st: The Peninsular Block has undergone block faulting.
Faulting created long troughs (rift valleys) between blocks.
The Narmada and Tapi flow westward through these troughs.
ex.a: Because block faulting in the Peninsular Block created rift valleys that these rivers now occupy.

topics.rl: The marble rocks gorge of the Narmada at Bhedaghat near Jabalpur lies in this ancient faulted landscape.

topics.t: The Himalaya and the Indo-Ganga-Brahmaputra Plain: structure
topics.h: Drill 2 km into the Ganga plain and you may still be in river mud. That huge trough was dug by the rising Himalaya and filled by their rivers.
p: The Himalaya and other Peninsular mountains are young, weak and flexible in geological structure, unlike the rigid Peninsular Block. They are still subject to endogenic and exogenic forces, resulting in faults, folds and thrust plains.
They are tectonic in origin and dissected by fast-flowing rivers in their youthful stage. Gorges, V-shaped valleys, rapids and waterfalls indicate this youthful stage.
A cross-section of the Himalaya shows parallel ranges rising from the plains: the Shiwalik, the Lesser (Middle) Himalaya, the Great Himalaya and, beyond, the Trans-Himalaya.
The Indo-Ganga-Brahmaputra Plain was originally a geo-synclinal depression that reached its maximum development during the third phase of Himalayan mountain formation, about 64 million years ago.
Since then it has been filled by sediments from Himalayan and Peninsular rivers. The average depth of alluvial deposits is 1,000–2,000 m.

ex.q: Why do Himalayan rivers have gorges, rapids and waterfalls while Peninsular rivers have shallow valleys?
st: The Himalaya are young and still rising, giving steep slopes.
Fast rivers cut down actively, forming gorges, V-shaped valleys, rapids and waterfalls (youthful stage).
The Peninsula is old and stable, worn down over a long time.
Its rivers have shallow, graded valleys with low gradients.
ex.a: Because the Himalaya are young and rising, while the Peninsula is old and worn down.

topics.rl: Hydropower projects like Tehri on the Bhagirathi use the steep, youthful Himalayan river gradients.

topics.t: Physiographic divisions and the Himalayan ranges
topics.h: If you drove from Kashmir to Kanniyakumari and then took a boat to the Andamans, you would cross all six physiographic divisions of India.
p: The physiography of an area is the outcome of structure, process and the stage of development.

India is divided into six physiographic divisions: (1) the Northern and North-eastern Mountains; (2) the Northern Plain; (3) the Peninsular Plateau; (4) the Indian Desert; (5) the Coastal Plains; (6) the Islands.
Map work: mark these six divisions on an outline map of India.

The Northern and North-eastern Mountains consist of the Himalaya and the north-eastern hills. The Himalaya are a series of parallel ranges: the Greater Himalayan range (including the Great Himalaya and the Trans-Himalayan range), the Middle Himalaya and the Shiwalik.

ex.q: Name the physiographic division of each: Jaisalmer, Lucknow, Hyderabad, Port Blair, Kochi coast, Shimla.
st: Jaisalmer → Indian Desert.
Lucknow → Northern Plain.
Hyderabad → Peninsular Plateau.
Port Blair → Islands.
Kochi coast → Coastal Plains.
Shimla → Northern and North-eastern Mountains.
ex.a: Desert, Northern Plain, Peninsular Plateau, Islands, Coastal Plains, Northern Mountains.

topics.rl: State tourism campaigns often market India's diversity: Himalayan treks, Thar safaris, Deccan heritage, Kerala backwaters and Andaman beaches, one for each physiographic division.

topics.t: Orientation, size and regions of the Himalaya
topics.h: The Himalaya are not a straight wall. They curve like a giant bow across northern India, changing direction as they go.
p: In north-western India, the Himalayan ranges run from north-west to south-east.
In Darjeeling and Sikkim, they lie in an east–west direction. In Arunachal Pradesh, they run from south-west to north-east. In Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram, they run north–south.
The Great Himalayan range, also called the central axial range, is about 2,500 km long from east to west; its width varies from 160 to 400 km from north to south.

Based on relief, alignment of ranges and other geomorphological features, the Himalaya are divided into regions: (i) Kashmir or North-western Himalaya; (ii) Himachal and Uttarakhand Himalaya; (iii) Darjeeling and Sikkim Himalaya; (iv) Arunachal Himalaya; (v) Eastern Hills and Mountains.

ex.q: If the Himalaya are 2,500 km long and on average 280 km wide, roughly what area do they cover?
st: Area ≈ length × width.
ex.a: About 7 lakh sq km (a rough estimate).

topics.rl: The curved alignment of the Himalaya helps block cold Central Asian winds and trap monsoon moisture over India.

topics.t: Kashmir or North-western Himalaya
topics.h: Saffron fields at Pampore, the Siachen glacier, the cold desert of Ladakh and K2, the second-highest peak on earth: all in the North-western Himalaya.
p: The Kashmir or North-western Himalaya comprise a series of ranges: the Karakoram, Ladakh, Zaskar and Pir Panjal. The north-eastern part is a cold desert (Ladakh) lying between the Greater Himalaya and the Karakoram.
Between the Great Himalaya and the Pir Panjal lies the famous valley of Kashmir and the Dal Lake. Important glaciers of South Asia, the Baltoro and the Siachen, are found here.
The region is famous for Karewa formations (thick deposits of glacial clay and other materials embedded with moraines), used for cultivating zafran, a local variety of saffron.

Important passes: Zoji La on the Great Himalaya, Banihal on the Pir Panjal, Photu La on the Zaskar and Khardung La on the Ladakh range. Fresh-water lakes: Dal and Wular; salt-water lakes: Pangong Tso and Tso Moriri. The region is drained by the Indus and its tributaries, the Jhelum and Chenab; the Jhelum meanders in the Kashmir valley.
Map work: K2 (Godwin Austen) in the Karakoram, and Nanga Parbat in the north-western Himalaya. The southern part has longitudinal valleys called duns, such as Jammu dun and Pathankot dun.

ex.q: Match each pass to its range: Zoji La, Banihal, Khardung La.
st: Zoji La → Great Himalaya (links Kashmir valley to Ladakh).
Banihal → Pir Panjal (links Jammu with the Kashmir valley).
Khardung La → Ladakh range.
ex.a: Zoji La: Great Himalaya; Banihal: Pir Panjal; Khardung La: Ladakh range.

topics.rl: The Jawahar Tunnel and newer road tunnels near Banihal keep the Jammu–Srinagar route open in winter when snow blocks the Pir Panjal.

topics.t: Himachal-Uttarakhand and Darjeeling-Sikkim Himalaya
topics.h: Dehra Dun's flat valley, Shimla's hill-station charm and Darjeeling's tea gardens: the middle Himalaya were shaped by structure, slope and rainfall.
p: Himachal and Uttarakhand Himalaya lie approximately between the Ravi in the west and the Kali (a tributary of the Ghaghara) in the east, drained by the Indus and Ganga systems. All three ranges are prominent: the Great Himalaya, the Lesser Himalaya (Dhaoladhar in Himachal Pradesh and Nagtibba in Uttarakhand) and the Shiwalik.

The Lesser Himalaya at 1,000–2,000 m attracted the British, who developed hill stations and cantonments like Dharamshala, Mussoorie, Shimla, Kasauli, Almora, Lansdowne and Ranikhet. Distinguishing features are the Shiwalik and 'dun' formations: Chandigarh-Kalka dun, Nalagarh dun, Dehra Dun (the largest), Harike dun and Kota dun. Pilgrim centres (Gangotri, Yamunotri, Kedarnath, Badrinath, Hemkund Sahib), the Valley of Flowers and the five Prayags (river confluences) are here; Shipki La is an important pass on the Satluj.

Darjeeling and Sikkim Himalaya lie between the Nepal Himalaya in the west and the Bhutan Himalaya in the east. They are known for fast-flowing rivers like the Tista, high peaks like Kanchenjunga, and deep valleys. The higher reaches are inhabited by the Lepcha tribes.
The British introduced tea plantations here because of moderate slopes, thick soil with high organic content, well-distributed rainfall and mild winters.

Compared with other sections, the Darjeeling-Sikkim and Arunachal Himalaya lack the Shiwalik; in their place, 'duar formations' are important and have been used for tea gardens. Nathu La in Sikkim is an important pass.

ex.q: Why did the British develop tea gardens in Darjeeling?
st: Moderate slopes allow drainage without waterlogging.
Thick soils rich in organic matter provide nutrients.
Rainfall is well distributed throughout the year.
Winters are mild.
These conditions suit tea.
ex.a: Moderate slopes, organic-rich soils, well-distributed rain and mild winters.

topics.rl: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, a UNESCO World Heritage site, climbs through the tea gardens of this region.

topics.t: Arunachal Himalaya and the Eastern Hills
topics.h: The Brahmaputra plunges through one of the world's deepest gorges near Namcha Barwa before entering India. Arunachal's rivers have the highest hydropower potential in the country.
p: The Arunachal Himalaya extend from east of the Bhutan Himalaya up to the Diphu pass in the east. The general direction is south-west to north-east. Important peaks are Kangtu and Namcha Barwa.

These ranges are cut by fast-flowing rivers from north to south, forming deep gorges. Important rivers are the Kameng, Subansiri, Dihang, Dibang and Lohit. They are perennial with a high rate of fall, giving the highest hydroelectric potential in India.
Many tribal communities live here; prominent ones from west to east include the Monpa, Nyishi, Adi, Mishmi and the Nagas. Most practise jhumming, also called shifting or slash-and-burn cultivation.

The Eastern Hills and Mountains include the Patkai Bum, Naga hills, Manipur hills and, in the south, the Mizo or Lushai hills. These are low hills inhabited by tribal groups practising jhum cultivation. The Barak is an important river of Manipur and Mizoram, and the Loktak lake lies at the centre of Manipur, surrounded by mountains.
Map work: also locate the Karakoram, the Garo-Khasi-Jaintia hills, the Aravali, Vindhyan and Satpura ranges, and the Western and Eastern Ghats.

ex.q: Why does Arunachal Pradesh have the highest hydroelectric potential in India?
st: Rivers like the Kameng, Subansiri, Dihang, Dibang and Lohit are perennial (fed by snow and heavy rain).
They flow through steep mountains with a high rate of fall.
Large, steady flow plus a steep drop gives great hydropower potential.
ex.a: Because its rivers are perennial and have a high rate of fall.

topics.rl: The Subansiri Lower Hydroelectric Project on the Arunachal–Assam border is one of India's largest hydro projects, using these steep rivers.

topics.t: The Northern Plain
topics.h: Walk south from the Shiwalik foothills: first boulders where streams vanish, then swampy tarai jungle, then the endless fertile fields of the Ganga plain.
p: The Northern Plain is formed by alluvial deposits of the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra. It extends about 3,200 km from east to west, with an average width of 150–300 km; the maximum depth of alluvium is 1,000–2,000 m. It is a featureless plain with a general elevation of 50–150 m above mean sea level.
From north to south it has three zones: the Bhabar, the Tarai and the alluvial plains.
Bhabar: a narrow belt 8–10 km wide parallel to the Shiwalik foothills at the break of slope. Streams deposit heavy rocks and boulders and at times disappear in this zone.

Tarai: south of the Bhabar, about 10–20 km wide, where streams re-emerge without proper channels, creating marshy and swampy conditions with luxuriant vegetation and varied wildlife (e.g. Dudhwa National Park). Forests have been cleared for agriculture and settlement.

Alluvial plains: old alluvium (Bhangar) and new alluvium (Khadar). They show mature-stage fluvial features: sand bars, meanders, oxbow lakes and braided channels. The Brahmaputra plains are known for riverine islands and sand bars; the river mouths form huge deltas such as the Sundarbans. Haryana and Delhi form the water divide between the Indus and Ganga systems.

ex.q: Why do streams disappear in the Bhabar and reappear in the Tarai?
st: At the foot of the Shiwalik, slopes break sharply.
Streams drop coarse boulders and pebbles, forming the porous Bhabar.
Water sinks into these porous deposits and the streams vanish.
Further south, in the Tarai, the water re-emerges as marshy, poorly channelled streams.
ex.a: The porous boulder deposits of the Bhabar absorb the water; it reappears in the lower, finer Tarai.

topics.rl: Majuli in the Brahmaputra, one of the world's largest river islands, shows the riverine islands typical of the Brahmaputra plain.

topics.t: The Peninsular Plateau and the Deccan
topics.h: The Peninsular Plateau is India's oldest and most stable landmass: an irregular triangle tilted so that most of its rivers run east to the Bay of Bengal.
p: Rising from about 150 m above the river plains to an elevation of 600–900 m is the irregular triangle called the Peninsular Plateau. Its outer extent is marked by the Delhi ridge (extension of the Aravali) in the north-west, the Rajmahal hills in the east, the Gir range in the west and the Cardamom hills in the south. The Shillong and Karbi Anglong plateau form its extension in the north-east.

It is made of a series of patland plateaus such as Hazaribagh, Palamu, Ranchi, Malwa, Coimbatore and Karnataka plateaus. It is one of the oldest and most stable landmasses of India; its general slope is from west to east, as shown by the flow of rivers.

Features include tors, block mountains, rift valleys, spurs, bare rocky structures, series of hummocky hills and wall-like quartzite dykes; the western and north-western parts have black soil (Deccan Trap). The north-western part has ravines and gorges, such as those of the Chambal, Bhind and Morena.
The plateau has three broad groups: the Deccan Plateau, the Central Highlands and the North-eastern Plateau.
The Deccan Plateau is bordered by the Western Ghats in the west, the Eastern Ghats in the east, and the Satpura, Maikal range and Mahadeo hills in the north.

ex.q: How do the rivers of the Peninsula show that the plateau slopes from west to east?
st: Major Peninsular rivers like the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri rise in the west.
They flow east into the Bay of Bengal.
Rivers flow down the slope.
So the general slope is from west to east.
ex.a: Most major rivers flow eastward, showing the plateau tilts from west to east.

topics.rl: The Chambal ravines of Bhind and Morena are a classic badland landscape and have been the target of soil conservation programmes.

topics.t: Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats and the Central Highlands
topics.h: Anaimudi in Kerala, at 2,695 m, is the highest peak of the Peninsula. The Western Ghats are a near-continuous wall; the Eastern Ghats are broken hills cut by great rivers.
p: The Western Ghats are known locally as the Sahyadri in Maharashtra, the Nilgiri hills in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and the Anaimalai and Cardamom hills in Kerala. They are higher and more continuous than the Eastern Ghats, with an average elevation of about 1,500 m, increasing from north to south. Important passes include the Thal Ghat, Bhor Ghat and Palghat.
Anaimudi (2,695 m), the highest peak of the Peninsular plateau, is on the Anaimalai hills, followed by Dodabetta (2,637 m) on the Nilgiri hills. Most Peninsular rivers rise in the Western Ghats.

The Eastern Ghats are discontinuous, low hills, highly eroded by rivers like the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. Important ranges: Javadi hills, Palconda range, Nallamala hills and Mahendragiri hills. The Eastern and Western Ghats meet at the Nilgiri hills.

The Central Highlands are bounded on the west by the Aravali range. The Satpura range, a series of scarped plateaus at 600–900 m, forms the northernmost boundary of the Deccan plateau and is a classic relict mountain. The Central Highlands include the Malwa plateau, Bundelkhand, Baghelkhand and the Chotanagpur plateau (rich in minerals, south of the Rajmahal hills). Their general elevation is 700–1,000 m, sloping towards the north and north-east.

The Aravali hills are highly eroded relict mountains; Guru Shikhar is their highest peak. Most tributaries of the Yamuna rise in the Vindhyan and Kaimur ranges and flow north-east (Betwa, Ken); the Banas is the only significant tributary of the Chambal that rises in the Aravali.

ex.q: Compare the Western and Eastern Ghats on three points.
st: Continuity: Western Ghats are continuous; Eastern Ghats are discontinuous.
Height: Western Ghats are higher (average about 1,500 m); Eastern Ghats are low.
Rivers: Western Ghats are the source of most Peninsular rivers; Eastern Ghats are cut through by these rivers.
ex.a: Western Ghats: continuous, higher, source of rivers. Eastern Ghats: discontinuous, low, dissected by rivers.

topics.rl: The Mumbai–Pune railway climbs the Bhor Ghat, a pass in the Sahyadri used since colonial times.

topics.t: North-eastern Plateau and the Indian Desert
topics.h: 180-million-year-old fossil tree trunks lie in the Thar near Jaisalmer. The desert was once under the sea.
p: The North-eastern Plateau is an extension of the Peninsular plateau. The north-eastward push of the Indian plate during the Himalayan origin created a huge fault between the Rajmahal hills and the Meghalaya plateau, later filled by river deposits; so the Meghalaya and Karbi Anglong plateau now stand detached from the main block (separated by the Malda fault).

The Meghalaya plateau has three parts named after tribal groups: the Garo, Khasi and Jaintia hills; the Karbi Anglong hills of Assam are an extension. It is rich in coal, iron ore, sillimanite, limestone and uranium. Heavy south-west monsoon rain has highly eroded it; Cherrapunji shows a bare rocky surface without permanent vegetation. Map work: Malwa, Chotanagpur, Meghalaya and Deccan plateaus; passes Shipki La, Nathu La, Palghat, Bhor Ghat and Thal Ghat.

The Great Indian Desert lies to the north-west of the Aravali hills. It is a land of undulating topography with longitudinal dunes and barchans. Rainfall is below 150 mm a year, giving an arid climate with low vegetation; hence it is called Marusthali.

During the Mesozoic era this region was under the sea, as shown by the wood fossils park at Aakal and marine deposits around Brahmsar near Jaisalmer (wood fossils about 180 million years old). Though its rock structure is an extension of the Peninsular plateau, its surface has been carved by physical weathering and wind.

Features: mushroom rocks, shifting dunes and oases (mostly in the south). The northern part slopes towards Sindh and the southern towards the Rann of Kachchh. Most rivers are ephemeral; the Luni in the south is significant. Some streams disappear after a distance, ending in a lake or playa (inland drainage); these brackish lakes are the main source of salt.

ex.q: What evidence shows that the Thar desert was once under the sea?
st: Fossil wood about 180 million years old is preserved at the wood fossils park, Aakal.
Marine deposits are found around Brahmsar near Jaisalmer.
These date to the Mesozoic era.
So the region was under the sea then.
ex.a: Wood fossils at Aakal and marine deposits near Brahmsar (Jaisalmer), from the Mesozoic era.

topics.rl: Sambhar Lake near Jaipur is a playa-type salt lake that has supplied salt for centuries, an example of inland drainage in a dry region.

topics.t: The Coastal Plains
topics.h: Every August, long snake boats race across Punnamada Kayal in Kerala for the Nehru Trophy. The backwaters are a gift of the Malabar coast.
p: India's coastal plains are divided into the western coastal plains and the eastern coastal plains.

The western coastal plains are an example of a submerged coastal plain; the ancient city of Dwaraka is believed to be submerged under water. Because of submergence, it is a narrow belt that provides natural conditions for ports and harbours: Kandla, Mazagaon, JLN port Navha Sheva, Marmagao, Mangalore and Cochin. It is narrow in the middle and broader towards the north and south.

Divisions of the west coast: Kachchh and Kathiawar coast in Gujarat, Konkan coast in Maharashtra, the Goan coast, and the Malabar coast in Karnataka and Kerala. Rivers flowing through the western coastal plain do not form deltas. The Malabar coast has kayals (backwaters) used for fishing, inland navigation and tourism; the Nehru Trophy Vallamkali (boat race) is held in Punnamada Kayal.
The eastern coastal plain is broader and is an example of an emergent coast. It has well-developed deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri.

Being emergent, the east coast has fewer ports and harbours; its continental shelf extends up to 500 km into the sea, making it difficult to develop good ports. Map work: Saurashtra, Konkan, North and South Kanara, Malabar, Coromandel and Northern Circar coasts.

ex.q: Why does the west coast have many natural ports while the east coast has fewer?
st: The west coast is a submerged, narrow coast with deep water close to the shore: natural harbours.
The east coast is an emergent coast with a broad continental shelf extending up to 500 km.
Shallow water far out to sea makes good ports difficult.
So the west coast has more natural ports.
ex.a: The submerged west coast has deep water near the shore; the emergent east coast has a wide, shallow shelf.

topics.rl: Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Nhava Sheva) near Mumbai, India's busiest container port, is on the submerged western coast.

topics.t: The Islands
topics.h: India's island territories range from the volcanic and mountainous Andamans to the flat coral atolls of Lakshadweep.
p: India has two major island groups: one in the Bay of Bengal (about 572 islands/islets) and the other in the Arabian Sea.

Andaman and Nicobar Islands: roughly between 6°N–14°N and 92°E–94°E. The two principal groups of islets are Ritchie's archipelago and the Labyrinth island. The Andaman group in the north is separated from the Nicobar group in the south by the Ten Degree Channel.

These islands are believed to be elevated portions of submarine mountains; some smaller islands are volcanic. Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is the only active volcano in India. Important peaks: Saddle Peak (North Andaman, 738 m), Mount Diavolo (Middle Andaman, 515 m), Mount Koyob (South Andaman, 460 m) and Mount Thuiller (Great Nicobar, 642 m). The coasts have coral deposits and beaches; the islands receive convectional rainfall and have equatorial vegetation.

Arabian Sea islands: Lakshadweep and Minicoy, scattered between 8°N–12°N and 71°E–74°E, about 280–480 km off the Kerala coast. The entire group is built of coral deposits. There are about 36 islands, of which 11 are inhabited.

The Eleventh Degree Channel broadly divides the group: Amini Island to the north and Cannanore Island to the south. The islands have storm beaches of unconsolidated pebbles, shingles, cobbles and boulders on the eastern seaboard. Exam tip: practise MCQs on hills, passes and islands; compare Himalayan and Peninsular regions, Bhabar and Tarai, and the west and east coasts; and label a physiographic map.

ex.q: Compare the islands of the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea in origin and relief.
st: Bay of Bengal (Andaman and Nicobar): elevated parts of submarine mountains, some volcanic; hilly, with peaks like Saddle Peak (738 m).
Arabian Sea (Lakshadweep): built entirely of coral deposits; low and flat.
So the Andamans are mountainous and partly volcanic; Lakshadweep is low coral.
ex.a: Andaman and Nicobar: hilly, submarine mountain tops, partly volcanic. Lakshadweep: low coral islands.

topics.rl: Ross Island (Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep) and Havelock (Swaraj Dweep) in the Andamans and the coral lagoons of Lakshadweep are major island tourism destinations.

topics.t: Drainage, drainage basins and watersheds
topics.h: Rain falling on the Delhi ridge can end up in the Arabian Sea or the Bay of Bengal, depending on which side of a line of high ground it falls.
p: The flow of water through well-defined channels is called drainage, and the network of such channels is a drainage system.
The drainage pattern of an area is the outcome of the geological time period, the nature and structure of rocks, topography, slope, the amount of water flowing and the periodicity of the flow.

A river drains water from a specific area called its catchment area. The area drained by a river and its tributaries is a drainage basin. The boundary line separating one drainage basin from another is the watershed.
The catchments of large rivers are called river basins, while those of small rivulets and rills are often called watersheds.
The difference is mainly of size: watersheds are small in area, while river basins cover larger areas.

ex.q: A village plans water harvesting for the small stream that drains its 15 sq km of hill slopes. Is this a river basin or a watershed approach?
st: The area drained by a small stream is small (15 sq km).
Catchments of small rivulets and rills are called watersheds.
So it is a watershed approach.
ex.a: A watershed approach.

topics.rl: India's Integrated Watershed Management Programme works village by village on small watersheds to conserve soil and rainwater.

topics.t: Drainage patterns and classification of Indian drainage
topics.h: From the air, rivers of the Ganga plain look like branches of a tree, while the streams around Amarkantak spread out like spokes of a wheel.
p: Dendritic: drainage resembling the branches of a tree, e.g. rivers of the northern plain. Radial: rivers originating from a hill and flowing in all directions, e.g. rivers from the Amarkantak range. Trellis: primary tributaries flow parallel to each other and secondary tributaries join them at right angles. Centripetal: rivers discharge from all directions into a lake or depression, e.g. Loktak lake in Manipur.

By discharge (orientation to the sea): the Arabian Sea drainage and the Bay of Bengal drainage, separated by the Delhi ridge, the Aravalis and the Sahyadris. About 77% of the drainage area (Ganga, Brahmaputra, Mahanadi, Krishna, etc.) drains into the Bay of Bengal; about 23% (Indus, Narmada, Tapi, Mahi, Periyar) drains into the Arabian Sea.

By size of watershed: major river basins (catchment above 20,000 sq km; 14 basins such as the Ganga, Brahmaputra, Krishna, Tapi, Narmada, Mahi, Pennar, Sabarmati, Barak); medium basins (2,000–20,000 sq km; 44 basins such as the Kalindi, Periyar, Meghna); minor basins (less than 2,000 sq km, many in low-rainfall areas).
By mode of origin, nature and characteristics: the Himalayan drainage and the Peninsular drainage.

ex.q: A river's catchment is 15,000 sq km. Which size category does it belong to?
st: Major: more than 20,000 sq km.
Medium: 2,000–20,000 sq km.
Minor: less than 2,000 sq km.
15,000 lies between 2,000 and 20,000 → medium.
ex.a: Medium river basin.

topics.rl: The Central Water Commission plans dams and flood forecasting basin by basin, using these major, medium and minor categories.

topics.t: The Himalayan drainage system
topics.h: The Kosi has shifted its course westward by over 100 km in about 200 years, swallowing villages and fields. That is why it is called the 'sorrow of Bihar'.
p: The Himalayan drainage system mainly includes the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra basins. Fed by both melting snow and precipitation, these rivers are perennial.
They pass through giant gorges carved by erosion carried on simultaneously with the uplift of the Himalaya. In their mountain courses they form deep gorges, V-shaped valleys, rapids and waterfalls.
On entering the plains, they form depositional features: flat valleys, oxbow lakes, floodplains, braided channels and deltas near the river mouth.
In the Himalayan reaches their courses are highly tortuous, but over the plains they show a strong meandering tendency and shift their courses frequently.
The Kosi, known as the 'sorrow of Bihar', brings huge sediment from its upper reaches and deposits it in the plains; its course gets blocked and the river changes its course.

ex.q: Why are Himalayan rivers perennial?
st: They are fed by melting snow and glaciers in summer.
They also receive monsoon rainfall.
So they have water throughout the year.
ex.a: Because they are fed by both snowmelt and rainfall.

topics.rl: The 2008 Kosi breach at Kusaha in Nepal sent the river into a new course and flooded large parts of north Bihar.

topics.t: Evolution of the Himalayan drainage
topics.h: Imagine one mighty river flowing along the entire Himalaya from Assam to Punjab. Geologists believe it really existed, and they call it the Indo-Brahma or Shiwalik river.
p: Geologists believe a mighty river called the Shiwalik or Indo-Brahma traversed the entire length of the Himalaya from Assam to Punjab and onwards to Sind, finally discharging into the Gulf of Sind near lower Punjab during the Miocene period, some 5–24 million years ago.
Evidence: the remarkable continuity of the Shiwalik, their lacustrine (lake) origin, and alluvial deposits of sands, silt, clay, boulders and conglomerates.

In time, the Indo-Brahma river was dismembered into three main drainage systems: (i) the Indus and its five tributaries in the west; (ii) the Ganga and its Himalayan tributaries in the centre; (iii) the Brahmaputra in Assam and its Himalayan tributaries in the east.

The dismemberment was probably due to the Pleistocene upheaval in the western Himalaya, including the uplift of the Potwar Plateau (Delhi Ridge), which became the water divide between the Indus and Ganga systems.
The down-thrusting of the Malda gap area between the Rajmahal hills and the Meghalaya plateau during the mid-Pleistocene diverted the Ganga and Brahmaputra to flow towards the Bay of Bengal.

ex.q: What split the Indo-Brahma river into the Indus and Ganga systems?
st: During the Pleistocene, the western Himalaya were uplifted.
The Potwar Plateau (Delhi Ridge) rose.
It became a water divide.
Water on one side drained to the Indus, on the other to the Ganga.
ex.a: The Pleistocene uplift of the Potwar Plateau (Delhi Ridge), which became the water divide.

topics.rl: Sediment layers in the Shiwalik hills near Chandigarh and Dehradun, rich in boulders and conglomerates, are the record of this ancient river.

topics.t: The Indus system: main river
topics.h: The Indus rises at over 4,000 m in Tibet as 'Singi Khamban', the Lion's Mouth, and the subcontinent's oldest civilisation grew along its banks.
p: The Indus is one of the largest river basins of the world: total area 11,65,000 sq km (3,21,289 sq km in India). Its total length is 2,880 km, of which 1,114 km is in India. It is the westernmost Himalayan river in India.
It originates from a glacier near Bokhar Chu in the Tibetan region at an altitude of 4,164 m in the Kailash range. In Tibet it is known as Singi Khamban, or Lion's mouth.

It flows north-west between the Ladakh and Zaskar ranges, passing through Ladakh and Baltistan. It cuts across the Ladakh range near Gilgit, forming a spectacular gorge, and enters Pakistan near Chillar in the Dardistan region.

Himalayan tributaries include the Shyok, Gilgit, Zaskar, Hunza, Nubra, Shigar, Gasting and Dras. Near Attock it receives the Kabul river on its right bank; other right-bank tributaries, the Khurram, Tochi, Gomal, Viboa and Sangar, rise in the Sulaiman ranges. It finally discharges into the Arabian Sea, east of Karachi.

Under the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) between India and Pakistan, the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Satluj) were allotted to India and the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) mainly to Pakistan. As NCERT puts it, India can use only about 20% of the total water of the Indus system, mainly for irrigation in Punjab, Haryana and southern and western Rajasthan.

ex.q: What percentage of the Indus's total length flows through India? (Total 2,880 km; in India 1,114 km; nearest whole number.)
st: Nearest whole number = 39%.
ex.a: About 39%.

topics.rl: Leh, the main town of Ladakh, lies on the banks of the upper Indus, where the river is still young and clear.

topics.t: The Indus system: Panjnad tributaries
topics.h: Punjab means 'land of five waters'. The five rivers, the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Satluj, together are called the Panjnad.
p: The Panjnad is the name given to the five rivers of Punjab: the Satluj, Beas, Ravi, Chenab and Jhelum. They join the Indus a little above Mithankot in Pakistan.

Jhelum: rises from a spring at Verinag at the foot of the Pir Panjal in the south-eastern part of the Kashmir valley. It flows through Srinagar and the Wular lake, then enters Pakistan through a deep narrow gorge and joins the Chenab near Jhang.

Chenab: the largest tributary of the Indus, formed by the Chandra and Bhaga, which join at Tandi near Keylong in Himachal Pradesh (hence also called Chandrabhaga). It flows 1,180 km before entering Pakistan. Ravi: rises west of the Rohtang pass in the Kullu hills of Himachal Pradesh and flows through the Chamba valley, draining the area between the south-eastern Pir Panjal and the Dhauladhar ranges.

Beas: originates from the Beas Kund near the Rohtang pass at about 4,000 m. It flows through the Kullu valley, forms gorges at Kati and Largi in the Dhaoladhar range, enters the Punjab plains and meets the Satluj near Harike.

Satluj: originates in Rakas Tal near Mansarovar at 4,555 m in Tibet, where it is known as Langchen Khambab. It flows almost parallel to the Indus for about 400 km before entering India through the Shipki La and comes out of a gorge at Rupar. It is an antecedent river and feeds the canal system of the Bhakra Nangal project.

ex.q: Name the river: (a) formed by the Chandra and Bhaga; (b) rises at Verinag and flows through Wular lake; (c) enters India through Shipki La.
st: (a) Chandra + Bhaga at Tandi → Chenab.
(b) Verinag spring, Srinagar and Wular lake → Jhelum.
(c) Antecedent river entering through Shipki La → Satluj.
ex.a: (a) Chenab; (b) Jhelum; (c) Satluj.

topics.rl: The Bhakra Nangal dam on the Satluj supplies irrigation canals that helped make Punjab and Haryana the granary of India during the Green Revolution.

topics.t: The Ganga: source, course and basin
topics.h: The Ganga flows through four states for 2,525 km, and its basin, the largest in India, is home to a huge share of India's people.
p: The Ganga is the most important river of India, both for its basin and its cultural significance. It rises in the Gangotri glacier near Gaumukh (3,900 m) in Uttarkashi district of Uttarakhand, where it is called the Bhagirathi, and cuts through the Central and Lesser Himalaya in narrow gorges.

At Devprayag, the Bhagirathi meets the Alaknanda; from here it is called the Ganga. The Alaknanda rises in the Satopanth glacier above Badrinath. It consists of the Dhauli and Vishnu Ganga, which meet at Joshimath or Vishnu Prayag.
Other tributaries of the Alaknanda: the Pindar joins at Karna Prayag, and the Mandakini or Kali Ganga meets it at Rudra Prayag.

The Ganga enters the plains at Haridwar. It flows first south, then south-east and east, before splitting into two distributaries, the Bhagirathi(-Hugli) and the Padma. It discharges into the Bay of Bengal near Sagar Island.

Length 2,525 km: Uttarakhand 110 km, Uttar Pradesh 1,450 km, Bihar 445 km, West Bengal 520 km. Its basin covers about 8.6 lakh sq km in India. The Ganga river system is the largest in India, with perennial rivers from the Himalaya in the north and non-perennial rivers from the Peninsula in the south.

ex.q: Check that the Ganga's length is shared correctly among the four states.
st: Uttarakhand 110 + Uttar Pradesh 1,450 = 1,560 km.
+ West Bengal 520 = 2,525 km.

topics.rl: The Namami Gange programme works to clean and conserve the Ganga across these states.

topics.t: Ganga tributaries: Yamuna, Chambal, Son, Ramganga and Damodar
topics.h: The Taj Mahal stands on the Yamuna, the Chambal's ravines hide gharials, and the Damodar was once called the 'sorrow of Bengal'.
p: The Son is the major right-bank tributary of the Ganga. It is a large south-bank tributary originating in the Amarkantak plateau; after forming a series of waterfalls at the plateau edge, it joins the Ganga near Arrah, west of Patna.

The Yamuna is the westernmost and longest tributary of the Ganga. It rises in the Yamunotri glacier on the western slopes of the Bandarpunch range and joins the Ganga at Prayag (Allahabad). Its right-bank tributaries from the Peninsula are the Chambal, Sind, Betwa and Ken; left-bank tributaries include the Hindan, Rind, Sengar and Varuna. Much of its water feeds the Western and Eastern Yamuna and Agra canals.

The Chambal rises near Mhow on the Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh and flows north through a gorge upstream of Kota in Rajasthan; the Gandhi Sagar dam (in Madhya Pradesh) is built on this gorge section. From Kota it flows past Bundi, Sawai Madhopur and Dholpur to join the Yamuna. It is famous for its badland topography, the Chambal ravines.

The Ramganga is a comparatively small river rising in the Garhwal hills near Gairsain. It turns south-west after crossing the Shiwalik, enters the plains of Uttar Pradesh near Najibabad and joins the Ganga near Kannauj.

The Damodar occupies the eastern margins of the Chotanagpur plateau, flowing through a rift valley to join the Hugli. The Barakar is its main tributary. Once called the 'sorrow of Bengal', it has been tamed by the Damodar Valley Corporation, a multipurpose project.

ex.q: Name the river: (a) westernmost and longest tributary of the Ganga; (b) known for badland ravines; (c) once the 'sorrow of Bengal'.
st: (a) Westernmost and longest tributary → Yamuna.
(b) Badland topography → Chambal.
(c) 'Sorrow of Bengal', tamed by the DVC → Damodar.
ex.a: (a) Yamuna; (b) Chambal; (c) Damodar.

topics.rl: The National Chambal Sanctuary protects gharials, dolphins and turtles along the Chambal's ravine-lined course.

topics.t: Ganga tributaries from the north: Gandak, Ghaghara, Kosi, Sarda and Mahananda
topics.h: Rivers from the Nepal Himalaya pour into the Ganga from the north, bringing water, fertile silt and sometimes devastating floods to UP and Bihar.
p: The important left-bank tributaries of the Ganga are the Ramganga, Gomati, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi and Mahananda.

The Gandak comprises two streams, the Kaligandak and Trishulganga. It rises in the Nepal Himalaya between the Dhaulagiri and Mount Everest, drains central Nepal, enters the Ganga plain in Champaran district of Bihar, and joins the Ganga at Sonpur near Patna.

The Ghaghara originates in the glaciers of Mapchachungo. After collecting the waters of the Tila, Seti and Beri, it cuts a deep gorge at Shishapani. The Sarda joins it in the plains before it meets the Ganga at Chhapra.

The Kosi is an antecedent river with its source north of Mount Everest in Tibet, where its main stream, the Arun, rises. After crossing the Central Himalaya in Nepal, it is joined by the Son Kosi from the west and the Tamur Kosi from the east, forming the Sapt Kosi with the Arun.

The Sarda or Saryu rises in the Milam glacier in the Nepal Himalaya, where it is called the Goriganga; along the Indo-Nepal border it is called the Kali or Chauk, and it joins the Ghaghara. The Mahananda rises in the Darjeeling hills and joins the Ganga as its last left-bank tributary in West Bengal.

ex.q: Arrange these left-bank tributaries from west to east by where they join the Ganga system: Ghaghara (at Chhapra), Gandak (at Sonpur), Mahananda (in West Bengal).
st: Chhapra lies west of Patna in Bihar → Ghaghara joins first.
Sonpur is opposite Patna → Gandak next.
The Mahananda joins in West Bengal, furthest east, as the last left-bank tributary.
ex.a: Ghaghara → Gandak → Mahananda.

topics.rl: The Gandak barrage at Valmikinagar on the India–Nepal border supplies irrigation canals to Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.

topics.t: The Brahmaputra system
topics.h: One river, many names: Tsangpo in Tibet, Siang or Dihang in Arunachal, Brahmaputra in Assam and Jamuna in Bangladesh.
p: The Brahmaputra, one of the largest rivers of the world, originates in the Chemayungdung glacier of the Kailash range near the Mansarovar lake.

It flows eastward for nearly 1,200 km through a dry, flat region of southern Tibet, where it is called the Tsangpo, meaning 'the purifier'. The Rango Tsangpo is its major right-bank tributary in Tibet.

It emerges as a turbulent river after carving a deep gorge in the Central Himalaya near Namcha Barwa (7,755 m), and comes out of the foothills as the Siang or Dihang. It enters India west of Sadiya town in Arunachal Pradesh. Flowing south-west, it receives the Dibang (Sikang) and Lohit on its left bank, and from there it is called the Brahmaputra.

In its 750 km journey through the Assam valley, its major left-bank tributaries are the Burhi Dihing and Dhansari (South); its right-bank tributaries are the Subansiri (an antecedent river from Tibet), Kameng, Manas and Sankosh. It enters Bangladesh near Dhubri; there the Tista joins it on the right bank and it is called the Jamuna, finally merging with the Padma to fall into the Bay of Bengal.

The Brahmaputra is well known for floods, channel shifting and bank erosion, because most of its tributaries are large and bring huge sediment due to heavy rainfall in the catchment. It has many riverine islands, such as Majuli.

ex.q: Trace the names of the Brahmaputra from source to sea.
st: Tibet: Tsangpo.
Arunachal foothills: Siang or Dihang.
After the Dibang and Lohit join in Assam: Brahmaputra.
In Bangladesh after the Tista joins: Jamuna, merging with the Padma.
ex.a: Tsangpo → Siang/Dihang → Brahmaputra → Jamuna.

topics.rl: Every monsoon, Assam's Kaziranga National Park floods as the Brahmaputra spills over, and animals move to raised highlands.

topics.t: Peninsular drainage and its evolution
topics.h: Most big Peninsular rivers rise just 50–100 km from the Arabian Sea, yet travel over 1,000 km east to the Bay of Bengal. Ancient geology explains why.
p: The Peninsular drainage system is older than the Himalayan one, as shown by its broad, largely graded shallow valleys and the maturity of its rivers.

The Western Ghats, running close to the west coast, act as the water divide between the major Peninsular rivers draining into the Bay of Bengal and the small rivulets joining the Arabian Sea. Most major Peninsular rivers, except the Narmada and Tapi, flow from west to east.

Rivers rising in the northern part of the Peninsula, the Chambal, Sind, Betwa, Ken and Son, belong to the Ganga system. Other major systems are the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. Peninsular rivers have fixed courses, an absence of meanders and non-perennial flow; the Narmada and Tapi, flowing through rift valleys, are exceptions and form estuaries.

Evolution, event 1: subsidence of the western flank of the Peninsula, leading to its submergence below the sea during the early Tertiary period, disturbed the symmetrical plan of rivers on either side of the original watershed.

Event 2: during the upheaval of the Himalaya, the northern flank of the Peninsular block subsided, causing trough faulting; the Narmada and Tapi flow in these trough faults and fill the cracks with detritus, so they lack alluvial and deltaic deposits. Event 3: slight tilting of the Peninsular block from north-west to south-east gave the whole drainage its orientation towards the Bay of Bengal.

ex.q: Why do the Narmada and Tapi flow west and form estuaries rather than deltas?
st: They flow through trough faults (rift valleys) formed when the northern flank subsided during the Himalayan upheaval.
These troughs are oriented east–west and open to the Arabian Sea.
The rivers fill the cracks with their detritus and carry little sediment to the mouth.
So they form estuaries, not deltas.
ex.a: Because they occupy west-trending rift valleys (trough faults) and lack alluvial and deltaic deposits.

topics.rl: The broad Narmada estuary near Bharuch, about 27 km long, is a contrast to the huge Godavari delta on the east coast.

topics.t: East-flowing Peninsular rivers
topics.h: The Kaveri flows almost all year, unlike most Peninsular rivers. Its secret: two monsoons feeding two different parts of its basin.
p: Mahanadi: rises near Sihawa in Raipur district of Chhattisgarh and runs through Odisha to the Bay of Bengal. Length 851 km; catchment 1.42 lakh sq km. Some navigation in the lower course. 53% of its basin lies in Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh, 47% in Odisha.

Godavari: the largest Peninsular river system, also called the Dakshin Ganga. It rises in Nasik district of Maharashtra. Length 1,465 km; catchment 3.13 lakh sq km (49% in Maharashtra, 20% in Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh, the rest in Andhra Pradesh). Principal tributaries: Penganga, Indravati, Pranhita and Manjra. It floods in its lower reaches south of Polavaram, where it forms a picturesque gorge; it is navigable only in the deltaic stretch and splits into branches after Rajahmundry.

Krishna: the second largest east-flowing Peninsular river; rises near Mahabaleshwar in the Sahyadri. Length 1,401 km. Major tributaries: Koyna, Tungabhadra and Bhima. Basin: 27% Maharashtra, 44% Karnataka, 29% Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

Kaveri: rises in the Brahmagiri hills (1,341 m) of Kodagu district, Karnataka. Length 800 km; drains 81,155 sq km. Its upper catchment gets rain in the south-west monsoon (summer) and the lower part in the north-east monsoon (winter), so it flows all year with less fluctuation. Tributaries: Kabini, Bhavani, Amravati. Basin: 3% Kerala, 41% Karnataka, 56% Tamil Nadu.
Smaller east-flowing rivers include the Subarnarekha, Baitarni, Brahmani, Vamsadhara, Penner, Palar and Vaigai.

ex.q: Why does the Kaveri carry water throughout the year with less fluctuation than other Peninsular rivers?
st: Its upper catchment (Karnataka) receives rain from the south-west monsoon in summer.
Its lower catchment (Tamil Nadu) receives rain from the north-east monsoon in winter.
So it gets water in two seasons.
Its flow is therefore more even across the year.
ex.a: Because different parts of its basin receive rain from both the south-west and north-east monsoons.

topics.rl: The Hirakud dam on the Mahanadi in Odisha is one of the longest earthen dams in the world, built for flood control and irrigation.

topics.t: West-flowing rivers and map work
topics.h: Near Jabalpur, the Narmada thunders over the Dhuandhar falls and cuts through gleaming marble cliffs at Bhedaghat.
p: Narmada: originates on the western flank of the Amarkantak plateau at about 1,057 m. It flows in a rift valley between the Satpura (south) and the Vindhyan range (north), forming a picturesque gorge in marble rocks and the Dhuandhar waterfall near Jabalpur. After about 1,312 km, it meets the Arabian Sea south of Bharuch, forming a broad 27 km long estuary. Catchment about 98,796 sq km. The Sardar Sarovar Project is built on it.
Tapi: rises at Multai in Betul district of Madhya Pradesh. Length 724 km; drains 65,145 sq km. About 79% of its basin is in Maharashtra, 15% in Madhya Pradesh and 6% in Gujarat.

Luni: the largest river system of Rajasthan west of the Aravali. It originates near Pushkar in two branches, the Saraswati and Sabarmati, which join at Govindgarh; from there it is called the Luni. It flows west till Telwara, then south-west to the Rann of Kachchh. The entire system is ephemeral.

Smaller west-flowing rivers: in Gujarat, the Shetruniji, Bhadra, Dhadhar, Sabarmati and Mahi; in Goa, the Mandovi and Zuari; in Karnataka, the Sharavati (which forms the Jog or Gersoppa falls); in Kerala, the Bharathapuzha (also called Ponnani; it rises near the Anaimalai hills), the Periyar (second largest in Kerala) and the Pamba (falling into Vembanad lake).

Map work: locate the Brahmaputra, Indus, Satluj, Ganga, Yamuna, Chambal, Damodar, Mahanadi, Krishna, Kaveri, Godavari, Narmada, Tapi and Luni; lakes Wular, Sambhar, Chilika, Kolleru, Pulicat and Vembanad; and the Palk Strait, Rann of Kachchh, Gulf of Kachchh, Gulf of Mannar and Gulf of Khambhat.

ex.q: What percentage of the Tapi basin lies outside Maharashtra?
st: Maharashtra share = 79%.
Outside Maharashtra = 100 − 79 = 21%.
(This is 15% in Madhya Pradesh + 6% in Gujarat.)

topics.rl: The Sardar Sarovar dam on the Narmada supplies drinking and irrigation water to Gujarat and parts of Rajasthan.

topics.t: Himalayan vs Peninsular rivers; using river water
topics.h: India has some of the world's mightiest rivers, yet many cities face water shortages. The problem is not just how much water flows, but when, where and how clean.
p: Origin: Himalayan rivers rise in glacier-covered Himalayan mountains; Peninsular rivers rise in the Peninsular plateau and central highland. Flow: Himalayan rivers are perennial (glacier melt and rain); Peninsular rivers are seasonal (monsoon rain). Regime: Himalayan rivers have high flow in summer from both snowmelt and monsoon; Peninsular river flow depends on rainfall and fluctuates.

Type of drainage: Himalayan rivers are antecedent and consequent, giving dendritic patterns in the plains; Peninsular rivers are superimposed and rejuvenated, giving trellis, radial and rectangular patterns.

Nature: Himalayan rivers have long courses through rugged mountains with headward erosion and river capturing, and meander and shift course in the plains; Peninsular rivers have smaller, fixed courses with well-adjusted valleys. Catchment: very large basins vs relatively smaller basins. Age: young and youthful, actively deepening valleys vs old rivers with graded profiles that have almost reached base level.

Problems in using river water: non-availability of sufficient water; river water pollution; load of silt; uneven seasonal flow; river water disputes between states; and shrinking of channels due to the extension of settlements towards the thalweg (deepest part of the channel).

Pollution from sewage, industrial and agricultural wastes has made stretches of the Ganga and Yamuna highly polluted; the Namami Gange programme aims to clean the Ganga. Inter-linking of rivers to transfer surplus water to deficit areas has been proposed; supporters stress drought relief and irrigation, while critics raise concerns about cost, displacement and ecology.

ex.q: Compare the Ganga and the Godavari on flow, age and drainage pattern.
st: Flow: Ganga is perennial (snow and rain); Godavari is seasonal (monsoon rain).
Age: Ganga is young and actively eroding in the mountains; Godavari is old with a graded profile.
Pattern: Ganga shows dendritic drainage in the plains; Peninsular rivers like the Godavari show trellis, radial or rectangular patterns.
ex.a: Ganga: perennial, young, dendritic. Godavari: seasonal, old, trellis/radial/rectangular.

topics.rl: The Ken–Betwa link project between Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh is India's first river-interlinking project to be taken up, and it has been debated for its benefits and environmental impact.

topics.t: Weather, climate and the monsoon type
topics.h: A rainy afternoon in Pune is weather. Pune's pattern of wet summers and dry winters, year after year, is its climate.
p: Weather is the momentary state of the atmosphere; climate is the average of weather conditions over a long period of time (more than thirty years).
Weather changes quickly, within a day or a week, while climate changes very slowly and may be noticed only after many years.
The elements of weather and climate are temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind, humidity and precipitation.
India has a 'monsoon' type of climate, which is found mainly in South and South-east Asia.
The monsoon regime emphasises the unity of India with the rest of South-east Asia, even though there are many regional variations within India.

ex.q: Classify: (a) 'It is 39°C and humid in Chennai today'; (b) 'Chennai gets most of its rain in October–November every year'.
st: (a) describes the state of the atmosphere at one moment → weather.
(b) describes the long-term average pattern → climate.
ex.a: (a) Weather; (b) Climate.

topics.rl: IMD issues daily weather forecasts, but its 30-year climate normals are what planners use to design dams and crop calendars.

topics.t: Diversity within India's monsoon climate and Koeppen's regions
topics.h: On the same winter night, Drass in Ladakh can drop to −45°C while Thiruvananthapuram stays at 22°C.
p: Temperature varies greatly: in summer, the Rajasthan desert may reach about 50°C while Pahalgam in Kashmir is around 20°C. On a winter night, Drass may be as low as −45°C while Thiruvananthapuram has 22°C.

Precipitation varies in form and amount: snowfall occurs in the Himalaya while the rest of India gets rain. Cherrapunji and Mawsynram in the Khasi hills receive over 1,080 cm a year, while Jaisalmer rarely gets more than 9 cm.
Seasons differ: most of India gets rain from June to September, but the Tamil Nadu coast gets most of its rain in October and November (early winter).
Differences in winds, temperature, rainfall, the rhythm of seasons and the degree of wetness or dryness create regional diversity within the overall monsoon unity.

Koeppen's scheme for India: Amw (west coast south of Goa), As (Coromandel coast of Tamil Nadu), Aw (most of the Peninsular plateau south of the Tropic of Cancer), BShw (north-western Gujarat, parts of western Rajasthan and Punjab), BWhw (extreme western Rajasthan), Cwg (Ganga plain, eastern Rajasthan, northern Madhya Pradesh, most of the North-east), Dfc (Arunachal Pradesh), E (Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand).

ex.q: How many times more rain does Mawsynram (about 1,080 cm) get than Jaisalmer (about 9 cm)?
ex.a: About 120 times more.

topics.rl: The same IMD monsoon forecast can mean floods in Assam and drought worries in western Rajasthan.

topics.t: Factors determining India's climate: location and relief
topics.h: Agra and Darjeeling lie at almost the same latitude, yet in January Agra averages about 16°C and Darjeeling only about 4°C.
p: Latitude: the Tropic of Cancer passes through the middle of India; the area south of it is tropical and the area north of it is subtropical (warm temperate), with greater extremes of temperature.
The Himalaya act as an effective climatic divide: they protect the subcontinent from cold northern winds and trap the monsoon winds, forcing them to shed their moisture within the subcontinent.

Distribution of land and water: India is flanked by the Indian Ocean on three sides in the south and a high, continuous mountain wall in the north. Land and water heat and cool differently, creating different air pressure zones in different seasons, which causes the reversal of monsoon winds.

Distance from the sea: coastal areas have an equable or maritime climate; interior areas far from the sea's moderating influence have extreme climates (continentality), e.g. Delhi, Kanpur and Amritsar.

Altitude: temperature decreases with height (Agra 16°C vs Darjeeling 4°C in January). Relief affects temperature, pressure, wind direction and speed and rainfall: windward slopes of the Western Ghats and Assam get heavy rain, while the southern plateau in their rain shadow stays dry.

ex.q: Why is Mumbai's climate more equable than Delhi's?
st: Mumbai is on the coast; the sea heats and cools slowly.
Sea breezes moderate Mumbai's temperature: maritime climate.
Delhi is far from the sea, so land heats and cools quickly: continental climate.
So Mumbai has a smaller temperature range.
ex.a: Because of distance from the sea: Mumbai is maritime, Delhi is continental.

topics.rl: Shimla and Ooty became summer capitals and hill retreats because altitude makes them far cooler than the plains.

topics.t: Pressure, winds and jet streams in winter
topics.h: January snow in Kashmir and winter showers in Punjab are delivered by storms that began over the Mediterranean Sea, carried by a river of fast wind high in the sky.
p: Three factors related to air pressure and winds shape India's climate: (i) the distribution of air pressure and winds on the earth's surface; (ii) upper air circulation, caused by global weather controls and the inflow of different air masses and jet streams; (iii) the inflow of western cyclones (disturbances) in winter and tropical depressions in the south-west monsoon period.

In winter, weather is governed by pressure in Central and Western Asia. A high-pressure centre develops to the north of the Himalaya, and dry continental winds blow from it towards the low pressure over the oceans to the south; in north-western India these winds meet the trade winds.

Jet streams: in winter, Western and Central Asia lie under westerly winds blowing at 9–13 km from west to east. The Tibetan highlands act as a barrier and split this jet stream into two branches: one north of the Tibetan highlands and a southern branch blowing eastward south of the Himalaya, over India (mean position in February about 25°N).

Western cyclonic disturbances enter India from the west and north-west in winter. They originate over the Mediterranean Sea and are brought into India by the westerly jet stream; a rise in night temperature generally signals their approach.

Tropical cyclones originate over the Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean (mainly October–December). With very high winds and heavy rain, they hit the Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha coasts and are very destructive.

ex.q: Why does winter rain in Punjab and snow in Kashmir come from the west?
st: Western disturbances originate over the Mediterranean Sea.
The westerly jet stream steers them eastward into India.
They bring rain to north-western plains and snow to the western Himalaya.
ex.a: Because western disturbances from the Mediterranean are carried in by the westerly jet stream.

topics.rl: IMD's winter bulletins regularly track 'western disturbances' that bring rain to Delhi and snow to Gulmarg and Shimla.

topics.t: Summer mechanism: ITCZ, monsoon trough and the easterly jet
topics.h: By mid-July, a band of low pressure stretches across the Ganga plain. Winds from as far as the Southern Hemisphere rush towards it, and that rush is our monsoon.
p: The Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is a low-pressure zone at the equator where trade winds converge, so air tends to rise there. In July it lies around 20°N–25°N over the Gangetic plain and is sometimes called the monsoon trough. It encourages a thermal low over north and north-west India.

Due to the shift of the ITCZ, the trade winds of the Southern Hemisphere cross the equator between 40°E and 60°E and, deflected by the Coriolis force, blow from south-west to north-east: the south-west monsoon. In winter the ITCZ moves south and winds reverse, blowing from the north-east: the north-east monsoon.

By the middle of July the westerly jet stream withdraws from the Indian region. An easterly jet stream flows over the southern Peninsula in June (maximum speed about 90 km/h); in August it is confined to about 15°N and in September to about 22°N.
The easterly jet stream steers tropical depressions into India. These depressions play a big role in distributing monsoon rain; their tracks are the areas of highest rainfall in India.

'Monsoon' means a seasonal reversal in wind direction. Our understanding of it has grown through observations from ships and aircraft, satellite data and research programmes such as the Monsoon Experiment (MONEX).

ex.q: Why do the south-east trade winds become south-west monsoon winds after crossing the equator?
st: The ITCZ shifts north to about 20°N–25°N in summer.
The trades of the Southern Hemisphere are drawn across the equator towards it.
North of the equator the Coriolis force deflects winds to the right.
So south-east trades turn into south-westerly winds: the south-west monsoon.
ex.a: Because the Coriolis force deflects them to the right after they cross the equator.

topics.rl: INSAT and other Indian weather satellites track the monsoon trough and depressions daily for IMD's forecasts.

topics.t: Onset of the monsoon, El Nino and the Southern Oscillation
topics.h: Every year around 1 June, all of India watches Kerala. When the monsoon arrives there, it races north to cover the country within about six weeks.
p: The classical explanation (going back to Edmond Halley) is differential heating of land and sea. In April–May, when the sun shines vertically over the Tropic of Cancer, the large landmass north of the Indian Ocean is intensely heated, creating an intense low over north-western India and Pakistan, while the ocean to the south stays at higher pressure. This thermal low pulls in the south-east trades across the equator.

The south-west monsoon is thus a continuation of the south-east trades, deflected towards India after crossing the equator (between 40°E and 60°E). The northward shift of the ITCZ is linked with the withdrawal of the westerly jet stream; the easterly jet that sets in along 15°N after this is held responsible for the burst of the monsoon.
Onset: the south-west monsoon sets in over the Kerala coast by about 1 June, reaches Mumbai and Kolkata between about 10 and 13 June, and by mid-July covers the entire subcontinent.

El Nino is a warm current that appears off the coast of Peru in some years (once every three to seven years), replacing the cold Peruvian (Humboldt) current and raising water temperature by about 10°C. It distorts equatorial atmospheric circulation, causes irregular evaporation of sea water and reduces plankton (and fish). The name means 'Child Christ' as it appears around Christmas. India uses it for long-range monsoon forecasting.

Southern Oscillation (SO): normally, when the tropical eastern South Pacific has high pressure, the tropical eastern Indian Ocean has low pressure; in some years this reverses. The pressure difference between Tahiti (Pacific) and Darwin (northern Australia) is used to predict monsoon intensity; a negative difference suggests below-average and late monsoons. El Nino and SO together are ENSO.

ex.q: The monsoon reaches Kerala on 1 June and covers the whole country by 15 July. How many days does it take?
st: Days left in June after 1 June: 30 − 1 = 29.
Days in July up to 15 July: 15.
Total = 29 + 15 = 44 days.
ex.a: 44 days (about six weeks).

topics.rl: IMD's April long-range forecast discusses whether El Nino conditions are expected, because an El Nino year often raises fears of a weak monsoon.

topics.t: Monsoon arrival, rain-bearing systems, burst and breaks
topics.h: Mumbai's first monsoon downpour, with thunder and lightning, can drop the temperature by several degrees in an hour. That's the 'burst'.
p: By early June the low pressure over north-western India becomes powerful enough to attract the trade winds of the Southern Hemisphere. Crossing the equator and passing over warm waters, they bring abundant moisture; following a south-westerly direction, they are the south-west monsoon.

Rain begins abruptly. The sudden onset of moisture-laden winds with violent thunder and lightning is called the 'burst' of the monsoon. It may come in the first week of June on the coasts of Kerala, Karnataka, Goa and Maharashtra, but be delayed to the first week of July in the interior. Day temperatures fall by 5°C–8°C between mid-June and mid-July. The monsoon covers the country in about a month.
The monsoon approaches the landmass in two branches: the Arabian Sea branch and the Bay of Bengal branch.

Two rain-bearing systems: the first originates in the Bay of Bengal (tropical depressions) and brings rain to the plains of north India; the second is the Arabian Sea current, which brings rain to the west coast. Rain on the Western Ghats is mostly orographic; its intensity depends on offshore meteorological conditions and the position of the equatorial jet stream along East Africa. The paths of Bay of Bengal depressions are set by the position of the monsoon trough, whose axis oscillates.

A break in the monsoon is when rain fails for one or more weeks after a few rainy days. In northern India, breaks occur when rain-bearing storms are infrequent along the monsoon trough (ITCZ); on the west coast, dry spells occur when winds blow parallel to the coast.

ex.q: Why might the Konkan coast have a dry week in the middle of July?
st: West-coast rain needs moist winds blowing onto the Western Ghats.
If winds blow parallel to the coast, they do not rise up the Ghats.
Without uplift, there is little orographic rain.
So a dry spell (break) occurs.
ex.a: Because the monsoon winds are blowing parallel to the coast.

topics.rl: Farmers watch for monsoon breaks: a long break in July can wilt freshly sown kharif crops like soybean and cotton.

topics.t: Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches; nature of monsoon rainfall
topics.h: Mawsynram, on the crest of the Khasi hills, receives the highest average annual rainfall in the world, while the Tamil Nadu coast stays fairly dry in the same season.
