p: Arabian Sea branch splits into three: (i) one is obstructed by the Western Ghats; climbing to 900–1,200 m, it gives the windward Sahyadri and west coastal plain 250–400 cm of rain, then descends and warms, leaving a rain-shadow east of the Ghats; (ii) another strikes the coast north of Mumbai, moves along the Narmada and Tapi valleys into central India (the Chotanagpur plateau gets about 15 cm from it) and joins the Bay of Bengal branch in the Ganga plains; (iii) a third strikes Saurashtra and Kachchh, passes over west Rajasthan along the Aravali with scanty rain, and joins the Bay of Bengal branch in Punjab and Haryana. Together they bring rain to the western Himalaya.

Bay of Bengal branch strikes Myanmar and south-east Bangladesh; the Arakan Hills deflect much of it towards India, so it enters West Bengal and Bangladesh from the south and south-east. It splits: one branch moves west along the Ganga plains up to Punjab; the other moves up the Brahmaputra valley, giving widespread rain; a sub-branch strikes the Garo and Khasi hills, where Mawsynram gets the world's highest average annual rainfall.
The Tamil Nadu coast stays dry in this season because (i) it lies parallel to the Bay of Bengal branch and (ii) it is in the rain shadow of the Arabian Sea branch.

Characteristics of monsoon rainfall: seasonal (June–September); largely governed by relief (over 250 cm on the windward Ghats); declining with distance from the sea (Kolkata about 119 cm, Patna 105 cm, Allahabad 76 cm, Delhi 56 cm in the season); wet spells interrupted by breaks; heavy downpours causing runoff and soil erosion; over three-fourths of India's rain comes in this season; uneven spatial distribution (12 cm to over 250 cm); and uncertain onset and withdrawal.

ex.q: Using the monsoon-season rainfall figures, how much less rain does Delhi get than Kolkata?
st: Kolkata ≈ 119 cm; Delhi ≈ 56 cm.
Difference = 119 − 56 = 63 cm.
This shows rainfall declining with distance from the sea along the Bay of Bengal branch.
ex.a: About 63 cm less.

topics.rl: Cherrapunji and Mawsynram in Meghalaya compete for the title of wettest place on earth, both thanks to the Bay of Bengal branch hitting the Khasi hills.

topics.t: The cold weather season
topics.h: In January, Punjab may shiver near freezing at night while Thiruvananthapuram enjoys a balmy 31°C afternoon. The cold season is a northern story.
p: Meteorologists recognise four seasons: the cold weather season, the hot weather season, the south-west monsoon season and the retreating monsoon season.

The cold weather season begins from mid-November in northern India and lasts till February; December and January are the coldest months in the northern plain. Mean daily temperature stays below 21°C over most of northern India; nights can go below freezing in Punjab and Rajasthan. Reasons: distance from the sea (continental climate), snowfall in the nearby Himalaya creating cold waves, and cold winds from the Caspian Sea and Turkmenistan bringing cold waves, frost and fog around February.

Temperature decreases from south to north. The Peninsula has no well-defined cold season because of the sea's moderating influence and nearness to the equator; e.g. Thiruvananthapuram's mean maximum is about 31°C in January and 29.5°C in June.

Pressure and winds: feeble high pressure over the northern plain and slightly lower pressure in the south; light winds (3–5 km/h) blow outward from the north-west, westerly or north-westerly down the Ganga valley, northerly in the delta and north-easterly over the Bay of Bengal. Winter monsoon winds generally do not cause rain because they blow from land to sea and carry little moisture.

Exceptions: weak temperate cyclones from the Mediterranean (western disturbances) give rain in Punjab, Haryana, Delhi and western UP; though meagre, it is very useful for rabi crops (the winter rain known locally as 'mahawat'), and falls as snow in the lower Himalaya, sustaining summer river flow. This rain decreases from west to east in the plains. In October–November, the north-east monsoon picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and gives torrential rain to the Tamil Nadu coast, southern Andhra Pradesh, south-east Karnataka and south-east Kerala.

ex.q: Why do north-east winter winds give heavy rain to Tamil Nadu but not to most of India?
st: Over most of India, winter winds blow from land to sea and are dry.
Over the Bay of Bengal, the north-east winds pick up moisture.
They then strike the Tamil Nadu coast.
So Tamil Nadu gets rain while the rest of India stays dry.
ex.a: Because only after crossing the Bay of Bengal do these winds become moist.

topics.rl: Wheat farmers in Punjab and Haryana welcome a few winter showers from western disturbances, as they help the rabi crop.

topics.t: The hot weather season and its local storms
topics.h: Mango showers ripen Kerala's mangoes, blossom showers bring out coffee flowers, and Bengal's Kalbaisakhi storms help tea, jute and rice. Summer storms have names and jobs!
p: With the sun's apparent northward movement towards the Tropic of Cancer in March, temperatures rise in north India; April, May and June are summer months there. In March the highest temperature, about 38°C, is on the Deccan Plateau; in April, 38°C–43°C in Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh; in May the heat belt moves north, and in north-west India temperatures around 48°C are not uncommon.
The hot season in south India is milder because of the moderating ocean: temperatures stay between 26°C and 32°C. Due to altitude, the hills of the Western Ghats remain below 25°C.

Pressure and winds: excessive heat and falling pressure in the north. The ITCZ moves north, centred at about 25°N in July; the monsoon trough extends from the Thar desert to Patna and the Chotanagpur plateau. In the north-west, hot, dry winds called 'loo' blow in the afternoon, often into midnight. Evening dust storms are common in May in Punjab, Haryana, eastern Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.

Local storms: (i) Mango shower: pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and coastal Karnataka that help mangoes ripen early. (ii) Blossom shower: makes coffee flowers blossom in Kerala and nearby areas. (iii) Nor'westers: dreaded evening thunderstorms in Bengal and Assam, called 'Kalbaisakhi' (calamity of the month of Baisakh) in Bengal and 'Bardoli Chheerha' in Assam; useful for tea, jute and rice. (iv) Loo: hot, dry, oppressive winds in the northern plains from Punjab to Bihar, strongest between Delhi and Patna.

ex.q: Name the local storm: (a) evening thunderstorm in Bengal in April; (b) pre-monsoon shower in Kerala that ripens mangoes; (c) hot dry afternoon wind between Delhi and Patna.
st: (a) Evening thunderstorm in Bengal → Nor'wester (Kalbaisakhi).
(b) Ripens mangoes → mango shower.
(c) Hot, dry wind in northern plains → loo.
ex.a: (a) Kalbaisakhi (Nor'wester); (b) Mango shower; (c) Loo.

topics.rl: Coffee growers in Kodagu and Wayanad wait anxiously for the 'blossom shower' in March–April that triggers flowering.

topics.t: Retreating monsoon and the traditional Indian seasons
topics.h: Ancient Indian calendars split the year into six seasons, from Vasanta to Shishira. Modern meteorologists use four, including the 'October heat' of the retreating monsoon.
p: October and November are the months of the retreating monsoon. By the end of September the south-west monsoon weakens as the low-pressure trough of the Ganga plain moves south with the sun's southward march.

The monsoon retreats from western Rajasthan by the first week of September and from Rajasthan, Gujarat, the western Ganga plain and the Central Highlands by the end of September. By early October the low pressure covers the northern Bay of Bengal, by early November it moves over Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and by mid-December it leaves the Peninsula entirely.

This season has clear skies and rising temperature while the land is still moist; the high temperature and humidity make the weather oppressive, known as 'October heat'. In the second half of October temperatures fall rapidly in the north.

The weather is dry in north India but rainy in the eastern Peninsula, where October and November are the rainiest months. Cyclonic depressions from the Andaman Sea cross the east coast; these destructive tropical cyclones target the thickly populated deltas of the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. A bulk of the Coromandel coast's rainfall comes from these depressions and cyclones.

Traditional six seasons of two months each: Vasanta (spring, Chaitra–Vaisakha, March–April), Grishma (summer, Jyaistha–Asadha, May–June), Varsha (rainy, Sravana–Bhadra, July–August), Sharada (autumn, Asvina–Kartika, September–October), Hemanta (pre-winter, Margashirsa–Pausa, November–December) and Shishira (winter, Magha–Phalguna, January–February).

ex.q: Why is October oppressive in many parts of India even after the rains end?
st: The monsoon withdraws and skies become clear.
Clear skies let temperatures rise.
The land is still moist, so humidity stays high.
High temperature plus high humidity makes it oppressive: 'October heat'.
ex.a: Because of high temperature combined with high humidity after the rains (October heat).

topics.rl: Chennai gets most of its annual rain in October–December from depressions and cyclones of the retreating monsoon season.

topics.t: Distribution of rainfall in India
topics.h: India's average annual rainfall is about 125 cm, but that average hides places with over 1,000 cm and places with under 50 cm.
p: India's average annual rainfall is about 125 cm, with great spatial variation.

High rainfall (over 200 cm): the west coast, the Western Ghats, the sub-Himalayan areas of the north-east and the hills of Meghalaya. In some parts of the Khasi and Jaintia hills, rainfall exceeds 1,000 cm. (In the Brahmaputra valley and adjoining hills it is less than 200 cm.)

Medium rainfall (100–200 cm): southern Gujarat, east Tamil Nadu, the north-eastern Peninsula (Odisha, Jharkhand, Bihar, eastern Madhya Pradesh), the northern Ganga plain along the sub-Himalaya, the Cachar valley and Manipur.
Low rainfall (50–100 cm): western Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, Haryana, Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, eastern Rajasthan, Gujarat and the Deccan Plateau.

Inadequate rainfall (less than 50 cm): parts of the Peninsula, especially in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Maharashtra, Ladakh and most of western Rajasthan. Snowfall is restricted to the Himalayan region.

ex.q: Classify by rainfall zone: Konkan coast, Odisha, Punjab, Ladakh.
st: Konkan coast (west coast) → high, over 200 cm.
Odisha (north-eastern Peninsula) → medium, 100–200 cm.
Punjab → low, 50–100 cm.
Ladakh → inadequate, less than 50 cm.
ex.a: Konkan: high; Odisha: medium; Punjab: low; Ladakh: inadequate.

topics.rl: Low-rainfall Punjab grows huge amounts of rice and wheat only because of canal and tube-well irrigation.

topics.t: Variability of rainfall and the monsoon as the axis of agriculture
topics.h: In Kerala, the monsoon almost never fails; in western Rajasthan, one year can bring floods and the next a severe drought. That uncertainty is called variability.
p: Variability of rainfall is measured by the coefficient of variation: C.V. = (Standard deviation ÷ Mean) × 100. It shows how much rainfall deviates from the mean; actual rainfall in some places deviates by 20–50%.

Variability less than 25% exists on the west coast, Western Ghats, north-eastern Peninsula, eastern Ganga plains, north-east India, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and south-western Jammu and Kashmir; these areas get over 100 cm a year.

Variability over 50% exists in western Rajasthan, northern Jammu and Kashmir and the interior Deccan plateau; these areas get less than 50 cm a year. The rest of India has 25–50% variability with 50–100 cm of rain. So, generally, the lower the rainfall, the higher its variability. Map work: compare the annual rainfall map with the variability map.

The monsoon is the axis around which India's entire agricultural cycle revolves, because about 64% of people depend on agriculture for their livelihood, and agriculture itself is based on the south-west monsoon.
Except the Himalaya, all parts of India have temperatures above the threshold level for growing crops throughout the year, and regional variations in the monsoon climate help grow a variety of crops.

ex.q: A place has mean annual rainfall of 40 cm and a standard deviation of 22 cm. Find its coefficient of variation.
ex.a: 55%, high variability, typical of dry areas like western Rajasthan.

topics.rl: Crop insurance under PM Fasal Bima Yojana is especially important in high-variability districts where monsoon failure is common.

topics.t: Monsoon and economic life; global warming
topics.h: A good monsoon can lift farm incomes, tractor sales and even stock markets. A failed one can mean drought, debt and higher food prices.
p: Variability of rainfall brings droughts or floods every year in some part of the country. Agricultural prosperity depends on timely and adequately distributed rain; if it fails, farming suffers, especially where irrigation is not developed.
A sudden monsoon burst causes soil erosion over large areas. Winter rainfall from temperate cyclones in north India is highly beneficial for rabi crops.
Regional climatic variation is reflected in India's vast variety of food, clothes and house types (e.g. sloping roofs in rainy regions, thick walls in hot deserts).

Global warming: climate is changing due to natural and human-induced causes. Rising greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide since the industrial revolution, are causing global warming. The mean annual surface temperature of the earth has increased over the past 150 years, and it is projected that global average temperature may rise by about 2°C by 2100.

Higher temperatures melt polar ice caps and mountain glaciers; the resulting sea-level rise would submerge coastal areas and islands such as the Maldives and low-lying deltas. Reducing emissions is a shared global concern. Exam tip: practise seasons and local storms, climate factors, the monsoon mechanism with jet streams and El Nino, why Tamil Nadu gets winter rain, rainfall distribution and variability, and the monsoon's role in economic life.

ex.q: Give two ways the monsoon helps and two ways it harms the Indian economy.
st: Helps: timely, well-distributed rain boosts kharif harvests.
Helps: winter rain from western disturbances benefits rabi crops in the north.
Harms: variability brings floods or droughts every year somewhere.
Harms: sudden bursts cause soil erosion.
ex.a: Helps: good kharif harvests, rabi benefit from winter rain. Harms: floods/droughts, soil erosion.

topics.rl: RBI and the government watch monsoon progress closely because it affects food inflation, rural demand and overall growth.

topics.t: Natural vegetation and the types of forests
topics.h: Oak forests in Uttarakhand, rainforests in the Andamans, mangroves in the Sundarbans and cactus-like shrubs in Rajasthan: India's vegetation follows its rainfall and temperature.
p: Natural vegetation is a plant community that has been left undisturbed over a long time, so that its species have adjusted to the climate and soil conditions as fully as possible.
Forests grow wild without human help; planted vegetation such as gardens and orchards is not natural vegetation.

India's vegetation varies: temperate vegetation in the Himalaya, tropical rainforests in the Western Ghats and Andaman and Nicobar Islands, mangroves in the deltas, and desert and semi-desert vegetation like cacti and thorny bushes in Rajasthan.
Variation in vegetation is mainly due to climate (rainfall and temperature) and soil.

India's forests are classified into five major types: (i) tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen; (ii) tropical deciduous; (iii) tropical thorn; (iv) montane; (v) littoral and swamp forests. Map work: mark these on an outline map of India.

ex.q: Is a mango orchard in Ratnagiri natural vegetation? Is a sal forest in Jharkhand?
st: Natural vegetation grows without human help and is left undisturbed for long.
A mango orchard is planted and tended → not natural vegetation.
A sal forest grows wild → natural vegetation.
ex.a: Orchard: not natural vegetation; sal forest: natural vegetation.

topics.rl: The Forest Survey of India's maps show how India's vegetation belts closely follow rainfall belts.

topics.t: Tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen forests
topics.h: In the Western Ghats rainforest, some trees tower 60 m high, and the forest never looks bare because different trees shed leaves at different times.
p: Tropical evergreen forests are found on the western slope of the Western Ghats, the hills of the north-eastern region and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
They grow in warm, humid areas with annual precipitation over 200 cm and mean annual temperature above 22°C.

They are well stratified: shrubs and creepers near the ground, short trees, then tall trees reaching 60 m or more. There is no definite time for leaf fall, flowering and fruiting, so they appear green all year. Species: rosewood, mahogany, aini and ebony.

Semi-evergreen forests occur in the less rainy parts of these regions, with a mix of evergreen and moist deciduous trees; undergrowth climbers give them an evergreen character. Species: white cedar, hollock and kail.

Under colonial rule, forests were exploited commercially and their structure changed: oak forests in Garhwal and Kumaon were replaced by chir pine, needed for railway sleepers, and forests were cleared for tea, rubber and coffee plantations.

ex.q: Why do tropical evergreen forests look green all year?
st: The climate is warm and wet throughout the year.
There is no definite season for trees to shed leaves.
Different trees shed, flower and fruit at different times.
So the forest as a whole stays green.
ex.a: Because there is no definite time for leaf fall; trees shed at different times.

topics.rl: Silent Valley in Kerala and the forests of Arunachal Pradesh preserve some of India's finest evergreen forests.

topics.t: Tropical deciduous forests
topics.h: In summer, a dry deciduous forest in Madhya Pradesh looks like a grassland dotted with bare trees. After the monsoon, it bursts back into green.
p: Tropical deciduous forests are the most widespread forests of India, also called monsoon forests. They grow where rainfall is 70–200 cm and are divided into moist and dry deciduous.

Moist deciduous forests grow where rainfall is 100–200 cm: north-eastern states along the Himalayan foothills, eastern slopes of the Western Ghats and Odisha. Species: teak, sal, shisham, hurra, mahua, amla, semul, kusum and sandalwood.

Dry deciduous forests cover vast areas with 70–100 cm rainfall, in the rainier parts of the Peninsula and the plains of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. They grade into moist deciduous on wetter margins and thorn forests on drier ones. Species: tendu, palas, amaltas, bel, khair and axlewood.

In the dry season, trees shed their leaves completely and the forest looks like a vast grassland with naked trees. In higher-rainfall parts, they form a parkland landscape of teak and other trees with patches of grass.
In western and southern Rajasthan, vegetation cover is very scanty due to low rainfall and overgrazing.

ex.q: A forest receives 150 cm of rain and has teak, sal and sandalwood. Classify it.
st: 150 cm lies in 100–200 cm.
Teak, sal and sandalwood are moist deciduous species.
So it is a moist deciduous forest.
ex.a: Tropical moist deciduous forest.

topics.rl: Sandalwood from the moist deciduous forests of Karnataka has long been prized for perfumes and carvings.

topics.t: Tropical thorn forests
topics.h: The khejri tree, sacred to the Bishnoi community, survives in Rajasthan where few others can, with deep roots and small leaves.
p: Tropical thorn forests occur in areas receiving less than 50 cm of rainfall. They consist of a variety of grasses and shrubs.
They include semi-arid areas of south-west Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
Plants remain leafless for most of the year and give the appearance of scrub vegetation. Tussocky grass grows up to 2 m as undergrowth.
Important species: babool, ber, wild date palm, khair, neem, khejri and palas.

ex.q: Why do plants of thorn forests have few leaves for most of the year?
st: Rainfall is below 50 cm, so water is scarce.
Leaves lose water through transpiration.
Staying leafless reduces water loss.
So plants look like scrub most of the year.
ex.a: To reduce water loss in a very dry climate.

topics.rl: Rajasthan's farmers grow khejri trees in their fields for fodder and its pods (sangri), a classic dryland adaptation.

topics.t: Montane forests of the Himalaya
topics.h: Drive from Dehradun to Kedarnath and the forest changes like floors of a building: sal and deciduous trees, then oak, then pine and deodar, then fir and birch, then alpine meadows.
p: In mountainous areas, the decrease in temperature with increasing altitude leads to corresponding changes in natural vegetation. Montane forests are classified as northern mountain forests and southern mountain forests.

In the Himalaya, deciduous forests occur in the foothills, succeeded by wet temperate forests between 1,000 and 2,000 m. In the higher hills of north-eastern India, hilly areas of West Bengal and Uttarakhand, evergreen broad-leaf trees such as oak and chestnut dominate.

Between 1,500 and 1,750 m, pine forests are well developed, with chir pine a very useful commercial tree. Deodar, a highly valued endemic species, grows mainly in the western Himalaya; its durable wood is used in construction.
The chinar and the walnut, which sustain Kashmir's famous handicrafts, belong to this zone. Blue pine and spruce appear at 2,225–3,048 m, and temperate grasslands occur at many places.

Higher up there is a transition to alpine forests and pastures: silver firs, junipers, pines, birch and rhododendrons occur at 3,000–4,000 m. At still higher altitudes, mosses and lichens form tundra vegetation.

ex.q: Arrange in order of increasing altitude: blue pine and spruce, oak and chestnut, mosses and lichens, silver fir and birch.
st: Oak and chestnut: wet temperate forests at 1,000–2,000 m.
Blue pine and spruce: 2,225–3,048 m.
Silver fir and birch: 3,000–4,000 m.
Mosses and lichens: highest, tundra vegetation.
ex.a: Oak and chestnut → blue pine and spruce → silver fir and birch → mosses and lichens.

topics.rl: Kashmir's walnut-wood carving and papier-mâché crafts depend on chinar and walnut trees of the temperate Himalayan zone.

topics.t: Transhumance, slopes and southern montane forests
topics.h: Every summer, Gaddi shepherds of Himachal and Bakarwals of Jammu and Kashmir move their flocks to high meadows, and return before the snows. This seasonal movement is transhumance.
p: Temperate grasslands and alpine pastures are used extensively for transhumance (seasonal movement of herders with their animals) by tribes such as the Gujjars, Bakarwals, Bhotiyas and Gaddis.
The southern slopes of the Himalaya carry thicker vegetation than the drier north-facing slopes because they receive relatively higher precipitation.

Southern mountain forests are found in three areas of Peninsular India: the Western Ghats, the Vindhyas and the Nilgiris. Being closer to the tropics and only about 1,500 m above sea level, they are temperate in higher regions and subtropical in lower regions, especially in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.

The temperate forests are called sholas in the Nilgiris, Anaimalai and Palani hills. Trees of economic significance include magnolia, laurel, cinchona and wattle. Such forests are also found in the Satpura and Maikal ranges.

ex.q: Why are the south-facing slopes of the Himalaya more densely forested?
st: South-facing slopes face the monsoon winds.
They receive more precipitation.
North-facing slopes are drier.
More moisture supports thicker vegetation.
ex.a: Because they receive more precipitation than the drier north-facing slopes.

topics.rl: Cinchona, from which quinine for malaria was made, was grown in the Nilgiris and Darjeeling hills.

topics.t: Wetlands and the Ramsar Convention
topics.h: Siberian cranes once wintered at Bharatpur, and lakhs of flamingos still visit Chilika. Wetlands are lifelines for birds and people.
p: India has a rich variety of wetland habitats, covering about 3.9 million hectares in total. About 70% of this comprises areas under paddy cultivation.

Two sites, Chilika Lake (Odisha) and Keoladeo National Park (Bharatpur, Rajasthan), are protected as waterfowl habitats under the Convention on Wetlands of International Importance, the Ramsar Convention.

India's wetlands fall into eight categories: (i) reservoirs of the Deccan plateau and lagoons and wetlands of the south-west coast; (ii) vast saline expanses of Rajasthan, Gujarat and the Gulf of Kachchh; (iii) freshwater lakes and reservoirs from Gujarat eastwards through Rajasthan (Keoladeo) and Madhya Pradesh; (iv) delta wetlands and lagoons of India's east coast (e.g. Chilika); (v) freshwater marshes of the Gangetic plain; (vi) floodplains of the Brahmaputra and marshes and swamps of the north-east and Himalayan foothills; (vii) lakes and rivers of the montane region of Kashmir and Ladakh; (viii) mangrove forests and other wetlands of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

ex.q: Of India's 3.9 million hectares of wetlands, about 70% is under paddy. Roughly how many million hectares is that?
st: = 2.73 million hectares.
ex.a: About 2.73 million hectares.

topics.rl: India today has many more Ramsar sites, such as Loktak, Wular and the Sundarbans, recognising their global value.

topics.t: Mangrove forests
topics.h: Mangrove roots poke up out of the mud like snorkels, letting the trees breathe in salty, waterlogged soil.
p: Mangrove forests grow along coasts in salt marshes, tidal creeks, mud flats and estuaries. They consist of a number of salt-tolerant (halophytic) plant species.
Criss-crossed by creeks of stagnant water and tidal flows, they shelter a wide variety of birds.
According to NCERT, mangroves in India spread over 6,740 sq km, which is about 7% of the world's mangrove forests.
They are highly developed in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the Sundarbans of West Bengal; other significant areas are the Mahanadi, Godavari and Krishna deltas.
Mangroves are being encroached upon and need conservation.

ex.q: Why can mangroves grow where most trees would die?
st: Coasts and estuaries have salty, waterlogged soil.
Most trees cannot tolerate salt.
Mangroves are salt-tolerant (halophytic).
So they thrive in tidal creeks and mud flats.
ex.a: Because they are salt-tolerant species adapted to tidal, salty conditions.

topics.rl: The Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest shared by India and Bangladesh, is home to the Royal Bengal tiger.

topics.t: Forest cover and the National Forest Policy
topics.h: A plot can be recorded as 'forest' on paper yet have hardly any trees. That is why India distinguishes forest area from forest cover.
p: Forest area is the area notified and recorded as forest land, irrespective of whether trees exist; it is based on State Revenue Department records. Forest cover is the area actually under forest canopy, measured from aerial photographs and satellite imagery.
Forests give direct economic benefits (timber, fuel, fodder, minor forest produce) and indirect social and environmental benefits (soil and water conservation, climate regulation, biodiversity).
India adopted a forest policy in 1952, modified in 1988; the new policy emphasised sustainable forest management, conserving and expanding forest reserves while meeting local needs.

Aims of the policy: (i) bring 33% of the geographical area under forest cover; (ii) maintain environmental stability and restore forests where the ecological balance is disturbed; (iii) conserve the country's natural heritage, biological diversity and genetic pool; (iv) check soil erosion and the extension of desert lands, and reduce floods and droughts.

Further aims: (v) increase forest cover through social forestry and afforestation on degraded land; (vi) increase forest productivity to provide timber, fuel, fodder and food for forest-dependent rural people, and encourage the substitution of wood; (vii) create a massive people's movement involving women to plant trees and stop felling. The Forest Survey of India, headquartered at Dehradun, maps forest cover.

ex.q: India's geographical area is about 3.28 million sq km. What area would 33% forest cover represent? (Million sq km, two decimals.)
st: ≈ 1.08 million sq km.
ex.a: About 1.08 million sq km.

topics.rl: The Forest Survey of India's biennial 'India State of Forest Report' uses satellite data to measure actual forest cover across states.

topics.t: Forests and life; social forestry
topics.h: For many tribal communities, the forest is home, kitchen, pharmacy and temple. Social forestry tries to bring some of those benefits to villages and cities too.
p: For many tribal communities, forests are home, livelihood and existence: they provide food, fruits, edible leaves, honey, nourishing roots and wild game, as well as materials for building houses and items for the arts.

Tribal communities live in harmony with nature and have deep knowledge useful for forest development. They should be made growers of minor forest produce, not merely gatherers, and should participate in conservation.

Social forestry means the management and protection of forests and afforestation on barren lands to help environmental, social and rural development. The National Commission on Agriculture (1976) classified it into urban forestry, rural forestry and farm forestry.

Urban forestry: raising and managing trees on public and private lands in and around cities: green belts, parks, roadside avenues, industrial and commercial green belts. Rural forestry: agro-forestry (trees and crops on the same land, including waste patches, giving food, fodder, fuel, timber and fruit) and community forestry (trees on public or community land such as village pastures, temple land, roadsides, canal banks, strips along railway lines and schools).

Community forestry benefits the community as a whole and lets landless people take part in tree raising and share benefits otherwise limited to landowners. Farm forestry: farmers grow trees on their farms for commercial and non-commercial purposes; state forest departments distribute seedlings free to small and medium farmers; field margins, grasslands and land around homes and cow sheds can be used.

ex.q: Classify: (a) neem trees planted along a canal bank by the panchayat; (b) a farmer growing poplar along his wheat fields; (c) a green belt around an industrial estate.
st: (a) Trees on community land (canal bank) → community forestry (rural forestry).
(b) Trees on a farmer's own land → farm forestry (also agro-forestry).
(c) Green belt in an urban area → urban forestry.
ex.a: (a) Community forestry; (b) Farm forestry; (c) Urban forestry.

topics.rl: Poplar and eucalyptus planted on farms in Punjab and Haryana supply plywood and paper industries, a big success of farm forestry.

topics.t: Wildlife of India and causes of its decline
topics.h: India has only about 2.4% of the world's land but about 4–5% of all known plant and animal species.
p: India has a rich heritage of wildlife: about 4–5% of all known plant and animal species on earth are found in India.
India's great diversity of ecosystems, preserved through the ages, explains this richness.
Causes of decline: (i) industrial and technological advancement increased exploitation of forest resources; (ii) more land cleared for agriculture, settlements, roads, mining and reservoirs.

More causes: (iii) lopping for fodder and fuelwood and removal of small timber by local people; (iv) grazing by domestic cattle harming wildlife habitat; (v) hunting as a sport by the elite in the past, and rampant commercial poaching today; (vi) forest fires.
Wildlife conservation matters because wildlife is part of our natural heritage and supports ecotourism, which brings income and awareness.

ex.q: Identify the cause of wildlife decline: (a) a new mine cutting through elephant forest; (b) villagers lopping branches for fodder; (c) poachers killing rhinos for horn.
st: (a) Clearing land for mining → habitat loss from development.
(b) Lopping for fodder and fuelwood → local pressure on forests.
(c) Killing for trade → commercial poaching.
ex.a: (a) Land clearing for mining; (b) Lopping for fodder; (c) Commercial poaching.

topics.rl: Ecotourism in parks like Jim Corbett and Kaziranga provides jobs to local guides, drivers and homestay owners.

topics.t: Wildlife conservation: laws and protected areas
topics.h: Stories like the Panchatantra and the Jungle Book show how deeply animals are woven into India's culture; laws now give them legal protection too.
p: India has a long tradition of protecting wildlife, reflected in stories such as the Panchatantra and the Jungle Book.

The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 provides the main legal framework. Its two objectives: to protect the endangered species listed in its schedule, and to provide legal support to conservation areas classified as national parks, sanctuaries and closed areas.
The Act was comprehensively amended in 1991, making punishments more stringent and adding protection for specified plant species and endangered animals.
India now has more than 100 national parks and over 500 wildlife sanctuaries.

Map work: national parks such as Corbett (Uttarakhand), Kaziranga (Assam), Ranthambore (Rajasthan), Shivpuri (Madhya Pradesh) and Simlipal (Odisha); bird sanctuaries such as Keoladeo Ghana (Bharatpur, Rajasthan) and Ranganathittu (Karnataka); wildlife sanctuaries such as Periyar (Kerala), Rajaji (Uttarakhand), Mudumalai (Tamil Nadu) and Dachigam (Jammu and Kashmir).

ex.q: How many years after the Wild Life (Protection) Act was it comprehensively amended?
st: Act passed: 1972.
Amended: 1991.
ex.a: 19 years.

topics.rl: Kaziranga's one-horned rhinos and Ranthambore's tigers are protected under the Wild Life (Protection) Act.

topics.t: Project Tiger, Project Elephant and other projects
topics.h: In 2006, India counted about 1,411 tigers. By 2018 the count had roughly doubled to 2,967, one of the world's great conservation comebacks.
p: Project Tiger was launched in 1973 to ensure a viable population of tigers in India for scientific, aesthetic, cultural and ecological values, and to preserve areas of biological importance as natural heritage. It began with 9 tiger reserves and has since grown to over 50 reserves across many states.
Tiger numbers estimated by All-India surveys rose from about 1,411 in 2006 to 2,967 in 2018 (the figure used in NCERT). The next survey, in 2022, estimated about 3,682 tigers.
Project Elephant was launched in 1992 to assist states with free-ranging populations of wild elephants, protecting elephants, their habitats and migration corridors.
Other projects include the Crocodile Breeding Project, Project Hangul (for the Kashmir stag) and the conservation of the Himalayan musk deer.

ex.q: By how many did India's estimated tiger population rise between 2006 (1,411) and 2018 (2,967)?
ex.a: 1,556 tigers, more than doubling.

topics.rl: Corbett, the first national park under Project Tiger, and new reserves like those in central India have helped tiger numbers grow.

topics.t: Biosphere reserves
topics.h: India's first biosphere reserve, the Nilgiri, spreads across three states and links famous parks like Bandipur, Nagarhole, Mudumalai and Silent Valley.
p: A biosphere reserve is a unique and representative ecosystem of terrestrial and coastal areas, internationally recognised within UNESCO's Man and Biosphere (MAB) Programme. It has three objectives: conservation, development, and logistics support (research, monitoring, education and training). India has 18 biosphere reserves, several of which are in UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves.

Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (1986), the first in India, includes the Wyanad wildlife sanctuary, Nagarhole, Bandipur and Mudumalai, the forested hill slopes of Nilambur, the Upper Nilgiri plateau, Silent Valley and the Siruvani hills, spread across Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka.

Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve, in Uttarakhand, includes parts of Chamoli, Almora, Pithoragarh and Bageshwar districts. Its forests are mainly temperate; fauna include the snow leopard, black bear, brown bear and musk deer.

Sundarbans Biosphere Reserve lies in the swampy delta of the Ganga in West Bengal, with mangrove forests; the Royal Bengal tiger here has adapted to the saline, aquatic environment. Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve covers the Indian part of the Gulf of Mannar between India and Sri Lanka, with a chain of 21 islands, estuaries, beaches, coral reefs, seaweeds and mangroves, and rich marine biodiversity.

Other biosphere reserves include Nokrek, Manas, Great Nicobar, Similipal, Dibru-Saikhowa, Dehang-Debang, Pachmarhi, Khangchendzonga, Agasthyamalai, Achanakmar-Amarkantak, Kachchh, Cold Desert, Seshachalam and Panna. Exam tip: expect MCQs on forest types (e.g. sandalwood), Project Tiger, Nanda Devi's location and forest policy targets; definitions of natural vegetation and biosphere reserves; social forestry; and map marking of mangroves and biosphere reserves.

ex.q: Which three states share the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve?
st: It includes Wyanad (Kerala), Nagarhole and Bandipur (Karnataka), and Mudumalai and the Nilgiri plateau (Tamil Nadu).
So it spans three states.
ex.a: Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka.

topics.rl: The Gulf of Mannar's coral reefs and dugongs (sea cows) are protected within its biosphere reserve near Rameswaram.

topics.t: Change and the meaning of a disaster
topics.h: Mountains rise over millions of years; a flash flood rises in minutes. Nature changes at every speed, but we call some changes disasters.
p: Change is a continuous natural process. It varies in speed (fast or slow), magnitude and intensity: from the slow uplift of mountains to sudden earthquakes.
Nature treats change as value-neutral; it is humans who perceive changes as good or bad, desirable or undesirable, depending on how they affect us.
Activity idea: list environmental changes over long periods (e.g. formation of landforms, climate change) and short periods (e.g. floods, landslides), and classify them as desirable or undesirable.

A disaster is an undesirable occurrence resulting from forces largely beyond human control. It strikes quickly with little or no warning, causes or threatens serious disruption of life and property, including death and injury to many people, and needs efforts beyond those normally provided by statutory emergency services.

ex.q: Is the slow formation of the Ganga delta over thousands of years a disaster? Is a cyclone that kills thousands in a day a disaster?
st: A disaster strikes quickly and causes serious loss of life and property.
Delta formation is slow and gradual and creates fertile land → not a disaster.
The cyclone strikes suddenly with huge losses, needing large-scale relief → a disaster.
ex.a: Delta formation: not a disaster; the cyclone: a disaster.

topics.rl: The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) is deployed when a calamity exceeds what local emergency services can handle.

topics.t: Human-made disasters, hazards and changing patterns
topics.h: The 1984 Bhopal gas tragedy shows that disasters are not only natural. Some are made by human mistakes.
p: Some disasters are human-induced: the Bhopal gas tragedy, the Chernobyl nuclear disaster, wars, release of CFCs and greenhouse gases, and environmental pollution (noise, air, water and soil).
Some human activities indirectly intensify disasters: deforestation, unscientific land use and construction in fragile areas can trigger landslides and floods.
Human-made disasters can, to an extent, be prevented; natural disasters cannot be prevented but can be mitigated and managed.

A natural hazard is an element of circumstances in the natural environment that has the potential to cause harm to people, property or both, e.g. ocean currents, steep slopes and unstable structures in the Himalaya, or extreme conditions in deserts and glaciated areas. A hazard becomes a disaster when it actually strikes and causes large losses.

Disasters are becoming more frequent and larger in magnitude. One reason is that, with technology, people increasingly settle in hazard-prone areas such as floodplains, steep slopes and coasts, so perceptions and patterns of disasters have changed.

ex.q: Is a steep, unstable Himalayan slope a hazard or a disaster? What if it collapses onto a village?
st: A hazard is a natural condition with potential to cause harm.
The unstable slope is a hazard.
When it collapses and kills people or destroys property, it becomes a disaster.
ex.a: The slope is a hazard; the collapse affecting the village is a disaster.

topics.rl: Unplanned construction on steep slopes in hill towns has been linked to worse landslide damage during heavy monsoon rains.

topics.t: International efforts: Yokohama Strategy and IDNDR
topics.h: Disasters cross borders, so countries came together in Yokohama, Japan, in 1994 to plan a 'Safer World'.
p: Important milestones in disaster management include the establishment of the National Institute of Disaster Management in India, the Earth Summit at Rio de Janeiro (1992) and the World Conference on Disaster Management at Yokohama, Japan (May 1994).

The UN General Assembly in 1989 took up natural disaster reduction, leading to the 'Yokohama Strategy and Plan of Action for a Safer World' in 1994. The decade 1990–2000 was declared the International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction (IDNDR).

The World Conference on Natural Disaster Reduction was held at Yokohama, Japan, from 23 to 27 May 1994. It recognised that human and economic losses from disasters are rising and that poor and developing countries are hit hardest.
Each country has the sovereign responsibility to protect its citizens from natural disasters. Priority should be given to developing, least developed, land-locked and small island developing states.
Countries should develop and strengthen national capacities and legislation, and promote regional and international cooperation for capacity building, technology sharing and mobilising resources.

ex.q: How many days did the Yokohama World Conference last, from 23 to 27 May 1994 inclusive?
st: Counting both the first and last days: 4 + 1 = 5.
ex.a: 5 days.

topics.rl: India's National Institute of Disaster Management in New Delhi trains officials in planning and response, building national capacity as Yokohama urged.

topics.t: Classification of natural disasters and India's vulnerability
topics.h: Locust swarms, cold waves, avalanches and tsunamis are all natural disasters, but they come from very different parts of the earth system.
p: Natural disasters are classified into four categories: atmospheric, terrestrial, aquatic and biological.
Atmospheric: blizzards, thunderstorms, lightning, tornadoes, tropical cyclones, droughts, hailstorms, frost, heat waves or loo, and cold waves.
Terrestrial: earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides, avalanches, subsidence and soil erosion.

Aquatic: floods, tidal waves, ocean currents, storm surges and tsunamis. Biological: plants and animals as colonisers (e.g. locusts), and insect infestation and fungal, bacterial and viral diseases such as bird flu and dengue.

India is highly vulnerable to disasters because of its large size, great physical diversity, unique geo-climatic conditions and very large population; social and economic inequalities can make some groups even more vulnerable.

ex.q: Classify: (a) heat wave in Rajasthan; (b) avalanche in Kashmir; (c) storm surge in Odisha; (d) locust attack in Gujarat.
st: (a) Heat wave → atmospheric.
(b) Avalanche → terrestrial.
(c) Storm surge → aquatic.
(d) Locusts → biological.
ex.a: (a) Atmospheric; (b) Terrestrial; (c) Aquatic; (d) Biological.

topics.rl: The 2020 locust swarms that damaged crops in Rajasthan and Gujarat were a biological disaster.

topics.t: Earthquakes in India: causes, regions and zones
topics.h: The Indian plate creeps north by about a centimetre a year. That tiny push builds enormous stress along the Himalaya.
p: Earthquakes are among the most unpredictable and highly destructive natural disasters. Those of tectonic origin are the most devastating and widespread.

The Indian plate is moving about 1 cm per year towards the north and north-east. This movement is constantly obstructed by the Eurasian plate, so stress builds up and is released as earthquakes, especially along the Himalayan arc.
The most vulnerable regions are Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, the Darjeeling subdivision of West Bengal and all the north-eastern states.

Central-western India has also had damaging earthquakes: Gujarat (1819, 1956 and 2001) and Maharashtra (1967 and 1993). The 1993 quake hit Latur and Osmanabad, along the Bhima (Krishna) fault, within the supposedly stable Peninsular block.

India is divided into five earthquake zones: very high damage risk, high damage risk, moderate damage risk, low damage risk and very low damage risk zones. Map reading: identify these zones on the earthquake hazard map of India.

ex.q: At about 1 cm per year, how far will the Indian plate move in 10,000 years (in metres)?
st: Distance = 1 cm × 10,000 = 10,000 cm.
ex.a: About 100 m.

topics.rl: Building codes from the Bureau of Indian Standards require stronger, earthquake-resistant designs in the higher-risk seismic zones of India.

topics.t: Earthquakes: effects and mitigation
topics.h: Earthquakes rarely kill by shaking alone. It is collapsing buildings that cause most deaths, which is why safer construction saves lives.
p: Socio-environmental consequences: earthquakes destroy lives and property, settlements, infrastructure, transport and communication, industries and historical and cultural monuments; they can wipe out whole towns in moments.
Effects on the ground (NCERT table): fissures, settlements, landslides, liquefaction and earth pressure, possibly with chain reactions.
Effects on man-made structures: cracking, sliding, overturning, buckling and collapse. Effects on water: waves, hydro-dynamic pressure and tsunami.

Mitigation: (i) establish seismological centres for regular monitoring and fast dissemination of information; GPS can help monitor plate movement. (ii) Prepare a vulnerability map of the country and spread risk information, educating people on how to reduce impacts.

(iii) Modify house types and building designs in vulnerable areas and discourage high-rise buildings, large industrial establishments and big urban centres there. (iv) Make earthquake-resistant designs mandatory and use light materials in major construction in vulnerable areas.

ex.q: Why are light building materials recommended in earthquake-prone areas?
st: During shaking, heavy materials (stone, concrete roofs) fall with great force.
Falling heavy debris causes most injuries and deaths.
Light materials cause less damage if they fall.
So light materials reduce casualties.
ex.a: Because light materials cause less harm if structures fail during shaking.

topics.rl: Traditional Assam-type houses with light bamboo and timber walls have long been considered safer in the earthquake-prone North-East.

topics.t: Tsunami
topics.h: On 26 December 2004, a massive undersea earthquake near Sumatra sent walls of water across the Indian Ocean, reaching the coasts of Tamil Nadu and the Andamans within hours.
p: A tsunami (also called a harbour wave or seismic sea wave) is a series of high waves caused when earthquakes or volcanic eruptions make the sea floor move abruptly, suddenly displacing ocean water.
In the deep ocean, a tsunami has a very long wavelength and limited wave height, so ships at sea are hardly affected and tsunamis are difficult to detect there.

A tsunami's speed depends on the depth of water: it races across the deep ocean at several hundred km/h, and as it approaches a shallow coast it slows down while its height rises, reaching 15 m or more, causing large-scale destruction of coastal settlements.

Tsunamis are frequently observed along the Pacific Ring of Fire, especially along the coasts of Alaska, Japan, the Philippines and other islands of South-east Asia, Indonesia, and also in the Indian Ocean. They cause the most damage on densely populated coasts.

The Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004 killed well over 2 lakh people across many countries (NCERT puts the toll at over 3 lakh; most later counts give about 2.3 lakh). After it, India joined the International Tsunami Warning System. Because losses are so large and widespread, mitigating tsunamis needs international cooperation.

ex.q: Why can a ship in the open ocean ride over a tsunami without noticing it?
st: In deep water, a tsunami's wavelength is very long.
Its height there is small.
So the sea surface rises only slightly and gradually under the ship.
The wave grows tall only near shallow coasts.
ex.a: Because in deep water the tsunami is a long, low wave.

topics.rl: INCOIS in Hyderabad runs the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre, set up after 2004, which can issue alerts within minutes of an undersea quake.

topics.t: Tropical cyclones in India
topics.h: A cyclone is a giant heat engine: it drinks warm sea water as vapour, releases its heat in towering clouds, and spins with winds averaging about 180 km/h at India's coasts.
p: Tropical cyclones are intense low-pressure areas between 30°N and 30°S, around which high-velocity winds blow. Horizontally they extend 500–1,000 km and vertically from the surface to 12–14 km.
A tropical cyclone is like a heat engine energised by latent heat released when moisture gathered over warm oceans condenses.

Initial conditions: (i) large, continuous supply of warm, moist air; (ii) strong Coriolis force to prevent filling of the central low (its absence near the equator prevents cyclones between 0° and 5°); (iii) unstable conditions through the troposphere; (iv) absence of strong vertical wind shear, which would disturb vertical transport of latent heat. Structure: a calm eye with clear sky, surrounded by an eye wall of spirally rising winds.

In India, cyclones originate in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea. Most originate between 10° and 15°N during the monsoon season; in the Bay of Bengal they mostly develop in October and November, and their place of origin shifts with the seasons.

Since cyclones draw energy from the sea, their force decreases with distance from it after landfall. Coastal areas are most vulnerable, struck by winds averaging about 180 km/h, often with a storm surge (abnormal rise in sea level) that floods settlements and fields. Map reading: wind and cyclone hazard zones of India.

ex.q: Why do cyclones not form between 0° and 5° latitude?
st: Cyclones need a strong Coriolis force to keep the central low from filling up.
The Coriolis force is absent at the equator and very weak near it.
Without it, air flows straight into the low.
So no cyclone develops between 0° and 5°.
ex.a: Because the Coriolis force is absent or too weak near the equator.

topics.rl: Odisha's network of cyclone shelters and early evacuation greatly reduced deaths in cyclones like Phailin (2013) and Fani (2019).

topics.t: Floods: causes and flood-prone regions
topics.h: Every monsoon, the Brahmaputra and Kosi spill over vast areas, while desert towns in Rajasthan sometimes face sudden flash floods.
p: A flood is the inundation of land and human settlements when water in river channels rises and spills over, usually when surface runoff exceeds the carrying capacity of channels and flows into low-lying floodplains.

Natural causes: intense rainfall, storm surges, prolonged rain, melting of ice and snow, reduced infiltration and a high load of eroded material. Human causes: indiscriminate deforestation, unscientific agricultural practices, disturbance of natural drainage channels and colonisation of floodplains and river beds.
Floods are common in China, India and Bangladesh. The Rashtriya Barh Ayog (National Flood Commission) identified 40 million hectares of land in India as flood-prone.

Assam, West Bengal and Bihar are among the most flood-prone states. Rivers of Punjab and Uttar Pradesh also flood occasionally. Rajasthan, Gujarat, Haryana and Punjab increasingly face flash floods, partly due to the monsoon pattern and partly due to human blocking of streams and channels. Tamil Nadu sometimes floods in November–January due to the retreating monsoon.

Contrast: floods in eastern India (Assam, Bihar, West Bengal) are frequent and widespread, caused by heavy monsoon rain, huge sediment loads and large Himalayan rivers; floods in western states are more often sudden flash floods linked with intense rain and blocked drainage. Map reading: flood hazard zones of India.

ex.q: Why are Assam and Bihar among the most flood-prone states?
st: They receive heavy monsoon rainfall.
Large Himalayan rivers like the Brahmaputra and Kosi carry huge sediment loads.
Sediment raises river beds, reducing channel capacity.
So rivers frequently overflow onto the plains.
ex.a: Heavy rain plus large, sediment-laden Himalayan rivers overflowing their channels.

topics.rl: The Central Water Commission issues flood forecasts for hundreds of river stations, helping districts in Assam and Bihar evacuate in time.

topics.t: Floods: consequences, benefits and control
topics.h: Floods can destroy crops and homes, yet on Majuli island in Assam, the yearly floods also leave behind fresh silt that grows excellent paddy.
p: Consequences: frequent inundation of farmland and settlements damages crops, roads, rails, bridges and houses; people and cattle are displaced, and economies suffer.
After floods, water-borne diseases such as cholera, gastro-enteritis and hepatitis spread.
Benefits: floods deposit fertile silt on farmland every year. Majuli in Assam, the largest riverine island in the world, gives good paddy crops after the annual Brahmaputra floods.
Control measures: building flood-protection embankments, constructing dams, afforestation, and discouraging major construction in the upper reaches of rivers.
Removing human encroachment from river channels and depopulating floodplains help reduce losses; in coastal areas prone to cyclonic floods, cyclone centres provide shelter.

ex.q: Give one harm and one benefit of annual floods in the Brahmaputra valley.
st: Harm: crops, houses, roads and bridges are damaged and people are displaced.
Benefit: fresh fertile silt is deposited, giving good paddy crops, as on Majuli.
ex.a: Harm: damage and displacement; benefit: fertile silt for paddy.

topics.rl: After floods, health departments in Bihar and Assam run camps to prevent cholera and diarrhoea outbreaks.

topics.t: Droughts: meaning, types and drought-prone areas
topics.h: Jaisalmer and Barmer get less than 90 mm of rain a year on average. For them, drought is not an event but a constant threat.
p: A drought is an extended period of shortage of water availability due to inadequate precipitation, excessive evaporation and over-use of water from reservoirs and other stores, including groundwater. It is a complex phenomenon involving meteorological, hydrological, agricultural, socio-economic and ecological elements.

Types: (i) meteorological drought: a prolonged period of inadequate rainfall, poorly distributed in time and space; (ii) agricultural drought (soil moisture drought): low soil moisture causes crop failure; an area with more than 30% of its gross cropped area irrigated is excluded from the drought-prone category; (iii) hydrological drought: water in aquifers, lakes and reservoirs falls below what precipitation can replenish; (iv) ecological drought: productivity of a natural ecosystem fails due to water shortage.
About 19% of India's area and 12% of its population suffer from drought every year. About 30% of the country's area is drought-prone, affecting around 50 million people.

Extreme drought: most of Rajasthan west of the Aravali (Marusthali) and the Kachchh region of Gujarat; districts like Jaisalmer and Barmer receive less than 90 mm average annual rainfall. Severe drought: parts of eastern Rajasthan, most of Madhya Pradesh, eastern Maharashtra, interior Andhra Pradesh and the Karnataka plateau, northern interior Tamil Nadu, southern Jharkhand and interior Odisha.

Moderate drought: northern Rajasthan, Haryana, southern Uttar Pradesh, the rest of Gujarat, Maharashtra except Konkan, Jharkhand, the Coimbatore plateau of Tamil Nadu and interior Karnataka. Droughts are frequent in central and western India because rainfall there is low and highly variable and many areas lie in rain shadows. Map reading: drought-prone areas of India.

ex.q: A district has 40% of its gross cropped area irrigated. Is it in the drought-prone category for agricultural drought?
st: Areas with more than 30% of gross cropped area under irrigation are excluded.
40% is more than 30%.
So it is excluded from the drought-prone category.
ex.a: No, it is excluded because irrigation exceeds 30%.

topics.rl: MGNREGA works like farm ponds and check dams are often prioritised in drought-prone districts of Maharashtra and Rajasthan.

topics.t: Droughts: consequences and mitigation
topics.h: Rajasthan's villagers have words for the worst droughts: akal for food, jalkal for water, trinkal for fodder, and trikal when all three fail together.
p: Consequences: crop failure causes scarcity of food grains (akal) and fodder (trinkal); inadequate rainfall causes shortage of water (jalkal); shortage of all three, trikal, is the most devastating.

Droughts cause large-scale death of cattle and other animals, migration of people and livestock, and spread of water-borne diseases (gastro-enteritis, cholera, hepatitis) when people are forced to drink contaminated water.
Short-term mitigation: provide safe drinking water, medicines for victims, fodder and water for cattle, and shift people and livestock to safer places.

Long-term mitigation: identify groundwater potential (aquifers), transfer river water from surplus to deficit areas, plan inter-linking of rivers, build reservoirs and dams, promote drought-resistant crops, and practise rainwater harvesting.
Remote sensing and satellite imagery help identify river basins that can be inter-linked and areas with groundwater potential.

ex.q: Classify these drought measures as short-term or long-term: (a) tankers supplying drinking water; (b) rooftop rainwater harvesting; (c) shifting cattle to fodder camps; (d) growing drought-resistant crops.
st: Immediate relief → short-term: (a), (c).
Lasting solutions → long-term: (b), (d).
ex.a: Short-term: (a), (c). Long-term: (b), (d).

topics.rl: Rooftop rainwater harvesting is compulsory for new buildings in many Indian cities, such as Chennai, to recharge groundwater.

topics.t: Landslides
topics.h: In August 1998, a massive landslide at Malpa in Pithoragarh, Uttarakhand, buried a village and a group of Kailash Mansarovar pilgrims.
p: A landslide is the rapid sliding of a large mass of bedrock or debris down a slope. Landslides are highly localised, controlled by geology, geomorphic agents, slope, land use, vegetation cover and human activities, so they are difficult and costly to monitor and predict.

Very high vulnerability zone: highly unstable, young mountainous areas of the Himalaya and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, high-rainfall steep slopes of the Western Ghats and Nilgiris, the north-eastern regions, earthquake-prone areas and areas of intense construction (roads, dams).
High vulnerability zone: areas with similar conditions but a different combination, intensity and frequency of factors; all Himalayan states and north-eastern states except the plains of Assam.

Moderate to low vulnerability: low-precipitation Trans-Himalayan Ladakh and Spiti, the stable Aravali, rain-shadow areas of the Western and Eastern Ghats and the Deccan; mining and subsidence areas in Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, MP, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Goa and Kerala. Other (safe) areas: Rajasthan, Haryana, UP, Bihar, West Bengal (except Darjeeling), Assam (except Karbi Anglong) and coastal regions of southern states.

Consequences: roadblocks, destruction of railway lines, and blocking of river channels by rock falls (which can cause floods), making movement risky and costly. Mitigation: restrict construction and settlements in vulnerable zones; limit agriculture to valleys and moderate slopes; large-scale afforestation; bunds to reduce water flow; and terrace farming instead of jhumming in north-eastern hill states. Project idea: a case study of the Malpa landslide.

ex.q: Why is terrace farming recommended instead of jhumming on north-eastern hill slopes?
st: Jhumming clears and burns forest on slopes, leaving soil loose.
Loose soil on steep slopes slides easily in heavy rain.
Terraces break the slope into steps and hold soil and water.
So terracing reduces landslides.
ex.a: Because terraces stabilise slopes, while jhum clearing loosens them.

topics.rl: The Border Roads Organisation constantly clears landslides on highways to Sikkim, Arunachal and Uttarakhand during the monsoon.

topics.t: Disaster management
topics.h: In 1999, the Odisha super cyclone killed about 10,000 people. In 2019, the very strong Cyclone Fani hit the same coast, but large-scale planned evacuation kept deaths far lower. Management makes the difference.
p: Cyclones are relatively easier to manage because they are more predictable in time and place. Measures include cyclone shelters, embankments, dykes, reservoirs and afforestation to reduce wind speed.
Losses from cyclones are higher in India, Bangladesh and Myanmar because of dense populations in coastal areas.

The Disaster Management Act, 2005 defines a disaster as a catastrophe, mishap, calamity or grave occurrence in any area, arising from natural or man-made causes, or by accident or negligence, which results in substantial loss of life or human suffering or damage to property or the environment, and is beyond the coping capacity of the affected community.

Disaster management has three stages: (i) pre-disaster: generating data and information, preparing vulnerability zoning maps, spreading awareness, disaster planning, preparedness and preventive measures; (ii) during disaster: rescue and relief operations such as evacuation, shelters and relief camps, and supply of water, food, clothing and medical care; (iii) post-disaster: rehabilitation and recovery of victims and capacity building.

A large part of India's area and population is vulnerable to disasters, so mitigation and preparedness are the best options. Project ideas: reports on the Malpa landslide, the 2004 tsunami, the Odisha and Gujarat cyclones, river inter-linking, the Tehri or Sardar Sarovar dam, the Bhuj or Latur earthquakes, life in a delta, or a rooftop rainwater harvesting model.

ex.q: Place each action in the right stage: (a) preparing a flood vulnerability map; (b) evacuating people by boat; (c) rebuilding houses with flood-resistant designs.
st: (a) Planning before the event → pre-disaster.
(b) Rescue during the event → during disaster.
(c) Rehabilitation and capacity building afterwards → post-disaster.
ex.a: (a) Pre-disaster; (b) During disaster; (c) Post-disaster.

topics.rl: The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) and state authorities run mock drills in schools, part of pre-disaster preparedness.

qa.q: Who first coined the term 'geography'?
qa.e: The Greek scholar Eratosthenes coined the word geography from 'geo' (earth) and 'graphos' (description).

qa.q: The literal meaning of the word 'geography' is:
qa.e: Geo = earth and graphos = description, so geography means description of the earth.

qa.q: Geography is best defined as the study of the earth as:
qa.e: Geography studies the earth's surface with humans at the centre: how people live on, use and change it.

qa.q: 'Areal differentiation' in geography refers to the study of:
qa.a: How places differ from and resemble each other
qa.e: Areal differentiation is about variations over space: why one area is different from or similar to another.

qa.q: Which one of the following is a cultural feature of the earth's surface?
qa.e: A canal is built by people, so it is part of the cultural environment. The others are natural features.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The cultural environment of a place changes over time.
Reason (R): Humans keep interacting with and modifying the physical environment.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Because people keep using and modifying nature, the landscape they create (fields, towns, roads) keeps changing. R is the cause of A.

qa.q: Ladakh has flat-roofed houses while Kerala has steep sloping roofs. A geographer would explain this mainly by:
qa.a: Differences in rainfall between the two regions
qa.e: Heavy rain in Kerala needs sloping roofs to drain water; dry Ladakh does not. This is a cultural feature shaped by a physical one.

qa.q: Which pair correctly matches the two parts of the environment that geography studies?
qa.e: Geography studies the physical (natural) environment and the cultural (human-made) environment and their interaction.

qa.q: Questions about the identification of patterns of natural and cultural features belong to which category?
qa.e: 'What' questions identify the patterns of features found over the earth's surface.

qa.q: Which question in geography is related to causal relationships between features and processes?
qa.e: The 'why' question seeks explanation, i.e., the causes behind the patterns and distributions.

qa.q: 'Geography is concerned with spatial attributes.' Here 'spatial' refers to:
qa.a: Location and distribution over the earth's surface
qa.e: Spatial means related to space on the earth's surface: where things are and how they are arranged.

qa.q: Which question would a geographer ask to study the DISTRIBUTION of coal mines in India?
qa.a: Where are coal mines located in India?
qa.e: Distribution is about location, so it is a 'where' question.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Geography is called a discipline of synthesis.
Reason (R): It studies the interrelationships and associations of phenomena over space.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Because geography brings together many phenomena and their links over space, it synthesises them. R explains A.

qa.q: Which question makes geography a scientific discipline rather than a descriptive list?
qa.e: Seeking causes (why) turns description into scientific explanation.

qa.q: A student notes that cotton textile mills are concentrated near cotton-growing areas of Maharashtra and Gujarat. She is studying:
qa.a: An interrelationship between phenomena in space
qa.e: She links one phenomenon (mills) with another (raw cotton) across space. That is studying interrelationships.

qa.q: Case: A geographer maps rainfall across India and finds that the western slopes of the Western Ghats get far more rain than the Deccan beyond them. She then explains it by the rain-shadow effect. Which sequence of questions did she follow?
qa.e: She identified the pattern (what: rainfall amounts), its distribution (where: windward vs leeward), and then the cause (why: rain shadow).

qa.q: In the early stages of human history, humans adapted to nature because:
qa.a: Their level of technology was low
qa.e: With simple tools and little technology, people had to adjust to natural conditions.

qa.q: The process by which humans, using technology, create a cultural landscape over nature is called:
qa.e: Humanisation of nature means humans imprint their culture on nature using technology.

qa.q: Which statement best describes 'environmental determinism'?
qa.e: Determinism holds that the physical environment determines how humans live.

qa.q: According to geographers, what is an index of the cultural development of a society?
qa.e: Technology shows how far a society has developed in its ability to use and change nature.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The relationship between humans and nature is dynamic.
Reason (R): The level of technology of human societies changes over time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: As technology changes, the way people use and modify nature changes, so the relationship is dynamic.

qa.q: Farmers in a dry region choose drip irrigation and millets over water-hungry rice. This reflects which idea?
qa.e: Nature sets limits (low water) but humans choose among possible options. That is possibilism.

qa.q: 'Technology loosened the shackles of environment on human beings.' Which example fits best?
qa.a: Air-conditioning allowing offices to work in 45 °C heat
qa.e: Air-conditioning frees people from the limits of extreme heat. The others show nature still controlling humans.

qa.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
qa.e: Low technology makes people adapt to nature (naturalisation of humans). High technology leads to humanisation of nature.

qa.q: Geography is a discipline of spatial synthesis, whereas history is a discipline of:
qa.e: History integrates events over time (temporal), geography over space (spatial).

qa.q: Climatology, a branch of physical geography, is most closely linked with:
qa.e: Both study the atmosphere; meteorology deals with weather processes and climatology with long-term patterns.

qa.q: Soil geography is closely related to which natural science?
qa.e: Pedology is the science of soils, so it supports soil geography.

qa.q: Which natural science is most closely linked with geomorphology?
qa.e: Landforms are shaped by rocks, structures and earth processes studied in geology.

qa.q: Biogeography draws mainly on which pair of sciences?
qa.e: Biogeography studies plants and animals over space, so it uses botany and zoology.

qa.q: Why is geography called an integrating discipline?
qa.a: It brings together knowledge from natural and social sciences over space
qa.e: Geography draws on many sciences and integrates their findings in a spatial framework.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Geography has close links with almost all sciences.
Reason (R): Geography studies only the physical features of the earth and ignores human activities.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true: every science deals with some reality that exists over space, so geography links with both natural and social sciences. R is false: geography studies both physical and cultural (human) features.

qa.q: In NCERT's diagram of geography's relation with other subjects, geography sits at the centre linked with:
qa.a: Natural sciences on one side and social sciences on the other
qa.e: The figure links physical geography to natural sciences and human geography to social sciences.

qa.q: Population geography is closely linked with:
qa.e: Demography is the statistical study of population, which is the base of population geography.

qa.q: What is considered the most effective tool of a geographer?
qa.e: Maps represent the earth's surface and spatial patterns, making them the geographer's key tool.

qa.q: A map converts the earth's surface from:
qa.e: The earth is three-dimensional; a map shows it on a flat, two-dimensional sheet.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a body-part metaphor used in geography?
qa.e: NCERT's examples include face of the earth, eye of the storm, mouth of a river, snout of a glacier, neck of an isthmus and profile of the soil. 'Crown of a delta' is not a standard term.

qa.q: Political geography is most closely related to:
qa.e: Political geography studies spatial aspects of states, boundaries and elections, linked with political science.

qa.q: GIS stands for:
qa.e: GIS is a Geographic Information System, a computer-based tool for storing and analysing spatial data.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Cartography and quantitative techniques link geography with mathematics.
Reason (R): Map-making and statistical analysis of spatial data use mathematical methods.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Map projections, scales and statistics are mathematical, so these techniques connect geography with mathematics.

qa.q: The 'profile' of the soil refers to:
qa.e: A soil profile is a vertical cut showing the soil's layers (horizons). The word is borrowed from the human face.

qa.q: The systematic approach in geography was introduced by:
qa.e: Humboldt introduced the systematic approach; Ritter developed the regional approach.

qa.q: Karl Ritter is associated with which approach?
qa.e: Ritter, a German contemporary of Humboldt, developed the regional approach.

qa.q: In the regional approach:
qa.a: The world is divided into regions and all phenomena of a region are studied
qa.e: Regional geography divides the world into regions at different levels and studies everything within a region.

qa.q: Studying natural vegetation all over the world and then classifying it into types such as equatorial rainforests and grasslands is an example of:
qa.e: One phenomenon studied globally, then typologies identified: systematic approach.

qa.q: Which pair shows dualism in geography?
qa.e: Dualism refers to the twin divisions physical vs human (and systematic vs regional).

qa.q: Humboldt and Ritter were both:
qa.e: Both were German geographers and contemporaries in the late 18th to mid-19th century.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Systematic geography is also called general geography.
Reason (R): It studies a phenomenon as a whole across the world before finding its patterns.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Because it studies a phenomenon generally (worldwide) rather than region by region, it is called general geography.

qa.q: A geographer studies population, agriculture, climate and transport of only the Kashmir valley. Her approach is:
qa.e: All phenomena in one region are studied together, which is the regional approach.

qa.q: Which of the following is NOT a branch of physical geography?
qa.e: Political geography is a branch of human geography. The others are physical geography.

qa.q: Plant geography and zoo geography are sub-branches of:
qa.e: Biogeography studies life forms over space and includes plant geography and zoo geography.

qa.q: Regional planning includes:
qa.e: Regional planning covers country or rural planning and town or urban planning.

qa.q: Remote sensing, GIS and GPS together form part of:
qa.e: These are geo-informatics techniques under 'methods and techniques'.

qa.q: 'Land and human interaction' or human ecology is part of which common aspect?
qa.e: Philosophy of geography includes geographical thought and land-human interaction (human ecology).

qa.q: Which branch belongs to the regional approach?
qa.e: Regional studies or area studies are based on the regional approach; the others are systematic branches.

qa.q: Social/cultural geography and economic geography are branches of:
qa.e: Both study human activities over space, so they belong to human geography.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Cartography is used only in the regional approach of geography.
Reason (R): Both systematic and regional geography need maps to present and analyse spatial data.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: cartography is a method common to both approaches, not only the regional one. R is true, and it is exactly why A is wrong.

qa.q: Which branch of physical geography studies landforms, their evolution and related processes?
qa.e: Geomorphology is the study of landforms and the processes that shape them.

qa.q: The study of climatic types and regions is part of:
qa.e: Climatology covers atmospheric structure, weather elements and climatic types and regions.

qa.q: Hydrology studies:
qa.a: The realm of water and its effect on life
qa.e: Hydrology covers oceans, lakes, rivers and other water bodies, and their effects on life forms.

qa.q: The fertility status and distribution of soils is studied in:
qa.e: Soil geography studies soil formation, types, fertility, distribution and use.

qa.q: Composition of air, temperature, pressure and winds are studied under which component?
qa.e: These are elements of the atmosphere studied in climatology.

qa.q: Food chains and ecological balance are studied under the:
qa.e: The biosphere includes life forms and their sustaining mechanisms such as food chains.

qa.q: Which pair is INCORRECTLY matched?
qa.e: Soils are formed on land and studied in soil geography, not as part of the atmosphere.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Geomorphology is a branch of physical geography.
Reason (R): It studies how the land surface and its landforms develop.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Because geomorphology deals with landforms of the lithosphere, it belongs to physical geography.

qa.q: According to NCERT, plains are mainly utilised for:
qa.e: Flat land and fertile soils make plains ideal for agriculture.

qa.q: Which landform provides pastures, forests, tourist spots and is a source of rivers?
qa.e: Mountains offer pastures, forests and scenic tourism, and rivers rise in them.

qa.q: Climate influences which of the following?
qa.a: House types, clothing and food habits
qa.e: Climate shapes how people build homes, dress and eat, and also affects crops and industries.

qa.q: Why is physical geography important for sustainable development?
qa.a: It helps evaluate and manage natural resources wisely
qa.e: Understanding landforms, climate, water and soils helps plan their use without harming the environment.

qa.q: Plateaus are particularly important because they provide:
qa.e: Plateaus such as the Chota Nagpur are storehouses of minerals and support forests.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Cropping patterns differ from region to region in India.
Reason (R): Plateaus such as the Chota Nagpur are rich in minerals and forests.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but the mineral wealth of plateaus does not explain why cropping patterns differ. Crops differ mainly because climate and soils differ.

qa.q: Which region and resource pair is correctly matched?
qa.e: The Chota Nagpur plateau is rich in coal, iron ore and other minerals.

qa.q: Soil is considered a resource mainly because it:
qa.e: Soil supplies nutrients and water to plants, making farming possible.

qa.q: The nebular hypothesis on the origin of the earth was first put forward by:
qa.e: The German philosopher Immanuel Kant proposed it; Laplace later revised it in 1796.

qa.q: In which year did Laplace revise the nebular hypothesis?
qa.e: Laplace revised Kant's nebular hypothesis in 1796.

qa.q: According to Chamberlain and Moulton, the material that formed the planets was:
qa.a: A cigar-shaped extension pulled out of the sun by a wandering star
qa.e: They proposed that a passing star drew out a cigar-shaped extension of solar material that condensed into planets.

qa.q: Which scientists supported the wandering star (binary) idea?
qa.a: Sir James Jeans and Sir Harold Jeffrey
qa.e: Jeans and later Jeffrey supported Chamberlain and Moulton's argument.

qa.q: The 1950 revision of the nebular hypothesis was given by:
qa.e: Otto Schmidt (Russia) and Carl Weizascar (Germany) revised it in 1950.

qa.q: In the revised nebular hypothesis, the solar nebula contained mostly:
qa.a: Hydrogen and helium along with dust
qa.e: The solar nebula was mostly hydrogen and helium with what may be called dust.

qa.q: Theories that involve a companion star coexisting with the sun are called:
qa.e: A companion to the sun makes it a pair (binary), hence binary theories.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In the revised nebular hypothesis, planets formed through accretion.
