qa.q: A sinuous ridge of coarse material deposited by a meltwater stream flowing beneath a glacier is a/an:
qa.e: Eskers form in ice-walled channels under the glacier.

qa.q: Drumlins are composed mainly of:
qa.e: Drumlins are mainly till with some gravel and sand.

qa.q: The long axis of a drumlin is:
qa.a: Parallel to the direction of ice movement
qa.e: Drumlins are streamlined along the ice-flow direction.

qa.q: The end of a drumlin that faces the glacier is called the:
qa.e: The stoss end is blunter and steeper; the opposite end is the tail.

qa.q: Broad flat alluvial fans of glacio-fluvial deposits that join together form:
qa.e: Meltwater deposits beyond the ice build outwash plains.

qa.q: Drumlins may measure up to about:
qa.a: 1 km in length and 30 m in height
qa.e: NCERT gives up to 1 km length and about 30 m height.

qa.q: Which is a correct difference between a glacial valley and a river valley?
qa.a: Glacial valley is U-shaped; river valley is V-shaped
qa.e: Ice bulldozes broad U-shapes; rivers cut narrow Vs.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Drumlins indicate the direction of glacier movement.
Reason (R): The blunt stoss end faces the oncoming ice and the tail points downstream.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Their asymmetric shape shows where the ice came from and where it went.

qa.q: High rocky coasts are also known as:
qa.e: High rocky coasts look drowned, so they are called submerged coasts.

qa.q: Which type of landforms dominate along high rocky coasts?
qa.e: Waves pound the steep coast, creating cliffs and other erosional features.

qa.q: The east coast of India is an example of a:
qa.e: Depositional forms like deltas and lagoons dominate the east coast.

qa.q: Along low sedimentary coasts, rivers appear to:
qa.a: Extend their length by building coastal plains and deltas
qa.e: Rivers deposit sediment and extend the land seaward.

qa.q: Which statement describes a high rocky coast?
qa.a: Highly irregular coastline with hill sides dropping sharply into water
qa.e: Rocky coasts are indented with steep slopes into the sea.

qa.q: Coastal processes are described as the most destructive because:
qa.a: They are the most dynamic, with waves, storms and tsunamis acting quickly
qa.e: Constant wave action and sudden storm or tsunami waves change coasts fast.

qa.q: Which pair is a correct difference between the two types of coast?
qa.a: Rocky: erosion dominant; sedimentary: deposition dominant
qa.e: Rocky coasts are eroded; sedimentary coasts are built by deposition.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Lagoons are common along the east coast of India.
Reason (R): The west coast of India is a high rocky retreating coast.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but a fact about the west coast cannot explain lagoons on the east coast. Lagoons form there because the low sedimentary east coast favours bars and spits that enclose water.

qa.q: Resistant masses of rock left standing isolated just off the shore after cliffs retreat are called:
qa.e: Sea stacks are remnants of cliffs or hills cut off by wave erosion.

qa.q: A wave-cut platform occurring above the average height of waves is called a:
qa.e: NCERT calls such a platform a wave-cut terrace.

qa.q: An offshore bar that is exposed due to further addition of sand is called a:
qa.e: When an offshore bar shows above water, it becomes a barrier bar.

qa.q: A barrier bar keyed up to one end of a bay is called a:
qa.e: Spits are attached at one end to a bay's headland.

qa.q: Beaches made of excessively small pebbles and even cobbles are called:
qa.e: Shingle beaches contain pebbles and cobbles rather than sand.

qa.q: The first natural buffer against storm and tsunami waves is formed by:
qa.e: Offshore bars absorb most of the force first, followed by barriers, beaches, dunes and mangroves.

qa.q: A lagoon forms when:
qa.a: Bars and spits nearly block the mouth of a bay
qa.e: Enclosed bay waters behind bars or spits become a lagoon.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Removal of mangroves can increase damage from cyclones and tsunamis.
Reason (R): Mangroves, beaches and dunes absorb the destructive force of storm waves.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Without these buffers, settlements take the full force of the waves.

qa.q: Which of the following is NOT a process of wind erosion?
qa.e: Wind causes deflation, abrasion and impact; plucking is glacial.

qa.q: Gently inclined rocky floors close to mountains at their foot in deserts are called:
qa.e: Pediments are rocky floors formed by lateral erosion and sheet flooding.

qa.q: The remnant of a mountain left standing on a pediplain is called a/an:
qa.e: In deserts, the remnant is an inselberg; on a river peneplain it is a monadnock.

qa.q: Shallow lakes in desert basins that hold water only briefly and often contain salts are:
qa.e: Playas form at basin centres and evaporate quickly, leaving salts.

qa.q: A playa plain covered up by salts is called:
qa.e: Salt-covered playas are alkali flats.

qa.q: Deflation refers to:
qa.a: Lifting and removal of dust and smaller particles by wind
qa.e: Deflation is wind blowing away fine particles.

qa.q: Besides wind, which other agent is dominant in shaping hot deserts?
qa.e: Rare, torrential rains produce sheet floods that shape desert landforms.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Pediments extend backwards at the expense of the mountain front.
Reason (R): The steep wash slope and free face retreat backwards through parallel retreat of slopes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Backwasting moves the slope back, enlarging the pediment.

qa.q: Crescent-shaped dunes with points directed away from the wind are called:
qa.e: Barchans have wings pointing downwind.

qa.q: Parabolic dunes form when:
qa.a: Sandy surfaces are partially covered with vegetation
qa.e: Vegetation holds the arms back, making a reversed barchan shape.

qa.q: A seif differs from a barchan in that it has:
qa.e: Seifs have a single wing due to shifting wind conditions.

qa.q: Dunes aligned perpendicular to the wind direction are:
qa.e: Transverse dunes lie across the wind.

qa.q: Longitudinal dunes form when:
qa.a: Sand supply is poor and wind direction is constant
qa.e: Poor sand supply with a steady wind builds long, low ridges.

qa.q: Mushroom rocks are shaped mainly by:
qa.e: Wind-borne sand abrades the lower part, leaving a broad cap on a slender stalk.

qa.q: Shallow depressions created by wind blowing away weathered material are called:
qa.e: Persistent wind removes loose material, creating deflation hollows.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Barchans form where the wind direction keeps changing from season to season.
Reason (R): A uniform surface and a steady wind let sand pile into a regular crescent shape.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: barchans form where the wind direction is constant and moderate. R is true; shifting winds give seifs instead.

qa.q: Which gas makes up the largest share of dry air by volume?
qa.e: Nitrogen forms 78.08% of dry air.

qa.q: According to NCERT, the percentage of oxygen in dry air is:
qa.e: Oxygen forms 20.95% of the volume of dry air.

qa.q: About 99% of the total mass of the atmosphere is found within what height of the earth's surface?
qa.e: Air is densely compressed near the surface; 99% of its mass lies within 32 km.

qa.q: At what height does oxygen become almost negligible?
qa.e: Oxygen is almost negligible at 120 km.

qa.q: Carbon dioxide and water vapour are found only up to a height of:
qa.e: NCERT states they occur only up to 90 km.

qa.q: Argon forms about what percentage of dry air?
qa.e: Argon is 0.93% by volume, the third most abundant gas.

qa.q: How many times greater is the percentage of nitrogen (78.08) than that of oxygen (20.95)? Choose the nearest whole number.
qa.e: 78.08 ÷ 20.95 ≈ 3.73, which is nearest to 4.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Mountaineers find it hard to breathe at great heights.
Reason (R): The density of air decreases rapidly with height.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Thinner air holds less oxygen per breath, making breathing hard.

qa.q: Carbon dioxide is meteorologically important because it is:
qa.a: Transparent to incoming solar radiation but opaque to outgoing terrestrial radiation
qa.e: It lets sunlight in but traps heat radiated by the earth.

qa.q: The gas largely responsible for the greenhouse effect, according to NCERT's discussion of atmospheric composition, is:
qa.e: CO₂ absorbs and re-radiates terrestrial radiation, causing the greenhouse effect.

qa.q: The rise in carbon dioxide in recent decades is mainly due to:
qa.e: Fossil fuel combustion releases CO₂.

qa.q: Ozone is found between which heights above the earth's surface?
qa.e: NCERT places ozone between 10 and 50 km.

qa.q: What does ozone do?
qa.a: Absorbs ultraviolet rays from the sun
qa.e: Ozone filters harmful UV rays.

qa.q: Which statement about the volume of atmospheric gases is correct?
qa.a: Other gases are nearly constant but CO₂ has been rising
qa.e: NCERT notes that only CO₂ volume has been rising markedly.

qa.q: Why would the earth be colder without carbon dioxide in the air?
qa.a: Less terrestrial radiation would be absorbed and returned to the surface
qa.e: CO₂ traps part of the heat radiated by the earth; without it, more heat would escape to space.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The volume of every gas in the atmosphere has been rising steadily in recent decades.
Reason (R): The volume of carbon dioxide has risen because of the burning of fossil fuels.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the volume of the other gases stays nearly constant; only carbon dioxide has been rising markedly. R is true.

qa.q: In the warm and wet tropics, water vapour may account for about what percentage of air by volume?
qa.e: Water vapour can reach about 4% in warm, humid tropics.

qa.q: Water vapour in the atmosphere:
qa.a: Decreases with altitude and from the equator towards the poles
qa.e: It is a variable gas, highest near the surface in warm, wet regions.

qa.q: Why is water vapour described as acting like a blanket?
qa.a: It absorbs insolation and preserves the earth's radiated heat
qa.e: It keeps the earth from becoming too hot or too cold.

qa.q: Dust and salt particles help form clouds because they:
qa.a: Act as hygroscopic nuclei for condensation
qa.e: Water vapour condenses around these particles to form droplets.

qa.q: Higher concentrations of dust particles are found in:
qa.e: Dry winds in subtropical and temperate regions carry more dust.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a source of dust particles in the atmosphere?
qa.e: Ozone is a gas, not a dust particle. Sea salt, pollen, ash, soot and meteor dust are sources.

qa.q: Water vapour in cold, dry polar regions may be:
qa.e: Cold, dry regions hold very little water vapour.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Dust particles are generally concentrated in the lower layers of the atmosphere.
Reason (R): Convectional currents can never carry dust upwards.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: convectional currents can carry dust to great heights.

qa.q: The average height of the troposphere is about:
qa.e: It averages 13 km, about 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the equator.

qa.q: The troposphere is thickest at the equator because:
qa.a: Strong convectional currents transport heat to great heights
qa.e: Intense heating drives strong convection that lifts the tropopause.

qa.q: All weather phenomena take place in the:
qa.e: The troposphere contains water vapour and dust, so all weather occurs here.

qa.q: In the troposphere, temperature decreases at the rate of 1°C for every:
qa.e: NCERT gives 1°C per 165 m.

qa.q: The air temperature at the tropopause over the equator is about:
qa.e: It is about −80°C over the equator and −45°C over the poles.

qa.q: The temperature on the ground is 28°C. What would it be at 990 m height, using a fall of 1°C per 165 m? (Answer in °C.)
The troposphere extends to about what height near the poles?
qa.e: It is about 8 km near the poles and 18 km at the equator.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The troposphere is the most important layer for all biological activity.
Reason (R): The air temperature at the tropopause is about −80°C over the equator.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but the temperature at the tropopause does not explain why the troposphere matters for life. It matters because it holds water vapour and dust, and all weather happens there.

qa.q: The ozone layer is located in the:
qa.e: The stratosphere contains the ozone layer, which absorbs UV radiation.

qa.q: The stratosphere extends up to a height of about:
qa.e: It lies above the tropopause and extends up to 50 km.

qa.q: In the mesosphere, temperature reaches about −100°C at a height of:
qa.e: Temperature falls to −100°C at 80 km, the top of the mesosphere.

qa.q: The upper limit of the mesosphere is known as the:
qa.e: The mesopause marks the top of the mesosphere.

qa.q: Which layer reflects radio waves transmitted from the earth?
qa.e: Electrically charged ions in the ionosphere reflect radio waves.

qa.q: The ionosphere lies between:
qa.e: NCERT places the ionosphere between 80 and 400 km.

qa.q: How thick is the mesosphere if it lies between 50 km and 80 km? (Answer in km.)

Assertion (A): Geographers are mainly concerned with the first two layers of the atmosphere.
Reason (R): Weather occurs in the troposphere, and the ozone of the stratosphere protects life.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: These two layers most directly affect life and weather on the surface.

qa.q: Which of the following is NOT an element of weather and climate?
qa.e: Latitude is a control of climate, not an element. The elements are temperature, pressure, winds, humidity, clouds and precipitation.

qa.q: Climate differs from weather in that climate is:
qa.a: The average weather over a long period
qa.e: Climate is long-term average weather; weather is short-term.

qa.q: Pressure differences in the atmosphere mainly cause:
qa.e: Air moves from high to low pressure, creating winds.

qa.q: In which layer do all six elements of weather operate?
qa.e: Weather, including clouds and precipitation, occurs in the troposphere.

qa.q: The instrument used to measure atmospheric pressure is the:
qa.e: A barometer measures air pressure.

qa.q: Which element is directly linked with water vapour in the air?
qa.e: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air.

qa.q: Which of these is a correct sequence of linked weather elements?
qa.e: Heating changes pressure, and pressure differences cause winds.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Precipitation depends on humidity and clouds.
Reason (R): Water vapour condenses to form clouds, from which precipitation falls.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Moisture in the air condenses into clouds, which then produce precipitation.

qa.q: Insolation means:
qa.e: Insolation is short for incoming solar radiation.

qa.q: On average, the earth receives how much energy at the top of its atmosphere?
qa.a: 1.94 calories per sq cm per minute
qa.e: NCERT gives 1.94 calories per sq cm per minute.

qa.q: The earth is farthest from the sun on:
qa.e: Aphelion falls on 4 July at about 152 million km.

qa.q: The position of the earth nearest to the sun is called:
qa.e: Perihelion (3 January) is the nearest position, at about 147 million km.

qa.q: What is the earth's distance from the sun at perihelion?
qa.e: At perihelion the earth is about 147 million km from the sun.

qa.q: Why does the variation in insolation between perihelion and aphelion not affect daily weather much?
qa.a: It is masked by land-sea distribution and atmospheric circulation
qa.e: Other factors are far more important for daily weather.

qa.q: The difference between the aphelion (152 million km) and perihelion (147 million km) distances is what percentage of the aphelion distance? (Nearest whole number.)
qa.e: 5 ÷ 152 × 100 ≈ 3.3%, nearest whole number 3%.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The earth intercepts only a very small portion of the sun's energy.
Reason (R): The earth receives insolation mostly in long wavelengths.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: insolation reaches the earth mostly in short wavelengths; it is the heated earth that radiates long waves.

qa.q: The earth's axis makes an angle of how many degrees with the plane of its orbit?
qa.e: The axis is inclined at 66½° to the orbital plane (23½° from the perpendicular).

qa.q: Which two factors have less influence on insolation?
qa.a: Transparency of the atmosphere and configuration of land (aspect)
qa.e: NCERT notes that the last two factors, transparency and aspect, have less influence.

qa.q: Slant rays deliver less energy per unit area because they:
qa.a: Spread over a larger area and pass through more atmosphere
qa.e: The same energy spreads out, and more is lost in a longer path through the air.

qa.q: The angle of inclination of the sun's rays depends mainly on:
qa.e: The higher the latitude, the more slanting the rays.

qa.q: Which of the following is NOT a factor affecting insolation received at the surface?
qa.e: Longitude does not change the angle or duration of sunshine; the others do.

qa.q: Compared to vertical rays, slant rays are subject to more:
qa.e: A longer path through the atmosphere means more absorption, scattering and diffusion.

qa.q: If the axis is inclined at 66½° to the orbital plane, what is its inclination from the perpendicular? (Answer in degrees.)

Assertion (A): Polar regions receive less insolation per unit area than equatorial regions.
Reason (R): At high latitudes the sun's rays are slanting and spread over a larger area.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Slant rays spread energy thinly and lose more in the atmosphere.

qa.q: Maximum insolation at the earth's surface is received over:
qa.e: Subtropical deserts have the least cloudiness, so most insolation reaches the ground.

qa.q: The blue colour of the sky is due to:
qa.a: Scattering of light by small particles
qa.e: Tiny particles scatter visible light, especially blue, across the sky.

qa.q: Insolation received at the surface varies from about 320 W/m² in the tropics to about:
qa.e: NCERT gives about 70 W/m² at the poles.

qa.q: The equator receives comparatively less insolation than the tropics because:
qa.e: Heavy cloud cover at the equator reflects and absorbs insolation.

qa.q: Within the troposphere, much of the near-infrared radiation is absorbed by:
qa.a: Water vapour, ozone and other gases
qa.e: Water vapour, ozone and other gases absorb near-infrared radiation.

qa.q: At the same latitude, insolation is generally:
qa.a: More over continents than over oceans
qa.e: NCERT notes that continents receive more insolation than oceans at the same latitude.

qa.q: How many times greater is tropical insolation (320 W/m²) than polar insolation (70 W/m²)? (One decimal place.)
qa.e: 320 ÷ 70 ≈ 4.57, which rounds to 4.6.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The rising and setting sun looks red.
Reason (R): Light is scattered within the atmosphere.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: At low sun angles, light travels through more air and scattering leaves mainly red light.

qa.q: The transfer of heat through horizontal movement of air is called:
qa.e: Advection is horizontal transfer of heat by moving air.

qa.q: The vertical heating of the atmosphere by rising air currents is:
qa.e: Convection is vertical transfer, confined to the troposphere.

qa.q: Convective transfer of energy is confined to the:
qa.e: Convection occurs only in the troposphere.

qa.q: The 'loo' of northern India in summer is an outcome of:
qa.e: The loo carries heat horizontally, which is advection.

qa.q: Conduction is most important in heating:
qa.a: The lower layers of the atmosphere
qa.e: Air in direct contact with the ground is heated by conduction.

qa.q: In middle latitudes, most diurnal variations in daily weather are caused by:
qa.e: NCERT states that advection alone causes most of these variations.

qa.q: Conduction stops when:
qa.a: Both bodies attain the same temperature or contact is broken
qa.e: Heat flows only while there is a temperature difference and contact.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Horizontal movement of air is relatively more important than vertical movement in transferring heat.
Reason (R): Convective transfer of heat is confined to the troposphere.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but where convection occurs does not explain why horizontal transfer matters more. The reason is that advection causes most of the day-to-day weather changes in middle latitudes.

qa.q: Terrestrial radiation is emitted in the form of:
qa.e: The heated earth radiates long-wave energy.

qa.q: The atmosphere is heated mainly:
qa.a: Indirectly, by terrestrial radiation from below
qa.e: The atmosphere is largely transparent to insolation and absorbs the earth's long-wave radiation.

qa.q: Which gases particularly absorb long-wave terrestrial radiation?
qa.a: Carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases
qa.e: Greenhouse gases like CO₂ absorb long-wave radiation.

qa.q: Planck's law states that the hotter a body:
qa.a: The more energy it radiates and the shorter the wavelength
qa.e: Hotter bodies radiate more energy at shorter wavelengths.

qa.q: Specific heat is defined as the energy needed to raise the temperature of:
qa.a: One gram of a substance by 1°C
qa.e: It is the energy to raise 1 g of a substance by 1°C.

qa.q: How does the earth maintain a nearly constant temperature over time?
qa.a: Heat received from the sun is finally returned to space
qa.e: The atmosphere and earth radiate back to space what they receive.

qa.q: Why is it cooler at higher altitudes even though they are closer to the sun?
qa.a: The atmosphere is heated from below by terrestrial radiation
qa.e: Since the air is heated from the ground up, temperature generally falls with height.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The sun emits short-wave radiation and the earth emits long-wave radiation.
Reason (R): The hotter a body, the shorter the wavelength of its radiation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: By Planck's law, the much hotter sun radiates shorter waves than the cooler earth.

qa.q: Out of 100 units of insolation, how many units are reflected or scattered back to space before reaching the surface?
qa.e: 27 from clouds + 2 from snow and ice + 6 scattered = 35 units.

qa.q: How many units are reflected back from the tops of clouds?
qa.e: Clouds reflect 27 units, the largest share of the albedo.

qa.q: The reflected amount of radiation is called the earth's:
qa.e: Albedo is the reflected part of incoming radiation.

qa.q: How many units of insolation are absorbed by the earth's surface?
qa.e: Of the 65 absorbed units, 51 are absorbed by the surface and 14 by the atmosphere.

qa.q: How many units of insolation are absorbed within the atmosphere directly?
qa.e: The atmosphere directly absorbs 14 units of incoming insolation.

qa.q: How many units are reflected from snow and ice-covered areas?
qa.e: Snow and ice reflect 2 units in NCERT's heat budget.

qa.q: Why does the earth as a whole neither warm up nor cool down on average?
qa.a: Incoming insolation is balanced by outgoing radiation
qa.e: Energy received equals energy returned to space: the heat budget balances.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Deforestation and snow melt can change the earth's albedo.
Reason (R): Albedo is the amount of radiation reflected by surfaces and clouds.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Changing a surface changes how much radiation it reflects, i.e., the albedo.

qa.q: Of the 51 units radiated by the earth, how many go directly to space?
qa.e: 17 units escape directly; 34 are absorbed by the atmosphere.

qa.q: How many units does the atmosphere receive through latent heat of condensation?
qa.e: Latent heat of condensation contributes 19 units.

qa.q: How many units does the atmosphere receive through convection and turbulence?
qa.e: Convection and turbulence carry 9 units to the atmosphere.

qa.q: The total radiation the atmosphere sends back to space is:
qa.e: 14 (from insolation) + 34 (from terrestrial radiation) = 48 units.

qa.q: Total radiation returning to space from the earth and the atmosphere is:
qa.e: 17 + 48 = 65 units, equal to the 65 units absorbed.

qa.q: Of the 34 units of terrestrial radiation absorbed by the atmosphere, how many are absorbed directly?
qa.e: 6 units directly, 9 by convection and turbulence, 19 by latent heat.

qa.q: The heat budget is said to be balanced because:
qa.a: Radiation returned to space (65 units) equals the insolation absorbed (65 units)
qa.e: Absorbed and returned energy match at 65 units.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Latent heat of condensation is the largest single way the surface transfers heat to the atmosphere in the heat budget.
Reason (R): It contributes 19 of the 34 units absorbed by the atmosphere from the earth.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: 19 units is more than 9 (convection) or 6 (direct absorption), so it is the largest.

qa.q: There is a surplus of net radiation between:
qa.e: NCERT gives the surplus zone as 40°N to 40°S.

qa.q: Regions near the poles have:
qa.e: Polar regions lose more energy than they receive.

qa.q: How is surplus heat from the tropics redistributed?
qa.a: Polewards by winds and ocean currents
qa.e: Atmospheric and oceanic circulation move heat towards the poles.

qa.q: Without poleward transfer of heat, what would happen?
qa.a: The tropics would keep heating and high latitudes would freeze
qa.e: Transfer prevents progressive heating of the tropics and permanent freezing of the poles.

qa.q: A place at 55°N is likely to have:
qa.e: 55°N lies poleward of 40°N, in the deficit zone.

qa.q: On a graph of net radiation against latitude, the curve is:
qa.a: Positive in low latitudes and negative towards the poles
qa.e: Low latitudes show surplus (positive) and high latitudes deficit (negative).

qa.q: How many degrees of latitude wide is the surplus belt from 40°S to 40°N?
qa.e: 40 + 40 = 80 degrees of latitude.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The earth's heat budget balances for the planet as a whole.
Reason (R): Every latitude receives exactly as much radiation as it loses.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: low latitudes have a surplus and polar regions a deficit; heat transfer balances them.

qa.q: The normal lapse rate of temperature is:
qa.e: Temperature falls by about 6.5°C for every 1,000 m rise.

qa.q: Heat differs from temperature because heat is:
qa.a: The molecular movement of particles, while temperature measures how hot or cold something is
qa.e: Heat is energy of molecular motion; temperature is its measurement in degrees.

qa.q: Places near the sea have a smaller range of temperature mainly because:
qa.a: The sea heats and cools slowly, and sea and land breezes moderate temperature
qa.e: Water's slow heating and cooling moderates coastal climates.

qa.q: Why do places near sea level record higher temperatures than places at high elevations?
qa.a: The atmosphere is heated from below by terrestrial radiation
qa.e: Air is warmed from the ground up, so temperature falls with height.

qa.q: A coast washed by a warm ocean current will generally be:
qa.a: Warmer than a coast with a cold current
qa.e: Warm currents raise coastal temperatures.

qa.q: Sea-level temperature is 35°C. What is the temperature at 3,000 m using the normal lapse rate of 6.5°C per 1,000 m? (Answer in °C, one decimal place.)
Which of these is NOT a factor controlling temperature distribution?
qa.e: Longitude does not control temperature; latitude, altitude, distance from sea, air masses and currents do.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Inland places have a larger range of temperature than coastal places at the same latitude.
Reason (R): Land heats up and cools down more quickly than water.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Rapid heating and cooling of land makes inland ranges larger (continentality).

qa.q: Isotherms are lines joining places having equal:
qa.e: Iso = equal; therm = temperature.

qa.q: In January, Northern Hemisphere isotherms deviate:
qa.a: Northwards over oceans and southwards over continents
qa.e: Oceans stay warmer and continents get colder in winter.

qa.q: Which warm ocean currents make the North Atlantic warmer in January?
qa.a: Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift
qa.e: The Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift bend the isotherms north.

qa.q: The highest annual range of temperature, more than 60°C, is found over:
qa.e: Extreme continentality in north-eastern Eurasia gives the largest range.

qa.q: In July, temperatures over 30°C are noticed over:
qa.e: NCERT notes over 30°C in subtropical continental Asia along 30°N.

qa.q: Isotherms in the Southern Hemisphere are more regular because:
qa.e: Large oceans make temperature changes gradual, so isotherms are smoother.

qa.q: The least annual range of temperature, about 3°C, is found between:
qa.e: NCERT gives the least range, 3°C, between 20°S and 15°N.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In January, isotherms bend northwards over Europe and the Siberian plain.
Reason (R): Over land in winter, temperature decreases sharply.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: over the cold continents in January, isotherms bend southwards (towards the equator); they bend north over the warmer North Atlantic. R is true, and it is why they bend south over land.

qa.q: Inversion of temperature means:
qa.e: In an inversion the normal decrease with height is reversed.

qa.q: The ideal condition for temperature inversion is:
qa.a: A long winter night with clear skies and still air
qa.e: Clear, calm, long nights let the ground lose heat fast, cooling the air near it.

qa.q: Over which region is temperature inversion normal throughout the year?
qa.e: The cold polar surface keeps the lowest air cooler than the air above.

qa.q: Surface inversion promotes:
qa.a: Stability in the lower layers of the atmosphere
qa.e: Cold air below warm air resists rising, so the air is stable.

qa.q: Dense fogs on winter mornings are linked with:
qa.e: Under inversion, cool air and moisture near the ground produce fog, and smoke and dust collect too.

qa.q: The flow of cold, dense air down hill slopes at night into valleys is called:
qa.e: Cold air drains downslope like water and collects in valleys.

qa.q: Air drainage protects plants on hill slopes because:
qa.a: Cold air collects in valley bottoms, leaving slopes warmer
qa.e: Frost forms in valley bottoms where cold air pools, sparing the slopes.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Smoke and dust collect near the ground during a surface inversion.
Reason (R): Inversion creates stable air that does not rise easily.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Stable air traps pollutants beneath the inversion layer, spreading them horizontally.

qa.q: Atmospheric pressure is defined as:
qa.a: The weight of a column of air in a unit area from sea level to the top of the atmosphere
qa.e: Pressure is the weight of the overlying air column per unit area.

qa.q: The average atmospheric pressure at sea level is about:
qa.e: NCERT gives 1,013.2 millibars at sea level.

qa.q: In the lower atmosphere, pressure decreases by about 1 mb for every:
qa.e: NCERT states about 1 mb per 10 m increase in elevation.

qa.q: Which instrument is used to measure air pressure?
qa.e: Mercury or aneroid barometers measure pressure.

qa.q: Why don't we experience strong upward winds even though the vertical pressure gradient is large?
qa.a: It is balanced by a nearly equal and opposite gravitational force
qa.e: Gravity pulls air down with almost the same force as the vertical pressure gradient pushes it up.

qa.q: Sea-level pressure is 1,013 mb. What is the approximate pressure at 800 m, using 1 mb per 10 m? (in mb)
Air at the earth's surface has higher pressure because:
qa.e: Gravity compresses air near the surface, increasing density and pressure.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Pressure decreases with height in the lower atmosphere.
Reason (R): There is less air above a higher place, so the weight of the air column is smaller.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Higher up, the column of air pressing down is shorter and lighter.

qa.q: Lines connecting places having equal pressure are called:
qa.e: Isobars join places of equal pressure.

qa.q: Why is pressure at weather stations reduced to sea level before drawing isobars?
qa.a: To eliminate the effect of altitude on pressure
qa.e: Altitude changes pressure, so values are standardised to sea level for comparison.

qa.q: Closely spaced isobars indicate:
qa.a: A steep pressure gradient and strong winds
qa.e: Rapid change of pressure over short distance means strong winds.

qa.q: A high-pressure system is enclosed by isobars with:
qa.a: The highest pressure at the centre
qa.e: In a high, pressure increases towards the centre.

qa.q: The pressure gradient is:
qa.a: The rate of change of pressure with respect to distance
qa.e: It is the change in pressure per unit distance.

qa.q: Two places 100 km apart have pressures of 1,012 mb and 1,004 mb. What is the pressure gradient in mb per 100 km?
qa.e: Difference = 1,012 − 1,004 = 8 mb over 100 km.

qa.q: Widely spaced isobars on a map indicate:
qa.e: Far-apart isobars mean pressure changes slowly with distance.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Small differences in horizontal pressure are significant for weather.
Reason (R): They determine wind direction and velocity.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Even small horizontal differences drive winds, which shape weather.

qa.q: The high-pressure belts found along 30°N and 30°S are the:
qa.e: Subtropical highs lie around 30° latitude in both hemispheres.

qa.q: The low-pressure belts along 60°N and 60°S are called:
qa.e: Subpolar lows lie around 60° latitude.

qa.q: Near the equator, sea-level pressure is:
qa.e: The equatorial low (trough) is a belt of low pressure.

qa.q: Pressure belts shift because of:
qa.a: The apparent movement of the sun
qa.e: As the zone of maximum heating shifts, the belts oscillate north and south.

qa.q: In the Northern Hemisphere winter, the pressure belts move:
qa.e: They follow the sun, shifting south in northern winter and north in summer.

qa.q: Near the poles the pressure is:
qa.e: Cold, dense air creates the polar highs.

qa.q: How many degrees of latitude separate the subtropical high (30°N) from the subpolar low (60°N)?
qa.e: 60 − 30 = 30 degrees.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Pressure belts are not permanent in position.
Reason (R): Pressure belts shift because of the changing phases of the moon.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: the belts oscillate with the apparent movement of the sun, which shifts the zones of maximum heating; the moon plays no part.

qa.q: Wind moves from:
qa.e: Air flows down the pressure gradient, from high to low.

qa.q: The Coriolis force deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the:
qa.e: Deflection is to the right in the NH and to the left in the SH.

qa.q: The Coriolis force is:
qa.a: Maximum at the poles and absent at the equator
qa.e: It is directly proportional to the angle of latitude.

qa.q: The influence of frictional force on wind generally extends up to:
qa.e: Friction is greatest at the surface and extends up to about 1–3 km.

qa.q: Why are tropical cyclones not formed near the equator?
qa.a: The Coriolis force is zero there, so the low fills up instead of intensifying
qa.e: Without Coriolis deflection, air flows straight into the low and fills it.

qa.q: The Coriolis force was described in 1844 by a physicist from:
qa.e: It is named after the French physicist Coriolis.

qa.q: The pressure gradient force acts:
qa.e: It acts at right angles to isobars, from high to low pressure.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Wind deflection due to the Coriolis force is greater when wind velocity is high.
Reason (R): The Coriolis force is caused by the earth's rotation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but the cause of the Coriolis force (rotation) does not explain why faster winds are deflected more.

qa.q: A geostrophic wind blows:
qa.e: When the pressure gradient and Coriolis forces balance, wind flows parallel to isobars.

qa.q: Geostrophic winds occur in the upper atmosphere about:
qa.e: At 2–3 km, winds are free from surface friction.

qa.q: Around a low-pressure centre in the Northern Hemisphere, winds blow:
qa.e: Cyclonic circulation in the NH is anticlockwise.

qa.q: Around a high-pressure centre in the Northern Hemisphere, winds blow:
qa.e: Anticyclonic circulation in the NH is clockwise.

qa.q: Over a high-pressure area, air generally:
qa.a: Subsides from above and diverges at the surface
qa.e: Sinking air spreads outwards at the surface, giving clear weather.

qa.q: The wind circulation around a low is called:
qa.e: Around lows it is cyclonic; around highs, anticyclonic.

qa.q: Around a low-pressure centre in the Southern Hemisphere, winds blow:
qa.e: In the SH, cyclonic circulation is clockwise.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Low-pressure areas are often associated with clouds and rain.
Reason (R): Air converges and rises over low-pressure areas.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Rising air cools and condenses, forming clouds and precipitation.

qa.q: The ITCZ is a zone where:
qa.a: Trade winds converge and air rises
qa.e: At the ITCZ, easterlies from both hemispheres converge and the heated air rises.

qa.q: The cell of circulation in the tropics is called the:
qa.e: The tropical cell is the Hadley cell.

qa.q: The surface winds of the Ferrel cell are the:
qa.e: In the middle latitudes, surface winds are westerlies.

qa.q: In the polar cell, cold dense air subsides near the poles and blows towards the middle latitudes as the:
qa.e: Air flowing out of the polar highs is deflected into polar easterlies.

qa.q: Air rising at the ITCZ reaches the top of the troposphere at about:
qa.e: NCERT gives an altitude of up to about 14 km.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a factor affecting the pattern of planetary winds?
qa.e: The moon's phases do not control planetary winds.

qa.q: What maintains the general circulation of the atmosphere?
qa.a: Transfer of heat from lower to higher latitudes
qa.e: Redistribution of surplus tropical heat drives the circulation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A subtropical high forms around 30°N and S.
Reason (R): Air moving polewards from the ITCZ accumulates, cools and sinks around these latitudes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Sinking air in the Hadley cell builds the subtropical high.

qa.q: The appearance of warm water off the coast of Peru is known as:
qa.e: Warm central Pacific water replacing the cold Peruvian current is El Nino.

qa.q: The change in pressure conditions over the Pacific between the Central Pacific and Australia is called the:
qa.e: This pressure see-saw is the Southern Oscillation.

qa.q: ENSO stands for the combination of:
qa.e: ENSO = El Nino + Southern Oscillation.

qa.q: During El Nino, the warm water replaces which current?
qa.e: Warm water displaces the cold Peruvian (Humboldt) current.

qa.q: Which effect is associated with strong ENSO years?
qa.a: Drought in Australia and sometimes in India
qa.e: NCERT lists drought in Australia and sometimes India, floods in China and rain on South America's arid west coast.

qa.q: The most pronounced effect of the seasonal shift of pressure and wind belts is seen in:
qa.a: The monsoons, especially over South-east Asia
qa.e: Monsoon winds result from the seasonal shift of heating and pressure belts.

qa.q: How do oceans influence the atmosphere in the general circulation?
qa.a: They provide energy and water vapour to the air
qa.e: Oceans supply heat and moisture, while winds drive ocean currents.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): ENSO is of no use in long-range weather forecasting.
Reason (R): In strong ENSO years, large-scale variations in weather occur over the world.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: ENSO is closely monitored and used for long-range forecasting in many parts of the world, including for India's monsoon. R is true, and it is the very reason ENSO is useful for forecasting.

qa.q: During the day, the wind blows from the sea to the land because:
qa.a: Land heats faster, creating lower pressure over land
qa.e: Warmer land has rising air and low pressure, drawing air in from the sea.

qa.q: A land breeze blows:
qa.a: From land to sea at night
qa.e: At night land cools faster, so pressure is higher over land.

qa.q: The wind that blows up the valley during the day is the:
qa.e: Heated slopes draw air upslope and up the valley by day.

qa.q: Cool air of high plateaus and ice fields draining into valleys is called:
qa.e: Katabatic winds are cold, dense air draining downslope.

qa.q: Warm, dry winds on the leeward side of mountains are warmed by:
qa.a: The adiabatic process as the air descends
qa.e: Descending air is compressed and warms adiabatically after losing moisture on the windward side.

qa.q: The Chinook is a warm leeward wind associated with the:
qa.e: The Chinook blows down the eastern slopes of the Rockies; the Foehn is its counterpart in the Alps.

qa.q: At night, mountain slopes cool and dense air:
qa.a: Descends into the valley as the mountain wind
qa.e: Cold, dense air flows down into the valley at night.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Warm leeward winds can melt snow in a short time.
Reason (R): After losing moisture on the windward side, the descending air warms up and is dry.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Warm, dry descending air rapidly melts and evaporates snow.

qa.q: An air mass is a large body of air with:
qa.a: Little horizontal variation in temperature and moisture
qa.e: Air masses are nearly uniform horizontally in temperature and humidity.

qa.q: The homogeneous surfaces over which air masses form are called:
qa.e: Air masses take on the character of their source regions.

qa.q: An air mass forming over a warm tropical ocean is classified as:
qa.e: Maritime = over sea; tropical = warm.

qa.q: Continental polar (cP) air masses form over:
qa.a: Very cold snow-covered continents in high latitudes
qa.e: cP air masses originate over cold, snowy high-latitude continents.

qa.q: How many major source regions of air masses does NCERT identify?
qa.e: There are five major source regions.

qa.q: Which air mass would be warm and dry?
qa.e: Continental = dry; tropical = warm.

qa.q: The 'm' in mT and mP stands for:
qa.e: m = maritime (formed over oceans).

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Air masses are classified according to their source regions.
Reason (R): Fronts generally occur in the middle latitudes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but where fronts occur does not explain how air masses are classified. Air masses are classified by source region because they take on the temperature and humidity of the area where they form.

qa.q: The boundary zone between two different air masses is called a:
qa.e: A front is the meeting zone of two air masses.

qa.q: The process of formation of fronts is known as:
qa.e: Frontogenesis means formation of fronts.

qa.q: When cold air moves towards a warm air mass, the contact zone is a:
qa.e: The advancing cold air defines a cold front.

qa.q: A front that remains stationary is called a:
qa.e: When neither air mass advances, the front is stationary.

qa.q: An occluded front forms when:
qa.a: An air mass is fully lifted above the land surface
qa.e: When a cold front overtakes a warm front, the warm air is fully lifted off the surface.

qa.q: Fronts are characterised by:
qa.a: Steep gradients in temperature and pressure
qa.e: Different air masses meeting produce sharp contrasts.

qa.q: Fronts generally occur in:
qa.e: NCERT notes that fronts occur in the middle latitudes.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The passage of a front brings abrupt changes in weather.
Reason (R): Fronts cause air to rise, forming clouds and precipitation, and separate air masses of different temperatures.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Crossing from one air mass to another, with rising air and clouds, changes weather suddenly.

qa.q: Extra-tropical cyclones form along the:
qa.e: They develop where cold polar air meets warmer air along the polar front.

qa.q: The area of warm air wedged between the warm front and the cold front is the:
qa.e: The warm sector lies between the two fronts.

qa.q: An extra-tropical cyclone dissipates when:
qa.a: The cold front overtakes the warm front and the front is occluded
qa.e: Occlusion lifts the warm air off the surface, ending the system.

qa.q: Extra-tropical cyclones generally move from:
qa.e: They move with the westerlies, from west to east.

qa.q: Which statement about extra-tropical cyclones is correct?
qa.a: They can originate over both land and sea
qa.e: Unlike tropical cyclones, they can form over land and sea.

qa.q: Compared with a tropical cyclone, an extra-tropical cyclone:
qa.e: It covers a larger area but has lower wind speeds than a tropical cyclone.

qa.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, the circulation of an extra-tropical cyclone is:
qa.e: Cyclonic circulation in the NH is anticlockwise.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Cumulus clouds develop along the cold front.
Reason (R): The cold front approaches from behind and pushes the warm air up.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Forced rapid uplift of warm air builds cumulus clouds.

qa.q: Tropical cyclones in the Atlantic are called:
qa.e: Atlantic tropical cyclones are hurricanes.

qa.q: For a tropical cyclone to form, the sea surface temperature should be higher than:
qa.e: A large sea surface above 27°C is a key condition.

qa.q: The energy that intensifies a tropical cyclone comes from:
qa.e: Latent heat released by condensation fuels the storm.

qa.q: The calm region at the centre of a tropical cyclone, with subsiding air, is the:
qa.e: The eye is calm; the strongest winds are in the eye wall.

qa.q: Where are the maximum winds and torrential rain found in a tropical cyclone?
qa.e: The eye wall has strong spiralling ascent, maximum wind and heavy rain.

qa.q: Why does a tropical cyclone weaken after landfall?
qa.a: Its supply of moisture from the sea is cut off
qa.e: Without moisture, condensation and its energy stop.

qa.q: A cyclone travels 300 km per day. How many days will it take to travel 1,500 km?

Assertion (A): Tropical cyclones crossing 20°N generally recurve.
Reason (R): Such recurving cyclones are more destructive.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are stated by NCERT, but being more destructive does not explain why they recurve.

qa.q: Over the Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean, the whole tropical cyclone system is about how wide?
qa.e: NCERT gives a diameter of about 600–1,200 km for the storm over these seas; the strongly circulating core around the eye is 150–250 km across.

qa.q: Thunderstorms are caused by:
qa.a: Intense convection on moist, hot days
qa.e: Strong heating of moist air drives rapid uplift and cumulonimbus growth.

qa.q: A thunderstorm is a well-grown:
qa.e: Towering cumulonimbus clouds produce thunder and lightning.

qa.q: A spiralling wind descending from a severe thunderstorm like an elephant's trunk is a:
qa.e: Tornadoes descend from severe thunderstorms with very low central pressure.

qa.q: Tornadoes over the sea are called:
qa.e: NCERT calls tornadoes over the sea water spouts.

qa.q: Hailstorms occur from thunderstorms when:
qa.a: Clouds extend to heights with sub-zero temperatures
qa.e: Freezing temperatures high in the cloud form hail.

qa.q: Tornadoes generally occur in:
qa.e: NCERT notes that tornadoes generally occur in the middle latitudes.

qa.q: In violent storms, potential and heat energies are converted into:
qa.e: Storms convert stored energy into the energy of motion.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A thunderstorm with insufficient moisture can generate dust storms.
Reason (R): Strong winds from the storm lift dust when there is little rain.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Without moisture to bring rain, the storm's winds raise dust.

qa.q: Absolute humidity is expressed in:
qa.e: It is the weight of water vapour per unit volume of air.

qa.q: Relative humidity is:
qa.a: The percentage of moisture present compared with full capacity at a given temperature
qa.e: RH compares the actual vapour with the maximum the air can hold at that temperature.

qa.q: Water vapour in the atmosphere varies by volume from:
qa.e: NCERT gives a range of zero to four per cent.

qa.q: Air at a certain temperature can hold 40 g/m³ of vapour but contains 10 g/m³. What is its relative humidity?
The capacity of air to hold water vapour depends entirely on:
qa.e: Warmer air can hold more water vapour.

qa.q: If air is heated without adding moisture, its relative humidity will:
qa.e: Heating raises capacity while actual vapour stays the same, so RH falls.

qa.q: Air has a capacity of 50 g/m³ and RH of 60%. How much water vapour does it hold (g/m³)?

Assertion (A): Relative humidity changes when air temperature changes, even if moisture stays the same.
Reason (R): The capacity of air to hold moisture depends on its temperature.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Changing temperature changes the denominator (capacity) in the RH formula.

qa.q: The temperature at which saturation occurs in a sample of air is called the:
qa.e: At the dew point, air becomes saturated.

qa.q: Air that holds moisture to its full capacity at a given temperature is:
qa.e: Saturated air cannot hold any more vapour at that temperature.

qa.q: Relative humidity is greatest over:
qa.e: NCERT notes it is greater over oceans and least over continents.

qa.q: Evaporation is the change of water from:
qa.e: Evaporation turns liquid water into vapour.

qa.q: Which of these does NOT increase evaporation?
qa.e: Saturated air cannot take more moisture, so evaporation slows.

qa.q: Movement of air increases evaporation because it:
qa.a: Replaces the saturated layer with unsaturated air
qa.e: Fresh dry air keeps absorbing moisture.

qa.q: The heat absorbed when water changes into vapour is called:
qa.e: Evaporation absorbs latent heat, which is released later during condensation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A glass of cold water 'sweats' on a humid day.
Reason (R): Relative humidity is greater over the oceans than over the continents.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but the pattern of humidity over oceans and land does not explain the sweating glass. It sweats because air touching it cools to its dew point and the vapour condenses.

qa.q: Condensation is the transformation of:
qa.e: Condensation turns vapour into liquid water.

qa.q: Condensation is caused by:
qa.e: Cooling reduces the air's capacity, so vapour condenses.

qa.q: When water vapour changes directly into a solid form, it is called:
qa.e: NCERT calls direct vapour-to-solid change sublimation.

qa.q: Particles of dust, smoke and sea salt around which condensation occurs are called:
qa.e: They are hygroscopic (water-absorbing) nuclei.

qa.q: The most favourable condition for condensation is:
qa.e: Cooling air to its dew point is the main cause.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a condition under which condensation takes place?
qa.e: Raising temperature increases capacity, so it does not cause condensation.

qa.q: Condensation depends upon:
qa.a: The amount of cooling and the relative humidity of air
qa.e: The more humid the air and the greater the cooling, the more condensation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Fog is common in industrial cities in winter.
Reason (R): Smoke provides plenty of nuclei for condensation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: More nuclei plus winter cooling make condensation into fog easier.

qa.q: For dew to form, the dew point must be:
qa.e: Dew is liquid, so the dew point must be above 0°C.

qa.q: Frost forms when:
qa.a: Condensation takes place below the freezing point
qa.e: Below 0°C, moisture is deposited as ice crystals.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT an ideal condition for dew formation?
qa.e: Dew needs calm air; wind mixes the air and prevents cooling of surfaces.

qa.q: A cloud with its base at or very near the ground is called:
qa.e: NCERT describes fog as a cloud at or near the ground.

qa.q: Smog is:
qa.e: In urban and industrial areas, fog mixed with smoke is smog.

qa.q: The difference between mist and fog is that:
qa.a: Mist contains more moisture than fog
qa.e: In mist, each nucleus has a thicker layer of moisture; fogs are drier.

qa.q: Clouds are masses of minute water droplets or ice crystals formed by condensation:
qa.a: In free air at considerable elevations
qa.e: Clouds form high above the surface, unlike dew or frost.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Mists are frequent over mountains.
Reason (R): Rising warm air up the slopes meets a cold surface.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Warm moist air cooling against cold slopes condenses into mist.

qa.q: Cirrus clouds are formed at a height of about:
qa.e: Cirrus are high clouds at 8,000–12,000 m.

qa.q: Clouds that look like cotton wool with a flat base are:
qa.e: Cumulus are puffy patches with flat bases.

qa.q: Layered clouds covering large portions of the sky are:
qa.e: Stratus means layered.

qa.q: Black or dark grey clouds that are extremely dense and opaque are:
qa.e: Nimbus clouds are dark, dense and low.

qa.q: Which of these is a middle cloud?
qa.e: Middle clouds are altostratus and altocumulus.

qa.q: Clouds with extensive vertical development include:
qa.e: Cumulus and cumulonimbus grow vertically.

qa.q: Clouds are classified on the basis of their:
qa.e: NCERT groups clouds by height, expanse, density and transparency or opaqueness.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Cirrus clouds are always white.
Reason (R): Cirrus clouds form very close to the ground, below 1,000 m.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: cirrus are high clouds formed at about 8,000–12,000 m; they are thin and feathery, which is why they look white.

qa.q: Precipitation occurs when:
qa.a: Condensed particles grow so heavy that air cannot hold them against gravity
qa.e: Growing droplets or crystals eventually fall under gravity.

qa.q: Snowfall takes place when the temperature is:
qa.e: Below 0°C, moisture falls as snowflakes.

qa.q: Snowflakes are formed from crystals that are:
qa.e: Moisture is released as hexagonal crystals that form flakes.

qa.q: Sleet consists of:
qa.a: Frozen raindrops and refrozen melted snow-water
qa.e: NCERT defines sleet this way.

qa.q: Sleet occurs when:
qa.a: A layer of air above freezing overlies a sub-freezing layer near the ground
qa.e: Raindrops freeze as they fall through the cold layer near the ground.

qa.q: Hailstones have:
qa.e: Successive coatings of ice form concentric layers.

qa.q: Which forms of precipitation are limited in occurrence and sporadic in time and space?
qa.e: NCERT notes that sleet and hail are limited and sporadic.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Dew and fog are not forms of precipitation.
Reason (R): Precipitation is moisture that falls to the earth after condensed particles grow heavy.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Dew forms on surfaces and fog stays suspended; neither falls as precipitation.

qa.q: Rainfall caused by heated air rising in convection currents is:
qa.e: Heated air rises, cools and condenses, giving convectional rain.

qa.q: Convectional rain is very common in:
qa.e: Intense heating near the equator drives daily convection.

qa.q: In orographic rainfall, the slopes that receive greater rainfall are the:
qa.e: Air rises and cools on the windward side, giving more rain.

qa.q: The area on the leeward side of a mountain that receives less rainfall is the:
qa.e: Descending, warming air on the leeward side gives little rain.

qa.q: Why are leeward slopes dry?
qa.a: Descending air warms and its capacity to hold moisture increases
qa.e: Warming air can hold more moisture, so condensation and rain stop.

qa.q: Orographic rain is also known as:
qa.e: NCERT also calls it relief rain.

qa.q: Convectional rainfall is usually:
qa.a: Heavy, with thunder and lightning, but short-lived
qa.e: It comes in short, intense bursts.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The leeward slopes of the Western Ghats receive more rain than the windward slopes.
Reason (R): Moist winds rise and cool on the windward side, and descend and warm on the leeward side.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the windward (western) slopes get far more rain; the leeward side is a rain-shadow area. R is true, and it is exactly why the leeward side stays drier.

qa.q: In general, as we proceed from the equator towards the poles, rainfall:
qa.e: Rainfall generally decreases poleward.

qa.q: Between 45° and 65° N and S, rainfall is first received on the:
qa.e: The westerlies bring moisture to western margins first.

qa.q: Between 35° and 40° N and S of the equator, rain is heavier on:
qa.e: NCERT notes heavier rain on eastern coasts in this belt.

qa.q: Rainfall is more over oceans than over landmasses because:
qa.a: Oceans are great sources of water
qa.e: Abundant evaporation over oceans supplies moisture.

qa.q: Where mountains run parallel to a coast, rainfall is greatest:
qa.e: Moist winds rise against the mountains on the windward side.

qa.q: Compared with the interior of continents, coastal areas generally receive:
qa.e: Coasts are closer to moisture sources.

qa.q: The westerlies influence rainfall mainly between which latitudes?
qa.e: NCERT links the westerlies with 45°–65° N and S.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Western Europe gets rainfall throughout the year.
Reason (R): It lies in the westerly belt, where western margins of continents receive rain first.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Moist westerlies from the Atlantic bring rain to western Europe year-round.

qa.q: Which region receives over 200 cm of rainfall per annum?
qa.e: The equatorial belt, windward western coasts of cool temperate zones and monsoon coasts get over 200 cm.

qa.q: Areas in the rain-shadow zone of the interiors of continents and high latitudes receive:
qa.e: These are the driest regimes.

qa.q: The central parts of tropical lands and the eastern and interior parts of temperate lands receive:
qa.e: NCERT puts these in the 50–100 cm regime.

qa.q: Interior continental areas generally receive moderate rainfall of:
qa.e: NCERT gives 100–200 cm for interior continental areas.

qa.q: In which region is rainfall distributed evenly throughout the year?
qa.e: The equatorial belt gets rain in all seasons.

qa.q: Mediterranean lands receive most of their rainfall in:
qa.e: Mediterranean climates have dry summers and rainy winters.

qa.q: Why is the seasonal distribution of rainfall important?
qa.a: It decides how effective the rainfall is for crops and water supply
qa.e: Even good totals are less useful if all rain falls in a short season.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Coastal areas of monsoon lands receive heavy rainfall of over 200 cm.
Reason (R): Moist monsoon winds from the oceans bring heavy rain to these coasts in summer.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Onshore monsoon winds deliver large amounts of moisture to coastal areas.

qa.q: Koeppen's classification of climate is:
qa.e: It is based on observed temperature and precipitation data.

qa.q: Genetic classification of climate organises climates according to their:
qa.e: Genetic means based on origin or causes.

qa.q: Koeppen identified a close relationship between climate and the distribution of:
qa.e: He related temperature and precipitation values to vegetation.

qa.q: Which capital letter in Koeppen's scheme stands for dry climates?
qa.e: B denotes dry climates; A, C, D and E are humid.

qa.q: How many major climatic groups did Koeppen recognise (excluding highlands)?
qa.e: Five groups: four based on temperature (A, C, D, E) and one on precipitation (B).

qa.q: Koeppen's scheme was developed in:
qa.e: It was developed in 1918 and modified later.

qa.q: Koeppen's classification is based on:
qa.a: Mean annual and mean monthly temperature and precipitation
qa.e: He used mean annual and mean monthly temperature and precipitation data.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Four of Koeppen's major climatic groups are based on temperature.
Reason (R): The B group is based on precipitation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but B being based on precipitation does not explain why the others are based on temperature.

qa.q: In Koeppen's scheme, the small letter 'f' indicates:
qa.e: f = no dry season.

qa.q: The small letter 's' indicates:
qa.e: Small s = summer dry season; capital S = steppe.

qa.q: For a climate to be in group A (tropical), the average temperature of the coldest month must be:
qa.e: A climates have the coldest month at 18°C or more.

qa.q: Group B (dry) climates are those in which:
qa.e: Dryness is defined by evaporation exceeding precipitation.

qa.q: In group D climates, the average temperature of the coldest month is:
qa.e: D (cold snow forest) has the coldest month at −3°C or colder.

qa.q: The capital letter W within the B group stands for:
qa.e: BW = desert; BS = steppe.

qa.q: A place where the average temperature of all months is below 10°C belongs to group:
qa.e: E (cold/polar) climates have all months below 10°C.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Mediterranean climate is written as Cs.
Reason (R): It is a warm temperate climate with a dry summer.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: C (warm temperate) + s (summer dry) gives Cs.

qa.q: Which climate type is found in the Amazon Basin, western equatorial Africa and the East Indies?
qa.e: These equatorial areas have the tropical wet (Af) climate.

qa.q: The Indian subcontinent mainly has which Koeppen climate type?
qa.e: NCERT lists the Indian subcontinent under Am.

qa.q: In the tropical wet (Af) climate, rain usually falls as:
qa.e: Strong daily convection brings afternoon thundershowers.

qa.q: In the Aw climate compared with Af:
qa.a: The wet season is shorter and the dry season longer
qa.e: Aw has less, more variable rain and a severe dry season.

qa.q: Tropical humid climates are hot and humid mainly because of:
qa.a: The overhead sun throughout the year and the presence of the ITCZ
qa.e: Constant high sun and the rising air of the ITCZ make them hot and wet.

qa.q: The natural vegetation of the Af climate is:
qa.a: Tropical evergreen forests with dense canopy
qa.e: Year-round heat and rain support dense evergreen forests.

qa.q: In the Af climate, the maximum daily temperature is around 30°C and the minimum around 20°C. What is the daily range?
qa.e: 30 − 20 = 10 degrees.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Diurnal ranges of temperature in the Aw climate are greatest in the dry season.
Reason (R): Aw climates have a longer wet season than Af climates.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true: clear dry-season skies allow strong daytime heating and rapid night cooling. R is false: Aw has a shorter wet season and a longer, more severe dry season than Af.

qa.q: Dry climates extend over latitudes from about:
qa.e: NCERT gives 15°–60° north and south.

qa.q: At low latitudes, dry climates occur in the subtropical high mainly because:
qa.a: Subsidence and inversion of temperature do not produce rainfall
qa.e: Sinking, stable air prevents cloud formation.

qa.q: NCERT cites a shade temperature of 58°C, recorded on 13 September 1922, at:
qa.e: NCERT cites 58°C at Al Aziziyah, Libya, on 13 September 1922. (The World Meteorological Organization later rejected this reading, but it is the textbook figure.)

qa.q: Subtropical steppe and desert climates (BSh and BWh) occur at latitudes:
qa.e: BSh and BWh are low-latitude dry climates.

qa.q: In middle latitudes, dry climates are confined to:
qa.a: Interiors of continents beyond the reach of maritime winds
qa.e: Moist ocean winds do not reach these interiors, often ringed by mountains.

qa.q: Fog is common in coastal deserts that border:
qa.e: Cold currents cool the air above, causing fog but little rain.

qa.q: Desert rainfall is ineffective in building soil moisture because it:
qa.e: Brief heavy showers run off or evaporate quickly.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Variability of rainfall affects life in the steppe more than in the desert.
Reason (R): Steppe communities depend on grasslands that fail when rains fail, often causing famine.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: People and herds in the steppe depend on rain-fed grass, so failure hits harder.

qa.q: Warm temperate (C) climates extend from about:
qa.e: NCERT places C climates between 30° and 50°.

qa.q: The Mediterranean climate is characterised by:
qa.a: Hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters
qa.e: Subtropical high in summer and westerlies in winter give this pattern.

qa.q: Which of these regions has a Mediterranean (Cs) climate?
qa.e: Central California is a classic Mediterranean region.

qa.q: The humid subtropical climate with dry winters (Cwa) is found mainly in:
qa.a: North Indian plains and South China interior plains
qa.e: NCERT names these two areas for Cwa.

qa.q: Which climate type is found poleward of the Mediterranean climate on the west coasts of continents?
qa.e: Cfb lies poleward of Cs on western margins, e.g. north-western Europe.

qa.q: In the humid subtropical (Cfa) climate, rainfall:
qa.e: Unstable air masses give rain in all seasons.

qa.q: Mediterranean lands have summer temperatures around 25°C and winter temperatures below 10°C. If winter is 8°C, what is the annual range?
qa.e: Range = 25 − 8 = 17 degrees.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Winters in the marine west coast (Cfb) climate are warmer than expected for their latitude.
Reason (R): These regions are under strong marine influence.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: The ocean (and warm currents like the North Atlantic Drift) moderates winter temperatures.

qa.q: Cold snow forest climates (D) occur in the Northern Hemisphere between:
qa.e: NCERT gives 40°–70°N in Europe, Asia and North America.

qa.q: The cold climate with dry winters (Dw) occurs mainly over:
qa.e: Dw is typical of north-eastern Asia.

qa.q: A monsoon-like reversal of wind in the Dw region is caused by:
qa.a: A pronounced winter anticyclone that weakens in summer
qa.e: Seasonal change of the anticyclone reverses winds.

qa.q: The Df climate occurs:
qa.a: Poleward of the marine west coast climate and mid-latitude steppe
qa.e: NCERT places Df poleward of Cfb and BSk.

qa.q: Highland climates are governed mainly by:
qa.e: Elevation and relief control highland climates.

qa.q: Why are D climates absent in the Southern Hemisphere?
qa.a: There are no large continental areas at 40°–70°S
qa.e: D climates need large continental interiors in those latitudes; the Southern Hemisphere is mostly ocean there.

qa.q: Annual precipitation in the Dw climate is low, about 12–15 cm. What is the difference between these two limits?

Assertion (A): In highland climates, large changes in mean temperature occur over short distances.
Reason (R): The cold climate with dry winters (Dw) occurs mainly over north-eastern Asia.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but the location of Dw climates has nothing to do with highlands. Highland temperatures change quickly because temperature falls with altitude and height changes sharply over short distances.

qa.q: Polar climates exist poleward beyond:
qa.e: NCERT places polar climates beyond 70°.

qa.q: The tundra climate is named after:
qa.a: Its vegetation of low mosses, lichens and flowering plants
qa.e: Tundra refers to the vegetation type.

qa.q: Permafrost means:
qa.e: In the tundra, the subsoil stays frozen permanently.

qa.q: The ice cap (EF) climate occurs over:
qa.e: NCERT names interior Greenland and Antarctica.

qa.q: In the ice cap climate, even in summer the temperature is:
qa.e: Temperatures stay below 0°C all year.

qa.q: Ice cap regions receive:
qa.e: Cold air holds little moisture, so precipitation is very low.

qa.q: During summer, tundra regions have:
qa.e: High latitudes get very long summer days.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Ice cap regions receive very heavy precipitation throughout the year.
Reason (R): Very cold air can hold only a small amount of moisture.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: ice cap (EF) regions receive very little precipitation. R is true, and it explains why precipitation there is so low.

qa.q: Europe witnessed the 'Little Ice Age' from:
qa.e: NCERT dates the Little Ice Age to 1550–about 1850.

qa.q: Which of these provides clues about wet and dry periods in the past?
qa.e: Ring widths vary with moisture, recording wet and dry years.

qa.q: According to archaeological findings, the Rajasthan desert experienced a wet and cool climate around:
qa.e: NCERT notes wet, cool conditions around 8,000 BC.

qa.q: Milankovitch oscillations refer to:
qa.a: Cycles in the earth's orbit, wobble and axial tilt
qa.e: These orbital cycles alter the insolation received.

qa.q: Volcanic eruptions can lower the earth's temperature because:
qa.a: Aerosols reduce the solar radiation reaching the surface
qa.e: Aerosols in the atmosphere block some sunlight for years.

qa.q: The most important anthropogenic cause of climate change is:
qa.e: Human activities raise greenhouse gases, which trap heat.

qa.q: The last major peak glacial period was about 18,000 years ago and the present inter-glacial began about 10,000 years ago. How many years separate them?

Assertion (A): Climate change is a natural and continuous process.
Reason (R): Geological, biological and historical evidence shows repeated warm, cold, wet and dry periods.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: The record of repeated changes shows that climate keeps changing naturally.

qa.q: Which gas has the largest concentration among greenhouse gases in the atmosphere?
qa.e: NCERT states CO₂ has the largest concentration of GHGs.

qa.q: The greenhouse effect occurs because the atmosphere:
qa.a: Transmits incoming solar radiation but absorbs outgoing long-wave radiation
qa.e: Like a greenhouse, it lets light in but traps heat.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a primary greenhouse gas of concern?
qa.e: The primary GHGs are CO₂, CFCs, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone. Nitrogen is not one.

qa.q: The effectiveness of a greenhouse gas depends on:
qa.a: Increase in its concentration, its lifetime and the wavelength it absorbs
qa.e: NCERT lists these three factors.

qa.q: Forests and oceans are described as:
qa.e: They absorb CO₂ from the atmosphere.

qa.q: Atmospheric CO₂ is rising at about what rate annually, according to NCERT?
qa.e: NCERT gives about 0.5 per cent annually.

qa.q: The time taken for atmospheric CO₂ to adjust to changes in sources and sinks is:
qa.e: NCERT gives 20–50 years.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Deforestation increases the concentration of CO₂ in the atmosphere.
Reason (R): Forests use CO₂ in their growth.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Removing trees removes a CO₂ sink, so more CO₂ remains in the air.

qa.q: The depletion of ozone concentration in the stratosphere is called the:
qa.e: Large ozone depletion, especially over Antarctica, is called the ozone hole.

qa.q: Large depletion of ozone occurs over:
qa.e: The ozone hole is most marked over Antarctica.

qa.q: The chemicals mainly responsible for destroying stratospheric ozone are:
qa.e: CFCs drifting into the stratosphere destroy ozone.

qa.q: The Kyoto Protocol was proclaimed in:
qa.e: It was proclaimed in 1997 and came into effect in 2005.

qa.q: Under the Kyoto Protocol, 35 industrialised countries were to reduce emissions by 2012 to:
qa.e: The target was 5% below 1990 levels by 2012.

qa.q: Which is a likely effect of global warming?
qa.a: Rise in sea level inundating coastal areas and islands
qa.e: Melting ice and thermal expansion raise sea level.

qa.q: How many years passed between the proclamation of the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and its coming into effect (2005)?

Assertion (A): The ozone hole allows more ultraviolet rays to reach the lower atmosphere.
Reason (R): Stratospheric ozone normally absorbs ultraviolet rays.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: With less ozone, less UV is absorbed, so more passes through.

qa.q: The earth is called the blue planet because:
qa.a: About 71% of its surface is covered by water
qa.e: Most of the earth's surface is covered by water.

qa.q: According to NCERT's table, oceans hold about what percentage of the earth's water?
qa.e: Oceans hold about 97.3% of the water on the earth.

qa.q: Most of the earth's fresh water is stored in:
qa.e: About 2% of all water is in ice caps and glaciers, far more than rivers or lakes.

qa.q: Which of these holds the smallest share of the earth's water?
qa.e: Rivers hold only a tiny fraction of the earth's water.

qa.q: If 97.3% of water is in oceans and about 2% in ice caps and glaciers, roughly what percentage is left for all other stores (groundwater, lakes, atmosphere, rivers, soil, life)?
About what percentage of the earth's surface is covered by water?
qa.e: Water covers about 71% of the surface; land covers about 29%.

qa.q: Which statement about fresh water is correct?
qa.a: Easily usable fresh water is a very small fraction of all water
qa.e: Most water is salty or frozen, so usable fresh water is scarce.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Even a water-rich planet can face fresh water shortages.
Reason (R): Most of the earth's water is saline ocean water or locked in ice.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Because little water is fresh and accessible, shortages can occur.

qa.q: The hydrological cycle refers to:
qa.a: The circulation of water among oceans, atmosphere, land and organisms in all its forms
qa.e: It is the continuous exchange of water in liquid, solid and gas forms.

qa.q: Water lost to the atmosphere from plants and land surfaces together is called:
qa.e: Evapotranspiration combines evaporation and transpiration.

qa.q: Water seeping into the ground from the surface is called:
qa.e: Infiltration moves surface water into the soil and groundwater.

qa.q: Ice changing directly into water vapour is called:
qa.e: Sublimation moves water from ice straight to vapour.

qa.q: Which process returns water from the atmosphere to the earth?
qa.e: Precipitation brings water down as rain, snow, sleet or hail.

qa.q: Springs are an outlet of:
qa.e: Groundwater discharges at the surface as springs.

qa.q: Why is water considered a cyclic resource?
qa.a: It continuously circulates between the earth's stores
qa.e: The same water moves endlessly through the cycle.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Many parts of the world face water stress even though water is a cyclic resource.
Reason (R): Demand for water is rising while usable fresh water is limited.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Rising demand and limited fresh water lead to stress, so careful management is needed.

qa.q: The four major divisions of the ocean floor are:
qa.a: Continental shelf, continental slope, deep sea plain and oceanic deeps
qa.e: These four divisions are based on depth and relief.

qa.q: The average width of continental shelves is about:
qa.e: NCERT gives about 80 km as the average.

qa.q: The largest continental shelf in the world is the:
qa.a: Siberian shelf in the Arctic Ocean
qa.e: The Siberian shelf stretches to about 1,500 km.

qa.q: The gradient of the continental slope varies between:
qa.e: The slope is steeper than the shelf, at 2°–5°.

qa.q: Continental shelves are important as sources of fossil fuels because:
qa.a: Massive sedimentary deposits accumulate on them over long periods
qa.e: Thick sediments over time become oil and gas sources.

qa.q: The steep drop at the end of the continental shelf is called the:
qa.e: The shelf ends at the shelf break.

qa.q: The continental slope reaches a depth of 3,000 m at its seaward edge and begins at 200 m. What depth range does it cover?

Assertion (A): The continental slope boundary indicates the end of the continents.
Reason (R): The continental slope is the shallowest part of the ocean floor.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: the continental shelf is the shallowest part; the slope is steeper (2°–5°) and descends from about 200 m to 3,000 m to the ocean basins.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five oceans recognised by geographers?
qa.e: The five oceans are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. The Mediterranean is a sea, not an ocean.

qa.q: The flattest and smoothest regions of the world are:
qa.e: Deep sea (abyssal) plains are the flattest regions on earth.

qa.q: Deep sea plains are covered with:
qa.a: Fine-grained sediments like clay and silt
qa.e: Fine sediments settle on abyssal plains.

qa.q: The depth of deep sea plains varies between:
qa.e: NCERT gives 3,000–6,000 m.

qa.q: Oceanic deeps are about how much deeper than the surrounding ocean floor?
qa.e: Trenches are about 3–5 km deeper than the surrounding floor.

qa.q: Oceanic trenches are significant for studying plate movements because they are:
qa.a: Associated with active volcanoes and strong earthquakes
qa.e: Trenches mark subduction zones with intense tectonic activity.

qa.q: Which ocean has the largest number of explored deeps?
qa.e: 32 of the 57 explored deeps are in the Pacific.

qa.q: What percentage of the 57 explored deeps lie in the Pacific? (Nearest whole number.)

Assertion (A): Trenches occur at the bases of continental slopes and along island arcs.
Reason (R): They are associated with active volcanoes and strong earthquakes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but the association with volcanoes does not explain where trenches are located; both result from plate subduction.

qa.q: A mountain with a pointed summit rising from the seafloor but not reaching the surface is a:
qa.e: Seamounts have pointed tops below sea level.

qa.q: A flat-topped seamount is called a:
qa.e: Guyots are flat-topped, showing gradual subsidence.

qa.q: Iceland is an example of:
qa.a: A part of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge rising above sea level
qa.e: Iceland is part of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

qa.q: The best known submarine canyon in the world is the:
qa.e: NCERT names the Hudson Canyon.

qa.q: Low islands of coral reefs surrounding a central depression are called:
qa.e: Atolls are coral rings around lagoons.

qa.q: The Emperor seamount is an extension of the:
qa.e: It extends from the Hawaiian Islands in the Pacific.

qa.q: Seamounts are mostly of which origin?
qa.e: Seamounts are volcanic in origin.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Submarine canyons often extend from the mouths of large rivers.
Reason (R): They are deep valleys cutting across continental shelves and slopes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but describing canyons as valleys across shelves does not explain why they begin near river mouths.

qa.q: The average temperature of the surface water of oceans is about:
qa.e: NCERT gives about 27°C.

qa.q: Surface ocean temperature decreases from the equator towards the poles at about:
qa.e: The general rate is 0.5°C per degree of latitude.

qa.q: Offshore winds affect ocean temperature by:
qa.a: Driving warm surface water away and causing upwelling of cold water
qa.e: Removing warm surface water brings colder water up from below.

qa.q: Why are Northern Hemisphere oceans warmer than those of the Southern Hemisphere?
qa.a: They are in contact with a larger extent of land
